t.woerden centrum@52.1,4.9:
Woerden is a small Dutch town on the Oude Rijn, the old Rhine, halfway between Utrecht and Leiden, in the middle of the Green Heart of Holland, a landscape of polders, meadows, ditches and cows. Its centre is a compact old town ringed by canals, with a castle, a big church and a windmill on the old ramparts. The Romans were here too: Woerden lies on the line of the Lower German Limes, and the remains of a Roman fort lie beneath the town centre.

The Roman fort at Woerden, known in Latin as Laurium, guarded the Rhine frontier, and excavations have turned up wooden ships, timber structures and everyday objects preserved in the wet soil. The Limes in the Netherlands is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site. The town's museum displays some of the finds, and markings in the streets show where the fort stood.

Woerden later became a fortified town, and its castle, built in the fifteenth century, still stands. The town was a strategic point on the Old Dutch Waterline, the defensive system of flooded land that protected Holland, and in 1672, when French troops occupied it, the town suffered terribly. Woerden is also known as a cheese town: it is the heart of a dairy region, and in summer it holds a traditional cheese market, where farmers bring their wheels of Gouda-style cheese to be weighed and sold.

Riding here is flat and relaxed. The roads follow canals and dykes through polders, past farms and windmills, and they are narrow, with lots of cyclists. The Dutch take cycle lanes seriously, so be aware. The roads along the Oude Rijn and toward the lakes of the Nieuwkoopse Plassen and the Reeuwijkse Plassen are scenic, especially in the soft light of the early morning or evening.

Woerden has fuel, food and all services. Local specialities are cheese, of course, and the bakeries sell stroopwafels. The best time to visit is in summer, when the cheese market runs, or in spring, when the meadows are full of birds and the polders turn green.
t.fort near heemstede@52.3,4.6:
Between Haarlem and the bulb fields of the Dutch coast, near the town of Heemstede and the hamlet of De Glip, lies a squat, grassy fort surrounded by a moat. This is the Fort near Heemstede, built around the turn of the twentieth century as part of the Defence Line of Amsterdam, a ring of forts, dykes and flooding zones around the city, and now part of the UNESCO-listed Dutch Water Defence Lines.

The Defence Line of Amsterdam, the Stelling van Amsterdam, was designed to protect the capital by flooding the land around it, creating a water barrier too deep for soldiers to wade but too shallow for boats. The forts were built at points where roads, railways or dykes crossed the flood zone, which were the weak spots. Most were built from concrete, an innovation at the time, and covered with earth. The system was never tested in war and soon became obsolete with the arrival of aircraft, but it is an impressive piece of engineering. The Fort near Heemstede guarded the railway and roads crossing the line here.

The area around Heemstede is a landscape of old country estates, woods and dunes on one side and the bulb fields on the other. In spring, from late March to May, the fields around Hillegom, Lisse and Bennebroek are carpeted with tulips, hyacinths and daffodils in stripes of brilliant colour, and the Keukenhof gardens draw huge crowds. Haarlem, a few kilometres away, is a lovely old city with a big market square, the Frans Hals museum and canals.

The riding here is flat and gentle, along canals, through villages and past the bulb fields, with a lot of cyclists and traffic on the main roads. The dune roads toward Zandvoort and the coast offer a change of scenery, with sea views and wind. Zandvoort has a racing circuit in the dunes, which hosts the Dutch Grand Prix.

Heemstede has fuel and food. Local specialities include herring, which is eaten raw with onions from a stall, and Dutch apple pie. The bulb season in spring is the most popular time to visit; the roads can be clogged with visitors, so go early on a weekday.
t.van nellefabriek@51.9,4.4:
The Van Nelle factory, on the edge of Rotterdam, is one of the most beautiful industrial buildings ever made. Built between 1925 and 1931 for a company that processed coffee, tea and tobacco, it is a long, light building of glass and steel, with curtain walls that let daylight flood into the workspaces. The designers, Johannes Brinkman and Leendert van der Vlugt, created what became an icon of modernist architecture, a factory of light and air for its workers. It was added to the UNESCO list in 2014.

The factory reflected the ideals of the time: functional design, hygiene, light and a better working environment. The building is arranged in sections that follow the production process, with glass-enclosed conveyor bridges connecting the buildings. On top, a round tea room offers views over the city. The factory closed as a production site in the 1990s and has been converted into offices and event spaces, and it is generally not open to casual visitors, though tours are sometimes organised.

Rotterdam itself is a city of modern architecture, rebuilt after its centre was destroyed by German bombing in May 1940. The Markthal, the cube houses, the Erasmus Bridge and the skyline of towers along the Maas make it the most architecturally adventurous city in the Netherlands. The port of Rotterdam is the largest in Europe, stretching for kilometres toward the sea. Delfshaven, nearby, is one of the few historic areas to have survived the bombing, and it was from here that the Pilgrim Fathers set sail in 1620.

Riding in Rotterdam is urban and busy, with lots of cyclists, trams and traffic lights. The roads around the city are flat, and the polders and dykes to the north, toward Delft and Gouda, offer a calmer ride. Wind can be strong. The port area, with its giant cranes and container terminals, is an interesting ride on a quiet day.

Rotterdam has every service. Local food includes fresh herring, kibbeling, battered fish, and Indonesian food, a legacy of colonial history. The Van Nelle factory is best seen in the evening light, when the glass glows.
t.sint pieterskerk belfort@50.9,4.7:
Leuven is a university town through and through. Its university, founded in 1425, is the oldest in the Low Countries, and its students fill the streets, cafés and squares, giving the city a youthful energy. At its heart is the Grote Markt, dominated by two buildings: the Town Hall, a Gothic masterpiece covered in hundreds of statues, and opposite it, the Church of St Peter, a great Gothic church whose tower was never finished but which is part of the UNESCO-listed Belfries of Belgium and France.

The church, built in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, was badly damaged in both world wars. In August 1914, German troops burned much of the city, including the university library, an act that caused international outrage. The library was rebuilt after the war with American funds and was damaged again in 1940. Inside St Peter's, the treasury holds two famous paintings by Dirk Bouts, including the Last Supper, one of the masterpieces of Flemish painting. The tower has a carillon.

Leuven is also a beer city. It is the home of Stella Artois, whose brewery dominates the north of the town, and of AB InBev, one of the world's largest brewers. The Oude Markt, a square lined with bars, is said to be the longest bar in Europe, and in the evening it is packed with students. The Groot Begijnhof, a seventeenth-century beguinage, now part of the university, is a peaceful enclave of brick houses and cobbled streets.

Riding in Leuven is urban and slow, with many one-way streets, cobblestones and pedestrian zones. The city centre has restricted access, so park outside and walk. The countryside around Leuven, toward the Hageland to the east, with its low hills, vineyards and orchards, and the Dijle valley to the south, offers pleasant riding on quiet roads. Belgian roads can be rough, with cobbled sections in villages.

Leuven has every service. Local food includes stoofvlees, a beef stew made with beer, and waffles. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, though Belgium can be wet at any time.
t.seventeenth century canal ring area of a:
Nobody rides a motorbike into the Amsterdam canal ring for the curves. You come because in the early seventeenth century, the city at the height of its Golden Age planned an extension of startling ambition: three main canals, the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht, laid out in concentric arcs around the medieval core, lined with tall, narrow merchants' houses with gabled roofs and hoisting beams. Work began in 1613, and the result, a UNESCO site since 2010, is still one of the most admired examples of urban planning in the world.

Walking along the canals, you see the wealth of the period in every detail: the elaborate gables, the stone steps, the large windows that let in the light. The houses were built on wooden piles driven into the soft ground, and many of them lean slightly, which adds to their charm. Behind the facades, gardens and courtyards hide, and some houses are open as museums, like the Museum Van Loon on the Keizersgracht or the Anne Frank House on the Prinsengracht, where the young diarist hid from the Nazis.

As a rider, be prepared for the realities of the city. Bicycles rule the streets here, in their tens of thousands, and their riders have little patience for motor vehicles. The streets along the canals are narrow, often one-way, and shared with pedestrians, delivery vans and trams. Parking is scarce and expensive, though there are designated areas for motorcycles. The best approach is to leave the bike at a secure parking garage on the edge of the centre, or at a park-and-ride, and explore on foot, by bicycle or by boat. A canal cruise is a touristy cliché, but it really is the best way to see the city from the perspective it was designed for.

Fuel stations are rare in the centre, so fill up before entering. The city has endless options for food and drink: brown cafés with old wooden interiors, herring stands, Indonesian rice tables, and modern restaurants. The surrounding countryside offers flat, scenic rides along dikes and polders, especially north to the Zaanse Schans windmills and the old fishing towns of Volendam and Marken, or the Beemster polder, another UNESCO site.
t.terril 34@50.6,2.4:
A terril is a slag heap, a mountain of waste rock dumped beside a coal mine, and in the flat land of northern France these man-made hills are the closest thing to relief for miles around. Terril 34 is one of hundreds that dot the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, a UNESCO site since 2012, which recognises not only the heaps but also the pithead frames, miners' housing estates, schools, churches and railway lines that made up the landscape of coal mining in the region for nearly three centuries. This one sits near Norrent-Fontes and Lillers, at the western end of the basin, where it meets the chalk hills of Artois.

Many terrils have been reclaimed by nature, with birch woods, grasslands and rare plants that thrive on the warm, dark soil, and some are now nature reserves or viewpoints, with paths to the top. Climbing one gives you a view over the plain, with church towers, villages, fields and other terrils on the horizon, and an appreciation of the scale of the industry that once dominated life here. The last mine in the region closed in 1990, and the towns are still dealing with the economic and social legacy.

Riding in this area is mostly flat, with straight roads through farmland and villages, and the wind is a constant companion. The real reward is the history and the atmosphere. A short distance east, the twin terrils of Loos-en-Gohelle, among the highest in Europe, and the Louvre-Lens museum are well worth a visit. To the west and south, the hills of Artois offer gentler curves, and the battlefields of the First World War, including the Canadian memorial at Vimy Ridge and the French necropolis of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, are a sombre reminder of the region's suffering.

Lillers, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Béthune, a little further, is a lively town with a belfry and a beautiful main square. Local food is hearty and comforting: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, potjevleesch, a terrine of mixed meats, and of course chips, often from a friterie van. The local beers are excellent, and the people are known for their warmth and hospitality.
t.sonian forest reserve forestiere du tict:
The beeches in the Sonian Forest grow so tall and straight that people call it the cathedral forest, and once you stand under them on a misty autumn morning the name stops sounding like tourist talk. This great woodland on the southeastern edge of Brussels covers thousands of hectares, and most of the famous columns of grey trunks were planted in the late eighteenth century, when the Austrian Habsburgs ruled these lands and their foresters reshaped the old wood. A few patches, including the Tict reserve near La Hulpe and Waterloo, are left to grow wild with no felling at all, and they form part of the UNESCO listing for the ancient and primeval beech forests of Europe, a chain of reserves stretching across the continent.

In the strict reserves, dead trees are left where they fall, and that is precisely the point: rotting wood feeds beetles, fungi, woodpeckers and bats, and the forest slowly rebuilds itself the way it did before anyone managed it. Paths run along the edges, and the light that filters through the canopy in May, bright green and soft, is worth the trip alone.

This is not a riding destination in itself. The forest is crossed by the Brussels ring road and a few main roads with heavy commuter traffic, and the forest lanes are for walkers, horses and cyclists. Treat it as a pause: park at one of the forest entrances, walk twenty minutes into the trees, and let the noise drop away. The roads south of here, into Walloon Brabant, become quieter and more rolling, with farmland, castle farms and small villages, and the Ardennes are less than two hours away for real curves.

Waterloo, three kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and everything practical, and of course the battlefield where Napoleon met his end in 1815, with the Lion's Mound, a vast artificial hill topped by a cast-iron lion, the panorama painting and the memorial museum. La Hulpe has a lovely château park, and Hoeilaart, on the Flemish side, was once famous for growing grapes in heated glasshouses. Belgian waffles and a strong local beer on a terrace make a fine end to the walk.
t.halletoren ou belfort@51.0,3.3:
Tielt is a working town in the heart of West Flanders, a place of farmers' markets, textile history and flat roads, and its belfry rises above the market square like a stubborn finger pointing at the clouds. The Halletoren, the hall tower, stands on top of the old cloth hall, the building where merchants once inspected and traded woollen cloth, the source of Flanders' wealth in the Middle Ages. The belfry is one of the group of Belgian and French belfries that UNESCO listed together, symbols of the civic freedom that the cities of Flanders won from their lords, where the town charters were kept and the bells rang to call citizens to arms or to work.

Tielt's tower is modest compared to the giants of Bruges or Ghent, but that is part of its charm: you get a real market square, with cafés, shops and locals going about their business, rather than a tourist set. The town suffered in both world wars, and much of what you see has been rebuilt, but the proportions remain.

The riding around Tielt is about the Flemish countryside: flat, open fields of potatoes, maize and vegetables, poplar rows, farmhouses with red-tiled roofs, and villages built around tall church towers. Roads are generally well surfaced but narrow, with many roundabouts, cycle paths and speed bumps in villages, and the wind blowing in from the North Sea can be fierce. Cobbled sections appear here and there, especially in villages, and they are slippery when wet. The real joy is the sense of space and the light, which painters have loved for centuries.

Tielt has fuel, shops and plenty of cafés and restaurants. Try a plate of stoofvlees, beef stewed in beer, with fries, or waterzooi, a creamy stew from nearby Ghent. Flanders is famous for its beers, and the local cafés serve a huge range, from Trappist ales to sour reds. Bruges and Ghent are both less than an hour away, and the coast is a little further. For a different kind of history, the battlefields of the First World War around Ypres are a short ride to the southwest.
Tienen means sugar to most Belgians. The town in the east of Flemish Brabant has been the home of Belgium's largest sugar refinery since the nineteenth century, and the smell of sugar beet being processed hangs over the town in autumn during the campaign, when trucks loaded with beets roll in from the surrounding fields. The Sint-Germanuskerk, the church of Saint Germanus, with its massive tower serving as the town's belfry, stands near the huge Grote Markt, one of the largest market squares in Belgium, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of the belfries of Belgium and France. The tower, a mix of Romanesque and Gothic, has a carillon whose bells ring out over the town.

The museum Het Toreke, in a former prison on the square, tells the history of the town and the region, from the Romans to the sugar industry. Tienen also has a beautiful Gothic church, the Onze-Lieve-Vrouw-ten-Poelkerk, and a number of old houses and gardens.

The landscape around Tienen is known as Haspengouw, or Hesbaye, a gently rolling plateau of fertile loess soil, with fields of sugar beet, wheat and potatoes, orchards of apples, pears and cherries, and small villages. In spring, when the orchards are in blossom, the area is especially beautiful. The riding is relaxed, with quiet roads winding through the countryside, little traffic and gentle hills, but the wind can be strong on the open plateau. Some village roads are cobbled.

Tienen has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and the Grote Markt is lined with terraces. Hoegaarden, about five kilometres away, is the home of the famous white beer, a cloudy wheat beer flavoured with coriander and orange peel, revived in the 1960s after the last local brewery had closed, and now known worldwide. Leuven, about twenty kilometres west, is a lively university town with a spectacular Gothic town hall and the largest beer-brewing company in the world. Local food includes Luikse wafels, Liège waffles with caramelised sugar, and stews made with local beer.
t.monument commemoratif charles mathieu@50:
Lourches is a small mining town in the Nord department, on the banks of the Escaut river, between Denain and Valenciennes, in the heart of the old coal mining basin that stretched across northern France. The memorial named after Charles Mathieu is one of the elements listed as part of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin UNESCO site, alongside pitheads, slag heaps, miners' housing and the buildings of the mining companies. I do not know the details of who Charles Mathieu was, and I would rather not guess; memorials of this kind in the basin often honour engineers, managers or miners connected with the local pits, and the plaque on site will tell you more than I can.

The Denain and Valenciennes area was one of the most industrialised in France, with coal mines, steelworks and factories, and it suffered greatly when they closed in the late twentieth century. The towns are full of reminders of that past: rows of brick miners' houses, called corons, mining company churches and schools, and slag heaps, some of which have become nature reserves or leisure areas. Nearby, at Wallers-Arenberg, the old mine with its three headframes has been transformed into a film and media centre, and it was used as a location for the film adaptation of Émile Zola's Germinal, set in this very region.

The riding in this area is mostly flat, with straight roads between towns, many roundabouts and some heavy traffic around Valenciennes. The Escaut valley offers some green spaces, with canals, wetlands and towpaths, and the Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers forest, a large woodland to the north, provides quieter, shaded roads. The weather is often grey and rainy, and the wind can be strong, but the light on a clear evening, over the slag heaps and brick towns, has its own beauty.

Escaudain, about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and services, and Denain and Valenciennes have more. Local food is hearty and comforting: carbonnade, beef stewed in beer, maroilles cheese, which has a powerful smell and a mild taste, and the many local beers. The people of the mining basin are known for their warmth, solidarity and sense of humour, and the local dialect, ch'ti, is a source of great pride.
t.stadhuis met belfort@51.2,3.6:
Eeklo is the capital of the Meetjesland, the flat, green region of East Flanders between Ghent and Bruges, close to the Dutch border, and its town hall with a belfry, the Stadhuis met Belfort, stands on the market square as the symbol of the town. It is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO, a group of civic towers that embodied the freedom and power of the medieval towns of Flanders. Eeklo's belfry is modest compared with those of Bruges and Ghent, but it has its own charm, rising above a town that most visitors pass through without stopping.

The Meetjesland takes its name, according to one explanation, from the measured plots of land, meetjes, created when the region's marshes and forests were reclaimed in the Middle Ages, and the landscape is still a patchwork of fields, meadows, ditches and rows of trees. Further north, toward the Dutch border, the polders of the creek region, with their winding creeks and dikes, are a reminder of the battle against the sea.

The riding here is flat and peaceful, with quiet roads winding through fields and villages, and many cycle paths. The N9 road between Ghent and Bruges passes through Eeklo, and it is busy, but the smaller roads to the north, toward Kaprijke, Sint-Laureins and the polders, are much more pleasant, with farms, windmills and church towers on the horizon. The wind is a constant factor, and the weather changes quickly, with rain often coming in from the sea. Some village roads are cobbled, and these can be slippery when wet.

Eeklo has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and the market square has terraces where you can sit with a beer and watch the town go by. Ghent and Bruges, both about twenty to thirty kilometres away, are two of the most beautiful cities in Europe, with canals, medieval buildings and lively squares. Local food includes waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish from Ghent, Flemish stew with fries, and of course the local beers, served in their own glasses. The coast, with its long beaches, is less than an hour's ride away.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de comines@5:
Comines is one of those towns the border runs straight through. The river Lys, the Leie to the Flemish, divides French Comines from Belgian Comines-Warneton, and you can cross from one country to the other on a bridge without noticing much more than a change in the shape of the street signs. On the French side the town hall and its belfry stand over the main square, a tall brick tower in the Flemish style with a pointed roof and a carillon, part of the group of belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO.

What you see is not old in the way it looks. The front line of the First World War ran close by, Ypres is barely twenty kilometres to the north, and Comines was badly smashed in the fighting. The town hall and belfry were rebuilt after the war in a confident regional revival style, which is why the brickwork looks so crisp. That rebuilding is a statement in itself: these towers were symbols of civic freedom in the medieval Low Countries, and putting them back up was a way of saying the town was still standing.

Comines has a sense of humour too. Its best-known festival, the Fête des Louches, involves wooden ladles being thrown from the town hall to the crowd below, a custom tied to a local legend and celebrated every autumn. If you happen to pass on that weekend, expect closed streets and a lot of cheerful noise.

As for riding, this is flat Flanders. The roads follow the Lys through Wervik and Wervicq-Sud, past brick farms, tobacco country history and the odd stretch of cobbles that will rattle your fillings. Wind off the North Sea is the main variable and it can be relentless across the open fields. The interest lies less in the corners than in the layers of history: a few minutes north and you are among the war cemeteries and memorials of the Ypres Salient, quiet places worth a pause.

Comines has twelve thousand people, so fuel, bakeries and bars are all here, and the Belgian side is a handy option for a coffee or a frites stop. Park near the square, look up at the clock and enjoy the fact that you are standing in two countries within a short walk.
t.beffroi de gravelines@51.0,2.1:
Gravelines sits right where the river Aa meets the Channel, between Calais and Dunkirk, and it still wears its walls. The town is wrapped in Vauban-era fortifications, a star of brick ramparts, bastions and water-filled moats that you can walk or ride around, and in the middle of it rises the belfry, one of the towers listed by UNESCO among the belfries of northern France and Belgium. It is a solid, sober tower rather than a showpiece, built to watch, warn and ring the hours for a frontier town that changed hands more than once.

The history here is seaborne. In 1588, off this stretch of coast, the English fleet sent fireships into the anchored Spanish Armada and the running fight that followed, usually called the Battle of Gravelines, broke the Armada's formation for good. Thirty years earlier a land battle near the town had gone the other way for the French. Walk out to the mouth of the Aa at Grand-Fort-Philippe and you look over the same grey water, now busy with fishing boats and the occasional sailing club dinghy.

Modern Gravelines has another landmark you cannot miss: the nuclear power station on the coast just east of town, one of the largest in Europe. It makes for a strange backdrop to a seventeenth-century fortress, and the warm water it releases is said to be good for the local fish farming.

The riding is coastal and flat, so honesty is in order: you come here for atmosphere, not for corners. The D940 heads west along the Côte d'Opale towards Calais and the white cliffs of Cap Blanc-Nez, and that stretch is a lovely ride with big skies, dunes and sea light that changes by the minute. Wind is the defining feature and gusts off the Channel can be fierce, especially in autumn. Watch for cobbles inside the ramparts and the tight gates through the walls.

With thirteen thousand people, Gravelines has fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of brasseries; fish and seafood are the obvious order, and moules-frites never feels wrong this close to the water. The ramparts make a fine place to walk off lunch and look out across the moats while the bike cools down.
t.grand beguinage of leuven@50.9,4.7:
Step through the gate of the Groot Begijnhof in Leuven and the city noise drops away. Cobbled lanes, small brick houses with white window frames and stepped gables, little bridges over the arms of the river Dijle, and a Gothic church in the middle: this is one of the largest béguinages in the Low Countries, part of the Flemish Béguinages group listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Béguines were women who lived devout lives in community without taking the permanent vows of nuns. They could own property, work, and leave if they chose, which in the Middle Ages was a rare form of independence. From the thirteenth century they built enclosed little towns like this one across Flanders. Leuven's béguinage was home to hundreds at its height, and the last béguines died in the twentieth century. In the 1960s the Catholic University of Leuven bought the whole complex and restored it, and today it is housing for students and visiting academics, which keeps it alive rather than turning it into a museum.

Leuven itself is a university city through and through. The university was founded in 1425 and its students fill the bars of the Oude Markt, a square lined almost entirely with cafés. The Gothic town hall is a stone lacework of statues, and the city is home to one of the world's largest brewing companies, so beer is not hard to find.

Riding inside the city is slow going, with cobbles, cyclists in great numbers, buses and a ring road that can be confusing. Park near the béguinage and walk. South of the city, though, things get more interesting: the Meerdaal and Heverlee forests offer shaded roads through beech and oak, and the Dijle valley towards Wavre and the Brabant countryside has gentle hills, sunken lanes and small villages that make good riding on a weekday morning. Belgium's roads can switch from smooth to rough without warning, and cobbled stretches are common in villages.

Leuven has everything practical: fuel on the ring and outskirts, bakeries, supermarkets, and endless places for food. Try the local fries from a proper frituur, or a Flemish stew made with dark beer, and then take a slow walk along the béguinage's little canals before you head out of town.
t.het belfort of halletoren@50.8,3.3:
On the Grote Markt of Kortrijk a tower stands alone in the middle of the square, as if the building it belonged to had wandered off. In a sense it did. The Belfort, or Halletoren, was once part of the cloth hall, the trading heart of a medieval textile town, and when the hall disappeared the tower stayed. It is one of the belfries of Belgium and France on the UNESCO list, and it has a pair of local celebrities at the top: two gilded figures, Manten and Kalle, who strike the hours on the bell. Kortrijk people are fond of them, and you will see their likenesses on all sorts of souvenirs.

The town's great moment came in 1302, when Flemish town militias, mostly craftsmen on foot, faced the heavy cavalry of the French king on the fields near the Groeninge stream and beat them soundly. Hundreds of golden spurs were collected from the fallen knights and hung in the Church of Our Lady as trophies, and the Battle of the Golden Spurs remains a founding story of Flemish identity. There is a museum about it near the park where the fighting took place.

Kortrijk is a busy small city on the river Leie, with the medieval Broel towers guarding an old bridge, a béguinage tucked behind the church, and plenty of modern design and shopping around the centre. Riding through it means traffic lights, cobbles, cyclists and one-way streets, so park near the market and explore on foot.

For riding, head east or south. The Flemish Ardennes around Oudenaarde, half an hour away, are low hills famous among cyclists for the cobbled climbs of the Tour of Flanders, and the lanes between them make an entertaining, if bumpy, playground on a motorbike. Westwards, the hills of Heuvelland near the French border, including the Kemmelberg, offer short climbs and wide views over the old battlefields of the First World War. The weather is changeable all year, and wet cobbles are treacherous, so take care on any stretch of stone.

With over seventy thousand people, Kortrijk has fuel, workshops and good food everywhere. Sit on a terrace on the Grote Markt with a Flemish beer and a portion of frites, and wait for Manten and Kalle to do their job on the hour.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de calais@51:
Most riders know Calais as the place where the ferry or the tunnel train spits them out onto French tarmac, and they head south without a backward glance. Spare it an hour. The town hall is a surprise, a grand building in Flemish Renaissance style finished in the early twentieth century, and its belfry, one of the tallest in the region, rises well above the rooftops as a landmark you can see from the port. It forms part of the UNESCO list of belfries in Belgium and France, alongside towers that are centuries older.

In front of it stands one of the most famous sculptures in the world: Auguste Rodin's Burghers of Calais. It commemorates an episode from 1347, during the Hundred Years' War, when the English king Edward III besieged the town for nearly a year. Six leading citizens offered their lives in exchange for sparing the town, walking out with ropes around their necks. In the end they were spared, so the story goes, after the queen pleaded for mercy. Rodin portrayed them not as heroes but as frightened men, and the bronze figures stand at ground level so you look them in the eye.

Calais also has a long history of lace making, and the lace museum in an old factory tells that story well, along with the Channel crossings that have shaped the town for centuries.

The riding starts the moment you leave town. The coast road west towards Cap Blanc-Nez and Cap Gris-Nez climbs over chalk cliffs with the Channel on your right, and on a clear day the white cliffs of Dover are plainly visible across the water. The road dips through villages like Wissant, with dunes and wide sandy beaches, and the light can be wonderful in the evening. Wind is a constant companion, and in a westerly gale it can push a bike sideways, so keep a loose grip and a careful line.

Calais has fuel, supermarkets and everything a traveller needs, including plenty of shops geared to people stocking up before crossing. For lunch, the brasseries near the town hall do solid French food, and the fish restaurants near the port serve local catch with very little fuss. It is a decent place to begin or end a continental trip.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville d armentiere:
Armentières is a textile town on the river Lys, right on the Belgian border, a quarter of an hour west of Lille. Its name is familiar to many English speakers from the bawdy marching song of the First World War, Mademoiselle from Armentières, which British soldiers sang on their way to the front lines nearby. The town paid a terrible price for being so close to that front: it was shelled, occupied and largely destroyed by 1918. The town hall and its belfry were rebuilt in the 1920s and 1930s in a confident Flemish style, and the tower now belongs to the UNESCO group of belfries of Belgium and France.

Armentières has its own quirky tradition, the Fête des Nieulles, when small biscuits are thrown down from the town hall to the crowd below, a custom dating back centuries and linked to a local legend about the end of a feast. The town also parades giants, the huge wicker figures that are a beloved part of street festivals across northern France and Belgium.

Around the town, the landscape is mostly flat, with farms, canals and brick villages. The interest lies to the north-west, where the Monts de Flandre rise from the plain: Mont Noir, Mont des Cats and, across the border, the Kemmelberg. They are only small hills, but in this flat country they feel like mountains, and the lanes that climb them have steep sections, tight bends and sweeping views. The Trappist abbey on Mont des Cats makes a well-known cheese, and the nearby villages are full of estaminets, traditional taverns serving Flemish food and local beer.

The area is also full of reminders of war. Military cemeteries, memorials and museums dot the countryside, and a ride through the old front line between Armentières and Ypres is both beautiful and humbling. Weather is changeable, with rain, wind and fog common throughout the year, and cobbled stretches in villages need care, especially when wet.

Armentières has fuel, shops and plenty of brasseries. For lunch, try a carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, or a potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats served with chips, and finish with a strong coffee before heading out to the hills.
t.beffroi de saint riquier@50.1,1.9:
Saint-Riquier is a small village in the Somme, a few kilometres from Abbeville, and it punches far above its weight. In the early Middle Ages it was the site of Centula, one of the most important monasteries of the Carolingian empire, ruled by Angilbert, a courtier and son-in-law of Charlemagne, who made it a centre of learning and prayer with hundreds of monks. The great abbey church you see today is later, a Gothic building with a richly carved facade, but the scale of the place still reflects that history. The belfry, a solid square tower in the village, was a symbol of the townspeople's rights and is one of the belfries listed by UNESCO in Belgium and France.

The abbey buildings host exhibitions, and every summer the village holds a festival of classical music, filling the church with concerts. The rest of the year, Saint-Riquier is quiet, with a handful of houses, shops and cafés around the square.

The Somme valley is gentle countryside: chalk plateaus, fields of wheat and sugar beet, small woods and the wide valley of the river with its marshes, ponds and poplars. To the west, the Bay of the Somme is a vast estuary where the tide goes out for miles, home to seals, birds and salt meadows where sheep graze, giving their meat a distinctive flavour. Abbeville, the nearest town, was heavily bombed in 1940 but has a fine Gothic church and makes a good base.

The riding is relaxed rather than thrilling: straight roads across the plateau, gentle curves in the valleys and very little traffic on the back roads. The coast road along the bay offers wide views and the chance to stop at villages like Saint-Valery-sur-Somme and Le Crotoy, popular with visitors in summer. Wind and rain are frequent, and the roads can be slippery with mud near farms.

Saint-Riquier has a few local services but no guarantee of fuel. Abbeville, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and everything else. Try a ficelle picarde, a pancake rolled with ham and mushrooms and baked with cream and cheese, or local sheep from the salt meadows, followed by a gâteau battu, a rich brioche.
Hesdin is a small market town in the green valley of the Canche, in the Pas-de-Calais, and it owes its existence to an act of destruction. The original town, a few kilometres upstream, was razed in 1553 by the forces of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, and a new fortified town was built here the following year as a strongpoint on the frontier between France and the Habsburg Netherlands. The grid of streets and the large market square still follow that plan. On the square stands the town hall, a former palace of the Habsburg governors, with a beautifully carved Renaissance balcony from which proclamations were read, and its belfry is part of the UNESCO list of belfries in Belgium and France.

The town's best-known son is the Abbé Prévost, the eighteenth-century writer whose novel Manon Lescaut inspired operas by Massenet and Puccini. A short ride to the north lies Azincourt, the site of the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, where the army of Henry V of England defeated a much larger French force. A museum in the village tells the story, and the battlefield itself is now peaceful farmland.

The Canche valley is lovely, a green, gentle landscape of meadows, woods, small villages and a river full of trout. The river winds west towards the sea at Étaples and Le Touquet, and the valley roads follow it closely, with gentle curves and little traffic. To the east and south, the land rises onto chalk plateaus with wide, open views, and the Authie valley offers another quiet route.

The weather in this corner of France is changeable, with frequent rain and wind, and sudden showers can make the roads slippery. Cobbles are found in the old town centre, and the narrow streets around the square can be busy on market day, when stalls fill the square with produce, cheeses and local specialities.

Hesdin and neighbouring Marconne have shops, cafés and basic services, but for a wider choice of fuel the nearest larger town is Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise, about twenty-one kilometres away. Sit on the square with a coffee and look up at the Renaissance balcony, or try a local beer and a plate of Maroilles, the strong cheese of the north, on bread.
t.belfort@51.1,3.7:
Ghent has three towers standing in a row, and the middle one is the belfry, rising over the old centre between St Bavo's Cathedral and St Nicholas' Church. Begun in the fourteenth century, it was the town's watchtower, bell tower and strongroom, where the charters granting the city its privileges were locked away. On its spire sits a gilded dragon, the city's mascot, keeping an eye on things. The belfry, with the cloth hall attached to its base, is part of the UNESCO list of belfries of Belgium and France, and you can climb it, partly by lift, for one of the best views over the rooftops, canals and spires.

Ghent's story is one of rebellious wealth. In the Middle Ages it was among the largest cities north of the Alps, rich on cloth woven from English wool, and its citizens repeatedly defied counts, dukes and kings. The great bell Roland once called the people to arms, and the emperor Charles V, born in Ghent, punished the city for a revolt by forcing its leaders to walk barefoot with nooses around their necks, which is why locals are still sometimes called noose-bearers. In St Bavo's hangs the Ghent Altarpiece by the Van Eyck brothers, one of the most important paintings in European history.

The city today is lively, young and less crowded than Bruges. The Graslei and Korenlei, two quays lined with guild houses facing each other across the river Lys, are beautiful at dusk, and the Gravensteen, a grim stone castle of the counts of Flanders, stands in the middle of town.

Riding in Ghent requires patience. The city centre has a traffic plan that divides it into sectors you cannot drive between directly, plus a low-emission zone, and cyclists and trams are everywhere. Park on the edge of the centre and walk. Outside the city, the roads through the Leie valley to the south-west lead past villages where painters once worked, and the Flemish Ardennes, with their cobbled climbs, are within easy reach. Rain and wind are frequent companions.

Ghent has every service, including fuel on the ring roads. Try Gentse waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish, and cuberdons, purple cone-shaped sweets with a syrupy centre, sold from carts in the old town.
t.major mining sites of wallonia@50.4,3.8:
Grand-Hornu, on the edge of the Borinage coalfield west of Mons, looks less like a coal mine than a neoclassical palace. In the early nineteenth century the industrialist Henri De Gorge built it as a model colliery, with workshops, offices and stables arranged around a vast oval courtyard of brick arches, and hundreds of houses for workers, each with its own garden, laid out in streets around it. It was a revolutionary idea at the time, combining industry and housing in one planned complex. Mining ended in the mid-twentieth century, and after years of neglect the site was restored. Today it houses a museum of contemporary art and a design centre, and it is one of the four Major Mining Sites of Wallonia listed by UNESCO in 2012.

The Borinage was the heart of Belgium's coal industry, and life here was harsh. Vincent van Gogh lived among the miners in the late 1870s as a lay preacher, sharing their poverty and sketching their lives, and that experience shaped his decision to become an artist. The houses where he lived, in Wasmes and Cuesmes, can be visited. The landscape still bears the marks of mining, with terrils, conical slag heaps now covered in birch and grass, rising above the brick towns.

Mons, a few kilometres east, is a handsome city with a Baroque belfry, also a World Heritage site, and a famous festival, the Doudou, held every year on Trinity Sunday, when Saint George fights a dragon in the main square amid enormous crowds.

The riding in this part of Hainaut is mostly urban and suburban, with brick towns merging into one another, traffic lights and cobbles. Surfaces can be rough, and tram rails and wet setts are slippery. The landscape opens up to the south, towards the woods and farmland near the French border, and the canals offer flat roads along the water. Rain is common, and roads can be greasy.

Saint-Ghislain and Quaregnon, both about two kilometres away, have fuel and shops, and Mons has everything you need. Try a plate of frites with a Belgian beer, or a local tarte al djote, a savoury tart made with chard and cheese from nearby Nivelles, and take a walk around the great oval courtyard.
t.beffroi de l ancienne maison communale d:
On 26 March 1918, with the German spring offensive smashing through the British lines and threatening to split the Allied armies apart, French and British leaders met in the town hall of Doullens, a small town on the river Authie, north of Amiens. In a room on the first floor, they agreed to give the French general Ferdinand Foch the coordination of all Allied forces on the Western Front, a decision that many historians see as a turning point of the war. The room, now known as the Salle du Commandement Unique, can still be visited, with a stained glass window commemorating the meeting. The belfry of the old town hall, a solid tower from the late Middle Ages, is part of the UNESCO group of belfries of Belgium and France.

Doullens also has a large citadel, one of the biggest in the north of France, with massive walls and bastions built over centuries to guard the frontier. It sits on a hill above the town, and parts of it can be visited on guided tours.

The Authie valley is green and gentle, with meadows, woods and small villages, and the river is clear and full of trout. To the south lie the battlefields of the Somme, where in 1916 one of the bloodiest battles in history was fought. Memorials, cemeteries and museums are scattered across the landscape, including the Thiepval Memorial and the Newfoundland memorial park at Beaumont-Hamel, where the trenches are still visible in the grass.

The riding is gentle rather than exciting: rolling chalk plateaus with wide views, straight roads between villages and gentle curves in the valleys. Traffic is light, and the roads are generally in good condition, though farm vehicles and mud are common. Weather is changeable, with frequent rain and wind, and fog can settle in the valleys in the morning.

Doullens has around six thousand inhabitants, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a pâté de canard d'Amiens, a duck pâté baked in pastry, or a ficelle picarde, and look out for macarons d'Amiens, soft almond biscuits, for later. A visit to the town hall room, followed by a ride south to the Somme battlefields, makes a moving day.
t.mill network at kinderdijk elshout@51.9,:
Nineteen windmills stand in two rows along the canals at Kinderdijk, their sails turning slowly against the wide Dutch sky, and it is one of the most iconic sights in the Netherlands. They were built in the eighteenth century to pump water out of the Alblasserwaard, a low-lying polder between the rivers Lek and Noord, which would otherwise be flooded. Each mill lifted water from a lower canal to a higher one, and from there it was let out into the river. Over time steam, diesel and electric pumping stations took over the job, and the most recent ones still keep the polder dry today. The mill network was listed by UNESCO in 1997.

The name Kinderdijk means child's dike, and it comes from a legend about the great Saint Elizabeth's flood of 1421, when a wooden cradle was found floating on the floodwater with a baby and a cat inside, the cat jumping from side to side to keep the cradle balanced. Some of the mills are still inhabited by millers, and a few are open to visitors, giving a glimpse of life inside, with cramped living quarters around the machinery.

The area is a classic Dutch landscape: flat green polders, ditches, cows and sheep, lined by dikes along the rivers, where long barges glide by. Herons stalk the ditches, and in winter, when the canals freeze, the mills are a romantic backdrop for skaters. Nearby Schoonhoven is a small, fortified town known for its silversmiths.

The riding is flat and relaxed. Narrow roads run along the tops of the dikes, with views over the rivers and polders, and small ferries cross the rivers at several points, a charming way to get around. Traffic is moderate, but the dikes are popular with cyclists, so ride gently. Wind is a constant companion, and in autumn and winter, fog and rain are common. The area around Kinderdijk can be busy with tourists, especially in summer, so arrive early or late.

Alblasserdam, about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. Try a plate of poffertjes, small fluffy pancakes dusted with sugar, or a herring sandwich, and walk or cycle along the canals to see the mills up close.
t.stadhuis met belfort@51.0,4.1:
Dendermonde sits where the Dender gives up and pours itself into the Scheldt, and the old town hall on the Grote Markt is the thing you aim for when you roll in. Its belfry is one of the Flemish and Walloon towers grouped together by UNESCO as the Belfries of Belgium and France, and the reason those towers matter is simple: in the medieval Low Countries a belfry was the civic answer to the church spire. It held the town charters, the bell that called the citizens, and the watchman who looked out for fire and for armies. Dendermonde needed the watchman more than most, because a town at a river junction is a town everybody wants, and it was besieged, burned and rebuilt more than once, most brutally in 1914 when German troops set much of it alight.

The riding around here is Flanders in its purest form. Flat, yes, but not boring if you choose the dike roads along the Scheldt, where the river swings in long tidal loops and the wind comes off the polders with nothing to stop it. Expect brick villages, poplar rows, cyclists in tight packs on Sunday mornings and the occasional stretch of cobbles that will rattle your mirrors loose. Lebbeke and Zele are a few kilometres off, and Ghent, Antwerp and Brussels all lie within an easy hour, which is exactly why traffic thickens at commuter times. Mid-morning and early evening light on the river is the best of it.

The town has a story it tells every ten years or so: the Ros Beiaard, a giant horse carried through the streets with the four Aymon brothers on its back, a legend from the Charlemagne cycle that Dendermonde treats as its own. If you are not lucky enough to hit the procession, the béguinage a short walk away gives you a quiet courtyard of whitewashed houses and a sense of how lay religious women lived here for centuries.

Practically, this is a stop that gives you everything. Dendermonde is a town of over forty thousand, so fuel, cafés and bakeries are never far, and the market square has terraces where you can park the bike within sight. Order a local beer if you are done for the day, or a strong coffee and a waffle if you are not, and watch the bell tower count the quarters while the square goes about its business.
t.la citadella d arras@50.3,2.8:
The people of Arras call their citadel la belle inutile, the beautiful useless one, and they say it with affection. Vauban built it in the late seventeenth century, after Louis XIV took Artois from Spain, as part of the chain of fortresses meant to lock France's northern border. Its star-shaped ramparts, bastions and moats are textbook Vauban, but the border moved north before the fortress ever saw a serious siege, hence the nickname. It is one of the twelve sites grouped as the Fortifications of Vauban on the UNESCO list since 2008. Its later history is darker: during the Second World War, the Germans executed resistance fighters in the moat, and a memorial there lists their names.

The town centre is a short ride away and far from useless. The Grand-Place and the Place des Héros form two vast squares lined with tall Flemish baroque gabled houses on arcades, and the town hall's belfry, part of the UNESCO Belfries of Belgium and France, rises above them. Much of it was destroyed in the First World War and rebuilt faithfully afterwards. Beneath the squares lie the boves, old chalk quarries and cellars, and on the edge of town the Wellington Quarry tells the story of the New Zealand tunnellers who dug a network of tunnels to hide thousands of soldiers before the Battle of Arras in 1917. Arras was also the birthplace of Robespierre.

The Artois countryside is open and rolling, with big fields of wheat and beet, and the landscape is scattered with the war cemeteries of the Western Front, white headstones in neat rows. Vimy Ridge, with the towering Canadian memorial, is a short ride north, and the roads there are fast, straight and windy. Traffic around Arras is moderate, with roundabouts and ring roads, and the town centre has cobbles in places.

Arras has fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of restaurants and brasseries around the squares. Try the local andouillette, a sausage made with tripe, if you are brave, or a plate of moules-frites. The sweet speciality is the cœur d'Arras, a heart-shaped gingerbread biscuit, and the region's beers, many brewed by small producers in northern France, are excellent.
t.maison atelier horta@50.8,4.4:
From the street, the house at Rue Américaine in Saint-Gilles is pleasant but unassuming, a narrow town house of stone and iron among many others. Inside, it becomes something else entirely: a flowing space of curving wrought iron, stained glass, mosaic floors and woodwork that seems to grow like plant tendrils, all bathed in light from a glass roof over the stairwell. Victor Horta, one of the founders of Art Nouveau, built it as his home and studio between 1898 and 1901, and it is now a museum dedicated to his work. In 2000, it was listed by UNESCO together with three other Horta town houses in Brussels, including the Hôtel Tassel, often cited as the first true Art Nouveau building.

Horta's genius lay in using modern materials, iron and glass, to create organic, light-filled spaces, and in designing everything, from the façades to the door handles. Many of his buildings were demolished in the decades after his death, most notoriously the Maison du Peuple, and their loss helped kick-start the heritage movement in Brussels. Today, the streets of Saint-Gilles and Ixelles still hold many fine Art Nouveau façades, if you know where to look.

Riding in Brussels is not much fun. The city is congested, with complex junctions, trams, cobbles, one-way streets and impatient drivers. The city has a low-emission zone, so check the current rules for your bike before you go. Parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, but keep your gear secure. For better riding, head south into the Sonian Forest, a vast beech wood on the edge of the city, or toward the rolling countryside of Walloon Brabant, with its farms and abbeys.

Brussels has fuel, food and accommodation everywhere. Saint-Gilles is a lively district, with cafés, bars and restaurants around the Parvis, the square in front of the church. Try frites, double-fried and served with mayonnaise, moules-frites, stoemp, mashed potatoes with vegetables and sausage, and of course, Belgian beer and chocolate. A waffle eaten standing at a street stall is a small, sticky joy.
t.belfort en schepenhuis beffroi et maison:
Aalst's Schepenhuis, the old aldermen's house on the Grote Markt, is reckoned to be the oldest surviving town hall in the Low Countries, its oldest parts going back to the thirteenth century, and its belfry, added later, carries the bells that once regulated the town's life. Together they are part of the UNESCO listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France. In front of them stands a statue of Dirk Martens, who set up one of the first printing presses in the Southern Netherlands here in the 1470s and later printed works by Erasmus and Thomas More.

Aalst is a busy, working town on the Dender, with a strong local identity. It is best known for its carnival, three days of parades, satire and excess before Lent, when the whole town dresses up and takes to the streets. The carnival was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage, then removed in 2019 after a controversy over floats judged antisemitic, a decision that the town debated fiercely. Whatever your view, the carnival remains the heartbeat of the town, and the locals talk about it all year round.

The riding around Aalst is flat to gently rolling, with busy roads around the town and quieter lanes through the countryside, past farms, fields and villages. South of Aalst, the Flemish Ardennes begin, a region of short, steep hills with cobbled climbs made famous by the Tour of Flanders cycling race, such as the Muur van Geraardsbergen, crowned by a chapel. On a motorcycle, they are fun but slippery when wet, and you will share them with plenty of cyclists. The weather is changeable, with frequent rain and wind.

Aalst, with seventy-seven thousand inhabitants, has everything: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants. The Grote Markt is lined with terraces where you can sit with a beer and watch the town go by. The locals proudly call themselves Ajuinen, the onions, after an old trade in the vegetable, and you will see onions on everything from shop signs to carnival costumes. For lunch, order a plate of stoofvlees, beef stewed in beer, with fries. The local breweries produce excellent beers, but save them for the end of the ride.
t.beguinage de sint amandsberg gent@51.1,3:
The Great Béguinage of Sint-Amandsberg looks like a small walled town of its own, tucked into a residential suburb just east of the centre of Ghent. When the city expanded in the 1870s and the old béguinage of St Elisabeth was in the way, the beguines, lay religious women who lived in community without taking permanent vows, moved here to a new complex of neo-Gothic houses, convents and a church, all laid out around streets, squares and gardens behind a wall and gate. The move was funded by the Duke of Arenberg, and the whole place was finished in just a few years. It is one of the thirteen Flemish Béguinages on the UNESCO list since 1998, and although the beguines are gone, the houses are still lived in, and the atmosphere is calm and quiet.

Ghent itself is one of the most beautiful cities in Belgium, and less touristy than Bruges. Its medieval centre is full of gabled houses, canals, bridges and churches, and the Gravensteen, a castle in the middle of the city, looks like something out of a storybook. St Bavo's Cathedral holds the Ghent Altarpiece by the van Eyck brothers, one of the most important paintings in the world. The city is lively, with a big student population, plenty of bars and a famous summer festival.

Riding into Ghent requires some care. The city centre has a strict traffic plan, with zones that cars and motorcycles cannot cross directly, and much of the centre is pedestrianised or restricted. There are cobbles, trams and lots of cyclists. It is best to park outside the centre and explore on foot. For riding, the countryside around Ghent is flat, with quiet lanes along the Leie and Scheldt rivers, through villages and past castles.

Ghent has everything, including fuel on the ring roads. Try Gentse waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish with vegetables, or stoverij, beef stewed in beer. Cuberdons, cone-shaped purple sweets with a syrupy centre, are a local speciality, often sold from carts in the market. Ghent mustard, sold by weight from a shop near the Vrijdagmarkt, is a good souvenir.
t.chateau dampierre@50.4,3.5:
Anzin, on the northern edge of Valenciennes, is where coal mining in northern France began on an industrial scale. In the eighteenth century, the Compagnie des mines d'Anzin became one of the largest companies in France, and its mines, workers' housing, slag heaps and buildings shaped the landscape of the region. Château Dampierre is one of the buildings linked to that history, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin, inscribed in 2012, which preserves more than a hundred sites across a vast area: pits, headframes, miners' cités, churches, schools and the great black spoil heaps known as terrils. The big miners' strike at Anzin in 1884 helped inspire Émile Zola's novel Germinal.

Valenciennes itself is a lively town, the birthplace of the painter Antoine Watteau, with a fine art museum and a centre rebuilt after heavy damage in the two world wars. The countryside around is flat, with fields, canals and woods, and the terrils, some now covered in vegetation, rise like strange green pyramids above the plain. A few kilometres away, in the forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers, the Trouée d'Arenberg is a long, straight stretch of rough cobbles through the trees, one of the most feared sectors of the Paris–Roubaix cycling race.

The riding in the area is mostly urban and flat, with busy roads, roundabouts and traffic lights. The roads through the forest and along the canals are quieter, with some nice stretches. If you want to try the cobbles of the Paris–Roubaix sectors, be aware that they are very rough and slippery when wet, and some are closed to motor vehicles. The weather is changeable, with frequent rain and wind.

Anzin and Valenciennes have fuel, shops and restaurants. The local cuisine is hearty: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer with gingerbread, welsh, melted cheese and beer over bread and ham, and potjevleesch, a terrine of different meats in jelly. Local beers, brewed by small breweries, are excellent. Maroilles, a strong, soft cheese with an orange rind, is used in many dishes, including a tart called flamiche.
t.stadhuis@50.9,3.1:
The pin drops you on the Grote Markt of Roeselare, in the middle of West Flanders, and not in Bruges as the ride title might suggest. Bruges is half an hour north, and the two make a good pairing, but Roeselare deserves to be taken on its own terms: a working town of some fifty-six thousand people, built on textiles, food processing and trade, with a town hall on its market square that anchors the centre. Like most Flemish towns, Roeselare grew around a market and a civic building that announced the burghers' independence from lords and bishops, and the tradition of the town hall as the symbol of local self-government is still very much alive here.

Two things make Roeselare famous well beyond Belgium. The first is beer: this is the home of Rodenbach, the brewery whose sour red-brown ales aged in huge oak foeders define the Flemish red style. Order one on a terrace on the square and you will taste something closer to wine than lager. The second is cycling. West Flanders breathes bike racing, and Roeselare hosts KOERS, the museum of road cycling, a fine stop for anyone who rides on two wheels of any kind.

For motorcyclists, the surroundings are flat to gently rolling, laced with narrow concrete and brick roads between farms, poplar rows and villages with big brick churches. It is not dramatic riding, but it is relaxing, and the wind off the North Sea is your main opponent. Watch out for cobbles on village squares, cyclists in numbers you will not see elsewhere, and speed limits that drop to 30 or 50 in every built-up area, with cameras to enforce them.

The First World War is never far away in this province. Roeselare lay behind the German lines for most of the conflict, and the battlefields of the Ypres Salient, with Passchendaele and Tyne Cot, are only a short ride to the west. Fuel and food are trivially easy in town, so use the stop for a coffee, a waffle or a Rodenbach, then head north to Bruges or west toward the Salient.
t.petit beguinage de gent@51.0,3.7:
Push open a gate off a busy Ghent street and the noise drops away. The Klein Begijnhof, the Small Béguinage, is a walled enclave of whitewashed and brick houses with stepped gables around a green courtyard and a Baroque church. Béguines were lay women who lived in community, devoted to prayer and work but without taking permanent vows, and this béguinage was founded in the thirteenth century. Most of the present buildings date from the seventeenth century. Together with other Flemish béguinages, it is on the UNESCO World Heritage list, and it remains one of the calmest places in the city.

Getting here on a motorcycle needs a little planning. Ghent introduced a traffic circulation plan that divides the centre into sectors you cannot drive directly between, and a low emission zone covers the city centre. Older bikes may need registration, and the medieval core around the Graslei, Korenlei and Sint-Baafs Cathedral is largely closed to motor traffic. The sensible approach is to park on the edge of the centre and walk or take a tram. Cobbles, tram tracks and swarms of cyclists make riding in the core more stressful than fun anyway.

Once on foot, Ghent rewards you generously. The Gravensteen castle, the Belfry, the Van Eyck brothers' Adoration of the Mystic Lamb in Sint-Baafs, and the canalside guildhalls are all within a short walk. Students keep the city lively and food is excellent, from Ghent's own waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish, to the purple cone-shaped sweets called cuberdons.

Outside the city, the ride options are pleasant rather than thrilling: the Scheldt and Lys valleys offer winding lanes through villages, and the Flemish Ardennes to the south give some short, steep cobbled climbs familiar from cycling's spring classics. Fuel, coffee and everything else are easy. Come back to the béguinage late in the day, when the light slants across the courtyard and you might have it almost to yourself.
For almost three centuries, coal shaped the land between Valenciennes and Béthune in northern France, creating a landscape of pits, slag heaps, railway lines and miners' housing estates. The Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2012, and the Cités de la Justice et du Moulin in Auby are part of it: rows of brick houses built by the mining companies to house their workers, with gardens, churches, schools and shops, all organised around the pit. The cités are still inhabited, so treat them as neighbourhoods rather than museums.

The mining landscape tells a story of hard work, solidarity and disaster. The Courrières mine disaster of 1906, a short distance from here, killed more than a thousand miners and remains the deadliest mining accident in European history. The region also drew workers from Poland, Italy, North Africa and elsewhere, and its culture reflects that mix, with Polish churches and associations still active in many towns.

Riding through the basin is not about scenery in the conventional sense, but there is a strange beauty in it. The slag heaps, some of them over a hundred metres high, have become green hills with walking trails and views, and those at Loos-en-Gohelle are among the highest in Europe. Roads are flat, busy and built-up, with lots of roundabouts, traffic lights and speed cameras. Cobbles appear on some village roads, especially toward Arenberg, famous from the Paris-Roubaix cycle race.

Auby, a town of almost eight thousand, has fuel and basic services, and Douai, a few kilometres away, has a beautiful belfry, a lively market and plenty of restaurants. Lens, nearby, is home to the Louvre-Lens, a branch of the Paris museum built on a former mine site. Try the local specialities, such as maroilles cheese, carbonade flamande or a welsh, a hot dish of cheddar melted with beer over bread and ham.
Lille's town hall belfry is a child of the twentieth century. After the old town hall was lost, the architect Émile Dubuisson built a new one in the 1920s and early 1930s in a working-class district south of the centre, and its belfry, rising about 104 metres, is the tallest civic belfry in Europe. Built of reinforced concrete and brick in an Art Deco reinterpretation of the Flemish tradition, it is part of the UNESCO-listed Belfries of Belgium and France, a group that celebrates the towers built by towns to symbolise their freedom and civic pride.

You can climb the belfry for a view across the city and the flat Flemish countryside, as far as Belgium on a clear day. At its base, the giants Lydéric and Phinaert, legendary founders of Lille, guard the entrance in stone. The neighbourhood around the town hall is lively and multicultural, a contrast to the elegant old town further north.

Lille itself is a city of over two hundred thousand people, the heart of a metropolitan area of more than a million, with Flemish and French heritage layered on top of each other. The Grand Place, the Vieille Bourse, the citadel built by Vauban, and the Palais des Beaux-Arts, one of the richest art museums in France, are all within walking distance. Food is hearty and northern: moules-frites, carbonade, potjevleesch, and waffles from Méert, a pastry shop since the eighteenth century.

For riders, Lille is a city stop rather than a riding destination. Traffic is heavy, cobbles are common, and the city has a low emission zone. Park the bike and explore on foot or by metro. Fuel is easy to find on the outskirts. From here, the ride options include the mining basin to the south, the Flemish hills to the north-west around Cassel, and the Belgian border, only a few minutes away, with Tournai, Kortrijk and Ypres all close by.
t.cite n 10@50.4,2.7:
Sains-en-Gohelle is a former coal town in the heart of the Nord-Pas de Calais mining basin, and Cité n°10 is one of its old mining estates, rows of brick houses built for miners and their families around a pithead. The basin, which stretches about 120 kilometres from the Belgian border towards the west, was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, and the cités, the slag heaps and the headframes are its most visible remains.

Cité n°10 is a garden city, built in the early twentieth century with houses set in gardens along curving streets, a model of the paternalistic housing that mining companies provided to attract and retain workers. The houses are modest but carefully designed, with variations in style and colour, and many are still inhabited. The slag heaps around the town, the terrils, are now covered in vegetation and form a striking landscape of artificial hills, some of which can be climbed for a view over the basin.

The riding here is not about mountains or bends; it is about history and atmosphere. The roads are flat or gently rolling, through towns and villages that blend into one another, with heavy traffic at times. The real reason to come is the landscape of memory. A few kilometres south lies the ridge of Notre-Dame de Lorette, site of fierce fighting in the First World War, with the largest French military cemetery and the Ring of Memory, a striking modern memorial listing the names of nearly six hundred thousand soldiers who died in the region. The Canadian memorial at Vimy Ridge is nearby too.

Sains-en-Gohelle has fuel and shops, and Lens, a few kilometres east, is a larger town with all services and the Louvre-Lens museum, a branch of the Paris Louvre built on a former mine site. The local cuisine is hearty: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, and maroilles, a strong local cheese. The light here is often grey and soft, which suits the brick and the green slag heaps. On a quiet weekday morning, the cité is calm and the memorials are almost empty, which makes the visit more moving.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de chabaud l:
At Condé-sur-l'Escaut, right on the Belgian border, the coal basin of northern France reaches its eastern end, and the old mining site of Chabaud-Latour shows how industry and nature have come to terms. A pit operated here for decades, and today what remains is a landscape of slag heaps, ponds formed by mining subsidence, woods and wetlands, part of the UNESCO site of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin.

Subsidence is the key to this landscape. As coal was extracted from underground, the ground above sank, and water filled the hollows, creating lakes and marshes where there had been farmland. These wetlands are now valuable habitats for birds, and the area is part of the Scarpe-Escaut regional natural park, which covers the valleys of these two rivers along the border. The slag heaps, once black and bare, are covered in trees and grassland, and some can be climbed for views over the flat country and into Belgium.

The riding here is not about mountains or fast bends. Roads are flat and often busy, passing through towns and villages that run into each other, and the landscape is a mixture of old industry, housing, fields and woodland. What draws you is the history and the atmosphere. The Escaut, the Scheldt in Dutch, flows north from here towards Antwerp, and canals and old towpaths cross the area. Cobbles appear on some minor roads, and they can be slippery in the wet. The weather is often grey and damp, with a soft light that suits the landscape.

Condé-sur-l'Escaut, a town of ten thousand, has fuel and shops, and Fresnes-sur-Escaut and Vieux-Condé are close by. Valenciennes, a larger city, is about fifteen kilometres south-west. The local food is hearty: carbonnade, beef braised in beer, and potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, both typical of French Flanders and Hainaut. Beer is a serious matter here, as across the border in Belgium. On a quiet morning, with mist over the ponds and herons standing in the reeds, it is hard to believe this was once a place of coal dust and noise.
t.nord pas de calais mining basin@50.5,3.5:
Black hills on a flat land. That is the image most people keep of the Nord-Pas de Calais coal basin, a band of former mining country stretching about 120 kilometres from the Belgian border westward towards Béthune, where for nearly three centuries coal was dug from deep underground. The slag heaps, the terrils, rise like pyramids above the towns, and the mining villages, the cités, line the streets in rows of brick houses. In 2012 the basin was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised as a living cultural landscape, with over three hundred elements protected.

Near Vieux-Condé and Hergnies, at the eastern end of the basin, coal was first found in the early eighteenth century, and mining spread westward over the following centuries. The life of the miners, with its hardships and its strong community spirit, was described by Émile Zola in Germinal, set in a fictional mining town in this region. The last pit in the basin closed in 1990, and the region has struggled with unemployment since, but it has also embraced its heritage, turning old pits into museums, cultural centres and parks.

The riding in the eastern part of the basin is flat and often busy, through towns and villages that blend into each other, but the Scarpe-Escaut regional natural park, created in 1968 as the first regional natural park in France, offers quieter roads through forests, wetlands and farmland. The forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers is the heart of the park, and the old mining site of Arenberg, in the forest, is now a media and cultural centre. The famous cobbled sector of the Paris-Roubaix cycle race, the Trouée d'Arenberg, runs through the forest, and riding it on a motorcycle is a jarring experience.

Vieux-Condé, two kilometres away, is a town of ten thousand with fuel and shops, and Condé-sur-l'Escaut and Valenciennes are nearby. The local food includes maroilles cheese, carbonnade and frites, and beer is a serious matter. The light here is often grey and soft, and the terrils, now green with vegetation, are good places to climb for a view over the land. Visiting the basin is a reminder of the human cost of the industrial age.
t.beffroi de thuin@50.3,4.3:
Thuin sits on a rocky spur above the Sambre, and from the river it looks like a town that climbed a hill to keep its feet dry. At the top stands the belfry, a tall square tower with an onion-shaped spire that was originally the bell tower of a collegiate church and survived when the church itself did not. Since 1999 it has been part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France, a reminder that towns in this region measured their freedom in bells, towers and charters.

Below the old upper town, terraced gardens cling to the slopes in tiers, held up by stone walls and linked by steep paths and stairways. The jardins suspendus, or hanging gardens, are a local pride, and the view from them across the valley is worth the climb in bike boots. Down by the water, Thuin has a long tradition of river boatmen, the bateliers, and a few old barges and the memory of that trade remain along the Sambre.

The riding around Thuin is better than you might expect for Wallonia's industrial fringe. The Sambre valley roads bend with the river, passing locks, wooded slopes and small brick villages, while to the south the land begins to rise into the Botte du Hainaut, the boot-shaped finger of Belgium that pokes into France around Chimay. Head that way for quieter lanes, forests and good flowing curves. Surfaces vary, and cobbles appear in town centres and on some steep streets in Thuin itself, which can be slippery when wet.

Thuin is a proper small town with fuel, shops and a choice of brasseries. Nearby Lobbes has an ancient collegiate church of Saint Ursmer with Carolingian roots, and the romantic ruins of the Abbey of Aulne lie a few kilometres down the valley, a beautiful place to stop in the evening light. Chimay, further south, is famous for its Trappist beer and cheese.

Local food leans hearty: try a Walloon dish of boulets in sauce, or something with the region's beer in it. Visit in spring when the gardens are waking up, or in autumn when the woods turn gold along the river. Climb up to the belfry, look out over the valley, and enjoy one of Belgium's more surprising viewpoints.
t.maison guiete@51.2,4.4:
In a leafy residential street in the southern suburbs of Antwerp, there is a white house that looks as if it has walked in from a different century. The Maison Guiette, as it is usually spelled, was designed by Le Corbusier in 1926 for the painter René Guiette, and it was his first building in Belgium. Since 2016 it has been one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of Le Corbusier's architectural work, alongside the Villa Savoye, the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille and buildings on several continents.

The house is a compact box of pure lines, with a big studio window on the upper floor, a roof terrace and a clear structure that let the painter live and work under the same light. Its strict geometry and white walls caused a stir among neighbours used to brick and ornament. It remains a private house, so treat it as something to admire from the street, quietly, without peering over hedges.

Riding here is city riding, pure and simple. Antwerp has a busy ring road, tram lines that grab front wheels, cobbled streets in the older districts and an enormous cycling population that moves with total confidence. Approach from the south rather than through the centre, take your time, and give the trams and bicycles the respect they demand. If you need a bit of air afterwards, head out along the Scheldt toward Hoboken or into the green belt of Mortsel and Edegem.

Practical matters are simple: you are surrounded by a city of half a million people, so fuel, food and coffee are never far away. Antwerp has an excellent café culture, and a short ride into the centre brings you to the cathedral, Rubens's house and the old Grote Markt with its guildhalls. Try a glass of De Koninck, the city's own beer, in a classic bar, or the local pralines and waffles if you need sugar for the ride home.

The appeal of a stop like this is the contrast.
