You go from the dense, gothic, Flemish heart of Antwerp to a little white manifesto of modern architecture in a quiet street, and it reminds you how much the twentieth century changed the way people live. Stop for five minutes, look at the clean lines against the trees, and imagine the reaction when it was new.
t.voormalig stadhuis lakenhal@51.2,4.8:
Rik Van Looy, one of the great Belgian cyclists of the 1950s and 1960s, was known as the Emperor of Herentals, which tells you something about the priorities of this town in the Kempen. Herentals lies on the flat heathland of the province of Antwerp, and in the middle of its market square stands the old town hall, built in the fourteenth century as a cloth hall, a lakenhal, when the town grew rich on wool and weaving. Its belfry is part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France, a symbol of civic pride and of the freedoms that merchants bought from their lords.

The building has the look of a sturdy Flemish townhouse with a spire on top, and it has served as a market, a courthouse and a meeting place over the centuries. Around it, the square is lined with cafés and shops, and the old town gates of Herentals, the Zandpoort and Bovenpoort, still stand at the edges of the centre. The Gothic church of Saint Waldetrudis is worth a look too, with a famous carved altarpiece inside.

The Kempen is not a place for mountain passes. The roads are flat and mostly straight, threading through pine forests, heathland and small villages, with canals like the Albert Canal and the Kempisch Canal running through the landscape. It is pleasant, easy riding with scents of pine and heather, but you will share the roads with very large numbers of cyclists, especially on weekends, and the speed limits are enforced. Look out for cycle paths crossing the road, tractors and the odd cobbled section in villages.

With twenty-five thousand inhabitants, Herentals will not leave you hunting for petrol or a sandwich. The market square cafés serve good Belgian beer, and you will find frites stands and bakeries nearby. In late summer the heathland around Kasterlee and the Kempen woods turns purple with flowering heather, a lovely sight from the saddle.

If you want history with your coffee, sit on the square and look up at the belfry, imagining the clatter of looms in medieval Herentals. If you want cycling lore, ask a local about Van Looy, and be ready for a long answer full of affection and pride.
t.cites du champ fleuri et du garage@50.3,:
Coal made this corner of northern France, and coal left it with a landscape unlike anywhere else in the country: slag heaps rising like black pyramids from the fields, pithead frames standing over old shafts and long rows of brick miners' houses lining the streets of every town. The Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin was listed by UNESCO in 2012, and the Cités du Champ Fleuri et du Garage, near Masny and Lewarde, are among its typical housing estates, built by mining companies to house workers and their families close to the pits.

The cités are rows of brick houses with small gardens, often arranged around churches, schools and community buildings, and each company had its own style. Walking through them gives a sense of the paternalistic world of the mining companies, which provided housing, schools and healthcare in exchange for loyalty and hard work. Just next door at Lewarde, the Centre Historique Minier occupies a former pit and is the largest mining museum in France, with guided tours, some led by former miners.

The riding here is flat, with straight roads crossing farmland, mining towns and villages. It is not a land of curves, but it has its own character. Not far away, the cobbled sectors of the Paris-Roubaix cycling race, including the famous Trouée d'Arenberg in the forest near Wallers, are an experience on two wheels of any kind, though they are rough, slippery when wet and demand respect. Traffic can be heavy near towns, and the weather is often grey and windy.

Aniche, about five kilometres away, and Douai a little further, have fuel, shops and restaurants. Masny and Lewarde have small bakeries and bars. Local food is hearty and warming: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, and chips cooked in beef fat. The region's beers are excellent.

The landscape has a stark, haunting beauty, especially in the low light of autumn and winter, when the slag heaps stand out against the sky. Many have been reclaimed by nature, with trees, wild flowers and birds, and some can be climbed for views over the basin. Ride through the cités slowly, look at the gardens and the brick, and think of the generations who went down the pits from these houses.
t.beffroi de bethune@50.5,2.6:
The belfry of Béthune has been standing in the middle of the Grand Place since the fourteenth century, and it has survived more than most of the buildings around it. In 1918 the town centre was almost completely destroyed by German shelling, and the square was rebuilt in the 1920s in a mix of Flemish and Art Deco styles, with tall, ornate façades in brick and stone around the old tower. The belfry, a symbol of the town's ancient freedoms, is part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France, and climbing its stairs gives a fine view over the rooftops and the flat land around.

Béthune sits at the western edge of the old mining basin of the Pas-de-Calais, between the Artois hills and the plains of Flanders. To the east the landscape is dominated by slag heaps, including the twin terrils of Loos-en-Gohelle, among the highest in Europe, and by the brick towns and cités of the mining companies. To the south lie the battlefields of the First World War, including the ridge of Notre-Dame de Lorette, with its vast military cemetery and the striking Ring of Remembrance, which lists the names of nearly six hundred thousand soldiers of all nations who died in the region.

The riding is mostly flat to gently rolling, with straight roads through farmland and towns, and more interesting stretches in the Artois hills to the south and west. Traffic can be heavy near the towns and on the main roads, and the weather is often grey, windy and wet. Cobbled streets appear in town centres.

Béthune is a market town of some thirty thousand souls, and nobody leaves it hungry or on reserve. The Grand Place is lined with cafés and brasseries, and the local food includes hearty dishes like carbonnade, welsh, a cheese and beer dish on toast, and maroilles tart, made with the strong-smelling cheese of the north. The Louvre-Lens museum, about twenty kilometres away, is a superb modern art museum in a former mining site.

The northern light is at its softest in May and September, and the rain is at least warmer then. Stand in the Grand Place, look up at the belfry and around at the rebuilt façades, and you will see a town that has refused, more than once, to disappear.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville d aire sur l:
Aire-sur-la-Lys is the kind of small French town that rewards a slow walk with no plan. Its belfry rises from the eighteenth-century town hall on the Grand Place, an elegant classical building topped by a tall tower with a lantern and a carillon, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France. Across the square stands the Bailliage, a richly decorated Renaissance building from around 1600, with arches, carved figures and a little loggia, which once housed the guard and the town's officials. A few streets away, the great collegiate church of Saint-Pierre, built in a flamboyant Gothic style, rises above the rooftops.

The town sits on the River Lys, which flows from here through Flanders into Belgium, and is laced with canals and small waterways. For centuries it was a fortified frontier town, changing hands between France, Burgundy and Spain, and its streets are lined with old brick and stone houses, some with Spanish-style gables. The atmosphere is quiet and provincial, with a weekly market that brings the square to life.

The riding around Aire is gentle. To the north lies the marshland of the Audomarois near Saint-Omer, a maze of canals and vegetable gardens, and to the south and west the land rises into the Artois hills, with rolling farmland, small valleys and quieter, curvier roads through villages like Fruges. Isbergues, next door, is an industrial town known for its steelworks. Traffic is moderate, and the weather often grey and windy, with rain never far away.

Aire-sur-la-Lys is a town of around ten thousand people, with fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and Isbergues nearby offers more choice. Local food includes the hearty dishes of French Flanders: potjevleesch, carbonnade, chicory gratin and cheeses from the region. A glass of local beer in a café on the Grand Place, with the belfry overhead, is a fine way to pass an hour.

Visit in spring or summer, when the market fills the square and the canals reflect the sky. In autumn and winter the light is soft and low, and the town has a sleepy, melancholic charm. Either way, Aire is a good place to slow down, eat well and admire the work of builders who wanted their town to look as proud as any in Flanders.
t.leiden roomburg besjeslaan@52.1,4.5:
The Rhine ends in a whimper rather than a bang. After its long journey from the Alps, its old main branch, the Oude Rijn, winds quietly through the flat polders of South Holland past Leiden toward the North Sea, and for the Romans this sluggish waterway was the northern frontier of the empire. At Roomburg, on the edge of Leiden and Leiderdorp, stood the fort of Matilo, guarding the river and the canal that linked it with the Meuse, and today its site is part of the Roomburgerpark, a green space with information points and outlines marking where the fort stood. It belongs to the Lower Germanic Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Leiden itself, just a couple of kilometres away, is one of the most charming cities in the Netherlands. It has the oldest university in the country, founded in 1575, canals lined with gabled houses, windmills and museums, and it was the birthplace of Rembrandt. The National Museum of Antiquities in Leiden holds Roman finds from the region, as well as Egyptian treasures, and is well worth a visit.

The riding here is flat, of course, and the roads are dominated by cyclists, who have their own paths, traffic lights and priority in many situations. Be alert at junctions and roundabouts, where cyclists may cross in front of you, and expect narrow roads along the canals and dykes. Wind is a constant companion, often strong and from the west. North of Leiden the bulb fields around Lisse bloom in spring, a spectacular sight of colour stretching across the polders.

Leiderdorp and Leiden have all the fuel, food and coffee you could need. Dutch food is simple but satisfying: raw herring with onions from a street stall, cheese from Leiden itself, flavoured with cumin, and pancakes, poffertjes and apple pie in cafés. A Leiden specialty is hutspot, a mash of potatoes, carrots and onions, which the city eats on 3 October to celebrate the end of the Spanish siege in 1574.

Come in spring for the bulb fields, or in summer for long evenings on the canals. Autumn and winter bring wind, rain and grey skies, but also cosy cafés. Stroll through Roomburgerpark, look at the quiet river and remember that this placid green ditch was once the edge of the Roman world.
t.beffroi de gembloux@50.6,4.7:
Gembloux grew up around a Benedictine abbey founded in the tenth century, and for most of its history the monks ran the show. The abbey buildings, rebuilt in a grand classical style in the eighteenth century, now house a university faculty of agricultural sciences, fitting for a town surrounded by some of the richest farmland in Belgium. The belfry, a solid tower that was once part of a church and later became the town's civic symbol, stands in the centre and is part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France. Climbing it gives views over the rooftops and across the open fields of the Hesbaye.

The town has a long and sometimes violent history. In 1578 Spanish forces crushed a Dutch rebel army at the Battle of Gembloux, and in May 1940 French troops fought a fierce battle here against German armoured divisions in one of the first big tank engagements of the Second World War. Memorials and cemeteries in the area recall the fighting.

The riding around Gembloux is flat to gently rolling, with straight roads across open farmland, fields of wheat, sugar beet and potatoes, and small brick villages. It is easy riding rather than thrilling, but the valley of the Orneau to the south and the Meuse valley around Namur, about fifteen kilometres away, offer more relief, with rocky cliffs, forests and twisting roads. Traffic can be heavy near Namur and on the main roads, and the weather is changeable, often grey and windy.

Gembloux has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the town centre has several cafés around the main square. Namur, the capital of Wallonia, has a magnificent citadel on a rocky spur above the confluence of the Sambre and Meuse, and a lively old town with restaurants and bars.

Local food includes Walloon dishes like boulets liégeois, meatballs in a sweet and sour sauce made with local syrup, and tarte au sucre, a rich sugar tart. Belgian beer is everywhere, with dozens of local and abbey brews to try, of course only when the riding is done. The Hesbaye looks its best in June, with the wheat high, and in the misty mornings of October. Stand at the foot of the belfry, look up, and remember that this calm farming town has seen armies clash on its doorstep more than once.
t.cite du rivage ancienne@50.4,3.6:
Brick terraced houses, small gardens and a straight street running toward the Escaut: at first glance the Cité du Rivage in Bruay-sur-l'Escaut looks like any working-class neighbourhood in northern France. It is part of something much larger. In 2012, UNESCO listed the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin, a landscape of pit villages, headframes, slag heaps and railways stretching over a hundred kilometres, as a monument to three centuries of coal. This cité is one of its many fragments, an early housing development built by the mining companies to keep their workers close to the pits.

The history here is old by coalfield standards. The Compagnie des mines d'Anzin, based just next door, was founded in the eighteenth century and became one of the most powerful industrial companies in France. Émile Zola studied the region's mines and the great strike of 1884 at Anzin before writing Germinal, his novel of miners' lives and revolt. Walk along these streets and imagine the long rows of houses filled with families whose lives revolved around the pit, the shift whistle and the company store.

The Escaut, called the Scheldt further downstream in Belgium, runs through the town, canalised and lined with old industrial sites. The landscape is flat and urban, with Valenciennes a few kilometres away and the forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand to the west, a large green island in the middle of the former coalfield. Riding here is not about curves: it is about urban roads, roundabouts, cobbled sections in old streets and traffic around Valenciennes. The rewards are elsewhere, in the history and in the sense of a region reinventing itself.

Fuel, food and services are everywhere. The local cooking is northern and generous: carbonnade flamande, beef braised in beer, potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, waffles and fries. Local beers are excellent but best kept for the evening. If you are following the mining heritage trail, Valenciennes makes a good base, with hotels, a lively centre and a museum of fine arts. As for the cité, take a slow ride or walk along its streets and look at the details: the brick patterns, the identical doors, the gardens that now bloom where miners once grew vegetables to make ends meet.
A steel tower with a big wheel at the top: once you have seen one headframe, you start to spot them all across the north of France, but each one marks a place where men went down into the dark. The headframe of the Fosse Dutemple, between Valenciennes and Petite-Forêt, is one of the survivors, kept as part of the UNESCO-listed Nord-Pas de Calais mining basin. Under it, cages once dropped miners hundreds of metres to the coal seams; now it stands as a monument, its pulleys still against the sky.

The surroundings are a mixture of housing estates, retail parks and pockets of greenery that have grown over old industrial land. To the west lies the forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers, one of the largest in the north, and within it, at Wallers, the former Arenberg pit, where a huge mining complex has become a film and media centre. Riders who follow cycling will know the name for another reason: the Trouée d'Arenberg, a straight, brutal stretch of cobbles through the forest, is one of the most feared sections of Paris-Roubaix. Riding it on a motorcycle is legal but rattling; the cobbles are irregular, sometimes greasy, and the bike will tell you exactly what it thinks of them.

Beyond the cobbles, the riding is flat and urban, with a lot of roundabouts and traffic around Valenciennes. The canals, the slag heaps rising like green pyramids and the old railway lines give the landscape a character of its own, and the light on a clear winter afternoon, low and golden over the brick and steel, can be wonderful. Rain is frequent, so be wary of painted lines and cobbles when wet.

Petite-Forêt and the surrounding towns have fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Valenciennes, a few kilometres away, offers a full range of services and a pleasant centre with a lively square. Northern food is filling and comforting: maroilles cheese, in a tart or just with bread, welsh made with cheddar, beer and ham, and frites from a roadside stand. The headframe itself is best seen from close by, with time to read the information boards and imagine the noise of the winding engine, the rattle of the cages and the miners lining up for the shift.
t.cite du moulin@50.4,2.9:
Around Lens the slag heaps rise from the plain like a chain of black pyramids, and the twin cones at Loos-en-Gohelle, among the highest in Europe, are visible for miles. The Cité du Moulin sits in this landscape at Fouquières-lès-Lens, next to Harnes and Billy-Montigny, one of the pit villages built by the mining companies and now part of the UNESCO-listed mining basin. It is a quiet residential area today, but its streets tell the story of the coalfield's most terrible moment.

On 10 March 1906, an explosion tore through the galleries of the Courrières mining company, whose pits lay around these towns. More than a thousand miners died, making it the worst mining disaster in European history. Days later, survivors who had been lost underground for three weeks emerged, and the anger that followed the slow and confused rescue effort sparked strikes across the region. Memorials and a mass grave in nearby Méricourt keep the memory alive, and families here still know the names.

Today the area is reinventing itself. Lens has the Louvre-Lens, a branch of the great Paris museum built on the site of a former pit, its long glass and aluminium halls displaying masterpieces in a vast single gallery. The Stade Bollaert-Delelis is the home of RC Lens, whose fans, many descended from Polish and Italian miners, are among the most passionate in France. The slag heaps have become nature reserves, with rare plants and birds, and some can be climbed for views across the flat land.

For riding, expect flat roads, roundabouts, cobbles in old streets and plenty of traffic around Lens and Hénin-Beaumont. Wind sweeps across the plain and rain is frequent. The appeal lies in the history and the strange beauty of the slag heaps at sunset. Fuel and food are easy to find: Harnes and Fouquières-lès-Lens have shops and stations, and Lens has everything. Try a plate of frites with a carbonnade, or a slice of tarte au maroilles. If you have time, combine the cité with the Louvre-Lens and a ride up to the twin slag heaps; between them, they tell the story of a region that went down into the earth and came back up.
t.belfort met lakenhal@50.9,2.9:
Every evening at eight o'clock, traffic stops under the Menin Gate in Ieper and buglers of the local fire brigade play the Last Post for the soldiers of the British Empire who died in the Ypres Salient and have no known grave. The ceremony has been held almost every evening since 1928, interrupted only during the German occupation in the Second World War. Walk from the gate to the Grote Markt and you come to the Cloth Hall and its belfry, a huge Gothic building that dominated medieval Flanders, when Ypres was one of the great cloth towns of Europe.

What you see is largely a reconstruction. The city was destroyed in the First World War, and the Cloth Hall was reduced to a stump. After long debate, Ieper decided to rebuild, and the work took decades. Today the belfry is one component of the World Heritage inscription for the belfries of Belgium and France, and the hall houses the In Flanders Fields Museum, which tells the story of the war in the Salient through the experiences of ordinary people. Ieper also has a curious tradition: the Kattenstoet, a cat festival held every few years, recalls the medieval practice of throwing cats from the belfry, now replaced, thankfully, with stuffed toys.

The countryside around the town is flat and green, dotted with farms, villages and the white headstones of war cemeteries. Zonnebeke, with the memorial museum of Passchendaele and the vast Tyne Cot cemetery nearby, lies a few kilometres east. Poperinge, to the west, is known for its hops and for Talbot House, a club for soldiers during the war. The riding is gentle, on narrow lanes between fields, with cobbles in some villages and a lot of farm traffic. Wind and rain are frequent, and the light over the fields can be soft and melancholy.

Ieper has fuel, hotels, restaurants and cafés. Flemish cooking is substantial: stews with beer, fries, waffles, and in Poperinge, hop shoots in spring. Belgian beer is legendary, but best enjoyed after parking the bike for the night. If you arrive in the evening, park near the centre and walk to the Menin Gate before eight; the crowd is quiet and the ceremony short. Afterwards, the square is lit up and the belfry rises above the rebuilt facades, a stubborn monument to a town that refused to stay in ruins.
t.cite de rimbert@50.5,2.5:
West of Béthune, the coalfield starts to run out of flat land. The first chalk hills of Artois rise around Auchel and Cauchy-à-la-Tour, and the pit villages climb their slopes in neat rows of brick. The Cité de Rimbert is one of these, built by the mining company of Marles to house its workers, and it belongs to the long necklace of sites in the UNESCO-listed mining basin. Its houses, gardens and straight streets are a textbook example of company planning, with every family given a home, a vegetable plot and a short walk to the pit.

Auchel is a town of about eleven thousand that grew around coal and fell on hard times when the pits closed in the second half of the twentieth century. Neighbouring Bruay-la-Buissière, Marles-les-Mines and Burbure share the same story. But the landscape has softened. Slag heaps have turned green, and at Haillicourt, nearby, one of them has been planted with vines, producing a wine with a cheeky name inspired by the coal. Further west, the hills of Artois become rural, with farms, small valleys and woods of beech and oak.

The riding improves as you head west. Around Auchel, expect urban roads, roundabouts and cobbles in some streets, with traffic in rush hour. But leave the coalfield behind and the roads start to roll over the hills, with gentle bends and views across the farmland toward the coast. Weather here changes fast, with Atlantic showers blowing in and clearing again, and the wind can be strong on the open plateaus. Watch for mud from tractors on the minor roads, especially in autumn when the beet harvest is on.

Auchel has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and the larger towns of Béthune and Bruay-la-Buissière offer more choice. The food is northern and filling: carbonnade, potjevleesch, tarte au maroilles, waffles and frites. A coffee in a local bar will often come with a little biscuit and an opinion on the weather. Before you leave, take a slow look at the cité, its brick facades and the small details that make each house different despite the uniform plan. Then head west into the hills, where the coalfield fades and the green begins.
t.beffroi de mons@50.5,4.0:
Belgium has many belfries, but only one in the baroque style, and it rises above Mons on the hill where the medieval castle stood. Built in the seventeenth century, it is about eighty-seven metres tall, with a carillon of forty-nine bells, and it was listed by UNESCO with the other belfries of Belgium and France. A lift takes visitors to the top, where the view stretches across the Borinage, the old coal-mining country around the city, and over the rooftops of the old town. Inside, an interpretation centre tells the story of the tower.

Mons is the capital of Hainaut, a city of about ninety thousand, lively and full of students. Every year, on Trinity Sunday, it celebrates the Doudou, a festival in which a reliquary of Saint Waltrude is carried through the streets, followed by the Lumeçon, a mock battle between Saint George and a dragon in the main square, watched by a dense crowd that tries to grab hairs from the dragon's tail for luck. The festival is recognised by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity. The city was also the scene of the first and last British battles of the First World War, in August 1914 and November 1918.

The riding around Mons is gentle, with the Borinage to the west, a landscape of former mining towns and slag heaps, and the Hainaut countryside to the east and south, with farms, forests and villages. Vincent van Gogh lived in the Borinage as a young preacher, and his house in Cuesmes can be visited. The roads are generally good, but cobbles appear in town centres, and the city's streets climb steeply to the belfry. Weather is changeable, with rain and wind.

Mons has filling stations, supermarkets and inns. Food here is Walloon, with stews, rabbit with prunes, fries and local beers, including those from the nearby Trappist abbeys. The Grand-Place is lined with cafés and restaurants, and on its town hall a small bronze monkey is rubbed for luck by passers-by. Climb the belfry on a clear day, look out over the Borinage, then come down and give the monkey a pat; it cannot hurt.
t.ancienne halle avec beffroi@51.0,4.5:
The Grote Markt of Mechelen is one of the grandest squares in Belgium, and on its eastern side stands the old cloth hall with its belfry, a building with a curious history. The hall was built in the fourteenth century, when Mechelen was a rich cloth-making town, and the belfry was planned to be a tall tower, but it was never finished. Its stump was eventually given a pointed roof, and later a sixteenth-century extension in the Renaissance style was begun to house the Great Council of the Netherlands, but that too remained unfinished. The belfry is part of the UNESCO listing of the belfries of Belgium and France.

Mechelen was for a time the capital of the Low Countries. In the early sixteenth century, Margaret of Austria, governor of the Netherlands, held her court here and raised the young Charles V, the future emperor, in her palace. Her court attracted artists, musicians and scholars, and the city still has many buildings from that golden age. The tower of St Rumbold's cathedral, nearly a hundred metres tall, dominates the city, and it houses a famous carillon; Mechelen has a renowned school for carillon players, the oldest in the world.

The riding here is about getting in and out. Mechelen sits between Brussels and Antwerp, surrounded by busy motorways and ring roads, and the centre has pedestrian zones and cobbles. The surrounding countryside is flat, with fields, canals and villages, and the roads along the rivers Dijle and Nete are pleasant, with dykes and willows. Traffic around the city can be heavy. Weather is changeable, with rain and wind.

Mechelen has fuel, shops, restaurants and cafés. Local specialities include Mechelse koekoek, a breed of chicken, asparagus from the area in spring, and beer from the Het Anker brewery, which brews in a former béguinage building, including the strong Gouden Carolus, named after Charles V. The Grote Markt is lined with cafés, and a drink on a terrace facing the cloth hall and the cathedral tower is a fine way to spend an hour. Look up at the unfinished buildings, and admire the city's habit of starting ambitious projects and then thinking better of them.
t.flemish beguinages@51.0,4.5:
In the thirteenth century, a remarkable movement spread across the Low Countries. Women, often unmarried or widowed, chose to live together in communities devoted to prayer and work, without taking the permanent vows of nuns, keeping their property and the freedom to leave. They were called béguines, and their walled settlements, the béguinages, became towns within towns. The Groot Begijnhof of Mechelen, the great béguinage, is one of thirteen in Flanders listed by UNESCO, and at its height it housed well over a thousand women, making it one of the largest communities of its kind.

The béguinage is a quiet district of narrow streets, small houses and courtyards, near the river Dijle. The baroque church of St Alexius and St Catherine stands at its heart, with a rich interior. Unlike some béguinages, which are enclosed and compact, the Mechelen one is open and spread out, blending into the surrounding city. The last béguines in Belgium died in the early twenty-first century, and the houses are now occupied by ordinary residents, but the atmosphere of calm and retreat remains. Mechelen also has a smaller béguinage, the Klein Begijnhof, near the city centre.

The riding in and around Mechelen is mostly urban, with ring roads, traffic lights and cobbles in the old streets. If you come from Brussels or Antwerp, the motorways are fast but dull; the old roads through villages and along canals are more interesting. Bonheiden, to the east, has woods and heaths, and the river valleys of the Dijle and Nete offer pleasant rides on dykes and quiet lanes. Watch for cyclists, who are everywhere and have priority in many places, and for trams in the city.

Mechelen has fuel and every service. Food in the city is good, with Belgian classics such as stews, mussels and fries, and a wide range of beers, including those of the Het Anker brewery, whose buildings stand on land that once belonged to the béguinage. Park the bike on the edge of the old town, walk to the béguinage, and wander its streets without a plan. Look at the small statues of saints above the doors and the names of the houses; each one was once home to a woman who chose an independent life in an age when that was not easy.
t.cite barrois@50.4,3.2:
Rows of red-brick cottages, each with its garden, set along curving streets with trees: the Cité Barrois in Pecquencourt looks almost English, and that is no accident. In the later years of the coal era, the mining companies of northern France built garden cities for their workers, influenced by ideas from across the Channel about healthy housing and green space. This one is part of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012 as an entire landscape of pits, slag heaps, workers' housing, schools, churches and railways spread over more than a hundred kilometres.

Pecquencourt lies between Douai and Valenciennes, in the valley of the Scarpe, a flat country of canals, poplars and old industrial towns. Just a few kilometres away in Lewarde, the former Delloye pit is now the Centre Historique Minier, the biggest mining museum in France, where former miners have guided visitors through reconstructed galleries. It is the best place to understand what life here was like: the shifts, the danger, the strikes, the waves of immigration from Poland, Italy and North Africa that built these communities.

Riding here is not about curves. The roads are flat, straight and often busy, with plenty of roundabouts, speed bumps and towns that blur into each other. What the area has instead is texture: the conical black slag heaps, the terrils, rising out of the fields; the headframes of old pits; the brick everywhere. Some of the terrils are now nature reserves, home to rare plants and birds that thrive on the warm, dry slopes. Cobblestone lanes, made famous by the Paris-Roubaix cycle race, still cross the countryside around Wallers and the Arenberg forest nearby. On a motorcycle they are bone-shaking and treacherous in the wet, so treat them with respect.

Pecquencourt has the basics, and Douai, a short ride west, is a handsome town with a famous Gothic belfry, plenty of cafés, and every service you need, including fuel. The weather is changeable: rain can arrive at any time of year, and wind blows unchecked across the flat land. Spring and late summer are the best seasons. Stop for a beer in a local café, ask about the pits, and you may well hear a story or two from someone whose grandfather worked underground.
t.hotel de ville@50.5,3.0:
A town hall makes an odd target for a ride, but Carvin's is a good excuse to stop in a place most people only see from the A1. The town sits on the northern edge of the old coalfield, between Lens and Lille, and its civic buildings and squares reflect the confidence of a community that grew with the mines. Like many such places, Carvin's centre is a mix of brick, stone and post-war rebuilding, and the town hall faces a square with cafés, bakeries and a market on certain days.

The history around here is heavy. Courrières, just a few kilometres south, gave its name to the worst mining disaster in European history: in March 1906 an explosion swept through the Courrières company's pits and killed more than a thousand miners. Rescuers came from Germany to help, and a group of survivors emerged after nearly three weeks underground, which made headlines across the world. The disaster led to strikes and reforms in French mining safety, and there are memorials in the towns around.

The landscape is the Mining Basin, now a UNESCO World Heritage site: terrils, workers' housing estates, headframes and railway lines threaded through farmland and towns. The slag heaps near Carvin and Oignies are some of the most distinctive in the area, and at Oignies the former 9-9bis pit has been turned into a cultural centre and concert venue. Riding past them is a reminder of how big this industry once was.

As for the riding, Carvin is a town stop, plain and simple. The roads in and out are flat and urban, with roundabouts, traffic lights and speed bumps, and the A1 motorway runs close by. Expect trucks and commuter traffic at peak hours. If you are looking for bends, you will need to head west towards the hills of Artois, where the terrain begins to rise around Notre-Dame-de-Lorette and Vimy.

Practically, Carvin has everything: fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants. It is a good place for a coffee and a sandwich, or for a plate of frites from a friterie, a northern tradition that locals take very seriously. Weather is changeable, so carry rain gear. Take a moment in the square, watch the town go by, and think about the generations of miners who built this place.
t.cite de la parisienne@50.4,2.9:
Drocourt is the sort of place you could ride through without a second glance, and you would miss a small piece of the story of northern France. The Cité de la Parisienne is a mining housing estate on the edge of the town, a grid of brick houses built by the coal company for its workers and their families, part of the UNESCO-listed Mining Basin. The name comes from the company that dug coal here. Hénin-Beaumont and Rouvroy press in on either side, and the black cones of the slag heaps rise above the rooftops.

These estates followed a pattern. The earliest were long rows of identical houses, the corons, built cheaply near the pit; later came semi-detached houses with gardens, then garden cities with curving streets, schools, churches and sometimes even a dispensary and a football pitch. The companies controlled almost every part of life, and the communities that grew up were tight-knit and proud, with strong traditions of brass bands, pigeon racing and allotment gardening that survive to this day.

Lens, a short ride west, is the heart of this world, and two things there are worth your time. The Louvre-Lens museum, a satellite of the Paris Louvre, opened in 2012 on the site of a former pit, a long, low glass and aluminium building with a remarkable gallery where art from many centuries is displayed side by side. And the Stade Bollaert, home of RC Lens, is a cathedral of football in a town where the club is close to a religion.

The riding is flat and urban for the most part, with heavy traffic around Hénin-Beaumont and the A1 and A21 motorways. Roundabouts, speed bumps and traffic lights are constant companions. Head west towards the Artois hills or south towards Arras, and the roads open up, with long views over farmland and gentle bends. Watch for slippery cobblestones in some town centres, and for wet leaves in autumn.

Hénin-Beaumont has all the services you need: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and fast food. The weather is fickle, so pack waterproofs. A stop here is about history rather than scenery, but if you have a little time, walk through the estate, look at the houses and gardens, and imagine the sound of the pit siren calling the next shift.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de barlin@50:
Barlin is where the coalfield starts to run into hills. To the west, the land rises gently into the Artois uplands, and the mining town sits at the transition, its slag heaps, workers' houses and pit buildings now part of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site. It is a quieter corner than Lens or Douai, and the mix of industrial history and rolling countryside makes it a pleasant place to pause.

The mining landscape here includes terrils, some of them now covered with trees, and estates of brick houses built for the miners. Neighbouring Hersin-Coupigny and Bruay-la-Buissière were also major mining towns, and Bruay has an old mining estate turned into a heritage area. The region's mining culture is still visible in small details: the pigeon lofts behind the houses, the brass band halls, the miners' monuments in the squares.

The great sights nearby belong to the First World War. Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, the largest French military cemetery, crowns a ridge a few kilometres to the southeast, with a basilica, a lantern tower and tens of thousands of graves. Next to it stands the Ring of Remembrance, a vast elliptical memorial opened in 2014 that lists the names of almost six hundred thousand soldiers of all nationalities who died in the region, alphabetically, without regard to rank or side. A little further on, the Canadian memorial at Vimy Ridge, with its twin white pylons, overlooks the plain of Douai.

The riding improves as you head towards these ridges. The roads climb and fall over the hills, with gentle bends, short climbs and views across farmland and the old coalfield. They are not mountain roads, but after the flat land around Lens they feel lively. Traffic is moderate, heavier on weekends near the memorials, and the weather is fickle: rain, wind and low cloud can roll in at any time, so pack waterproofs and expect damp roads.

Barlin has a supermarket, a few cafés and bakeries; for a broader choice and reliable fuel, Bruay-la-Buissière and Béthune are close. The local friteries are a good bet for a quick lunch. Take a moment on the ridges, look out over the countryside, and you will see both the scars of war and the marks of industry spread out below you.
t.notre dame cathedral in tournai@50.6,3.4:
Five towers. That is what everyone remembers about Tournai's cathedral, and when you first see them rising above the rooftops of this old city on the Scheldt, they seem almost too many for one building. The cathedral of Notre-Dame is one of the great churches of Europe, with a massive Romanesque nave and transept from the twelfth century and a later Gothic choir, tall and light, built in the following century. The combination is a lesson in medieval architecture, and it earned the building a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list. It has been under long restoration after a storm in 1999 damaged the structure, so parts may be covered in scaffolding when you visit.

Tournai is one of the oldest cities in Belgium. It was a Roman settlement and later an early capital of the Franks; in 1653 workers digging near the church of Saint-Brice found the tomb of King Childeric, father of Clovis, with treasures including golden bees that Napoleon later adopted as a symbol. The city's belfry, the oldest in the country, is also listed, and the Pont des Trous, a medieval gateway bridge over the Scheldt, is a striking sight, though it was rebuilt in recent years to let larger barges pass.

The old town rewards a walk: the Grand-Place with its terraces, the narrow streets around the cathedral, the river quays. Tournai has a long tradition of tapestry weaving and stone carving, and there is a museum devoted to tapestry.

Riding into Tournai, expect city traffic, cobblestones in the centre and one-way streets. Park outside the core if you can and walk. Around the city, the land is mostly flat to gently rolling, with farmland and small villages. To the south and east, the Mont-Saint-Aubert rises above the plain, a modest hill with a road to the top and a view over the city. Heading west into France or north into Flanders, the roads are straight and fast, with roundabouts and towns.

Tournai has everything you need, including fuel, cafés and restaurants. Try a local beer at a café on the Grand-Place, with the five towers looming overhead. Flemish skies being what they are, keep the waterproofs on top of the luggage.
t.beguinage de kortrijk@50.8,3.3:
Step through a gate off a busy street in the centre of Kortrijk and the noise falls away. The béguinage is a tiny enclosed village of whitewashed houses, cobbled lanes and a small church, founded in the thirteenth century by Countess Joan of Constantinople for the beguines, lay women who lived a religious life without taking full vows. It is one of the Flemish béguinages that UNESCO listed together in 1998, and although it is small, it has a rare atmosphere of calm. A statue of the countess stands at the entrance.

Kortrijk is a city with a big story. In 1302, on the fields just outside the walls, an army of Flemish townsmen and craftsmen defeated the flower of French knighthood in the Battle of the Golden Spurs, named after the spurs collected from fallen knights and hung in a church. The date is still celebrated as the Flemish community holiday, and there is a museum in the city dedicated to the battle. Kortrijk was also badly damaged in both world wars, and much of its centre was rebuilt.

The Leie river runs through town, with the medieval Broel towers guarding an old bridge, and the riverbanks have been redesigned into a pleasant walking area. The Grote Markt, with its belfry and town hall, is lined with cafés.

Riding here is about the towns rather than the roads. Flanders is flat, and the roads are busy, with cyclists everywhere; bike lanes are part of the road system, and drivers here expect you to give cyclists room. South of the city, the land begins to rise into the Flemish Ardennes around Oudenaarde and Ronse, with short, steep cobbled climbs famous from the Tour of Flanders cycle race. On a motorcycle they are fun but slippery when wet, and narrow. The landscape is green and rolling, with farms and small villages.

Kortrijk has all the services you need, including fuel, supermarkets and many restaurants. Try the local beer, and look out for Flemish dishes such as stoverij, beef stewed in beer, served with fries. Showers come in off the North Sea with little warning. Visit the béguinage early in the day, when it is quiet, and let the city wait for a while.
t.beffroi de l eglise st eloi de dunkerque:
The belfry of Saint-Éloi stands alone, which is odd for a church tower. It was originally attached to the church, but after fires and rebuilding in earlier centuries, a street was cut between them, and the tower became a separate landmark. Today it is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO, and its carillon plays tunes across the centre of Dunkirk, including a local song. You can climb to the top for views over the port, the city and the North Sea.

Dunkirk's name is known around the world for the events of May and June 1940, when more than three hundred thousand Allied soldiers were evacuated from the beaches and harbour under fire, in Operation Dynamo. Ships of all sizes, including fishing boats and pleasure craft from England, crossed the Channel to rescue them. The city was badly damaged during the war, and much of the centre was rebuilt afterwards. The Dynamo museum tells the story, and the beach at Malo-les-Bains, with its long promenade and villas, is a place to reflect on what happened there.

Dunkirk also has one of the liveliest carnivals in France. For weeks before Lent, crowds in fancy dress, many men dressed as women, parade through the streets singing, and at the climax the mayor throws smoked herrings from the balcony of the town hall to the crowd below. It is loud, wet and joyful.

The riding around Dunkirk is flat and open, with the wind blowing straight off the sea. The roads are straight and often busy, with heavy traffic around the port and industrial zones. Inland, the countryside of French Flanders is a patchwork of fields, canals and villages with Flemish names. To the south, the Monts de Flandre, a line of small hills including Mont Cassel, rise above the plain, with winding roads and views; Cassel, a hilltop town with a windmill, is a lovely stop. Further along the coast, Bergues, with its walls and belfry, is worth a visit.

Dunkirk has fuel, supermarkets and many restaurants. Try the local specialties: potjevleesch, a cold terrine of meats in jelly, or moules-frites, washed down with a local beer. The wind here never seems to stop, and rain blows in off the Channel at short notice. Climb the belfry on a clear day, and you may see the white cliffs of England on the horizon.
t.stadshal met belfort@51.1,2.8:
Nieuwpoort's cloth hall and belfry look medieval, and in a sense they are: they follow the design of the thirteenth-century originals. But almost everything you see was rebuilt after the First World War, when the town was reduced to rubble. Nieuwpoort lay at the northern end of the Western Front, where the River Yser reaches the sea, and in October 1914 the Belgians made a decision that changed the course of the war. By opening the sluices of the canals and the river at high tide, they flooded the low-lying land between Nieuwpoort and Diksmuide, creating a barrier of water that stopped the German advance. The front line stayed there for four years, and the town was shelled into ruins. The belfry is part of the UNESCO listing of belfries of Belgium and France.

The sluices are still there, at a complex of waterways known as the Ganzepoot, the goose foot, and next to them stands the King Albert I Monument, a circular memorial to the king who led the Belgian army during the war. You can climb to the top for views over the waterways, the town and the polders where the flooding took place. A visitor centre underneath tells the story.

Modern Nieuwpoort is a seaside resort with a large marina, a fishing harbour and a long beach. Its fish market is famous, and restaurants along the harbour serve shrimp, mussels and fish fresh from the boats. The coast tram, one of the longest tram lines in the world, runs along the entire Belgian coast and passes through the town.

The riding along the coast is flat and often busy, especially in summer, with heavy traffic, cyclists and pedestrians. The coastal road runs through a series of resorts, with apartment blocks, shops and roundabouts. Inland, the polders are quieter, with straight roads, canals and farmland, and the Westhoek region, with its war cemeteries and memorials, lies to the south. Ypres, with its Menin Gate, is less than an hour away.

Nieuwpoort has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants and cafés. Try grey shrimp, peeled by hand and served stuffed into a tomato or folded into croquettes, a specialty of the Belgian coast. The wind off the sea can be fierce, and the weather changes quickly. Stand on the monument, look out over the polders, and imagine the floodwaters that saved a corner of Belgium.
t.the four lifts on the canal du centre an:
Picture a barge sitting in a huge iron tank full of water, rising more than fifteen metres into the air while another tank, counterweighted, sinks beside it. That is what happens at the four hydraulic boat lifts on the old Canal du Centre in Hainaut, built between the 1880s and 1917 to carry boats over a steep change in level between the basins of the Meuse and the Scheldt. They were engineering marvels in their day, cast-iron and steel giants powered by water pressure, and they are still in working order, though now mostly used by pleasure boats. UNESCO listed them, along with their surroundings, in 1998.

The lifts sit along a few kilometres of canal between La Louvière and Thieu, and the towpath beside them makes a lovely walk or short ride past locks, bridges and old industrial buildings. Boat trips run in summer, so you can experience the climb yourself. A short distance away stands the Strépy-Thieu boat lift, completed in 2002 on the new canal, a colossal concrete structure that lifts large barges over seventy metres in one go. Its scale is staggering, and there is a visitor area with views over the countryside.

This was the industrial heart of Wallonia, with coal mines, steelworks and factories, and the landscape still carries the marks: slag heaps, workers' housing, railway lines. Bois-du-Luc, near La Louvière, is a remarkably complete mining village, part of the UNESCO site of the Major Mining Sites of Wallonia. Nearby Binche is famous for its carnival, when the Gilles, in wax masks and ostrich-feather hats, dance through the streets throwing oranges.

The riding around here is mostly urban and suburban, with busy roads, roundabouts and traffic lights around La Louvière and Mons. Away from the towns, the countryside is gently rolling, with fields and small villages, and the roads become quieter and more pleasant. Cobbles appear in some village centres, slippery when wet. To the south, the Ardennes are a couple of hours away, with the best riding in Belgium.

La Louvière has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try a local beer or a plate of frites from a friterie. The weather is changeable, with rain likely at any time of year. Arrive in time to see a lift in operation; it is a strangely mesmerising sight.
t.stadhuis met belfort@50.8,3.6:
Oudenaarde's town hall looks like something carved from lace. Built in the early sixteenth century in the late Gothic style, it has a facade covered with pointed arches, niches and statues, and a slender belfry topped with a gilded crown on which stands a small knight known locally as Hanske de Krijger, Little John the Warrior. The building is one of the finest of its kind in Flanders, and it is listed by UNESCO among the belfries of Belgium and France. Inside, there are displays of the tapestries for which Oudenaarde was famous across Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, especially its verdures, woven scenes of forests and greenery.

Oudenaarde sits on the River Scheldt, in the heart of the Flemish Ardennes, and it has had its share of history. In 1708, during the War of the Spanish Succession, the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated a French army in a great battle just outside the town. Today, though, Oudenaarde is best known as the home of the Tour of Flanders, one of the great classics of cycle racing. The Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen, a museum devoted to the race, stands near the market square, and the finish line is close by.

The hills around town are where the race is won and lost: short, steep climbs, many of them cobbled, with names that every cycling fan knows, the Oude Kwaremont, the Paterberg, the Koppenberg. On a motorcycle, they are an interesting challenge, steep and slippery when wet, with rough stones and narrow lanes. Respect the cyclists who come from all over the world to ride them; they have priority in spirit if not in law.

The riding in the Flemish Ardennes is pleasant, with rolling hills, green fields, woods and villages, on narrow roads with many bends. Traffic is moderate, but cyclists are everywhere, especially at weekends. Further south, towards Ronse and the French border, the hills continue, with good views.

Oudenaarde has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants. Try the local brown beer, Oudenaards bruin, a sour-sweet ale brewed in the town for centuries. The market square is lined with terraces, and on a sunny day it is a lovely place to sit. Showers sweep in regularly, so keep a waterproof handy.
t.historic centre of brugge@51.2,3.2:
Bruges was once one of the richest cities in northern Europe, a trading hub where merchants from Italy, Germany, England and Spain bought and sold wool, cloth, spices and luxury goods. Its wealth came from its access to the sea through an inlet called the Zwin, and when that silted up in the fifteenth century, trade moved to Antwerp and Bruges slowly fell asleep. For centuries it was a quiet, poor town, and that is why its medieval centre survived almost intact. In the nineteenth century, writers and painters rediscovered it, and Georges Rodenbach's novel Bruges-la-Morte made it famous as a melancholy city of canals and bells. The historic centre was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

Today Bruges is one of the most visited cities in Europe, and in summer the streets can be packed. But early in the morning or late in the evening, the canals, bridges and gabled houses are magical. The Markt is dominated by the belfry, which you can climb, 366 steps to the top, for views over the rooftops. Nearby, the Burg square has the Gothic town hall and the Basilica of the Holy Blood, which houses a relic said to contain drops of Christ's blood. The Church of Our Lady holds a marble Madonna and Child by Michelangelo, one of the few works by him to leave Italy in his lifetime. The museums are full of Flemish masters, Van Eyck and Memling among them.

Riding into Bruges is not recommended. The centre is a maze of narrow, cobbled, one-way streets, many of them restricted to local traffic, and the traffic plan is designed to keep through traffic out. Park outside the ring road, where there are large car parks, and walk or cycle in. The city is compact, and everything is within easy walking distance.

The countryside around Bruges is flat, with canals, polders and farmland, and the roads are straight and often busy. The coast is only a short ride to the north, with the resort of Knokke-Heist and the Zwin nature reserve, now a haven for birds. Damme, a small town on the canal north of Bruges, is a pleasant stop.

Bruges has fuel on the outskirts, and food everywhere: chocolate, waffles, beer and mussels. Try a local beer in one of the old cafés. The North Sea weather is changeable, with rain and wind common.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers d auchy les:
Flat country hides its stories well, and the strip of land around Vendin-le-Vieil, Pont-à-Vendin and Annay looks at first like any other piece of French Flanders suburbia: rows of brick houses, a canal, a few fields, a tangle of roads. Look again and the pattern reveals itself. The terraced streets are company housing, laid out by mining firms for their workers, and the low hills on the horizon are not hills at all but spoil heaps from the pits that once ran under this ground. The whole Nord-Pas de Calais coal basin was listed by UNESCO in 2012 as a living cultural landscape, and the area around Auchy-les-Mines and its neighbours is part of that long chain of pits, cités and terrils stretching across the north of France.

What makes it worth a stop is the human scale. These were not anonymous suburbs but whole communities built around the shaft: housing, schools, churches, allotments and the pithead, all owned by the company. Families lived here for generations, and the culture that grew up, from pigeon racing to brass bands to the local Picard dialect, still colours the region. The pits closed in the second half of the twentieth century, the last in the basin in 1990, and the towns have been working out what to become ever since.

The riding is honest rather than dramatic. Roads are mostly flat and straight, threading between towns with roundabouts, speed bumps and traffic lights, and the Canal de la Deûle near Pont-à-Vendin adds a little water to the view. Cobbled stretches still turn up on old streets, and they get slippery in the rain that blows in so often from the Channel. The wind across this open country can be strong, especially on the bigger roads, so expect a bit of buffeting. The light is at its best in the long evenings of early summer, when the brick glows warm and the terrils throw long shadows.

As a pause, this area is easy. Vendin-le-Vieil and the larger towns nearby have fuel, bakeries, cafés and supermarkets, and in this part of France a friterie is never far away. Order frites with a sauce of your choice and a local beer if you are not riding on, sit on a bench and watch the street. It is not a postcard, and it does not pretend to be one, but it tells you more about how ordinary people built modern Europe than most cathedrals do.
t.terrils jumeaux 28@50.5,2.6:
Two near-perfect black cones rise from the farmland between Ruitz, Maisnil-lès-Ruitz and Haillicourt, and once you have spotted them you will keep seeing them for miles. These twin terrils, the spoil heaps of former coal pits, are among the tallest in the Nord-Pas de Calais basin and have become something of a regional emblem. They look volcanic, which in a way they are: shale and waste rock tipped there for decades by the mining companies, slowly settling into steep, smooth pyramids that turn purple-grey in rain and almost silver in bright sun.

What fascinates naturalists is how quickly nature moved back in. The dark surfaces heat up in summer far more than the surrounding fields, creating a warm, dry microclimate where plants and insects normally found much further south can survive. Birch, buddleia and pioneer grasses colonise the lower slopes, and some heaps even host rare lizards and orchids. Many terrils in the basin are now protected green spaces, crossed by walking paths and occasionally used for sport, and they belong to the mining landscape listed by UNESCO in 2012.

The roads around here roll a little more than in the flatter east of the basin, because you are on the edge of the Artois hills. Lanes run between small towns and big open fields of wheat, beet and potatoes, with modest climbs and a few genuinely enjoyable bends heading west toward the higher ground. Surfaces are generally good, but farm traffic leaves mud on the road in harvest season, and cobbles survive in some town centres. Wind is the constant companion in this open country. The best views of the twins come from a few kilometres out, from the west or south, when the low sun catches their flanks.

For the practical side, Haillicourt and the neighbouring towns of Bruay-la-Buissière and Barlin have fuel, bakeries, supermarkets and the inevitable friteries. There is no café on top of a terril, of course, and climbing these steep heaps is often forbidden for safety reasons, so look for marked paths rather than scrambling. Take a slow loop around them instead, stop somewhere on a farm track with the engine off, and listen to the larks over the fields. It is a strange pleasure, admiring a pile of mining waste, but these two have earned it.
t.fosse n 2 de flines@50.4,3.2:
The headframe is the giveaway. In the low, watery country between Lallaing, Anhiers and Flines-lez-Raches, the steel or concrete winding towers of old coal pits still stand as markers, and Fosse n°2 de Flines is one of the sites that recall the industry that shaped this corner of the Douai area. A fosse in the local vocabulary is a pit with its shafts, buildings and spoil heap, and around each one a small world grew: rows of brick housing, a church, a school, and the company offices that ran the lives of everyone underground and above it.

This eastern part of the Nord-Pas de Calais basin is different from the Artois hills further west. It is flat, wet and green, laced with drainage ditches, ponds and the Scarpe river, and parts of the land sank as coal was taken out beneath it, so marshes and lakes formed where there were none before. Some of these subsidence ponds are now nature reserves full of herons, coots and reed warblers. Mining, in other words, did not just leave scars; it rearranged the water, and the landscape is still adjusting.

Riding here is calm, low-gradient work. The roads link villages and towns in short straight sections, crossing canals and railway lines, with roundabouts at every turn and speed humps in residential streets. You will find patches of old pavé in some places, which can be treacherous after rain. The Scarpe valley toward Marchiennes and the forest of Marchiennes add a bit of shade and a softer feel, and the north side of the area drifts toward the forested country around Saint-Amand. Morning mist over the ponds in autumn can be beautiful, though it can also hang on longer than you would like.

Lallaing and Flines-lez-Raches are sizeable enough for fuel stations, bakeries and small supermarkets, and Douai, a short ride away, has the full range of cafés and restaurants as well as one of the finest belfries in the region. Take a break here to walk around the pit site and the nearby cités, look at the details of the housing, the gardens and the brickwork, and imagine the noise and dust of a working shaft. The quiet that has replaced it is pleasant enough, but it is a quiet with a lot of memory folded into it.
t.terril 125a@50.3,3.2:
On the southern edge of the coal basin, where Auberchicourt, Écaillon and Aniche run into one another, a long spoil heap rises above the brick roofs and the fields. Terril 125a is one of the many numbered heaps that the Nord-Pas de Calais inventory catalogues, and it belongs to the old concession of the Compagnie des mines d'Aniche, one of the historic coal companies of the region. Aniche itself is a reminder that the north was not only about coal: the town had a long glassmaking tradition, and the combination of fuel, sand and labour made the area an industrial hub well before the twentieth century.

Many terrils around here have been greened and opened to walkers. Birch and willow have taken root on the slopes, and paths lead up to viewpoints from which you can see across to Douai and the plain stretching toward Cambrai. In summer the black shale soaks up heat and makes a little island of warmth; on a cold day the wind up top is sharp. Some heaps were partly quarried away after the pits closed, their material reused in road building, so the profiles you see today are not always the original ones.

For riders, this is the gentler, greener side of the basin. Head south and the country quickly turns into the open farmland of the Ostrevent and the Cambrésis, with long straight roads, slight undulations and big skies. Toward the east, the Scarpe and Escaut valleys bring water and trees. Expect plenty of roundabouts and village speed limits, occasional cobbled streets and farm traffic in summer, and keep an eye out for mud near field entrances after harvest. The wind can push hard across these open plains, especially on the higher, straighter stretches.

Aniche, with around ten thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, and Douai is close if you want more choice for lunch. If you are curious about the industrial past, the Centre Historique Minier at Lewarde lies a short ride to the west and gives the most complete picture of mining life in the region. Otherwise, park up near the foot of the terril, walk the first section of the path for a view, and enjoy a quiet corner of northern France that rarely sees a visitor on a motorcycle.
t.fosse n 5@50.5,2.9:
Douvrin, Billy-Berclau and Wingles form a little triangle of brick towns at the northern edge of the Lens coalfield, and the old pit known as Fosse n°5 sits among them. It is not a famous site and does not need to be: its value lies in being one of the many pieces that make up the mining landscape UNESCO listed in 2012, a network of pits, housing estates, slag heaps, railways and public buildings stretching for over a hundred kilometres across the north of France. Seen from the saddle, the area is a patchwork of cités, fields, canals and newer industrial estates, with the occasional terril breaking the skyline.

The history here is about people as much as coal. Workers came from all over, first from the French countryside and Belgium, later from Poland, Italy and North Africa, and the mining towns became some of the most diverse places in France. Polish churches, Italian surnames and couscous on the menu at local cafés are part of that story. The pits gave work and shelter but also brought disasters, strikes and silicosis, and the communal memory of all that is still strong.

The roads around Douvrin are flat and practical. The Canal d'Aire runs close by, and following it gives you long, easy stretches with water on one side and old industrial buildings on the other. Elsewhere, expect towns blending into each other, roundabouts every few hundred metres, and the A21 and the N47 carrying heavy traffic. Old cobbles remain in places, and the cité streets often have speed humps and parked cars on both sides. It is not a region for knee-down riding; it is a region for reading the landscape at a moderate pace. Evening light is kind to the brick, and a dry day makes all the difference here.

Douvrin, Wingles and nearby La Bassée have fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, and Lens, with its striking Louvre-Lens museum built on a former pit site, is a short hop to the south. A coffee and a croissant at a local bar, a look at the pit buildings and the surrounding housing, and you will have absorbed more of the basin's character than any guidebook could give you. Ask an older local about the mine, and you may well get a story worth hearing.
t.terril 32@50.6,2.3:
Out on the western fringe of the coal basin, where the mining country fades into the farmland of the Lys valley and the edge of the Artois hills, Terril 32 rises near Norrent-Fontes, Mametz and Thérouanne. This is the far end of the seam, a long way from the dense cités around Lens and Douai, and the countryside feels it: smaller villages, more fields, more trees, and pits that were fewer and further between. The heap stands almost like a lone hill above the cropland, a reminder that coal reached even here.

Thérouanne, just down the road, offers one of history's harsher lessons. It was once a bishop's seat with a cathedral, but in 1553 the Emperor Charles V had the town besieged and then razed to the ground, ordering it effectively erased from the map after its capture. Today it is a quiet village, and archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of the lost cathedral. Aire-sur-la-Lys, a little further north, is the place to see what a prosperous small town of this region looks like, with a fine Renaissance building on the square and a belfry on the UNESCO list.

The riding improves noticeably once you leave the mining towns behind. The lanes west and south of Norrent-Fontes start to climb gently into the Artois, with fields rolling away on both sides, small woods, and a few corners that actually reward some lean. Surfaces are mostly decent but narrow, with farm machinery and the odd tractor coming the other way, and gravel can collect on bends after rain. The wind is less of a nuisance here than out on the open plain, and spring brings rapeseed in yellow blocks, while late summer smells of cut wheat and dust.

Food choices are better in Aire too, with cafés around the main square. If you just want a break, pull off on a farm track with a view of the heap, switch off and enjoy the stillness. It is a peaceful place, and the contrast between the black cone and the green fields is oddly beautiful.
t.ensemble minier de la belleforiere@50.4,:
Roost-Warendin, Waziers and Râches sit just north of Douai, where the old Scarpe floodplain met the coal seams, and the Belleforière mining ensemble is one of the clusters that shows how a pit site was organised. Shafts, buildings, workers' housing and spoil heaps were laid out together, with the railway linking them all, and in a few places the ensemble survives well enough that you can read it on the ground. Part of the regional mining landscape listed by UNESCO in 2012, it is a good example of how coal companies planned whole villages around their extraction.

The countryside is damp and green. Before the mines, these were wetlands and woods; after them, subsidence created new ponds and marshes, and some former industrial land has been handed back to nature. You will see herons stalking the ditches, poplars lining the canals, and a lot of sky reflected in water. In late autumn the fog can settle in thick, and in summer the reeds hum with insects. The contrast between the brick terraces and this soft, wet landscape is part of the charm.

The road network is dense and slow, as it is throughout the urban part of the basin. You will move through a series of towns with roundabouts, traffic lights, speed bumps and parked cars, and a few cobbled stretches that are lethal in the rain. Head east toward the forests of Marchiennes and Saint-Amand for a greener ride with shaded straights and a few easy bends, or south into Douai for the city and its tall Gothic belfry. Traffic thins out on Sunday mornings, which is the best time to see the cités without competing with lorries.

Roost-Warendin and Waziers both have fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, and Douai offers cafés, brasseries and the full town experience a few minutes away. Walk a little way into the housing estates to notice how the company designs varied over the decades, from long uniform terraces to semi-detached houses with gardens, an evolution that reflects changing ideas about workers' welfare. Then pick a bar, order a coffee or a Picard beer for later, and enjoy the quiet rhythm of a place that has had more than its share of hard work.
t.dutch water defence lines@52.6,4.8:
Forget mountains and passes: the Dutch defended Amsterdam with water. Between the 1880s and the 1920s, the army built a ring of forts around the capital at a distance of roughly fifteen to twenty kilometres, the Stelling van Amsterdam, designed to flood the surrounding polders to a depth too shallow for boats but too deep to wade through. Forty-odd forts, along with dykes, sluices and batteries, formed the ring, and the area north of the city near De Rijp and the Beemster was part of it. The Defence Line of Amsterdam gained World Heritage status in 1996, and in 2021 it was extended to include the older New Dutch Waterline further south, the whole now known as the Dutch Water Defence Lines.

The forts are low, grassy mounds with concrete walls, often surrounded by moats, and they blend into the landscape so well that you can ride past one without noticing. They were built just as military technology was changing fast, and by the time the system was completed, aircraft had made it largely obsolete. It was never tested in battle. Today many forts have been converted into museums, restaurants, art spaces and nature reserves, and the moats are home to waterfowl.

The landscape around De Rijp is classic North Holland: flat polders crossed by straight canals and dykes, black-and-white cattle, windmills and wide skies full of clouds. De Rijp itself is a charming little town with wooden houses and a past built on whaling and herring fishing. The Beemster polder, drained in the early seventeenth century, is a UNESCO site in its own right, with its geometric grid of roads and ditches. Riding here means straight roads, tight bends on dykes, narrow lanes, and the constant presence of cyclists, who have priority and know it. Wind is the main challenge, and it can blow hard across the open polders.

De Rijp has a few cafés and shops, and larger towns such as Uitgeest, Purmerend or Alkmaar offer fuel and every other service. Local specialities include Beemster cheese, herring and apple pie. Take a short walk around one of the forts to see how the moats and earthworks fit together, then ride the dykes back toward De Rijp for a coffee by the water. It is gentle, open country, and on a sunny day with a light breeze, it is a joy.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers d escaudain@:
Escaudain sits in the old heartland of the Compagnie des mines d'Anzin, the oldest and once the most powerful of the coal companies in northern France, and the landscape around it is pure mining country: rows of brick terraces, spoil heaps, old railway embankments and the occasional headframe standing like a monument. This is the Valenciennes end of the coalfield, close to the Belgian border, and it was here that coal mining in the north began in the eighteenth century. The town and its surroundings form one of the many components of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin, which UNESCO inscribed in 2012 as an evolving cultural landscape.

The area inspired one of the great novels of the nineteenth century. Émile Zola came to the Anzin region in 1884 during a miners' strike, and the experience fed directly into Germinal, his powerful novel about the lives and struggles of coal miners. The film adaptation of 1993 was shot at the former mine of Arenberg at Wallers, a short ride to the north, whose headframes and buildings now house a centre for image and media. Arenberg is also famous among cyclists for the Trouée d'Arenberg, the brutal cobbled section through the forest that features in the Paris-Roubaix race.

Riding in this area is honest work rather than pleasure. The roads link the mining towns, with many roundabouts, traffic lights and speed bumps, and the traffic around Denain and Valenciennes can be heavy. Cobbles appear in the old streets, and they are slippery in the rain. But the forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers, to the north, offers a pleasant change, with straight roads through the trees and small ponds formed by mining subsidence. The Arenberg cobbles themselves are for walking and cycling, so admire them on foot and spare your fillings.

Escaudain is a working town of about nine thousand people with fuel, bakeries, cafés and supermarkets, and Denain and Valenciennes have more services. Try a plate of frites from a local friterie, or a carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, a classic of the north. Visit Arenberg, take a look at the headframes, and imagine the scenes Zola described. It is a landscape of hard labour and deep pride, and the people here are warm and welcoming.
t.cites de guesnain@50.3,3.2:
A kilometre down the road from the workers' housing of Guesnain stands the best place in France to understand what coal really meant. The Centre Historique Minier at Lewarde occupies the old Delloye pit, which closed in 1971, and it walks you through the whole life of a mine: the lamp room, the showers where miners hung their clothes on chains up to the ceiling, the stables for the pit ponies, and a reconstructed gallery underground where you hear the noise of the picks and the creak of the props. Come here first, and every terrace and terril you pass afterwards will make more sense.

Guesnain's own cités tell the story in brick. The mining companies built housing in successive styles: the early corons, long monotonous rows of identical houses fronting the street, then the cités pavillonnaires with pairs of houses set in gardens, and later the garden cities with curving streets, trees and a more generous layout, a shift driven partly by paternalism and partly by the need to attract and keep workers. Here near Douai, all the patterns sit close together, and the estates are among the components of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin on the UNESCO list since 2012. Look for the details: the outhouses at the end of the gardens, the numbering on the doors, the communal ovens and the little chapels.

The riding is gentle and slow, through towns that blend into each other and farmland between them. Douai, a short ride north, has a magnificent Gothic belfry with a carillon, also on the UNESCO list, and the roads south toward the Ostrevent and the Scarpe valley open up into wider fields with long straights. Expect roundabouts, speed humps and pavé on old streets, and remember that rain turns those cobbles into ice. Wind can be strong across the open plain, and grey skies are the norm rather than the exception, though a sunny evening makes the brick glow.

Sin-le-Noble, about two kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and Douai has cafés, brasseries and restaurants of every kind. The museum itself has somewhere to eat, and the local food is northern comfort fare: carbonnade, potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, and maroilles, a pungent cheese. Allow a couple of hours for the museum, then ride slowly through Guesnain to see the estates with fresh eyes.
t.terril 14@50.5,2.5:
Auchel lies on the western rim of the coalfield, where the black seams run out against the chalk hills of the Artois, and Terril 14 rises above the town and its neighbour Marles-les-Mines as a long, dark ridge softened by birch and grass. The heap is built of shale and waste rock brought up from the pits of the old company that worked this corner of the basin, and like many of the terrils, it has been left to nature since mining ended. Its slopes are now home to plants that love warm, dry ground, and the summit offers a view over the rooftops of the mining towns toward the green hills to the west. It belongs to the vast mining landscape listed by UNESCO in 2012.

Auchel and Marles were classic mining towns, built almost entirely around the pits, with rows of company housing, churches, schools and football grounds. Football, in fact, is part of the story: the mining towns of the north produced generations of footballers, and the passion for RC Lens, the club of the coalfield, runs deep across the region. The miners' culture also included pigeon racing, brass bands, and the ducasse, the local fair held each year in every town.

The riding gets more interesting here than in the flatter east of the basin. West of Auchel, the land rises into the Artois hills, with the valley of the Clarence and the forests around Olhain offering winding roads, gentle climbs and real corners. The roads toward Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise and the upper valleys are quiet and pleasant, running through fields, woods and small villages with flint and brick churches. Surfaces are generally decent, but farm traffic and mud are common, and cobbles appear in town centres. The light in the Artois is lovely in late afternoon, when the low sun picks out the folds of the hills.
