Auchel is a town of over ten thousand people with fuel, bakeries, cafés and supermarkets, and Marles-les-Mines and Lillers are close by. Grab a sandwich américain, a baguette stuffed with a burger and frites, if you want to eat like a local, or a coffee and a pastry if you prefer something lighter. Take a short walk up the terril if a path is open, look out over the towns and the hills, and then head west into the Artois for some of the best riding in the region.
t.terril 244@50.6,2.3:
Way out at the western tip of the coalfield, near the villages of Mametz and Norrent-Fontes, Terril 244 marks the place where coal mining reached its limit. Beyond it, the land belongs to farmers, and the next towns, Aire-sur-la-Lys and Saint-Omer, have more to do with canals, marshes and markets than with mines. The heap stands as a solitary landmark in the fields, smaller than the giants further east, and its green-covered slopes blend into the landscape. It is one of the outlying components of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin listed by UNESCO, a reminder that the coalfield stretched for over a hundred kilometres from the Belgian border to here.

The country to the north is quite different. Saint-Omer, a historic town with a fine cathedral, sits beside the Audomarois marshes, a maze of canals and cultivated plots where farmers once moved vegetables by flat-bottomed boat, and some still do. The marshes are a UNESCO biosphere reserve and a haven for birds. Arques, next to Saint-Omer, is home to one of the world's largest glassworks, and the canal of Neufossé links the Lys with the Aa, part of the old waterway network of Flanders.

The riding west of the mining country is quiet and enjoyable. The roads from Mametz toward the Artois hills climb gently through fields and woods, with some real corners and pleasant views. Northward, the land flattens toward the marshes and the Flanders plain, with long straight roads and canals. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light outside the towns, and the main hazards are tractors and mud in harvest season. Wind across the open fields can be strong, and rain comes often, so a dry day is a gift. Late summer, with the wheat golden and the sky big, is a fine time to ride.

The villages near the terril are small, with few services, so plan to refuel in Aire-sur-la-Lys, about nine kilometres away, or in Saint-Omer. Aire has cafés and restaurants around its grand square, with its Renaissance bailiwick building and belfry. Try a waterzooi, a creamy fish or chicken stew from Flanders, or simply a coffee with a slice of tarte au sucre, a sugar tart of the north. Pause by the terril, then ride into the marshes or the hills, depending on your mood.
t.monument aux morts@50.5,2.5:
In the centre of Auchel, the war memorial stands as it does in every French town and village, listing the names of the men who died in the First and Second World Wars, and in mining towns these lists are often heartbreakingly long. But the memorials of the coalfield have a particular resonance, because the front line of the First World War ran through the edge of the mining basin, only a few kilometres east of here. The Germans occupied Lens and the eastern pits for most of the war, and when they withdrew in 1918, they flooded and sabotaged the mines, which took years to restore. Auchel and the western towns, on the Allied side, kept producing coal for the war effort under constant pressure.

The battlefields of Artois lie close by. The ridge of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, about twenty kilometres to the east, holds the largest French military cemetery, with tens of thousands of graves, and next to it the Ring of Remembrance, inaugurated in 2014, lists the names of nearly six hundred thousand soldiers of all nations who died in the region, alphabetically and without distinction of nationality or rank. Vimy Ridge, a little further on, has the towering Canadian memorial, honouring the Canadian soldiers who took the ridge in April 1917.

The riding from Auchel toward the battlefields is a mix of mining towns and open country. The roads east pass through Bruay-la-Buissière and Barlin before climbing onto the Lorette ridge, with views over the plain of Lens and the terrils on the horizon. The roads around Vimy and Souchez are quiet, with gentle curves and good surfaces, and the cemeteries and memorials appear constantly, a solemn landscape. Weather in the region is often grey, with rain and wind, and the ridge can be cold even in summer. Riding slowly is the only proper way here.

Auchel has fuel, cafés and shops, and the larger towns along the way have more services. The memorial sites have visitor centres, and the Lens' 14-18 museum at Souchez explains the war in the region. Take a moment at the Auchel memorial to read the names, then ride east to Lorette and walk around the Ring of Remembrance. It is one of the most moving places in Europe, and a reminder of how heavily the war fell on this land.
t.ensemble minier de la fosse n 7@50.5,2.6:
Picture a pit village at six in the morning in 1950: men walking to the headframe with their lunch tins, the siren calling the shift, the women already up and stoking the stoves, children getting ready for the company school. The ensemble around Fosse n°7, near Maisnil-lès-Ruitz and Barlin, preserves the setting for that daily routine: the pit buildings, the housing, the paths between them, and the terril rising nearby. It was a self-contained world, owned and run by the mining company, which provided houses, coal for heating, schools, churches and even doctors, in exchange for loyalty and hard work. The site is one of the many components of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin on the UNESCO list.

Life in the cités had its own rhythm and culture. Gardens were essential, providing vegetables and a bit of independence, and many men kept pigeons, racing them on weekends in clubs that still exist. The bains-douches, the pithead baths, allowed miners to wash before going home, a major improvement on the days when they arrived black from head to toe. The communal festivals, especially Sainte-Barbe on 4 December, the feast of the miners' patron saint, brought everyone together.

The riding around Barlin is a pleasant mix of mining country and the first hills of the Artois. The roads link the towns with frequent roundabouts and speed bumps, but head south or west and you quickly reach the countryside, with gentle climbs and curves through fields and woods. The twin terrils of Ruitz and Haillicourt are visible from many roads, and the Olhain forest, to the south, offers shaded roads and a leisure park. Surfaces are generally decent, though cobbles appear in some streets, and farm traffic is common. The weather is changeable, so carry rain gear.

Barlin, about two kilometres away, has fuel, bakeries, cafés and shops, and Bruay-la-Buissière, nearby, has more. Try a local beer from one of the small breweries of the north, if you have finished riding, with a plate of cheese from the region, such as maroilles or vieux-lille. Walk around the pit site and the housing, imagine the morning shift, and then ride into the Artois hills for a breath of fresh air. It is a landscape of memory, and it rewards a slow look.
t.funerary and memory sites of the first w:
Every evening at eight o'clock, traffic stops under the Menin Gate in Ypres, and buglers from the local fire brigade sound the Last Post in memory of the soldiers of the British Empire who died in the Ypres Salient during the First World War. The ceremony has been held almost every evening since 1928, interrupted only during the German occupation in the Second World War, and it draws crowds of all ages, many of them descendants of the fallen. The gate itself is inscribed with the names of more than fifty thousand soldiers whose bodies were never found. It is one of the sites included in the World Heritage inscription of the Funerary and Memory Sites of the First World War, inscribed in 2023.

Ypres, Ieper in Dutch, was almost completely destroyed during the war, and it was rebuilt afterwards in its medieval style, including the magnificent Cloth Hall with its belfry, which now houses the In Flanders Fields Museum, telling the story of the war in the region. Around the town, the countryside is dotted with cemeteries, memorials and bunkers. Tyne Cot, near Zonnebeke, is the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, with nearly twelve thousand graves, and the German cemetery at Langemark is a sombre, dark-toned contrast.

The riding around Ypres is gentle, through the flat and rolling countryside of West Flanders. The roads link the villages and the memorials, with good surfaces, light traffic outside the towns, and plenty of cyclists. The Kemmelberg, to the south, is a short, steep hill with a cobbled road made famous by cycling races, and the view from the top over the former battlefields is wide. Poperinge, to the west, is a hop-growing town with a famous wartime rest house for soldiers, Talbot House. Wind and rain are common, and the landscape can feel bleak in winter, but spring and summer bring green fields and poppies.

Ypres has fuel, cafés, restaurants and accommodation, and the town's market square is a great place for a meal. Try Flemish dishes such as stoverij, beef stew in beer, or waterzooi, and a Belgian beer if you are finished for the day. Arrive in time for the Last Post at eight, stand under the gate, and listen. Then ride out the next morning to Tyne Cot and the other cemeteries. It is a deeply moving experience.
t.corbulo s canal vlietwijk@52.1,4.5:
The Vliet, a calm green waterway running between Leiden and The Hague, looks like any other Dutch canal, lined with reeds, cyclists and the occasional houseboat. But it follows, more or less, the route of one of the oldest canals in Western Europe. In about AD 47, the Roman general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo ordered his soldiers to dig a canal linking the Rhine and the Meuse estuaries, so that boats could move supplies along the coast without risking the North Sea. The historian Tacitus says Corbulo did it partly to keep his troops busy. Traces of the Fossa Corbulonis have been found here at Vlietwijk, near Voorschoten, and the site is part of the Lower German Limes World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2021.

The Roman frontier here followed the Rhine to the sea, with forts at places like Leiden and Valkenburg. What survives is mostly underground, known from excavation: timbers, ditches, pottery and the occasional ship. Above ground, the landscape is a flat, intensively used mixture of meadows, suburbs, greenhouses and roads, threaded together by waterways.

As riding goes, this is not a destination for curves. Roads are busy, roundabouts frequent and cyclists have priority in many places. But it is a good stop on the way between Leiden and The Hague, and the area has a lot to offer once you get off the bike. Leiden, just to the north, is a beautiful canal city with the oldest university in the Netherlands, founded in 1575 as a reward for the city's resistance during the Spanish siege of 1574. Rembrandt was born there, and its museums include the national antiquities museum, full of Roman finds from these very canals.

The Hague, a short distance to the south-west, has the Mauritshuis, Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and the beach at Scheveningen. The coast to the west offers dunes and sea air, with long, open roads that are pleasant if not exciting.

Voorschoten has fuel and supermarkets, and both Leiden and The Hague have everything. Try Leidse kaas, a cheese flavoured with cumin, and on the coast fresh herring with onions in early summer. Expect wind, rain showers and sudden bursts of sun, sometimes within the same hour.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de dunkerque:
The tower of Dunkirk's town hall rises above the centre of a city rebuilt from the ruins of the Second World War, a brick and stone belfry that is part of the World Heritage Site of the Belfries of Belgium and France. Belfries were symbols of civic freedom in the medieval towns of Flanders and northern France, housing bells and sometimes the town's charters, and they stood as proud counterparts to church towers. Dunkirk actually has two listed belfries, the town hall tower and the separate Saint-Éloi belfry beside the church, a reminder of how much these towns valued their bells.

Most people know Dunkirk for one thing: the evacuation of 1940, when hundreds of thousands of British and French soldiers were taken off the beaches and harbour by an armada of ships and small boats under German fire. The city was heavily damaged and was one of the last places in France to be liberated, in May 1945. A museum dedicated to Operation Dynamo explains the story, and the beaches at Malo-les-Bains, east of the centre, look peaceful today, with wide sands and a promenade.

Dunkirk is also famous for its carnival, held in the weeks before Lent, when thousands of people in costumes and wigs parade through the streets, singing and dancing behind bands. The highlight is the throwing of smoked herrings from the balcony of the town hall, beneath this very belfry, to the crowd below. It is loud, joyful and slightly mad, and not for the shy.

The riding country is flat, windy and open, with long straight roads, canals and fields. The A16 motorway connects Dunkirk with Calais and Belgium, while smaller roads lead through the Flemish countryside to towns like Bergues, with its walls and its own belfry, and Cassel, on a hill with views over the plain. The wind off the North Sea can be strong, and rain is common.

The city has fuel, workshops, restaurants and hotels. Local food is Flemish: moules-frites, potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, and beer from the region's breweries. A walk on the beach at Malo after a day's ride, with the wind in your face and the lights of ships on the horizon, clears the head.
t.hotel van eetvelde@50.8,4.4:
Victor Horta built this house between 1895 and 1898 for Edmond van Eetvelde, a senior official who ran the affairs of King Leopold II's Congo Free State from Brussels, and it is impossible now to look at it without holding both of those facts at once: one of the most daring houses of the Art Nouveau age, paid for in a world shaped by the brutal exploitation of the Congo. Hôtel van Eetvelde stands on the Avenue Palmerston near the Square Ambiorix, in the European quarter, and with three other Horta houses it was inscribed in 2000 as the Major Town Houses of the Architect Victor Horta.

What made Horta radical was his use of iron and glass in a private home. At van Eetvelde he built a central octagonal hall lit from above by a glass dome, with slender iron columns branching like plant stems and mosaics and stained glass in greens and golds. The façade is more restrained than the interior, using exposed metal in a way that shocked many contemporaries. Interior visits are limited and usually need booking, so check before you plan around it.

Brussels is a hard city on a motorcycle. Traffic is dense, the tunnels and boulevards are confusing, trams have priority and cobblestones turn treacherous in the rain. The city has a low emission zone that does cover motorcycles, so check the rules for your bike's age and standard before you arrive. Speed limits are low across the region, and enforcement is real. Parking a bike on the pavement is not generally tolerated, but designated motorcycle spaces exist.

The good news is how quickly you can escape. The Sonian Forest, a vast beech wood, begins on the south-eastern edge of the city, and beyond it the roads of Walloon Brabant roll through farmland to Waterloo and the battlefield of 1815. Leuven, with its great Beguinage and university, is half an hour east.

The neighbourhood around the Square Ambiorix and the nearby Square Marie-Louise is full of other Art Nouveau façades, including Gustave Strauven's narrow, flamboyant Maison Saint-Cyr, and they deserve a slow hour on foot. Afterwards, frites from a stand and a Belgian beer in a café make a fair consolation for the traffic.
t.beffroi de namur@50.5,4.9:
The belfry of Namur is a stout, round tower with a bulbous slate roof, not at all the slender Gothic spire people imagine when they hear the word. It started life in the fourteenth century as part of the town walls, the Tour Saint-Jacques, and later became the belfry, holding the bell that rang the hours and the curfew. It is one of the many towers in the World Heritage Site of the Belfries of Belgium and France.

Namur sits where the Sambre meets the Meuse, and the great rock between the two rivers carries one of the largest citadels in Europe, a maze of walls, tunnels and bastions built and rebuilt over centuries by whoever held the town. Vauban and his Dutch rival Coehoorn both left their mark here during the wars of Louis XIV. You can ride up to the top and look down on the confluence, the town's slate roofs and the river barges sliding past. The old town below has narrow streets, squares with cafés and a relaxed provincial feel, despite being the capital of Wallonia.

For riders, Namur is the gateway to the Meuse valley and the Ardennes. The road south along the Meuse to Dinant is one of the classic rides of Belgium, following the river between limestone cliffs, past castles, rocks used by climbers and little riverside villages. The N92 on one bank and smaller roads on the other let you make a loop. From Dinant, roads lead into the Ardennes proper, with forests, valleys and some of the best curves in the Low Countries. Weekends bring a lot of bikes and some police attention, and wet leaves in autumn deserve caution.

Floreffe, eight kilometres west, has an abbey on a hill whose monks once brewed beer, and the name lives on in the abbey beers sold today. Namur's own drink is pékèt, a juniper spirit that flows freely during the town's festivals in September, when stilt fighters from the old town battle in a tradition going back centuries.

Fuel and services are everywhere in Namur. Park near the river and climb on foot to the belfry and the old town, or ride up to the citadel for the view and come down for a waffle.
t.sonian forest grippensdelle b@50.8,4.4:
Imagine a cathedral built entirely of beech trunks, grey and smooth, rising forty metres or more to a roof of leaves, and you have the Sonian Forest at its finest. This great wood on the south-eastern edge of Brussels, the Forêt de Soignes or Zoniënwoud, covers thousands of hectares, and its most remarkable stands, including the Grippensdelle reserve near Hoeilaart, are part of the transnational World Heritage Site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of Europe, inscribed in 2017.

The famous cathedral of beeches is not entirely natural. Much of it was planted in the late eighteenth century, when the Austrian Habsburgs ruled the Southern Netherlands and a landscape architect named Joachim Zinner replanted large parts of the forest with beech in tight rows. Those trees are now huge and old, and in the protected reserves the forest is being allowed to age and decay naturally, with fallen trunks left to rot and feed beetles, fungi and woodpeckers. The ground is rolling, with little valleys and ponds, and in spring a carpet of bluebells and wood anemones covers the floor before the canopy closes.

Hoeilaart, three kilometres away, has a curious claim to fame: for more than a century it grew table grapes in heated glasshouses, and the village still celebrates its grape festival. The remains of the glasshouses can be seen on the hillsides, and the local grapes were once exported far and wide. La Hulpe, to the south, has a large park and château that belonged to the Solvay family.

The roads through the forest are pleasant but busy. Several main routes cross it, carrying commuters into Brussels, and the Brussels ring road runs along its edge. Speed limits are low and cyclists are many. The smaller lanes around Hoeilaart, Overijse and Tervuren are quieter and more enjoyable, with short climbs and descents through woods and villages. The forest itself is best explored on foot; numerous car parks give access to the trails.

Hoeilaart has fuel and shops, and the nearby towns of Overijse and Tervuren have restaurants and cafés. Tervuren is also home to the AfricaMuseum, which has rethought its colonial collections in recent years. Walking among the beeches on a misty autumn morning, with the leaves turning copper and the city a world away, is one of the great pleasures of the Brussels area.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers des pinchonv:
The flat coalfield of northern France has one real hill near Liévin, and on top of it stand two tall white pylons carved with figures of grief. This is Vimy Ridge, taken by the Canadian Corps in April 1917, and the Canadian National Vimy Memorial looks out over the mining country below. Down on the plain, in Avion and Liévin, Pinchonval is a cité, a miners' housing estate of brick houses and gardens, and with dozens of other sites it makes up the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin, a World Heritage Site since 2012.

Pinchonval itself is a residential neighbourhood, not a museum, so treat it as you would any street where people live. What makes it interesting is the planning: the coal companies built entire towns, with houses, schools, churches and allotments, designed to attract workers and keep them close to the pits. The architecture shifts from early terraced corons to roomier garden cités, and the brick details, porches and gardens reward a slow walk.

This patch of France has a heavy past. The front lines of the First World War crossed it for years, and just west of Liévin the basilica of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette stands beside the largest French military cemetery, with the Ring of Remembrance nearby listing the names of nearly six hundred thousand soldiers of all nations who died in the region. In December 1974 a firedamp explosion at the Saint-Amé pit in Liévin killed forty-two miners, one of the last great disasters of French coal mining. In Lens, next door, the Louvre-Lens museum now occupies a former pithead site.

Riding here is mostly short hops between towns: roundabouts, speed bumps, the odd cobbled street and traffic around Lens. The stretches that lift your mood are the climbs onto Vimy and Lorette, short roads with wide views over a plain dotted with black conical slag heaps, some among the tallest in Europe at Loos-en-Gohelle.

Liévin, two kilometres away, has fuel and every service. Stop at a friterie for a cone of chips with a sauce of your choice; it is as much a part of the culture here as the pits ever were.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de wallers a:
Anyone who follows cycling knows the Trouée d'Arenberg, the arrow-straight cobbled lane through the forest near Wallers where Paris-Roubaix often breaks apart. What fewer know is that the lane passes the gate of a colliery, and that the colliery is one of the jewels of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage Site. Fosse Arenberg, with its three steel headframes and brick engine houses, closed in 1989, and a few years later Claude Berri filmed his version of Zola's Germinal here, using the pithead and the cités around it as a ready-made nineteenth-century mining town.

The site has been reborn as Arenberg Creative Mine, a centre for images and media research run with the University of Valenciennes, and the industrial buildings have been carefully preserved. Around it, the miners' houses of the cités still line the streets, and old slag heaps nearby have turned into wooded hills and wetlands rich in birds.

The forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers wraps all of this in green. It is one of the larger woods in the north, part of the Scarpe-Escaut regional nature park, with ponds formed by mining subsidence, oaks and birches, and in spring a din of frogs and birdsong.

On a motorcycle, the cobbles are something to look at rather than ride. The Arenberg trench is normally closed to motor traffic, and on any pavé a bike skates and shudders, worse in the wet. The surrounding roads through the forest and the villages are calm and flat, with cyclists in numbers on weekends and around the race in April, when the area fills with fans. Valenciennes, a short ride east, has the larger choice of shops, garages and hotels.

Wallers, two kilometres away, has fuel and a few shops and cafés. Northern France is beer country, with farmhouse ales brewed in small breweries across the region, and the food leans hearty: carbonnade flamande, beef braised in beer and spiced bread, is the one to order on a cold day.
t.cite des soeurs@50.5,2.6:
At the western edge of the coalfield, where the plain of the mining basin starts to buckle into the chalk hills of Artois, the town of Barlin grew up around its pits. The Cité des Soeurs is one of its housing estates, rows of brick miners' houses with gardens, and Terril 244, a slag heap now furred with trees, stands nearby like a man-made hill. Both belong to the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage Site, which covers more than a hundred kilometres of coal country from the Belgian border westwards.

What is striking in a cité like this is the sense of a planned world. The company decided where people lived, where their children went to school, where they prayed and often where they shopped, and the layout of the streets still reflects that order. The houses were rented to mining families, and many residents today are descendants of miners who came from across France and from Poland, Italy, Belgium and North Africa.

The region's character is strong and warm. People speak French with the local Picard flavour known as ch'ti, brass bands and choirs grew up around the pits, pigeon fanciers still race their birds, and the friterie and the local café remain institutions. The slag heaps, once black and bare, have become green hills where walkers, botanists and even vineyards have moved in; some terrils have trails to the top with views over the whole basin.

Barlin itself is for practical stops. The interesting riding lies west and south, where the roads climb into the Artois hills: quiet lanes between fields of wheat, beet and flax, small brick villages, and valleys like those of the Ternoise and the Canche running towards the coast. They are not dramatic, but they are pleasant, with gentle bends, little traffic and big skies. Expect wind, showers and the occasional tractor shedding mud.

Barlin has fuel, a supermarket and simple places to eat. If you want the full story of the coalfield, the Centre Historique Minier at Lewarde, east of Douai, has underground galleries and the best displays in the region, and it is worth the hour's ride.
The coal companies were not short of optimism when they named their housing. In Bruay-la-Buissière, two neighbouring cités were called the New World and the Flowers, and their brick houses with front gardens, laid out along tidy streets, were meant to sell a better life to the families who came from across France, Poland, Italy and North Africa to work the pits. They belong to the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage Site, and they remain ordinary homes, so look respectfully.

Bruay turned from a village into a town of tens of thousands in a few decades of coal, and in the 1930s the municipality built itself a sports park and an open-air swimming pool to match its ambitions. The Piscine Caneton is an Art Deco gem, all white curves, tiled basins and stepped terraces, restored in recent years and used again by local people in summer. Seeing it on a hot afternoon, full of children, you understand what such a place meant to families who spent their days underground or waiting for someone who was.

The landscape around shifts quickly. To the east is the dense ribbon of mining towns; to the west and south, the chalk hills of Artois open out into farmland, beech woods and small villages. Houdain, almost next door, is an old market town with a church and a long past before coal. The slag heaps around Bruay have been colonised by birch, heather and orchids, and some are now nature reserves.

Riding through the basin itself is stop and start, with roundabouts, speed bumps and patches of pavé. The pleasure is in the lanes to the west and south, and the run to Arras, about forty minutes away, where the two vast arcaded squares and the town hall belfry rebuilt after the First World War make one of the finest urban sights in northern France.

Bruay-la-Buissière has fuel, supermarkets and garages. A friterie lunch, chips with a hot sauce and a fricadelle, or a plate of carbonnade in a café, is how the town feeds itself. The pool, if it is open when you pass, is the most unexpected swim of the trip.
t.stoclet house@50.8,4.4:
From the street, the Stoclet House on the Avenue de Tervueren looks like a mansion carved out of a block of white marble and trimmed with bronze, with a stepped tower crowned by four male figures and a dome of copper laurel. It was built between 1905 and 1911 for the Belgian banker and art collector Adolphe Stoclet and designed by the Viennese architect Josef Hoffmann, with the artists and craftsmen of the Wiener Werkstätte creating everything from the furniture to the cutlery. Gustav Klimt designed the mosaic frieze in the dining room, one of his most famous works. The house was listed by UNESCO in 2009 as one of the most complete and refined works of the Vienna Secession.

The catch is that you cannot go in. The house is still privately owned and closed to the public, and there is no prospect of seeing Klimt's frieze in person. What you can do is ride or walk past slowly, admire the facade and the garden from the road, and appreciate the rigour of its geometry, which pointed the way toward modernism and Art Deco.

The Avenue de Tervueren itself is worth the ride. Laid out at the end of the nineteenth century by King Leopold II, it runs from the Cinquantenaire park in Brussels out to Tervuren, a broad, tree-lined avenue with fine villas and, in its later stretches, the edge of the Sonian Forest, a vast beech woodland on the south-eastern edge of the city. At the end of the avenue, the AfricaMuseum in Tervuren, founded in the colonial era, has been renovated to address the history of Belgian colonialism in the Congo, a difficult and important story.

Riding in Brussels can be stressful, with heavy traffic, cobblestones, tram rails and complex junctions, and the city has a low emission zone with rules for older vehicles, so check whether your bike is affected before riding in. Out in the Sonian Forest and beyond, the roads become quieter and more pleasant, with gentle curves through the woods.

Kraainem, about five kilometres away, and Brussels have fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. In the city, try moules-frites, mussels with fries, or a waffle from a street stall, and taste one of Belgium's many beers, from the light, sour lambics of the Brussels region to strong abbey ales. And look back at the Stoclet House as you pass, a jewel box of a building that most people only ever see from the street.
t.terril n 10@50.5,2.5:
In the western part of the Nord-Pas de Calais mining basin, around Bruay-la-Buissière, Divion and Marles-les-Mines, the horizon is shaped by terrils, the spoil heaps left by more than two centuries of coal mining. Terril number 10 is one of them, a dark cone of shale and waste rock that has slowly turned green as birch, broom and grasses have colonised it. The basin, with its pits, cités, railway lines and spoil heaps, was listed by UNESCO in 2012 as an evolving cultural landscape, recognising both the industrial history and the lives of the hundreds of thousands of miners who worked here.

Coal was first mined in the region in the eighteenth century, and by the early twentieth century the basin was one of the most important industrial areas in Europe, drawing workers from Poland, Italy, Belgium and North Africa. The last pit closed in 1990. The towns still carry the imprint of that era: rows of brick miners' houses, the corons, laid out in regular streets, with churches, schools and dispensaries built by the mining companies. The Polish community, in particular, left a deep mark, with churches, associations and family names.

Bruay-la-Buissière has a beautiful Art Deco swimming pool from the 1930s, restored and still in use, and the Stade-Parc, a park and sports ground also from that era. Some terrils in the area have been turned into nature reserves and walking areas, and from the top of the higher ones you get a surprising view over the flat landscape towards Artois.

The riding here is not spectacular, but it is interesting. The roads link mining towns with farmland in between, with frequent roundabouts, traffic lights and speed bumps in the built-up areas. To the south and west, the land rises into the hills of Artois, and small roads through villages towards Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise and the valley of the Ternoise are quieter and more rural. The weather is changeable, and the wind can be strong on the open plateau.

The food is northern comfort: frites, carbonade flamande, welsh, the cheddar and beer dish adopted by the north, and the strong Maroilles cheese. Divion and Bruay have fuel, shops and bars, and a friendly welcome. Locals take pride in their mining heritage, and if you show interest, they will tell you stories.
t.cite du n 7 de bethune@50.5,2.8:
Between Grenay, Mazingarbe and Vermelles, in the heart of the Gohelle, the Cité du n°7 is one of the mining villages built by the Compagnie des mines de Béthune for the workers of its pit number 7. The houses, laid out in tidy rows with gardens, still form a coherent neighbourhood, part of the UNESCO-listed mining basin. Each company built its cités in its own style, and the variety of brick patterns, porches and layouts is surprisingly rich once you start looking.

The most striking landmarks nearby are the twin terrils of Loos-en-Gohelle, at the former 11/19 pit, among the highest spoil heaps in Europe. Their perfect cones rise above the flat plain like a pair of black pyramids, visible for miles around. The site has become a centre for sustainable development and culture, and you can climb one of the terrils for a view over the whole basin.

This land was also the front line of the First World War. The Battle of Loos in 1915 was fought across these fields, and the ridge of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, a few kilometres to the south, was the scene of terrible fighting earlier the same year. On the ridge stands the French national necropolis, with tens of thousands of graves, and the Ring of Remembrance, a vast elliptical memorial inaugurated in 2014, inscribed with the names of almost six hundred thousand soldiers of all nationalities who died in the region, listed alphabetically regardless of side. It is a deeply moving place. Nearby Lens, a former mining capital, is home to the Louvre-Lens, a branch of the Paris museum opened in 2012 on the site of an old pit, with a long glass and aluminium gallery displaying masterpieces across five thousand years.

The riding is mostly urban and suburban, with dense traffic, roundabouts and speed bumps. Small roads up to the ridge of Lorette and through the villages of Artois to the south are more pleasant, with views over the plain and the terrils.

Mazingarbe, Grenay and Vermelles have fuel and shops, and Lens has everything. The local food is simple and generous: frites, potjevleesch, a terrine of several meats in jelly, and beer from local breweries. Visit the necropolis in the evening light, when the ridge is quiet.
t.terril 49@50.5,2.7:
Terril 49 rises above the fields between Vermelles, Mazingarbe and Noyelles-lès-Vermelles, one of the dozens of spoil heaps that punctuate the landscape of the Gohelle. Like many of them, it has gone green, with trees and scrub covering slopes once black and bare, and it has become a refuge for wildlife in a landscape of intensive farming and urban sprawl. Lizards, rare insects and birds of prey thrive on the warm, dry slopes of the terrils, which retain heat like stone.

The area around Vermelles was one of the most fought-over sectors of the Western Front. In the autumn of 1915, the British army launched the Battle of Loos here, its largest offensive of the year, and the first in which it used poison gas. The attack across open ground towards the German lines, including the formidable Hohenzollern Redoubt, cost tens of thousands of casualties in a few days. Among those killed was John Kipling, son of the writer Rudyard Kipling, whose grave was only identified decades later. The countryside is dotted with Commonwealth war cemeteries, carefully tended, and the Loos Memorial at Dud Corner records the names of over twenty thousand soldiers with no known grave.

Walking among the white headstones, in the middle of beet and wheat fields, you feel the weight of history in a landscape that looks so ordinary. The cemeteries are open, and visitors' books at the entrance record the names of descendants who come from all over the world.

The riding here is quiet farm roads between villages, with long straights, some sharp corners and occasional mud from tractors. The land is flat and open, and the wind blows hard from the west. It is not a destination for curves, but for remembrance and for the strange beauty of an industrial landscape slowly being reclaimed by nature. The spoil heaps make good landmarks for finding your way.

Vermelles and Mazingarbe have fuel and shops; Béthune, a little further, has a lovely main square with a belfry and plenty of restaurants. If you stop in a village café, the welcome will be warm, and if you are British, someone may mention a great-uncle buried nearby.
t.camus haut@50.5,2.9:
Camus Haut lies on the eastern edge of the mining basin, near Annay, Pont-à-Vendin and Harnes, where the canalised Deûle carries barges north towards Lille. The label refers to one of the many mining sites and cités of the area, and while the exact spot is hard to identify from a distance, the landscape tells you what kind of place it is: brick housing estates, old pit heads, spoil heaps going green, and the wide, flat horizon of the Gohelle.

A few kilometres to the south lie the sites of the Courrières mining disaster. On 10 March 1906, an explosion tore through the galleries of the Compagnie des mines de Courrières, killing more than a thousand miners, the worst mining catastrophe in European history. Twenty days later, thirteen survivors emerged after wandering through the dark galleries, an event that made headlines around the world. The disaster triggered strikes and led to reforms in mine safety, and rescue teams from Germany who came to help were remembered as an early example of international solidarity. A memorial and a mass grave in Méricourt commemorate the victims. Harnes, the nearest larger town, has a museum dedicated to the history of the school and to mining life, and the area has several other museums and heritage trails about coal and the people who extracted it. The towns are modest, often with high unemployment since the mines closed, but with a strong community spirit.

The riding here is practical rather than scenic. Roads connect towns through suburbs and industrial zones, and traffic can be heavy, especially near the A21 motorway and around Lens and Hénin-Beaumont. The towpaths and roads along the Deûle canal are quieter, and watching a heavily laden barge slide by is an unexpected pleasure.

The weather is typical of northern France: grey skies, frequent drizzle, sudden bright spells, and wind. In summer the long evenings are pleasant, and the green slopes of the terrils glow in the late sun.

Harnes and Pont-à-Vendin have fuel, shops and bakeries. For food, look for a friterie, a chip stand, which in the north is an institution. Ask for a fricadelle with your frites, and sit on a bench to watch the town go by.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de boulogne@:
Boulogne-sur-Mer has two faces: the busy fishing port down by the Liane estuary, the largest in France, and the Haute-Ville on the hill above, enclosed by thirteenth-century ramparts that you can walk all the way around. The belfry stands in the upper town, attached to the town hall, its lower part dating from the thirteenth century and the upper stages added later. It is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO, symbols of the freedom of medieval towns, which rang their bells to call citizens to arms, to work, or to assembly. You can climb it for a view over the rooftops, the port and the Channel.

Nearby, the basilica of Notre-Dame, with its huge dome, was built in the nineteenth century on the site of an older church that had been a famous place of pilgrimage. Below it lies a vast crypt, one of the largest in France. The château, a medieval castle at the corner of the ramparts, houses a museum with an unexpected collection of Egyptian and Greek antiquities.

Boulogne has always looked across the water. Julius Caesar may have sailed from here to Britain, and the Emperor Claudius certainly launched his invasion from the port, where a Roman lighthouse once stood. In 1803 to 1805, Napoleon gathered his Grande Armée in a vast camp around the town, preparing to invade England. The invasion never happened, but the Colonne de la Grande Armée, a tall column on the hill north of the town, commemorates it.

The riding along the Côte d'Opale is magnificent. The D940 runs north from Boulogne to Wimereux, Cap Gris-Nez and Cap Blanc-Nez, along cliffs and dunes, with views across the Channel to the white cliffs of Dover on clear days. The road climbs and dips, with open bends and strong winds. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic; spring and autumn mornings are quieter.

Boulogne has fuel, garages and plenty of restaurants. Eat fish: the local speciality is fresh herring, grilled or smoked, and the market on the quays sells the day's catch. Nausicaá, the national sea centre, is one of the largest aquariums in Europe if you want to spend a rainy hour.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers d estevelles:
Estevelles is a small town where the mining basin meets the waterways of the Deûle, between Pont-à-Vendin and Carvin. The label points to one of the mining ensembles of the area, part of the UNESCO-listed basin: a pit, a cité, perhaps a spoil heap, all together telling the story of how coal shaped every aspect of local life. The mining companies built not only houses but churches, schools, health centres and gardens, controlling their workers' lives from cradle to grave. The cités around here, with their neat rows of brick houses and small vegetable gardens, still house many descendants of miners.

The Deûle canal is the backbone of the area. It links the mining basin to Lille and to the Belgian waterways, and in the heyday of coal, barges loaded with coal left from the quays every day. The canal still carries freight, and its banks are now used by cyclists and walkers.

Lens, the former capital of the basin, is a short ride away, and it has two things worth knowing about. The first is the Louvre-Lens, opened in 2012, a long, low, luminous building on the site of an old pit, where the Galerie du Temps displays works from the Louvre's collections in chronological order, from antiquity to the nineteenth century. Its light-filled halls are a striking contrast to the industrial landscape outside. The second is Racing Club de Lens, whose Stade Bollaert-Delelis is one of the most passionate football grounds in France. On match days, the whole town wears the club's red and gold colours, the sang et or, and the atmosphere is extraordinary.

The riding is mostly through towns and suburbs, with frequent roundabouts, traffic lights and speed bumps. The roads along the canal are flatter and quieter. Beware of cobblestones in some old streets, and of the slick surface after rain. The wind blows across the plain with nothing to stop it.

Estevelles and Pont-à-Vendin have fuel and bakeries, and Lens has every service. For a meal, try a local brasserie: the north is beer country, and many dishes are cooked with beer, from carbonade to waterzooi. If you are here on a match day, expect the roads near Lens to be jammed.
t.beffroi de tournai@50.6,3.4:
Tournai is one of the oldest towns in Belgium, and it does not shout about it. Sitting on the Scheldt, which the French-speaking locals call the Escaut, it was a Roman settlement, then the first capital of the Franks: Childeric I, father of Clovis, was buried here, and when his tomb was found in 1653 it yielded gold, jewels and hundreds of golden bees that later inspired Napoleon's imperial emblem. The belfry on the Grand-Place was begun in the late twelfth century and is considered the oldest in the country. Climb its two hundred and fifty-odd steps and you look down on a town of grey stone and slate, and straight across at the five towers of the Cathedral of Notre-Dame, a Romanesque and Gothic giant listed by UNESCO in its own right.

The Grand-Place itself is a fine, slightly lopsided triangle, lined with cafés and old guild houses, where fountains spring from the pavement on summer days and children run through them. Down by the river, the Pont des Trous, a medieval bridge with defensive towers, was rebuilt with a higher arch a few years ago to let larger barges pass, after a long and heated local debate.

Tournai has been fought over endlessly: by the French, the English under Henry VIII, the Habsburgs and the armies of both world wars. That turbulent past has left a town with a bit of everything, from Romanesque houses to Art Nouveau facades.

On the bike, the area rewards patience more than speed. The countryside of Hainaut is gently rolling, with farms, small villages and roads that wander between them. South of town, the Pays des Collines around Ellezelles and Flobecq is the hilliest corner of the region, with lanes climbing short, steep ridges and offering long views; it is cycling country, so expect to share. Cobbles are frequent in old village centres, slick when wet. Belgium also has a dense network of speed cameras and average-speed zones, and limits change often, so stay alert.

Tournai has fuel and everything else. Eat a plate of local carbonnade or try the town's speciality, lapin à la tournaisienne, rabbit cooked with prunes and beer. Sit on the Grand-Place with a Trappist from nearby Chimay or one of the many local brews, and listen to the belfry bells mark the hours.
t.la grand place@50.8,4.4:
The Grand-Place in Brussels is a square so densely decorated with gold, stone and sculpture that visitors tend to stop at the entrance and just stare. The Gothic town hall, with its slender tower, fills one side, and the guildhalls of the old trades, brewers, bakers, butchers and others, line the rest, each topped with gilded statues and ornate gables. Most of it was rebuilt after a French bombardment in 1695 destroyed the centre of the city, and the speed and ambition of the reconstruction is part of the story.

The square was a market and a stage for centuries, and its history includes executions of Protestant noblemen in the sixteenth century and processions of guilds and royalty. Today it hosts markets, concerts and, every second August, a famous flower carpet laid out across the cobbles in thousands of begonias. A few streets away stands the Manneken Pis, a small bronze statue that draws crowds far out of proportion to its size, and the glass-roofed Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert offer elegant shopping and chocolate.

A square like this is not a riding destination. The centre of Brussels is largely pedestrian or restricted, with cobbles, tram lines and a low-emission zone that may affect older machines, so check the rules before riding in. Better to park at the edge, in a designated motorcycle bay or a garage, and walk in. The roads around the city are busy, with a ring road and tunnels that can be congested at rush hour, and the surfaces are generally good, apart from cobbles and potholes that can be treacherous in the wet.

Fuel is simple to find on the roads leading out of the centre, and the area around the square is full of cafés, bars and restaurants. Try moules-frites, a pot of mussels with fries, or a paper cone of chips with mayonnaise, and a Belgian waffle if you have room. The beers are justly famous, so leave the bike parked, enjoy one, and let the evening light turn the gold of the guildhalls to amber. Early morning, before the crowds arrive, is the best time to see the square at its quietest.
t.cite saint paul@50.5,2.9:
The mining basin of northern France is a flat, open country that seems to have been built entirely by hand, and among the first things you notice are the hills that nature never put there. They are the terrils, the slag heaps of the coal mines, some of them more than a hundred metres high, and around Courrières they punctuate the horizon between rows of brick houses. The Cité Saint-Paul belongs to this world: a miners' housing estate, laid out by the mining company with its rows of uniform houses, gardens, schools and a church, so that a worker could live, shop and pray within the company's reach.

Courrières has a name that still carries weight. On 10 March 1906 a coal-dust explosion tore through the pits here, and more than a thousand men and boys died, making it the worst mining disaster in European history. Rescue efforts went on for weeks, and a handful of survivors were found alive after twenty days underground. The event shook France, led to labour unrest and helped to bring in reforms for mine safety, and the memorials in the area keep its memory alive. UNESCO listed the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin in 2012, as an outstanding example of an industrial landscape and the communities it created.

Riding in the basin is not about corners. The roads are long, straight and often cobbled, running between villages that merge into one another, with level crossings and roundabouts and a lot of local traffic. The surface is generally fair, but the setts, called pavés, can be slippery in rain, so go gently. What you get instead is a sense of place: the angular silhouettes of pit-head frames, the red brick, the silent slag heaps now covered in birch and wildflowers. The light on a winter afternoon, low and amber on the brick, is particularly good.

Courrières, a couple of kilometres off, has fuel stations, bakeries, supermarkets and cafés, so you will not go hungry. Try a plate of carbonnade, beef stewed in beer, or a Maroilles tart made with the strong local cheese, and a glass of northern beer. The Louvre-Lens museum and the Vimy memorial, both close, are fine additions to a day, and an early start makes the whole ride easier.
The belfry of Douai rises above the town hall like a stone exclamation mark, a tall, square tower with a corner turret and a gilded lion at the top. Belfries were the symbols of medieval towns in Flanders and northern France, built to show that a town had won its freedoms, and to hold the bell that called citizens to meet, fight or put out fires. Douai's was begun in the fourteenth century and finished in the fifteenth, and it is one of the group of belfries of Belgium and France that UNESCO lists together.

Inside is a carillon of more than sixty bells, played by hand on a keyboard and also by an automatic drum, and the music drifts across the square on market days. Douai is also known for Gayant, a family of giants that has paraded through the streets every July since the sixteenth century: a huge figure of a man, his wife and their children, carried by teams of men beneath the costumes, to the delight of the crowds. The tradition is a local passion, and the town takes it with a straight face.

The town sits on the Scarpe river, with canals and quiet squares, and it was a university city under the Spanish crown before French rule. It lies just beyond the northern edge of the mining basin, and from the belfry on a clear day you can see the slag heaps on the horizon, including the twin terrils nearby. Riding in the centre is a matter of cobbles, one-way streets and narrow lanes, so park near the edge and walk. Outside, the roads across the plain are flat and fast, with long straights and sudden roundabouts, and the surfaces are generally good.

Douai has fuel in plenty, together with shops, cafés and restaurants, as do Lambres-lez-Douai and Cuincy. Sit with a coffee in the square and watch the clock, or try a waffle with brown sugar, a northern favourite. The belfry can sometimes be climbed on guided tours, so check hours at the tourist office, and bear in mind that the wind at the top can be sharp. Early morning gives you the quiet of the square and the best light on the stone.
t.batiment de la goutte de lait@50.5,2.5:
Mining companies in northern France did more than dig coal. They built housing, schools, churches, shops and clinics, so that workers' lives were shaped from birth to burial by the company, and the Goutte de Lait, the Drop of Milk, is a piece of that system. The name refers to the charitable clinics set up across France from the late nineteenth century to give mothers advice and clean milk for their babies, in an age when infant mortality was terrifying. In Auchel, the building belonged to the mining community, and it is listed as part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin.

Auchel and its neighbours Calonne-Ricouart and Cauchy-à-la-Tour sit on the southern edge of the basin, where the plain starts to roll into the hills of the Artois. The landscape here is greener than around Lens and Douai, with fields and woods behind the mining villages, but the terrils and pit-head buildings are still visible. Many of the miners who worked here came from Poland and other countries in the 1920s, and their influence survives in names, churches and clubs. The Marles mining company, which ran the pits around Auchel, shaped the town's streets and its civic life.

Riding in the area is easy and unhurried. The roads run in gentle undulations through villages of brick houses, with local traffic and the occasional lorry, and the surface is mostly good, apart from setts in some of the old centres. The nearby slopes give some bends and views, and the cycling and walking trails along old mine railways attract many visitors. The best time is spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the fields are bright.

Auchel is large enough for fuel, shops and cafés, and there is a market on certain days. Food is hearty: potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats, chips with a thick sauce, and rich local cheeses, along with beer rather than wine. If you are curious about the social history of the mines, the local museums are interesting, but check opening hours, since they can be limited. A short walk around the housing nearby shows the way a company could design a town.
t.beffroi d abbeville@50.1,1.8:
Abbeville stands on the river Somme a few kilometres before it widens into its famous bay, and the town has the air of a place that has been knocked about and picked itself up. Much of the old centre was destroyed by bombing in May 1940, in the German advance, and rebuilt in a plain, solid style after the war. The belfry, part of the town hall complex, belongs to the group of belfries of France and Belgium that UNESCO lists, and it stands as a symbol of the town's medieval privileges.

The Somme has a name that echoes through the twentieth century, though the great battle of 1916 took place further east. Abbeville lay behind the lines as a British base and hospital centre in that war, and the surrounding countryside holds many cemeteries and memorials. The Bay of the Somme, west of the town, is one of the finest estuaries in France, a wide expanse of sand, salt marsh and water, where seals bask on the sandbanks and migrating birds feed in their thousands. Saint-Valery-sur-Somme, on the bay's edge, is a pretty harbour town with a small steam railway.

For riders, Picardy is gentle, open and quietly rewarding. The roads cross rolling farmland of wheat, sugar beet and rape, passing villages with brick and flint houses, and the surfaces are generally good, with long straights and gentle curves. Wind can be strong near the coast, and summer weekends bring visitors to the bay, so traffic builds. Spring, with yellow rape fields, and early autumn, with misty mornings, are the best seasons. The light along the estuary, with its huge sky, is the sort that painters travel for.

Abbeville has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and Saint-Riquier, a short ride away, has a magnificent abbey church. Local specialities include the ficelle picarde, a pancake filled with ham and mushrooms and baked with cream, and flamiche, a leek tart, and the fish and shellfish of the bay are excellent. Take a moment in the town square, look up at the belfry and enjoy the unfussy character of a town that has been through a lot.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de grenay ma:
Take any road across the Artois plain around Grenay and you will see the shape of the mining basin on the skyline: conical slag heaps, called terrils, rising out of the farmland and cités, and tall brick pit-head buildings that once housed the winding gear. This area lies between Lens and Béthune, in a district called the Gohelle, and it was mined intensively from the nineteenth century until the last pit closed in 1990. The Grenay and Mazingarbe sites are part of the UNESCO-listed mining basin, which recognises both the buildings and the landscape, and the way company housing, railways and spoil heaps shaped one another.

The terrils are the surprise. Once bare and black, many have been colonised by birch, broom and wild orchids, and they now shelter rare plants and insects, plus birds that like warm, dry ground. Some can be climbed, and the views from the top, across the plain to other terrils and church towers, are unexpectedly good. The twin heaps at Loos-en-Gohelle, not far away, are the highest in Europe, at about 186 metres, and have become a symbol of the region's reinvention.

The area has another layer of history: this was front line country in the First World War. The battle of Loos in 1915 was fought here, among the mining villages, and the Vimy Ridge with its Canadian memorial and the French cemetery at Notre-Dame-de-Lorette stand a short distance to the north. Walking among the terrils, you are on ground that was fought over and mined at the same time.

The riding is flat and straightforward, with straight roads, cobbles in the old centres and heavy local traffic. The surfaces are generally fine, and the main hazards are slippery setts in the wet and sudden roundabouts. Spring and autumn bring good light and mild temperatures, and the winter sun on red brick has a glow of its own. Grenay and neighbouring Bully-les-Mines and Mazingarbe all have fuel, shops and cafés, so supplies are easy.
t.les cites des musiciens@50.5,2.5:
In Bruay-la-Buissière, the streets of one mining estate carry the names of composers, which is where the Cités des Musiciens get their name. The mining company laid out housing in neat rows of brick, with gardens, pavements and modest decorative touches, and gave the lanes names such as Mozart, Berlioz and Bizet, a gesture that mixes paternalism with a certain poetry. Whether the miners cared much about the choice is another question, but the estates have a distinctive atmosphere, and they are listed by UNESCO as part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin.

Bruay grew rapidly in the second half of the nineteenth century, when the Compagnie des Mines de Bruay opened its pits, and the town's population surged. The company provided houses, schools and shops, and in exchange expected loyalty and long hours. Life was hard and the work was dangerous, and the miners, known as gueules noires, black faces, developed strong traditions of solidarity, brass bands, pigeon racing and growing vegetables in their gardens. Many of those habits survive, and you may see pigeon lofts and neat allotments behind the houses.

The land around Bruay is part of the western basin, with terrils on the edges of town, including one marked as Terril 31, and fields beyond. It is not dramatic scenery, but it has a gritty charm, and the light on the red brick, especially under a low winter sun, can be beautiful. Riding is simple, with flat, often cobbled streets and quiet side roads. Be careful with setts in the wet, and with streams of local traffic at rush hour, and take your time in the estates, where children play in the street.

Bruay-la-Buissière is large enough for fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, and neighbouring Divion and Houdain have smaller services. Local food includes chips with mayonnaise, mussels in season, and strong cheese, with beer in plenty. A stroll through the cités, with respect for the people who live there, is the best way to understand the place, and a late afternoon in autumn, when chimney smoke curls into the air, is a good time for it.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de drocourt@:
Drocourt lies in the middle of the basin, between Lens and Douai, and its landscape tells the story of coal on a human scale. The pit-head frames and brick buildings of the old shafts, the spoil heaps sprouting trees and the long rows of miners' houses lie almost within sight of one another, and together they are listed as part of the UNESCO Mining Basin. Nearby is the old pumping house at the Sarteau shaft, a reminder that water was always the miners' enemy, and that huge machines had to keep the workings dry day and night.

The population of the mining towns changed dramatically after the First World War, when the mines recruited tens of thousands of workers from Poland to replace the dead and wounded. Polish families settled in the villages, built their own churches, formed choirs and clubs, and kept their language and customs for generations, and their influence is still visible in family names and in traditions such as the celebration of Saint Barbara, the patron saint of miners, on 4 December. The basin is one of the few places in France where Polish culture left such a mark.

Riding here is a quiet matter of straight roads, small towns and level crossings. The surface is generally fine, and the main roads carry commuter traffic, while the back lanes are calmer and often lined with old brick houses. The terrils are the landmarks, and many are open for walks, with paths that wind through birch woods to viewpoints. The best times are spring and autumn, when the light is clear and the air is mild. In winter, mist and low cloud can hide the heaps entirely.

Billy-Montigny, Rouvroy and Drocourt all have shops and cafés, and Billy-Montigny is large enough for fuel stations and supermarkets. Try a plate of potjevleesch or a bowl of soup, and look for a bakery selling the local pastries. The people of the basin are famously hospitable, and a conversation in a café can teach you more than any information board.
t.ensemble minier du n 9 de bethune@50.5,2:
Béthune was a mining town on the edge of the Artois, and Pit Number 9 of the Béthune company is one of the surviving complexes that UNESCO included in its listing of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin. A mining complex is more than a hole in the ground: there were the winding house and headframe, the screening and washing plants, the offices, the baths where miners scrubbed off the coal dust, the stables for the pit ponies and the railway sidings, and many of these structures stand near Vermelles. Brick, steel and slag dominate the scene, and a sense of effort and anonymity hangs over it.

Vermelles and the surrounding district have another history. In 1915 the area was a battlefield, with the British Army attacking German lines at the Battle of Loos, among the pit-heads and slag heaps, and the headframes themselves were used as observation posts. Many of the villages were wrecked, and mining resumed only after the war. Today a small number of memorials and cemeteries remain, quietly tended and often visited by British families.

In the town of Béthune itself, the belfry and the Grand'Place are also on the UNESCO list, as part of the group of belfries, and the contrast between the elegant square and the industrial heritage is striking. The belfry dates from the fourteenth century, and the Grand'Place was rebuilt in Flemish style after the First World War. Béthune is also known for the Charity of Saint Eloi, a medieval confraternity with elaborate processions.

Riding is flat and simple, with straight roads, cobbles in the town and busy roundabouts. Surfaces are generally good, though setts can be slick in the rain. Late spring and autumn are the best times. Mazingarbe, about four kilometres off, has fuel stations and supermarkets, and Vermelles has smaller services. Local cuisine is hearty, with stews, frites and beer, and a visit to the market in Béthune on market day is rewarding.
t.w arly pendjari complex@11.9,2.5:
West Africa's last great savanna wilderness sits where Niger, Benin and Burkina Faso meet. The W-Arly-Pendjari complex, named after the three parks that make it up, covers more than ten thousand square kilometres of grassland, riverine forest and rocky ridges, and holds the largest population of elephants in West Africa, along with lions, cheetahs, hippos and buffalo. The W takes its name from the double bend of the Niger river that traces the shape of that letter, and the whole complex was listed by UNESCO in 1996 and extended later.

I have to be plain about the present. The area lies in a region affected by armed groups, kidnappings and attacks, with the parks in Burkina Faso and the north of Benin and Niger seeing repeated violence in recent years, and foreign governments advise against travel here. The roads are tracks, there is no reliable fuel for hundreds of kilometres, and a breakdown means a long wait. This is not a place to take a motorcycle on the basis of a map pin, and anyone interested should speak to park authorities and specialised operators about whether any visit is safe.

If conditions improve, the experience is a dry-season one. From December to April the vegetation dies back, the waterholes shrink and the animals come to the rivers, and the heat is fierce by March. The rains from June to October turn tracks to mud and close the parks. Tsetse flies, mosquitoes and dust come with the territory.

For now, the better way to enjoy the place is from a distance, through the wildlife and conservation groups that work there, and by supporting the rangers, many of whom have paid a high price for their work. One day, when the borders are quiet, a slow drive through the grassland at dawn, with mist over the river and elephants at the water's edge, will be among the best things you can do in Africa.
t.sonian forest grippensdelle a@50.8,4.4:
Brussels has a cathedral of trees. The Sonian Forest, or Zoniënwoud, covers about four and a half thousand hectares on the south-eastern edge of the city, and most of it is beech, tall grey-barked trunks that rise like columns, with a canopy so dense that the forest floor under it is open and dim. Some trees are two centuries old, and the pattern of straight, evenly spaced trunks comes from the way the forest was managed in the eighteenth century under Austrian rule, when foresters planted the stands in a deliberate style. Parts of the forest were listed by UNESCO in 2021 as part of the ancient beech forests of Europe.

The label Grippensdelle refers to a hollow in the forest, and the A in the name suggests one of several nearby spots, so I cannot pin down a monument, but the character is plain. The paths run between mossy banks, with ponds, dips and old hunting rides, and walkers, cyclists and riders on horseback share them. In October, when the beech leaves turn copper and the ground is deep in mast, it is among the finest woods in northern Europe, and in spring, in April and May, bluebells and wood anemones fill the slopes.

The forest is shared by three regions of Belgium, Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels, and the rules differ at each boundary. Hoeilaart, a town of about ten thousand, has fuel and a long tradition of growing grapes under glass, and Sint-Genesius-Rode, French-speaking and nearly eighteen thousand strong, is a quiet commuter town with cafes. The country road between them follows the forest edge with gentle bends, though traffic into Brussels is heavy at rush hours.

Motorcycles are restricted on forest tracks, and the paved roads through the wood carry speed limits and cameras, so take it calmly. North of the forest, the road to Tervuren, with its great museum of Central Africa and a park laid out by Leopold II, makes a good half-day. After the ride, Belgian beer and frites are the obvious answer, and a stop at a waffle stand is not cheating. Weekdays are quieter, and the smell of wet leaves is a very good reason to go in November.
t.pompe a feu de la fosse du sarteau@50.5,:
Coal was first found in France not far from here. In 1720, prospectors working near Fresnes-sur-Escaut struck a seam, and within a few years the Anzin company was sinking shafts all along the valley of the Escaut, the river the Dutch and Belgians call the Scheldt. The Pompe à feu, the fire pump, is the old steam engine house at the Sarteau pit in Vieux-Condé, and its name comes from the early engines, which burned coal to make steam and pumped water out of the workings. Inside the red brick building the beam engine would have towered over the floor with its great rocking arm. The whole mining basin of Nord-Pas-de-Calais was listed by UNESCO in 2012 as an evolving cultural landscape, and the pit at Sarteau is one of the pieces of it.

The country here is a low, gentle plain on the edge of the Parc naturel régional Scarpe-Escaut, where canals, poplar lines and beet fields mix with the grey brick of mining settlements. The Belgian border is a few kilometres off, and the region feels like a corner of both countries. Brick, not stone, is the local material, and the little streets of workers' houses, in tidy rows with small gardens, repeat on every road.

The riding is not about curves. It is flat and mostly straight, on small roads between hedges and fields, with occasional cobbled sections known as pavé that the Paris-Roubaix cycle race made famous, and these can be slick when wet. Traffic is local, with the odd lorry from the nearby motorway. The lanes beside the river and canal are good for an easy loop, and spring brings blossom to the orchards. It can rain at any moment, and the sky is often a flat grey, which suits the brickwork.

Vieux-Condé and Condé-sur-l'Escaut each have about ten thousand people, so fuel and bakeries are close. Valenciennes lies a few kilometres south-west and offers a larger town centre with Flemish-style brick buildings and a good selection of cafes. A plate of local specialities, such as carbonade flamande, beef stewed in beer, and a mug of dark beer, make a sound lunch. Time spent in the pump house will explain the countryside better than any map.
t.cites de la clochette et notre dame@50.4:
Douai is a handsome old town on the river Scarpe, and its belfry is the thing to look for. The tall Gothic tower, topped with a lion, rises above the town hall and holds a carillon of bells, and it is one of the belfries of Belgium and France that UNESCO listed together. Every July the town stages a big parade of giants, huge wicker figures carried through the streets that represent Gayant, a giant from local legend, with his wife and children, a tradition that dates back centuries and which UNESCO recognises as intangible heritage. The Chartreuse museum, in a former monastery, holds paintings and sculpture from the town's long history.

The cités, the planned mining settlements of La Clochette and Notre-Dame, lie on the edge of the built-up area, near Waziers and Sin-le-Noble. They were built by the coal companies in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to house miners and their families, in rows of brick houses with gardens and, in places, a school, a church and a small square. The UNESCO listing of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais mining basin in 2012 includes a number of them. Looking at the layout, you see how the company planned a whole life around the pit.

Riding here is a flat, urban sort of business. The roads are straight, the traffic is steady, and the surface is mixed, with patches of cobbles and tram-like crossing lines near the old railway. The reward is the atmosphere of brick streets with miners' gardens, the terrils, black slag heaps now green with birch, rising on the horizon, and the quiet canals. In the morning, on a clear day, the air smells of wet brick and woodsmoke.

Douai has more than forty thousand people, so you will have no trouble finding fuel and a decent meal. It is a university and legal town with a lively market, and the cafes around the main square are good for people watching. Waziers and Sin-le-Noble are close. Take a few minutes in the market square at the foot of the belfry and listen for the bells, which ring out the hour with a cheerful chime.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de la fosse:
At Oignies the last coal in the whole Nord-Pas-de-Calais basin was brought up, and the pit closed in December 1990. That was the end of more than two and a half centuries of mining in northern France, and the buildings of pit number 9 and 9 bis survive as a monument and, remarkably, as a concert hall. The old headframes and sheds now host rock bands, and the site is one of the most striking pieces of the UNESCO-listed mining landscape. Two terrils, slag heaps from the mine, rise behind it, green with birch and bramble.

Nearby Courrières has a darker place in the story. In March 1906, an explosion and fire in the Courrières pits killed more than a thousand miners, the worst mining disaster in Europe, and it caused national mourning and a strike movement. The memorials in the cemeteries are quiet and moving.

The landscape is flat, brick-built and orderly, and the roads follow suit. Wide straight departmental roads link the villages, and the cobbled sections known as pavé appear without warning, so slow down on bends and watch for wet stones. The slag heaps are the only hills, and on a clear day the view from the top of one is wide, with the next terril and its twin visible across the fields. In spring the broom is yellow on the slopes, and after rain the heaps smell of wet earth.

Oignies, Courrières and Dourges are small towns with fuel, bakeries and cafes, and Lens and Lille are within easy reach. Climbing a terril on foot takes twenty minutes and rewards you with a view of how the mining landscape fits together. Wear boots, since the paths can be muddy, and pick a day when the cloud is high. A coffee in the village after a walk makes a pleasant ending.
t.cite deblock@50.4,2.9:
Sallaumines is one of those towns that merges into its neighbours until you cannot tell where one stops, and the whole built-up band between Lens and Hénin-Beaumont is mining country. Cité Deblock is one of the company housing estates that went up in the twentieth century as the mines expanded, with brick houses in rows or pairs, gardens at the front and back, and a layout planned by engineers who believed good housing kept a workforce loyal. The UNESCO listing of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais mining basin in 2012 covers a number of such estates, because together they show how an entire society was built around coal. I cannot say what makes Deblock specially different from its neighbours, but a slow ride through the streets tells you plenty.

Lens, three kilometres to the south, is the town to know. It is home to the Louvre-Lens, a branch of the Paris museum that opened in 2012 on the site of a former pit, in a long, low glass-and-aluminium building set in a landscaped park. It is also home to one of France's best-supported football clubs, Racing Club de Lens, whose supporters wear red and yellow and fill the Bollaert stadium with a noise that locals say you can hear across the town. Just outside Lens, the twin slag heaps of the old pits 11 and 19 at Loos-en-Gohelle are among the highest in Europe, and you can walk to the top of them.

For a rider, the plain is a flat grid of small roads with traffic lights, roundabouts and sections of cobbles. Take care at junctions, because the old setts become treacherous when wet. The more interesting riding is to the south-west, where the land rolls up into the Artois hills, with Vimy Ridge and the Canadian memorial about eight kilometres away. The great white memorial, surrounded by preserved trenches and shell-pocked ground, is one of the most moving places in northern France, and the grassy slopes around it are fenced because of unexploded shells.

Fuel and food are in the next street. Sallaumines, Méricourt and Noyelles-sous-Lens each have about ten thousand people or fewer, and the surrounding towns are bigger. Try a plate of frites with a carbonade or a waffle with sugar from a baker, and have a coffee in the square. The weather is mild but changeable, and the sky large.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de noeux les:
Noeux-les-Mines stands between Béthune and Lens, and its skyline is dominated by two things: tall slag heaps, the terrils, and the old pithead structures that survive from the coal years. I should be honest that I do not know every detail of the Cornuault pit complex named in the ride titles, but I know what an ensemble minier is. It is the surviving heart of a mine, with its headframe, winding house, baths and offices, plus the housing, school and church that went with it. The UNESCO listing of 2012 includes the Noeux-les-Mines area among its many components, for the sake of the whole landscape rather than any one building.

The Compagnie des mines de Béthune ran many of the pits here, and its engineers built a town in brick to serve them. The lines of cottages with their long gardens are reminders that miners kept vegetables, rabbits and pigeons. Racing pigeons were a passion in the mining villages. A little north-west, Béthune has a handsome belfry and a market square that was rebuilt in a Flemish style after the First World War, when the front line ran only a few kilometres to the east.

That front line is the other great story. To the south, the high ridge of Notre-Dame de Lorette holds the largest French military cemetery, with tens of thousands of graves, and a ring of remembrance beside it lists the names of the soldiers who died in the region. It is a short ride away, on straight roads and gentle hills, and silent in a way few places are. The memorial and the cemetery lie on the ridge, with a view over the plain and the terrils.

The riding between the stops is easy, on flat roads with moderate traffic and the occasional cobbled stretch. The surface is generally fine, though agricultural mud collects on the bends in autumn. Noeux-les-Mines has nearly twelve thousand people, so fuel and bakeries are there, along with Sains-en-Gohelle and Hersin-Coupigny nearby. Bring a jacket, because the wind across the plain is cold, and give yourself time at Lorette. It is a long way from a theme park.
t.cite du chateau des dames@50.5,2.6:
South of Bruay-la-Buissière the land stops being a miners' plain and starts to feel like Artois, with small rivers, wooded valleys and the first rolling hills. Gosnay and Labeuvrière are quiet villages on the edge of that country, and the Cité du Château des Dames is a small mining estate here, named after a château that I cannot place with any certainty.
