It is the sort of cité that you come across by accident, a cluster of brick houses with gardens, set a little apart from the village, built for the Compagnie des mines de Béthune or one of its neighbours. UNESCO's 2012 listing included many of these, and each has a slightly different plan.

Gosnay itself has a long history that has nothing to do with coal. A Carthusian monastery, the Chartreuse, was founded in the area in the Middle Ages, which gives the village a quiet, almost cloistered character. Nearby is the valley of the Clarence river, a small stream that wanders through meadows and woodland on its way to join the Lys, and a few farms still keep cattle on the wet ground.

The riding is the best of the day in this part of the basin. The roads around Gosnay and Labeuvrière wind gently through hedged fields and beech woods, with surfaces that are mostly smooth and traffic that is light. The slag heaps appear on the horizon like green pyramids, and the old railway lines have become cycle paths. In spring the hedgerows are in blossom, and in autumn the leaves lie wet on the corners. Morning mist is common, and the light in the evening makes the brickwork glow.

Gosnay has around twelve hundred inhabitants and Labeuvrière not many more, so do not count on a pump in the villages. Bruay-la-Buissière, three kilometres away, has twenty-four thousand people and all the services you could want, and Béthune is a short run further north. After a loop through the lanes, stop in Bruay for a coffee and a pastry from one of the bakeries.
t.belfries of belgium and france@50.2,3.2:
Cambrai gave its name to a fabric. Cambric, a fine light linen, was once woven and traded in this town, and the word survives in English. The town is also known for a small, translucent mint sweet called the bêtise de Cambrai, which the locals say was invented by mistake, and a visit to a confectioner is a pleasant way to spend ten minutes. The belfry is one of the group of belfries across northern France and Belgium that UNESCO listed together, as symbols of the independence of medieval towns, and in Cambrai it is a tall stone tower in the town centre, while the town hall nearby has two mechanical figures, Martin and Martine, who strike the hours.

The town is also remembered for a battle. In November 1917 the British Army launched an attack at Cambrai with several hundred tanks, the first large-scale use of armour, which broke through the German line before the advance was beaten back. The countryside to the south and west, a rolling plain of beet and wheat, still holds the traces, and the cemeteries along the roads are as well kept as parks. Before that, Cambrai was the see of the archbishop Fénelon, the author of an influential book on kingship, and the cathedral dedicated to Notre-Dame stands in the middle of the town.

Riding here is easy, wide and open, on the long roads that cross the Cambrésis. The plain is nearly flat, with endless fields, and the wind can be strong. Surfaces are generally good, and the villages are built in brick with small squares. The mining cités mentioned in the ride titles lie to the north-west, on the edge of the coal basin, and show a different side of the region. In harvest season tractors and sugar beet lorries fill the lanes, and the mud on the road makes corners slippery.

Cambrai has thirty-six thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and cafes on every ring road. The market square is a good place for a coffee and a sweet, and the evenings in summer are long. If you have time, stop at one of the war cemeteries, where the stones stand in neat rows under a big sky. It is a quiet end to a day.
t.chateau mercier et maisons d ingenieur@5:
Mining companies built for rank as well as for need. The ordinary miners got brick cottages in terraces, but the engineers and directors got something grander, detached houses with larger gardens and, for the top man, a house that was called a château and looked like one. Château Mercier at Mazingarbe belongs to that tradition, and the ride titles pair it with the engineers' houses. I do not know the history of this particular building, so I will not make one up, but the pattern is clear. A walk through the old cité shows you the whole hierarchy of a company town in a few hundred metres, from the pit and the cottages to the engineers' row and the director's lawn. UNESCO's 2012 listing of the mining basin covers this social geography as much as the machinery.

Mazingarbe is also a place of chemistry. The mine at Mazingarbe fed a nearby industrial complex that made fertiliser and chemicals from coal, and the plant has been a feature of the skyline for a century. Vermelles, a few kilometres to the south, had a different fame. In 1915 the village stood near the front line during the Battle of Loos, a failed British offensive in which gas was released and drifted back over the attackers, and the ground around still holds a number of cemeteries, including one known as Dud Corner, with a long wall inscribed with the names of the missing.

The roads here run straight between brick villages, with little elevation and plenty of lorries, and the cobbled sections known as pavé are common on side roads. It is not a place for a spirited ride, but it is a place for a thoughtful one. Early on a cold morning the mist hangs between the terrils and the air smells of coal smoke from old stoves.

Mazingarbe has about seven and a half thousand people, with fuel and a bakery or two, and the larger towns of Lens and Béthune are a short ride off. Take time to read the cemetery walls and note the dates and ages. Few people stay long at Dud Corner, and fewer talk. Then ride to a village square, order a coffee and let the day's pace settle down.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de libercour:
Libercourt is a young town by French standards. It grew in the early twentieth century around a coal company's pits and a railway line, on land that had been farm and marsh, and the planners laid it out from scratch, with straight streets, a station and cités of brick cottages in tidy rows. Many of the miners who filled them came from Poland, recruited in large numbers between the wars, and Polish names, church services and recipes marked the mining villages of the north for generations. I cannot give you details of the individual buildings the ride titles mention, but the whole place is a lesson in how a landscape can be designed around a single industry, which is why UNESCO included it among the mining sites listed in 2012.

Oignies lies next door, with its great pit and concert hall, so you can pair the two in an afternoon. The pit's headframes make a good counterpoint to the quiet streets of Libercourt, where a surprising amount of green has crept in: allotments, birch groves on old slag, and a canal edged with poplars. A few kilometres to the north lies Lille, the biggest city of the region, with a Flemish-looking Grand Place and a famous street market, the Braderie, in early September, when the whole centre fills with stalls and people eat mussels and chips.

The riding is flat, with long straight roads through the plain and numerous roundabouts. Be careful of cobbles on side roads and of wet tramlines near the railway. Traffic is brisk around the A1 motorway and the Lille-Lens axis, but small roads between villages are quiet. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons. In winter the fog on the plain can be thick, and a low sun in the evening gives the brick a deep red colour.

Libercourt has about eight thousand people, and the neighbouring towns are of a similar size, so fuel and food are not a problem. A baker or a frituur will do for lunch, and Lille is only twenty kilometres or so away for anything bigger. Take a walk through the cité streets and look at the doors and the gardens. People still grow beans and leeks in the back plots, as the miners did.
t.bois du cazier@50.4,4.4:
On the morning of 8 August 1956, a fire broke out in the Bois du Cazier coal mine in Marcinelle, near Charleroi, after a mechanical error in the shaft loaded a lift cage with a wagon and cut an oil pipe and electric cables. Smoke filled the galleries within minutes. Two hundred and sixty-two miners died, and only thirteen were rescued. Most of the dead were immigrants, and one hundred and thirty-six of them were Italian, men who had come to Belgium under a 1946 agreement that exchanged Italian labour for Belgian coal. The disaster remains a deep wound in Belgian and Italian memory, and it changed mining safety rules across Europe.

Today, the site is a museum and memorial, part of the UNESCO listing for the Major Mining Sites of Wallonia. The old buildings, the headframe, the sorting plant and the coking works stand as they were, and a memorial to the victims with their names is moving in its simplicity. The museum covers the history of mining, the lives of the miners and the story of the disaster. It also includes a glass museum, which gives a lighter touch of industrial heritage. A visit takes two or three hours and leaves you thoughtful.

The landscape around Charleroi is a surprise. For two centuries this was the Black Country of Belgium, with coal, steel and glass works, and it has the scars to show it. The terrils, the slag heaps, have become green hills covered in birch, and the old canals and railways have been turned into cycling and walking routes, the RAVeL network. Riding here is a mixture of urban streets, motorways and quiet roads through a patchwork of villages and woods. The cobbled sections can be rough, and rain makes them slippery, and the traffic around Charleroi's ring road is heavy at rush hours.

Charleroi has fuel at many stations, and Chatelet, a few kilometres away, has the same. The city is better than its reputation, with a lively art scene and good places to eat, and its Belgian beer and frites are as good as anywhere. Not far away, the Neolithic flint mines of Spiennes, near Mons, are another UNESCO site, and a dramatic reminder that people have been digging underground here for six thousand years.
t.valkenburg de woerd south@52.2,4.4:
For a few hundred years, the mouth of the Rhine was the edge of the world. West of Leiden, the river that once spilled into the North Sea along the Old Rhine channel marked the frontier of the Roman Empire, and the legions kept a line of forts along its banks. Valkenburg, a small village near the coast north of The Hague, was one of them, and the site of a fort known by the name Praetorium Agrippinae, which is the Roman name that archaeologists give to the Valkenburg fort. It sat on the south bank of the river, with a harbour, a bridge or two, and a settlement of traders and soldiers around it, and the finds from the area include timbers, shoes, and tools preserved in the damp clay.

The Lower Germanic Limes, as the whole frontier is called, was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2021, and the Valkenburg sites form a part of it. There is very little to see above ground. The Rhine moved, the coast changed, and later centuries piled sand and peat over the Roman land, so the experience is subtle, and you read the landscape through the information panels, the museum displays and your imagination. Still, standing on a dyke at sunset with the line of the old river at your feet is an unexpectedly strong feeling.

The riding here is flat and windy, in the classic way of the western Netherlands. Narrow roads run along dykes and canals between grass fields, with cows, sheep and the occasional windmill, and the sky is huge. The surface is smooth, the limits are strict and speed cameras are frequent, so keep to the numbers. Cyclists have priority in practice, and they are everywhere, so ride with courtesy and patience. A headwind can be a serious tiring force, and rain showers come and go quickly. Early morning and the evening are the most beautiful times, and spring brings the tulip fields of the nearby bulb district.

Valkenburg and Hoge Mors are small places with a few thousand people, and fuel is easy within a short ride, in Katwijk, Leiden or The Hague. Dutch bakeries sell good coffee and a slice of apple pie, and the beaches at Katwijk are a short run to the west.
t.onze lieve vrouwekathedraal@51.2,4.4:
Antwerp's cathedral tower is visible from almost anywhere in the city, and for good reason. The spire of the Cathedral of Our Lady rises about 123 metres above the old town, a slender, lacy Gothic needle that Napoleon is said to have compared with Mechelen lace. Work began in the middle of the fourteenth century and dragged on until the early sixteenth, by which time the city was the richest port in Northern Europe. The builders planned two towers but only finished one, and the unfinished stump of the second gives the facade its lopsided look.

Inside, the church is wide and airy, with seven aisles and a forest of slender columns, and it holds some of the greatest paintings by Peter Paul Rubens, including the Descent from the Cross and the Elevation of the Cross, which he painted in the early seventeenth century for this very building. Rubens lived and worked in Antwerp, and his house, a short walk away, is open to visitors. The walls are covered in the work of later painters too, and the cathedral's vast interior is cooler and quieter than the square outside.

The cathedral stands in the old town, near the Grote Markt, with its guild houses and the fountain of Brabo, the legendary soldier who threw a giant's hand into the river Scheldt, which gave the city its name, according to a folk etymology, from hand werpen, to throw a hand. The streets around are cobbled, narrow and busy with pedestrians and trams, and the area is a low-emission zone, so riders should check the rules and plan to park in a garage on the edge. On a motorbike, Antwerp's ring roads are fast, heavy with lorries from the port, and often congested, with the Kennedy tunnel under the Scheldt a famous bottleneck.

Antwerp is a large city of nearly half a million people, so fuel, food and everything else is easy. Wander the lanes at dusk, when the cathedral is lit and the cafes fill with people. Belgian beer, mussels and frites are all good here, and the local speciality, the Antwerpse handjes, are biscuits shaped like a hand. The diamond district near the central station is one of the world's main centres for the trade, and the station itself is a spectacular building worth a look.
t.corbulo s canal rozenrust@52.1,4.4:
In the year 47, a Roman general with time on his hands and a restless army decided to dig a canal. The Roman historian Tacitus records that Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, the commander on the Rhine frontier, kept his legions busy by having them cut a waterway of about twenty-three miles between the Rhine and the Meuse, so that ships could avoid the dangerous open sea. The Fossa Corbulonis, as it is known, probably linked the Old Rhine near Leiden with the Maas estuary, and its line seems to follow the later course of the Vliet, a waterway that still runs between Leiden and Delft. Scholars debate the exact route, but this area, between Voorburg and the Rozenrust district, is a natural candidate.

This part of the Netherlands was once densely Roman. Close by, at Voorburg, lay Forum Hadriani, the only Roman town in the Dutch coastal region, named after the emperor Hadrian and founded in the early second century, and traces of its streets, baths and harbour have been found under the modern suburbs. Many of these remains are under houses and gardens, so what you actually see is very little, a landscape of water, dykes and fields that hides its history in plain sight.

The riding around here is part of what makes the Netherlands a pleasure and a challenge. The country between The Hague and Rotterdam is flat, built up and crossed by canals, motorways and railway lines, and the minor roads are narrow and calm, with clipped hedges and canal views. Cyclists are everywhere and have priority at many crossings, and speed limits are low and enforced with cameras. Bring a rain jacket, as showers arrive suddenly, and note that wind is a serious factor on open stretches. Mornings and evenings are the quietest times, and midday weekend traffic around the big cities can be heavy.

Essesteijn and Kerkehout are small places, and fuel is easy in nearby Leidschendam, Voorburg, Delft or Rotterdam. A short ride south you reach the windmills of Kinderdijk, nineteen mills in a row along a canal, which are also a World Heritage site and a classic Dutch image. Stop at a canal-side cafe, order a coffee and a piece of apple tart, and watch the barges slide past, which is a very Dutch way to follow a Roman general's ditch.
t.hotel solvay@50.8,4.4:
Brussels is a city you ride into rather than through, and Avenue Louise is one of its grand approaches. The Hôtel Solvay stands on it, number 224, a townhouse that the architect Victor Horta designed in the 1890s for the industrialist Armand Solvay, whose family fortune came from soda production. Horta was in his early thirties when he started working on houses like this, and he was one of the founders of Art Nouveau. Here he gave everything a whiplash curve: the iron balcony, the stair rail, the stained glass, even the door handles. Several of his town houses are now on the UNESCO list together.

The house is not a museum you can wander into any day, and visits are normally arranged through guided tours or special openings, so check before planning around it. From the street you can still see the sinuous façade, the bay window and the iron work. It is worth a few minutes before you do anything else, because the rest of the avenue is a parade of shops, embassies and banks, and the contrast is part of the story.

The riding here is city riding, and honest advice is to take it slowly. Brussels has tram tracks, cobbles in the older streets, heavy commuter traffic and a low emission zone that applies to many vehicles, so look up the current rules for your bike before arriving. Weekends and early mornings are far more relaxed. The avenue runs from the Place Louise towards the Bois de la Cambre, a large park on the southern edge of the city, and a ride through the park and onto the Forêt de Soignes is a reminder that Brussels is surrounded by beech woods. Those woods are some of the grandest old beech forest in northern Europe.

For fuel, the city has plenty of stations, though they are scattered, and Drogenbos and Linkebeek on the southern edge are quieter places to fill up. Parking a motorbike on the pavement is a normal sight in Brussels, though rules change from one commune to another, so use marked bike bays when you see them. For something to eat nearby, a cone of Belgian fries, a waffle or a glass of one of the country's countless beers is never far away, and the cafés around the Place Louise are good for a coffee and a rest.
t.terril renard@50.3,3.4:
Climb the Renard slag heap near Denain and you are standing on two centuries of work. Terrils are the waste rock hauled out of a mine in wagons and tipped, one load after another, until the pile became a hill. This one, the Fox, lies barely a kilometre and a half from the middle of Denain, a town of twenty-one thousand people that grew fat on coal and steel. It is named after the Renard pit, and it was down the Renard pit in 1884 that Émile Zola was lowered while he researched Germinal, notebook in hand, listening to the men who worked the seam.

The coalfield ran in a long arc from here through Valenciennes and Douai to Lens and Béthune, and the whole landscape was shaped by it. Since 2012 the basin has been a World Heritage landscape, and the terrils are a large part of the reason, because nothing else says so plainly what the industry did to the land. From the top you can pick out other black cones on the plain, and the wind turbines beyond. Nature has quietly taken the heap over: birch, buddleia and thin-soil wildflowers, and birds that like warm, dry slopes. Paths wind up the flanks and it is an easy half-hour walk, dusty in summer and slick after rain.

The roads below are flat and gridded, joined by small roundabouts and lined with brick houses. Subsidence has left some surfaces rippled, and cobbles, the pavé, turn up where you least expect them. The famous cobbled roads of Paris-Roubaix lie not far to the north-west, and wet pavé will happily send a bike sideways, so give it respect.

Denain has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries; Lourches and Escaudain are small and close. Workaday cafes serve strong coffee, and a paper cone of frites is never far away. Pick a dry spring or autumn day, wear shoes you do not mind getting grey, and go up for the view.
t.cites de la victoire et des arbres@50.5,:
Houdain is a mining town in the Pas-de-Calais, a couple of kilometres from Bruay and a short hop from Béthune, and its workers' estates carry names that read like a municipal promise: Victory and Trees. They belong to the western end of the northern French coalfield, which stretches in a long band across the Nord and Pas-de-Calais and which was the engine of the region for more than two centuries. Here the company built housing on a scale that still surprises. Whole districts of identical brick houses, each with its own garden plot, were laid out in rows and crescents, so that miners and their families would live close to the pit and under the eye of their employer.

What strikes you today is how tidy and human the streets feel. The brick has aged to a soft orange, front gardens are packed with dahlias and vegetable rows, and mature trees line the avenues. It is easy to forget that this was a controlled system of work and housing, with rents, rules and often a company school and church. The coalfield was recognised as a World Heritage landscape in 2012 precisely because these estates survive in such quantity.

Riding here means flat country with long, straight roads, chains of villages that merge into one another, and pale sky. It is not twisty, and you will pass dozens of roundabouts. The surface can be bumpy where old galleries have caused subsidence under the tarmac. A ride through the cités is a gentle, low-speed affair, best done on a quiet Sunday when nobody is about and nobody minds a motorbike idling slowly past.

Houdain itself has a couple of shops and cafes for a coffee and a baguette; fuel is available in the town and in neighbouring Bruay-la-Buissière. Look for the black pyramids of slag heaps rising above the roofs, and give them a thought. Autumn is a good season, when the brick glows against grey cloud and the trees turn, and the fields around are in clean ploughed lines.
t.cite bellevue ancienne@50.4,2.9:
Cité Bellevue means beautiful view, and in this part of the Pas-de-Calais the joke, whether intended or not, is that the view is of other mining estates and a skyline of terrils. Noyelles-sous-Lens lies right beside Lens, the old capital of the coalfield, in a landscape that feels like one continuous town. The mines here were among the richest in France, and also among the most dangerous. The Courrières disaster of 1906, in which more than a thousand miners died, happened only a few kilometres away, and it remains the worst mining accident in European history.

That history hangs quietly over the streets. Rows of brick houses with steep roofs line the cité, many restored and repainted, and the old shared gardens are still tended by families who have been here for generations. After the pits closed in the 1980s and 1990s, the region went through a painful decline, but there has been a long and careful effort to preserve and reuse the buildings. In Lens, the Louvre-Lens museum opened on the site of an old pit, and its pale, glassy galleries sit among former slag heaps.

For the rider this is flat, urban fringe, with short straight streets and level crossings, roundabouts and pavé on side roads that can be greasy in the wet. The A21 and the regional roads move traffic fast, but the quieter streets between cités are slow and a little rough. It is not a place for thrilling riding, but it is rich in atmosphere. In the early morning, with mist lying over the fields and the brick faces turning pink, the place has a stillness that is oddly moving.

Lens is a big town, so petrol is no problem and Lens is a big town and Noyelles has shops and bakeries. Football fans will know that Lens is home to the red-and-gold supporters of RC Lens, whose Stade Bollaert-Delelis is one of the most atmospheric grounds in France. On match days, expect traffic and parking trouble, and avoid the centre if you can.
t.ensemble minier de la compagnie des mine:
Fresnes-sur-Escaut sits right beside the Belgian border, on the river Escaut, which flows north into Belgium as the Scheldt. In 1720, so the story goes, coal was found here for the first time in the Nord, and that find began the transformation of the region. The Compagnie des Mines d'Anzin, founded later in the eighteenth century, became one of the largest industrial enterprises in France and helped create the landscape you ride through today.

What remains is a mining ensemble listed among the sites of the coalfield landscape: headframes, company buildings and the housing that grew up around them. The place has the plain, sturdy look of old industry, with brick, iron and wide yards. Just a short way off lies the Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers forest, home of the famous Trouée d'Arenberg, a cobbled sector of Paris-Roubaix that is straight, brutal and lined by tall trees. You can find the cobbles from here with a little navigation, but be warned: they are punishing for road bikes and difficult for a loaded motorcycle, and a wet day turns them to ice.

The country is flat and quiet, with scattered villages, wooded stretches and the odd canal. The Escaut itself is a pleasant companion for a few kilometres, with towpaths, locks and fishermen. Traffic is light on the minor roads and heavy on the arterial ones towards Valenciennes. Surface quality varies; subsidence has left the roads wavy in places.

Fresnes has some seven and a half thousand people and enough bakeries and cafes for a break; fuel is in the town or in Condé-sur-l'Escaut and Valenciennes, which are close. Morning light on brick is warm and flattering, and in autumn the forest nearby turns russet. In this part of France, a plate of frites with a Belgian-style beer is never far away, as the border is so close.
t.cite bruno@50.4,3.0:
Dourges sits between Lens and Douai, in the very middle of the old coal basin, and the Cité Bruno is one of the rows of brick homes the mining company put up for its workers. What stays with you is the quiet. A district that once lay under smoke now has pigeons on the roofs, bicycles against the walls and hedges clipped square, and the street plan, with its straight lines and identical frontages, makes it feel like a stage set for a very ordinary life. Château Dampierre, the name that goes with this stop, is a reminder that the land around here also belonged to owners and gentry long before the pits, so there is a country-house layer under the industrial one.

The Dourges company was a major name in the basin, and its shafts fed the furnaces and factories of the Nord. Hedged inside the industrial belt nearby, at Noyelles-Godault, was a huge lead and zinc smelter, closed in the early 2000s, whose soils still worry the local authorities. The terrils around Dourges, by contrast, have become something close to nature reserves, with birch, gorse and rare birds colonising the dark slopes, and some of them now have trails you can follow for the view.

On a motorcycle, this is the least dramatic kind of riding, and also an odd kind of pleasure. The roads are long and straight, interrupted by level crossings and roundabouts, and there is a constant rhythm of brick, hedge and brick. Narrow lanes between the villages are patched and become greasy in rain. The main road between Lens and Douai clogs at rush hour, so avoid it if you can and take the back streets, slowly, in the early morning or on a Sunday.

Dourges is small and has a bakery and a few cafes, while fuel is in the neighbouring towns, and Lens and Douai offer everything you could want. Autumn is kind: mist hangs on the fields and the terrils look like natural hills.
t.beffroi de l eglise st martin de cambrai:
Cambrai's belfry is the tower of the church of Saint-Martin, a stout, plain-faced tower that rises over the roofs of a town of about thirty-six thousand people in the flat, open Cambrésis. Belfries in northern France and Belgium were symbols of civic freedom, built by town councils to hold the bells and the charters, and a group of them is on the World Heritage list. This one has a more modest charm than the giants of Bruges or Ghent, but it still announces the town from a long way off, across fields of sugar beet and wheat.

Cambrai has had a hard history. It lay on the frontier between France and the Spanish Netherlands, was besieged and captured many times, and was battered in both world wars. In November 1917 it gave its name to the Battle of Cambrai, where hundreds of British tanks were used together for the first time on a large scale. The town is also known for the cloth called batiste, said to be named after a medieval weaver, and for the minty sweets called bêtises de Cambrai, which you can buy in tins from shops in the centre. The writer and archbishop Fénelon once served here.

For a rider, the roads around Cambrai are a long, open trellis of straight lines across rolling farmland. Wind is a constant companion, and a strong crosswind can blow hard across the exposed plateau. The old town has narrow streets and some cobbles, so ride slowly there. The ring road around the centre is busy but easy.

Fuel, supermarkets and cafes are all in Cambrai itself, with plenty of places around the main square. It is a good place for a coffee and a pastry, and a quick walk to see the old gate and the cathedral. The light is best in April and September, and the fields in June are a deep, sheeted green. Take care on wet days, because the cobbles and tram-lined streets are slippery.
t.fosse mathilde@50.3,3.4:
Denain is remembered in French history for an afternoon in July 1712, when Marshal Villars crossed the Scheldt and smashed an allied army under Prince Eugene of Savoy, a victory that rescued France in the closing years of the War of the Spanish Succession and is still marked in the town. The Fosse Mathilde belongs to a later and quieter story. A fosse is the northern word for a pit, and these shafts were named for company directors and their families, so Mathilde was a lady before she was a hole in the ground.

Denain's wealth in the nineteenth century came from coal and then from steel, and the Anzin company, one of the biggest employers in France, sank pit after pit in the surrounding fields. Steelworks followed, and the town's population swelled and then, when the furnaces closed in the later twentieth century, fell. Standing here you see low brick halls, remnants of the pit head and the shape of terrils along the horizon. The scale of the buildings is modest next to the weight of the history, and that, oddly, is what moves people.

The riding is flat and urban, a grid of straight roads, level crossings and the odd patch of cobbles. Denain is a busy town, with roadworks and slow traffic at the usual hours. It is no place for corners, but it is good for an unhurried look at how industry carves a place into shape. Surfaces are patched in many places, and the pavé on some side streets is slippery when wet.

Fuel and food are easy in Denain. A short run to the west brings you to the Arenberg forest and the cobbled sector that appears in cycling lore, which you should attempt only on a dry day. In winter the landscape is grey and forbidding, but spring puts fresh green on the terrils and a softer light on the brick.
t.cites de beaurepaire@50.4,3.3:
Somain exists because of the railway. Several lines meet here, and the town grew up around the station, which still has the busy feel of a junction. The Cités de Beaurepaire were built by the Aniche mining company, one of the great concerns of the northern coalfield, and they show how a company could shape a landscape: neat brick rows, small squares, a few shared buildings, and gardens laid out to a plan. A local will tell you who lived in which house and which families still do; an outsider notices the symmetry first, and then the small signs of individuality, a painted door, a trellis, a satellite dish pointing the wrong way.

The Aniche company reached back to the eighteenth century and sank pits across the country between Douai and Valenciennes. Miners' lives were hard, and the strikes that shook the coalfield in the nineteenth century are well remembered. Nearby, old slag heaps have turned green with birch and gorse, and some have paths with views across the plain. The area has a strong tradition of brass bands, pigeon racing and cycling, and you will see pigeon lofts in the backyards.

Wind is the main fact of life on a bike here, since the plain is wide and open and there is nothing to break a crosswind, not a hedge, not a hill, only the odd line of poplars and the shoulder of a terril. Pick your day carefully and a ride here is calm and easy; pick badly and you spend it leaning at an angle. Roads are generally decent but bumpy where old workings have sunk, and the cobbles on older streets turn to glass in the wet. Sunday mornings are quiet, and the low light on the brick is lovely.

Somain has twelve thousand-odd inhabitants, so supermarkets, bakeries and fuel are all at hand. Douai, a short run west, has a fine belfry and a lively old centre. The region eats plainly and well: carbonnade flamande, potjevleesch and sugar tart. In autumn the beet harvest drags mud onto the tarmac, and in spring the fields glow yellow with rapeseed.
t.frontiers of the roman empire the lower@:
Where the old Rhine reached the North Sea, near the modern town of Katwijk, the Romans built a string of forts, and Valkenburg was one of them. The Dutch Valkenburg, a village near Leiden, not to be confused with its namesake in Limburg, was the site of a fort and harbour called Praetorium Agrippinae, a base on the northern frontier of the empire that stood on the south bank of the river. Along this stretch the Rhine formed the border of the Roman province of Lower Germany, and the line of forts, watchtowers and roads along it is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage listing.

Little shows above ground, since the Dutch landscape has always been busy burying things, but excavations here have turned up wooden structures preserved by waterlogged soil, including parts of the fort's timber walls, ships and personal items such as leather shoes and writing tablets. The Rhine itself later silted up and shifted, and the sea moved the coastline, so what was once a frontier river estuary is now a quiet lowland of canals, polders and dunes.

Riding in this part of Holland is flat, tidy and dominated by wind. The Rijndijk and its neighbouring roads run along old dikes, with water on both sides, and the air smells of cut grass and salt. In spring the nearby bulb fields around Lisse and Noordwijk are a carpet of tulips and hyacinths. Cyclists have priority everywhere, and cycle paths run alongside the roads, so look carefully at junctions. The Dutch enforce speed limits strictly, with cameras on many roads, and the weather can turn from sun to squalls within minutes.

Valkenburg is a small place, and the nearest bigger town is Rijnsburg, with Leiden a few kilometres away, where there are fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes. In Leiden you can see the Roman finds in the National Museum of Antiquities. Try fresh herring with onions, eaten from a stall by the canal, and a strong coffee with a slice of apple pie. The dunes at Katwijk, a short ride off, are a good place for a walk, and the best light comes in the evening.
t.corbulo s canal starrenburg@52.1,4.4:
Corbulo's canal is one of the oldest engineering works in the Netherlands, and it was dug by soldiers. In AD 47 the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, commanding the Roman army in Lower Germany, put his men to work cutting a canal between the Rhine and the Meuse, partly to keep them busy and partly to give ships a sheltered route that avoided the open sea, with its storms and raiding Frisians. The Fossa Corbulonis, as it was called, ran through the low country between modern Leiden and the Meuse mouth, and its line is thought to be followed today by the Vliet, a quiet waterway that runs between Leiden and Delft.

Starrenburg lies on this line, near Voorschoten, a pleasant commuter town with villas and willow-lined waterways. Near the site there was once a Roman settlement and harbour, and remains of bridges and moorings have turned up in the area. The canal itself is now a modest stretch of water with small boats and ducks, bordered by cycle paths, and the rhythm of the place is quiet and domestic, with allotments, windmills and tidy brick houses.

Riding here is a matter of small roads on dikes and canal banks, which wind a little and are mostly narrow. Surfaces are generally excellent, but there are many speed humps, narrow chicanes and cycle crossings, and cars are often parked on one side. Speed is strictly controlled, and cyclists swarm everywhere at school time and on summer evenings. The wind can be strong, and in winter fog collects along the water. Leave plenty of time and enjoy the slow pace.

Voorschoten, with some twenty-two thousand inhabitants, has petrol and shops, and Leiden is just beyond. The Vliet is a nice stretch for a walk, and the older villages of Leidschendam and Vlietwijk have decent places for coffee. Try a stroopwafel, a thin waffle sandwiched with syrup, warmed on top of a cup of tea. Spring and early summer are the best seasons, with the polders green and the light long.
t.belfort en hallen@51.2,3.2:
Bruges grew rich in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries as a cloth and trading port, and the belfry on its market square is the proudest sign of that wealth. Rising about eighty-three metres above the Markt, with an octagonal upper stage, few towers in Belgium are better known. The Hallen, the old market halls at its base, once held the town's cloth trade, and the belfry stored the town's charters and its bells, so that merchants and citizens could be called together and warned of fire or attack. It is also a part of the group of belfries of Belgium and France on the World Heritage list.

The climb up is 366 steps, steep and narrow, with a view at the top over the red roofs, canals and green fields toward the sea. The carillon has forty-seven bells, played by the town's carillonneur on a keyboard of wooden levers, and concerts are given several times a week in summer. On the Markt below, horse-drawn carriages pass, and on the east side the gabled guild houses stand like a row of stage sets. The town was a centre of Flemish painting, with Jan van Eyck and Hans Memling both working here.

Bruges is a place to arrive by bike or on foot, not by motorbike. The historic centre is a maze of cobbled streets, canals and one-way systems, with restrictions on vehicles and a large pedestrian zone around the Markt. Park outside the ring and walk in, or use one of the car parks near the station. Cobbles are slippery in rain and tourists are everywhere, so a motorbike in the centre is more bother than fun. The countryside to the east and the coast to the north are flat and pleasant, with tidy villages and tree-lined roads.

Bruges has about one hundred and seventeen thousand people, so fuel and food are easy outside the centre. Local fare means mussels and chips, waterzooi stew, and Belgian beer, with chocolate shops on every corner. Go at dawn or late in the evening to see the square at its quietest.
t.wortel@51.4,4.8:
Wortel is a village in the Belgian Kempen, near the Dutch border, and it is the Belgian member of a World Heritage group whose other two parts, Frederiksoord and Veenhuizen, lie in the Netherlands. The story begins in 1818, when a Dutch army officer, Johannes van den Bosch, founded the Society of Benevolence, an organisation with the grand idea of rescuing the urban poor by sending them to work on farms in the countryside. The first free colonies were founded in the Netherlands, at Frederiksoord, and in 1822 the society bought land at Wortel, then part of the same kingdom, and opened a colony there. When Belgium split away in 1830 the colony remained in Belgian territory.

The settlers were given a house, a plot of land and a cow, in return for working and living under strict rules, and many struggled on the poor sandy soil. Later the colonies became centres for orphans, vagrants and beggars, and the buildings grew into large institutions. In Wortel, the layout of fields, straight roads and brick farmhouses still follows the original plan, and the colony is a quiet, planned landscape in a region of heath, pine and farmland.

Hoogstraten, a few kilometres away, is the nearby town, known for its strawberries and for a huge Gothic church, with a tower that dominates the plain. The country here is flat and sandy, with straight roads between fields of strawberries, asparagus and nurseries growing trees and shrubs. Riding is easy but not thrilling, though the roads are generally good and traffic is light. Cyclists are numerous, and on summer weekends the cycle routes are crowded. Winter fog and spring rain are normal, and the smell of pine and damp earth is strong.

Hoogstraten has about eighteen thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and the Dutch border at Baarle is close. Try the local strawberries in season, and a Belgian beer in a village cafe. Antwerp is an easy ride away. The best seasons are spring, when the orchards flower, and summer, when the long evenings invite a slow ride.
t.rice terrace clusters of banaue bangaan@:
The terraces of Banaue are carved into the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, and the cluster at Bangaan is one of the most photographed, a tight village of thatched huts at the bottom of a steep amphitheatre of stone-walled paddies. The Ifugao people built these terraces over centuries, shaping the mountainsides with walls of stone and earth, and channelling mountain springs through bamboo pipes and canals so that water flows from one paddy to the next. Popular accounts say they are two thousand years old, but archaeologists now think most of what we see grew over the past four or five centuries. Either way, it is a monument of patient labour with hand tools, and it is a living landscape, still planted and harvested by hand.

UNESCO listed the terraces in 1995, and Bangaan is among five clusters included. Rice is planted in the rainy season and harvested around the middle of the year, so the colours change from the green of young shoots to gold at harvest, and in the dry months the paddies are bare and reflect the sky. Ifugao houses stand on stilts with pyramidal roofs, and carved wooden figures called bulul guard the rice. The Ifugao drink tapuy, a rice wine, at celebrations. Rice terraces are fragile, and many are threatened by landslides, young people leaving for the cities and erosion.

The road from Manila is long, around eight to nine hours, and the mountain roads in the Cordillera are narrow, twisting and often wet. In the wet months, landslides block roads and leave slippery clay and rock on the surface. Fog is common, and the drop-offs are steep, so ride in daylight and slow down. Jeepneys and trucks are the main traffic, and they stop without warning. The road toward Bontoc climbs high and gives sweeping views.

Banaue has fuel stations, guesthouses and small restaurants, but the villages beyond have little, so fill up and carry cash. Barlig, listed fifteen kilometres away, is a remote mountain town. Come in the dry season from November to April, but expect cool nights at altitude.
t.w national park of niger@12.3,2.3:
The W National Park gets its name from the shape of the Niger river, which makes a double bend here that looks like a letter W on the map. The park straddles the borders of Niger, Benin and Burkina Faso, and with neighbouring Arly and Pendjari it forms the largest protected savanna area in West Africa. This is the northern edge of the Sudanian savanna, where grassland and dry woodland meet the Sahel, and the river is the lifeline that holds everything together.

Wildlife is the main story. West African elephants, one of the last substantial populations, live in the park, along with hippos, buffalo, baboons, warthogs, roan antelope and a few lions. The Niger itself hosts hippo pods and, in theory, the rare West African manatee. Birdlife is rich along the river, with fish eagles, storks and bee-eaters. The rains run from roughly June to September, when tracks turn to mud and the grass grows tall, and the dry season from November to May is the time when animals gather at water and are easier to see.

I should be honest about the riding. This is not a place for casual travel. Tracks are rough, distances are long, and fuel and spare parts are scarce. There are no towns near the coordinates, and the nearest big services are in the capital Niamey, some distance away. Security in parts of the wider region has been unstable for years, and governments regularly advise against travel to areas near the borders. Any plan to come here needs current official advice, a local guide who knows the situation and permission from the park authorities.

If you do visit, the best season is the dry months, when the harmattan haze sometimes softens the horizon and the temperature is bearable in the morning. Go early, carry far more water than you think you need, and expect to share the track with cattle, goats and the occasional elephant. The park is one of the great wild places of West Africa and deserves informed care.
t.hotel tassel@50.8,4.4:
In 1893, a young architect named Victor Horta finished a town house in Brussels for a professor called Emile Tassel, and in doing so he changed the course of European design. The Hotel Tassel is generally regarded as the first true Art Nouveau building. Its facade looks restrained from the street, with a curved bay window and a bit of ironwork, but inside, the staircase is a revelation. Slim iron columns split into whiplash curves that spread across the walls and ceiling, mosaics ripple across the floor, and the whole space seems to grow like a plant.

What was new was the way Horta treated structure as decoration. The iron that held up the building was left visible and shaped into tendrils, and natural light poured down from a glazed roof over the stair. Rooms flowed into one another instead of being closed boxes. It is a very sensual kind of architecture, designed when cities were filling with heavy neo-classical stone. UNESCO included the Tassel house, along with three other Horta houses in Brussels, on the World Heritage list in 2000.

The house stands in a quiet residential street in the Saint-Gilles and Ixelles area, a short distance from the busy Avenue Louise. It is a private building that is not always open to visitors, and you may only see the facade, so check opening arrangements before you plan a visit. The neighbourhood has plenty of other Art Nouveau houses, so a slow walk around the streets nearby is rewarding. Look up at the facades, which are decorated with ironwork, stained glass and sculpted stone.

Riding in Brussels is a challenge. The city has cobbled streets, tram lines, tunnels and heavy traffic, and drivers can be impatient. Parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, but you should still lock the bike, and take valuables with you. Fuel is easy to find on the main roads, with Drogenbos, a smaller town to the south, a possible alternative. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the light is soft and the cafes spill onto the pavements. A Belgian waffle or a plate of frites is the right reward.
t.major town houses of the architect victo:
Victor Horta was born in Ghent in 1861, and by the end of the nineteenth century he was the most talked-about architect in Brussels. The four houses that UNESCO lists, the Hotel Tassel, Hotel Solvay, Hotel van Eetvelde and Horta's own house and studio, show how he developed his ideas. They were built for clients who wanted something modern: a professor, an industrialist, an administrator in the Congo Free State and the architect himself. Each uses iron, glass and curving lines in a different way.

Horta's own house, in Saint-Gilles, is now a museum, and it is the easiest of the four to visit. It lets you see how he lived and worked, and its stairwell, with a skylight, mirrors and a mosaic floor, is among the great interiors of the period. The others are mostly private. Hotel van Eetvelde, built for Edmond van Eetvelde, has a famous octagonal hall with a glass dome, and the Solvay house, for the Solvay chemical family, is a statement of wealth and taste. Together they form a small group in a few districts of the city.

It is a sad part of the story that many of Horta's other works were lost. The Maison du Peuple, a great socialist meeting hall with a glass and iron facade, was demolished in 1965, despite protests from architects around the world. That loss helped spark the movement to protect Brussels' architectural heritage. Today the houses are treated with great care, and the areas around them are conserved.

For riders, a day among the Art Nouveau houses is best done on foot, with the bike parked in a quiet street. Brussels has dense traffic, trams and cobbles, and it rewards a slow pace. Fuel is plentiful, and the city has a large number of workshops if you need help. Spring is the best time, with magnolia and cherry trees in the squares, and the evenings are long. If you like beer, ask a bar for something local. Brussels is a city that shows how much a small glass can hold.
t.bois du luc@50.5,4.1:
The coal that powered Belgium came from a ribbon of pits across Hainaut, and Bois-du-Luc is where the story is told best. The mining company here, the Societe de Bois-du-Luc, was founded in the late seventeenth century, making it one of the oldest in Europe, and it kept going until the pit closed in 1973. The site is now a museum and heritage centre, and it is listed by UNESCO as one of the Major Mining Sites of Wallonia, together with Grand-Hornu, Bois du Cazier and Blegny-Mine.

What makes it special is that the whole community survives. In the nineteenth century the company built a workers' village around the pit, with rows of neat brick houses, a school, a church, a bakery and a communal hall. It was an early example of the company town, and a model of paternalistic planning. The idea was that decent housing would produce a stable workforce, and the result is a lovely, orderly little district. Walking through it feels like stepping into a toy town, though the work done by the miners was anything but light.

The landscape around here is shaped by coal. Slag heaps, called terrils, rise from the plain as conical hills, now covered in birch and scrub, and they are a recognisable feature of the region. Nearby, the Canal du Centre has a famous set of hydraulic boat lifts, also on the UNESCO list, which were built to move barges up a steep slope. If you are interested in industrial heritage, this part of Belgium is one of the best places in Europe.

The roads are flat and often cobbled, running through small towns of brick houses, and the surface can be rough in places. Traffic is moderate, and the weather is changeable, with rain at any time of year. La Louvière, the nearest big town, has about seventy-six thousand people and all the fuel, food and repair services you need, and Le Roeulx has an old castle and a quiet main street. The region is also home to the carnival of Binche, with its Gilles in tall ostrich feather hats, held before Lent. Come in spring or autumn, and give yourself a few hours.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers du secteur d:
Coal made this corner of northern France, and for a century and a half it made it black. The mining landscape listed by UNESCO runs for a hundred and twenty kilometres across the old Nord and Pas-de-Calais coalfield, and the sector at this stop lies in the Valenciennes end of it, close to the Belgian frontier and the river Escaut, which the Belgians call the Scheldt. The pits of Anzin, the company that started the whole business in the middle of the eighteenth century, were the first great mines in France. A rider will not find a sign saying where the shaft stood, so treat the coordinates as a way into a district of brick towns, pit heads and slag heaps that have turned green.

Those heaps are the landmark you will actually see. The terrils, as they are called, rise abruptly out of flat farmland, and birch and broom have colonised most of them. Some are now nature reserves, and the Scarpe-Escaut regional park, just to the west, has made a point of keeping the wet hollows where the ground sank above old workings. Herons and reed warblers live in places that were once ploughed fields.

The riding is flat, straight and quiet, which is the honest description. Roads run between brick terraces of miners' housing, the cités, past level crossings and canal bridges, and through villages whose names finish in the same few syllables. Cobbled stretches appear without warning, as the north's cycling fans will tell you, and in wet weather they are slick as a plate. Wind from the North Sea sweeps across the open land, and rain is never far away. Vieux-Condé, with eleven thousand inhabitants, has fuel, a bakery and a few bars, and nothing else nearby is bigger.

If you want food, ask for the local fare: a carbonnade of beef cooked in beer, or a plate of frites with a fricadelle, bought in a roadside friterie with a queue out of the door. Belgian beer is a short ride away over the border, and the contrast in prices will show on the bill.

Come on a clear autumn day, when the low sun catches the brick and the leaves turn on the terrils, and the district looks better than its reputation.
t.maison syndicale lens@50.4,2.8:
Lens still wears its history on the surface. The town was flattened in the First World War, which fought over it for most of four years, and rebuilt in brick and concrete in the years after, so what you ride through now is mostly the work of the 1920s and 30s. The Maison syndicale, the union hall, is one of the buildings that belong to that rebuilding and to the world of the pits that surrounded the town, when coal paid the wages and the union bargained for the men who went down. It stands as a reminder that this was a place of organised labour as much as of industry.

Around the town the story deepens. At Courrières, a few kilometres east, an explosion in March 1906 killed more than a thousand miners, one of the worst mining disasters in European history, and the strikes that followed shook the country. To the west the twin slag heaps at Loos-en-Gohelle, the highest in Europe, rise like a pair of pyramids over the plain, and a short climb on foot brings a view over the whole basin. Vimy Ridge, where the Canadians fought in 1917, is a few minutes north, and its memorial is one of the most moving places in France.

The riding is easy in an almost lazy way. Roads are flat, straight and often cobbled, and the whole region is a magnet for cycling fans, so expect the occasional peloton on a weekend. Lens has thirty-eight thousand people and fuel at every corner. The Louvre-Lens museum, opened in 2012 on a former mining site, is a low glass-and-aluminium building set in a park, and worth an hour. The stadium, home to the football club that every local supports with unusual passion, wraps the town in red and yellow on match days, and traffic on those days is best avoided.

Eat in the town. A plate of local cheese from Maroilles, or a waterzooi, will keep you going. In winter the weather is raw and grey, and the damp gets under every layer. Spring and early autumn bring softer light, and the old brick houses glow when the sun finally breaks.
t.grands bureaux de la societe des mines d:
Every mining company in the north of France needed an office, and the one that held the pay books, maps and plans of the Lens pits needed a large one. The Grands Bureaux of the Société des Mines de Lens stand in the middle of the town as a monument to an organisation that employed tens of thousands of men and controlled whole districts: the housing, the schools, the shops, the churches and the clinics were all in the company's gift. The building was part of the reconstruction after the First World War, when the town had been reduced to rubble and the company set about rebuilding its pits and its headquarters in brick and stone.

It is a handsome, solid building, designed to impress, and it is a good place to think about how the mining basin worked. The company paid wages and ran the cités, the ordered streets of miners' houses with their gardens and washing lines. The Société des Mines de Lens was founded in the middle of the nineteenth century and ran until the French coal industry was nationalised in 1946. The last pit in the basin closed in 1990.

Riding in and around Lens is easy but unremarkable. The streets are flat and straight, with a good deal of cobbled paving and tram-like patches of rough tarmac, and the traffic is thick at rush hour. The town is a busy one, with thirty-eight thousand residents, and fuel stations are everywhere. For a coffee, find a brasserie near the station. For something more filling, a plate of potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats, is a Flemish speciality that has crossed the border into Artois.

If you have time, climb the slag heaps at Loos-en-Gohelle for a view that explains the landscape better than any museum. The twin cones are the highest in Europe, and on a clear day the whole plain is spread out below.

The weather in the north is changeable, with rain at any season. The best days are in late spring and early autumn, when the light is soft and the brick glows. Winter is raw, grey and damp.
t.cite des petits bois@50.4,2.8:
There is a particular kind of street in the old coalfield that outsiders mistake for suburban normality. Rows of identical brick houses, each with a small front garden, line a gently curving road, with a school at one end and a church at the other. These are the cités, built by the mining companies to house their workers, and the Cité des Petits Bois at Liévin is one of them. It belongs to the same family as the cités of the Solitude, named on this ride, and together they tell how a company could organise the life of its men from cradle to pit head.

Liévin itself is a town of thirty-four thousand people on the edge of Lens. It is known for its pits and for a tragedy: in December 1974 an explosion in one of the mines killed forty-two men, and the town still marks the anniversary. In happier times it is known for athletics, and the indoor stadium hosts a well-known meeting in the winter calendar.

As for the riding, expect more of the same as around Lens. The roads are flat and mostly straight, with cobbles in the older streets and speed bumps in the cités. Care is needed at the crossings, where the old railways cut the roads at odd angles. The traffic is thick on the main roads at rush hour, but the side streets are quiet, and a slow wander through a cité can be a quietly interesting half hour. The housing has often been renovated, with new roofs and brighter doors, and many of the residents are proud of the heritage that surrounds them. Please ride gently, since these are lived-in streets and not a museum.

Fuel and food are no trouble. There are stations on all main roads, and the cafes in the centre serve strong coffee and sandwiches filled with chips, a northern habit that foreigners find alarming and then adopt. The Éleu-dit-Leauwette district nearby is smaller but has a bakery or two.

In spring, when the gardens bloom and the allotments are planted, the cités look their best. In winter they are darker and wetter, and the brick takes on a hard grey tone.
t.chateau des douaniers@50.4,3.6:
Customs officers and smugglers have been playing the same game along the northern border for centuries, and Fresnes-sur-Escaut sits right on the line. The little town of seven and a half thousand people lies on the French bank of the river Escaut, a few kilometres from Belgium, in the country that was once part of the Spanish Netherlands and later the heart of the Anzin coalfield. The Château des Douaniers recalls the border guards who watched the lanes and the river for contraband, and the frontier traffic in coffee, tobacco, butter and spirits was an economic force for generations.

Around the town, the landscape is a gentle one of canals, poplars, pastures and brick villages, in the regional park of Scarpe-Escaut. The river was canalised long ago and is used by barges, and the towpaths are popular with walkers and cyclists. The pits closed decades ago, and the slag heaps are now covered in birch and grass. Across the border, Belgian Hainaut begins, with its own old mines and breweries. The basilica at Bonsecours, just over the line, is a local landmark and an easy detour.

The riding is quiet and easy. The roads are flat and mostly straight, linking villages with names that change from French to Walloon without much warning. Cobbles appear at the edges of towns, and farm traffic is frequent. The frontier is open, so you will cross it without noticing, apart from a change in road signs and the quality of the tarmac. Fuel is straightforward. Fresnes has stations on the main road, and Vieux-Condé, next door, with nearly eleven thousand inhabitants, has more. Cafes serve beer and simple food, and a plate of frites with a Flemish stew will cost less than you expect.

If you cross into Belgium, remember that speed limits and rules are different, and a motorbike has to carry its papers. The Belgians love their beer, and a stop at a village cafe over the border is an appealing prospect.

Early autumn and late spring are the best seasons, with clear skies and a soft light on the water. Summer is warm, and winter brings fog and drizzle that can linger for days.
t.stade parc@50.5,2.5:
There is nothing much in a name like Stade Parc to tell you where you are, but the coordinates put it in Bruay-la-Buissière, a former coal town in the Pas-de-Calais, in the heart of what the French call the bassin minier. This was once a landscape of pits, headframes and long rows of brick miners' housing, and in 2012 the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin was added to the UNESCO list as a cultural landscape. The stadium or park in the label is part of that story in a quieter way, because company towns like Bruay built sports grounds, brass bands and parks for their workers, and the community life around a pit was as important as the pit itself.

The country is flat and open, but it is not dull if you look at it properly. The most striking features are the terrils, the conical or flat-topped slag heaps, some of which have been grassed over and planted with birch and now carry walking trails, while others still show black. From a high one you can see a dozen others on the horizon, like a landscape of small mountains made by hand. Nearby, the Louvre-Lens museum stands on a former pit site, and the vast Notre-Dame-de-Lorette cemetery on its ridge commemorates the First World War dead, with the Vimy Ridge memorial a short ride away.

Riding here is about atmosphere rather than corners. The roads are straight, lined with brick terraces, and in places the surface is the famous pavé, the cobbles that make the Paris-Roubaix cycle race so brutal. Take them slowly, especially in the wet, and keep your hands light on the bars. The northern French weather is changeable, with a sharp wind off the plain, and a grey day can make the brick glow red. Spring brings blossom along the canal banks, and autumn mist hangs over the fields.

Bruay-la-Buissière has about twenty-four thousand people, so there is no trouble with fuel and food, and the neighbouring town of Béthune is the bigger centre with a handsome Grand-Place and belfry that was rebuilt after the First World War. Try a plate of carbonnade flamande or a local maroilles cheese, with a glass of beer, in one of the straightforward brasseries, and give the old miners' cafes a go if you find one open.
t.st martin s church@51.3,1.1:
St Martin's is a small flint-and-stone church on a low hill on the eastern edge of Canterbury, and it claims to be the oldest church in continuous use in the English-speaking world. The tradition is that it was already a Christian place of worship when Augustine arrived in 597 to convert the English, because the Frankish princess Bertha, who married King Æthelberht of Kent, had a chapel here and a bishop with her. Parts of the walls contain Roman brick, and the oldest part of the building is plainly very old, though experts argue about the details. The church is part of the World Heritage Site that also includes Canterbury Cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey.

The setting is pleasant rather than grand, with a churchyard of old gravestones, a view across the city to the cathedral towers, and the sound of a small bell. Sturry, three kilometres to the north-east, is a village on the River Stour, and the road between them runs through suburbs. Canterbury itself is a busy cathedral and university city of fifty-odd thousand people, with a medieval wall, a pedestrianised centre and a crowd of visitors for most of the year. Thomas Becket was murdered in the cathedral in 1170, and pilgrims have come ever since, as Chaucer's tales remind us.

Riding in and around Canterbury is mostly a matter of patience. The ring road is busy, and the centre is closed to most traffic, so park in one of the multi-storey car parks or the park-and-ride sites, and walk in. Surfaces are generally fine but the cobbled lanes around the cathedral are slippery in the wet. For real riding, take the quiet roads of the Kent Downs to the south, with rolling hills, orchards, oast houses and hedged lanes, or head for the Thanet coast. In May the apple and cherry blossom is lovely.

Fuel stations are on the edge of the city and along the A2, and supermarkets are plentiful. The cafes and pubs inside the walls range from tourist traps to proper old inns, and Kentish ale and cider are the sensible drinks. Spend an hour inside the church if it is open, which is not guaranteed, and then walk down the hill into the city for the cathedral. Choose a weekday morning in spring or autumn for the best light and the thinnest crowds.
t.grand beguinage de mechelen@51.0,4.5:
Mechelen's Grand Beguinage is a small town inside a town, and the first thing that hits you on walking through its gate is the silence. Behind the walls are cobbled lanes lined with small gabled houses, a quiet church, a green square and a canal arm of the Dijle river. For centuries this was the home of the beguines, women who lived a religious life without taking formal vows, supporting themselves by weaving, lace-making, nursing and teaching. The movement began in the Low Countries in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and at its height there were hundreds of beguinages. Mechelen's was one of the largest, and most of what stands today dates from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It was listed by UNESCO in 1998 as part of the group of Flemish beguinages.

The city around it is Mechelen, about halfway between Brussels and Antwerp, and in the early sixteenth century it was the capital of the Habsburg Netherlands, ruled by Margaret of Austria, who was a patron of the arts. Her court made the city rich, and you can still see the legacy in the old palaces and the great tower of St Rumbold's cathedral, a huge unfinished spire that dominates the skyline. Today it is a small lively city of some seventy-seven thousand people, known for its tapestry, its carillon school and its beer, the Gouden Carolus, brewed by a local brewery.

Riding here is Flemish flat. The roads are well surfaced, though cobbles in the old town can be slippery in the wet, and traffic around the ring road is busy at rush hour. Belgium has plenty of speed cameras. Fuel is simple to find, and Brussels and Antwerp, both half an hour away, can supply anything else.

Try the local delicacies: Mechelse koekoek, a chicken breed served in cream sauce, and the white asparagus of the region in spring, known as Mechelse asperges. Chocolate shops are everywhere in Belgium, and a stop at one is good manners.

The best months are May and June, when the beguinage gardens bloom, and September, when the light is mellow. Winters are grey but quiet, and you can often have the lanes to yourself.
t.rice terraces of the philippine cordille:
People say the rice terraces of the Ifugao are two thousand years old, though archaeologists now think the oldest of them may be a few centuries old, and either way the thing remains astonishing. Up in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, the Ifugao people shaped whole mountainsides into stairways of stone-walled paddies, fed by bamboo pipes and channels bringing water from the forest above. If the terraces were laid end to end, it is said, they would circle half the globe. They were built by hand, without machines, and they are still farmed by hand, with rice planted in the rains and harvested once a year. UNESCO listed them in 1995, and they remain one of the country's best-known cultural landscapes.

The most famous sites are around Banaue, Batad, Bangaan, Mayoyao and Hungduan. Batad, a steep amphitheatre of terraces reached only by a hike down a long path, is the classic view. Banaue has its terraces visible from the road, a kind of green spiral rising from the valley floor. The land is sacred: the Ifugao believe in rice gods called bulul, carved as wooden figures with arms folded and knees up, and rice wine, tapuy, is part of every festival.

Getting here is half the journey. Banaue lies about a day's ride from Manila, through the plains of central Luzon and then up through the mountains, with a final stretch of narrow, winding road, landslides and the occasional waterfall across the carriageway. Many riders also come from the north by the Halsema Highway from Baguio, the highest highway in the Philippines, crossing over two thousand metres through cloud forest, mist and cabbage terraces. Fuel is available in Lagawe and Banaue, but supplies can run short, so fill up whenever you pass a station.

Typhoons between July and October bring heavy rain and slides and can cut roads for days. The dry season, from November to April, is most reliable, with the terraces golden before harvest in April, or glossy green from May to June.

Wear good waterproofs and allow extra time, because the roads are slow and the scenery will slow you more.
t.valkenburg de woerd north@52.2,4.4:
On the coast between Leiden and Katwijk, Valkenburg is a village of fewer than four thousand people with a Roman past it rarely mentions. The Oude Rijn, the old Rhine, flows through here on its last stretch toward the North Sea, and for several centuries this river was the northern edge of the Roman Empire. A fort called Praetorium Agrippinae stood on the bank at Valkenburg, one of a string of forts that now form part of the Lower German Limes, which joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2021.

De Woerd, to the north of the village, takes its name from the Dutch word for a raised patch of ground, and that tells you something about the landscape: low, wet pasture and drained polder where a bit of height once mattered. Keep that in mind when you ride out here. The roads are flat and narrow, with water on either side, and the wind comes directly in from the sea. On a motorcycle you lean into it on exposed stretches and let the cyclists, who are ready for it, pass you on the bends.

Valkenburg is also known for its former naval air station, which closed in the mid-2000s and has since been turned over to housing and nature, and you can still read its outline on the map as a large flat open area. The village has quiet streets, a few small shops and a chance to see the countryside before the dunes begin. Rijnsburg, about two kilometres off, is a bigger neighbour with a flower-growing tradition and a place in philosophical history, since Baruch Spinoza lived there in the early 1660s and a small museum remembers him.

For fuel, the nearest larger town is Rijnsburg, and Katwijk with Leiden are close enough for anything else. For coffee, Katwijk's beachfront has terraces and fried fish, and cyclists will tell you the dune paths behind Katwijk are worth a walk. If your timing allows, aim for a calm morning in May, when tulip and hyacinth fields light up the horizon, and leave before the afternoon day-trippers arrive.
t.valkenburg centrum@52.2,4.4:
A Roman fort is a surprising thing to find in a Dutch village, but Valkenburg has one buried underneath it, and the old Rhine still runs past its doorstep. The centre of the village is a small cluster of houses, a church and a few shops around a bend of the Oude Rijn, a few kilometres from the dunes of the North Sea coast. Roman soldiers built a fort here, Praetorium Agrippinae, to guard the river frontier of the empire, and the site is part of the Lower German Limes, which is now a UNESCO World Heritage property.

Little of it is visible, because the Dutch landscape swallows its past quickly, and you need a little imagination. Still, the street plan and the river line help, and an information panel or museum visit in the area can fill in some detail. Archaeologists connect the first fort here with the reign of Caligula and his abandoned plan to invade Britain, which gives a sleepy Dutch village an unlikely place in imperial gossip.

On a motorcycle the village is gentle and low-speed, with narrow streets, speed bumps and a tide of bicycles. The surroundings are flat polder, and the roads that leave it follow canals and ditches, which means few real bends and plenty of straight sections with the sea wind pushing against you. Expect to share the road with cyclists, farm vehicles and, in spring, trucks carrying flowers from the bulb fields toward the auctions. The tulip season runs through April and early May, and the fields around Katwijk and Rijnsburg are lovely then, though riding along the narrow lanes in a crowd of tourists is less fun than it looks.

Fuel can be had in Rijnsburg or in the larger towns of Katwijk and Leiden, which are all within a few minutes. Coffee in the village is simple, and Katwijk has fish, beach and a wide promenade. If you have time, the university city of Leiden, with its canals and old botanical garden, is a proper place for lunch.

An early start on a quiet, clear morning shows the mist lifting off the river and the fields outlined in silver.
t.historic city of vigan@17.6,120.4:
Vigan survived the Pacific War almost whole, and that is the secret of its charm. Founded by the Spanish in the sixteenth century as a trading post at the mouth of the Mestizo River in Ilocos Sur, on the northwest coast of Luzon, it grew rich on Chinese silk, Ilocano goods and the galleon trade, and its merchants built houses of brick and stone with wooden upper floors and sliding capiz-shell windows. Together these make one of the best-preserved colonial towns in Southeast Asia, which UNESCO recognised in 1999.

The streets are cobbled, and the best known of them, Calle Crisologo, is lined with the old mansions, many of them now shops, hotels and cafés. Horse-drawn kalesas clop along the stones, and for the rider the central lanes are best handled on foot or at walking speed. Cobbles are rough and slippery after rain, and the town is crowded on weekends and holidays, so park the bike outside the heart and wander in. Heat and humidity are strong in summer, and typhoons between July and October can bring heavy rain and wind, so check forecasts.

The surrounding coast road is a pleasure. Running north and south through rice fields, tobacco, garlic and onion plots, it passes a series of old stone churches and small seaside towns, with the South China Sea sparkling on one side and the Cordillera on the other. Traffic is a lively mix of tricycles, buses, jeepneys and trucks, and drivers overtake with confidence. Dogs and chickens cross unexpectedly. The big Baroque churches of the region, such as Paoay and San Agustin, sit within a day's ride, and their thick buttresses were designed to withstand earthquakes.

Fuel is easy in Vigan, a city of nearly fifty thousand, and food is a high point. Try empanada, a crisp rice-flour pastry filled with egg and papaya, bagnet, deep-fried pork belly, and Vigan longganisa, a garlicky local sausage. Burnay jars, made of local clay and fired in wood kilns, are a fine souvenir, though awkward on a bike.

An early start gives you the town without the tour buses, and the golden hour on the cobbles is lovely.
t.rice terrace clusters of hungduan@16.8,1:
Rice terraces here follow the contours of the land like the lines of a map. Hungduan, in the province of Ifugao, high in the Cordillera Central of northern Luzon, is known for terraces built in a tight, spiralling pattern that some describe as a spider's web, climbing the steep sides of the Hapao river valley. They are part of the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras, which UNESCO recognised in 1995, and they were shaped, over many centuries, by Ifugao farmers working without machines, using stone walls and bamboo channels to guide water from the forest above.

The work continues. Ifugao farmers grow tinawon, a heritage rice that gives only one harvest a year, and the cycle shapes the landscape: terraces are flooded and planted around December to February, glow bright green in spring and early summer, and turn gold before harvest around June and July. The Ifugao also keep alive the hudhud, a long sung epic chanted by women at planting and harvest, which UNESCO has listed as intangible heritage. In Hapao, about seven kilometres away, the hot springs below the terraces are a pleasant way to ease aching muscles after the road.

Reaching Hungduan involves a mountain drive that is as interesting as the terraces. The roads are narrow and winding, often only one lane wide with few barriers, and landslides are common in the rainy season, from June to October, especially during typhoons. Surfaces can be broken, steep sections are concreted, and fog drifts in at altitude. Take it slowly, sound your horn on blind corners and watch for jeepneys, tricycles, pigs, children and the occasional water buffalo. Cooler air at altitude is welcome after the lowland heat, but carry a rain jacket.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Hungduan has little, and the nearest larger towns are Lagawe, the provincial capital, and Banaue, a long ride away on winding roads, so fill up before heading in. Small guesthouses and homestays serve rice, local vegetables and river fish, and the coffee grown in the Cordillera is surprisingly good.

Come in late April or May, when the terraces are green and the roads are mostly dry.
t.bruges@51.2,3.2:
Bruges was rich before it was pretty. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries it was one of the great trading ports of northern Europe, a place where merchants from Italy, Spain, the Hanseatic towns and England bought wool, cloth, spices and silver, and where the first stock-exchange-like dealings took place in a square named after a family called Van der Beurse.
