Then the channel to the sea silted up, trade moved to Antwerp, and the city went into a long sleep that preserved its medieval centre almost intact. A Belgian writer called it the dead city, and the label stuck for a century.

What survives is a maze of canals, brick gables, humped bridges and cobbled lanes. The Belfry rises over the market square at about eighty-three metres, and climbing its three hundred and sixty-six steps rewards you with a view across red roofs to the polder country beyond. The Basilica of the Holy Blood holds a relic said to have been brought back from the Crusades, and in the Church of Our Lady stands a marble Madonna and Child by Michelangelo, one of the few of his works to leave Italy in his lifetime. The Begijnhof, a peaceful court of whitewashed houses built for lay sisters, is quiet in the early morning, with daffodils in spring.

Eating and drinking are serious business. Frites are served in paper cones with mayonnaise, beer comes in glasses designed for each brand, and chocolate shops line half the streets. Mussels and chips are the classic dish, and carbonnade, a beef stew with beer, is the winter comfort.

For a rider the centre is a pleasure to leave on foot and a trial to cross by bike. Cobbles are slick when wet, much of the old town is closed to cars, and parking is controlled, so leave the bike at a car park near the ring road. Beyond the walls the roads are flat, straight and often lined with poplars, running toward the coast and the dunes. Fuel stations are easy to find on the ring and the main roads. Visit on a weekday in spring or autumn, and go early to avoid the coach tours.
t.brussels@50.9,4.4:
Brussels is a city that does not quite match its reputation. People think of meetings and regulations, and the capital of Europe is indeed full of both, but the town itself is full of odd, cheerful corners. The Grand-Place is the best-known, a cobbled square ringed by gilded guild houses and a lace-like town hall, and it is lovely at night when the lights come on. A few minutes' walk away, a small bronze boy relieves himself in a fountain and is regularly dressed in costumes by local clubs, which tells you something about the local sense of humour.

Around the centre the city is a museum of building styles. Art Nouveau was born here in the 1890s, with Victor Horta's houses full of whiplash curves and sinuous ironwork, and comics are an art form, with huge murals of Tintin and other characters on walls across town. The Atomium, a giant model of an iron crystal built for the world fair of 1958, stands on the northern edge and is better in person than in photographs. Eat waffles from a stall, frites with a spoonful of mayonnaise, or a pot of mussels. Beer is taken seriously, and the monastic and lambic varieties are worth trying with someone who knows the difference.

Riding in Brussels takes patience. The traffic is heavy, the tunnels are many, and the road surface is notoriously patchy, with cobbles, potholes and tram rails to avoid. Motorways ring the city and are lit at night, and low emission zone rules apply, so check your bike's compliance. The best escape is south-east into the Sonian Forest, a huge beech woodland of tall, silver-grey trunks, with quiet roads that are a revelation after the city. Further afield, the rolling farmland of Brabant and Wallonia offers gentle, well-kept roads and a succession of small towns with a belfry and a café on the square.

Fuel is easy on the outskirts and along the main roads, and the central districts have few stations. Rain can arrive at any time of year, so carry waterproofs. May and September are the best months, with decent weather and thinner crowds. Parking the bike in a secure garage is wise, because bikes are a target for thieves in busy areas of the centre.
t.ghent@51.1,3.7:
Ghent likes to think of itself as the city that Bruges forgot to be. It is a large, lively, slightly rebellious town at the meeting of the Leie and the Scheldt, and for centuries it was one of the biggest cities north of the Alps, a textile power whose weavers and guilds fought dukes and counts. The memory of that stubbornness lingers. Locals are known as the noose-bearers, after a day in 1540 when citizens were made to parade in nooses to atone for rebelling against Emperor Charles V, who was born in the town.

The centre is dramatic. Gravensteen, the castle of the counts, stands with its walls and towers right in the middle of town, complete with a moat and a set of grim medieval torture instruments in the displays. Along the waterfront, the Graslei and Korenlei quays are lined with tall merchants' houses with stepped gables, and the whole scene reflected in the canal at dusk is among the finest views in Belgium. Three towers dominate the skyline, the Belfry, the cathedral of Saint Bavo and Saint Nicholas' Church, and inside Saint Bavo hangs the Ghent Altarpiece by the van Eyck brothers, finished in 1432 and one of the great paintings of the world, with a startling clarity of detail that makes you lean in.

For a rider, the centre is largely closed to traffic, and trams and bikes dominate. Park at the edge, take a walk, and return when the evening cool arrives. Outside, the countryside is classic Flanders: flat, green, fringed by poplars, with farms and small canals. Roads are narrow and fast, with cyclists and tractors, and plenty of roundabouts, and the weather is changeable, so be ready for a shower. There is a speed camera culture here, and fines are real.

Food in Ghent is relaxed and good. Try waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish, and cuberdons, purple cone-shaped sweets sold from stalls, which have a soft, sticky centre. Fuel is easily found on the outskirts of a city of well over two hundred thousand people. Spring is lovely when the blossom opens, and the Ghent Festival in July fills the streets with music, though it is hard to find a parking space.
t.essex saltmarsh and suffolk villages sce:
Hadleigh Castle stands on a ridge above the Thames estuary, a ruin of crumbling towers that Constable painted in 1829 under a stormy sky. The pin sits beside it, near South Benfleet and Pitsea, on the edge of south Essex, where the land drops to the creeks and saltmarshes of the estuary. The sea is just beyond the marshes, with Canvey Island and the oil tanks across the creek, and the whole scene is wide, flat and grey-blue, with huge skies and a smell of mud and salt.

South Benfleet has an old place in English history. In 894, a Danish army held a fortified camp here, and King Alfred's forces attacked and defeated it, an event recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Nothing of the camp remains, but the creek and the church above it give a sense of the place. Hadleigh, a larger town, has the castle and a country park that climbs the hill, with views over the water toward Kent. Pitsea, once known for brickworks and a huge landfill, now has a country park with lakes and walking trails.

The riding is more varied than you would expect. The old Southend Road, the A13, is busy and often congested, and the roads around Benfleet are urban. But a short ride south, near the castle, there are quiet roads with sea views, and to the north the lanes through Rayleigh and Hockley rise gently into low wooded hills. The surface is generally good, but the traffic is heavy at weekends and on summer afternoons, when everyone heads for the coast.

Fuel, food and coffee are never far away. South Benfleet has supermarkets, cafés and fuel stations, and Southend, a few kilometres east, has a seafront with the longest pleasure pier in the world, a mile and a third out into the estuary, which is a good place for fish and chips if you like salt wind and seagulls.

The castle is the thing to see, and an early morning is best, before the dog walkers and the crowds, with the light coming low across the water. It is a hard spot to find a bad photograph, even on a grey day, since the cloud and the ruin suit each other.
t.peak district overnight escape scenic ro:
The Medway comes through Maidstone as a wide, slow river with old warehouses and a bridge, and the pin sits just upstream from the town, where the valley narrows and the roads follow the water between orchards and hop fields. This is the Weald of Kent, the Garden of England, and the landscape has the look of a place that has been farmed with great care for a very long time. Oast houses with their white-capped cowls appear in every village, a reminder of the hop-drying industry that once employed thousands of London families who came every September for the harvest.

Maidstone, with over a hundred thousand people, is the county town, with every kind of shop, fuel station and café, and it is a good place to restock. Marden and Yalding are smaller villages with a quieter character. Yalding stands where the Beult and the Teise join the Medway, and the long medieval bridge at the village is a lovely old structure, though the whole area floods in wet winters. Leeds Castle, on the east side of Maidstone, sits in the middle of a lake and is one of the most beautiful castles in England, with a bird park and a maze.

The riding is excellent, with narrow lanes that twist between orchards and old farm buildings, and the roads that follow the Medway valley are smooth and winding. South toward Marden and Staplehurst the country becomes flatter, with wide fields and straight roads, and the B and unclassified roads are quiet outside the weekend. Surfaces are generally good, but wet leaves, mud and farm traffic can be a hazard in autumn. The best time is late spring, when the cherry and apple blossom fill the orchards with white and pink, and in September, when the fruit is ripe and the hops are being picked.

For practical matters, there are fuel stations and cafés along the road into Maidstone, and village pubs throughout the valley, many with a garden. Farm shops sell apples, cider and local cheeses, and a short stop is a good way to taste what the county grows.

The ride is the Peak District Overnight Escape, and the route plainly uses this stop as a start, so make sure the tank is full and the bike is packed before you head north.
t.antwerp@51.2,4.4:
Antwerp is a city that made its fortune twice and will tell you about both. In the sixteenth century it was the richest trading port in northern Europe, a place of merchants, printers and painters on the Scheldt, until war and the closing of the river sent the money elsewhere. Then the port revived, and today it is the second largest in Europe, a vast maze of docks, cranes and chemical plants running north of the old town, with about four hundred and sixty thousand people living in the city itself.

At the centre, the Cathedral of Our Lady lifts its single tall spire above the old streets, and inside it hangs Rubens's Descent from the Cross, one of the great paintings of the Baroque. Rubens lived and worked in the city, and his house is a short walk away. Nearby, the Plantin-Moretus Museum preserves the printing house of the family who turned Antwerp into a publishing capital, with its sixteenth-century presses and type still in place. Around Central Station, a railway palace of stone and glass built in the early twentieth century, the diamond district still handles a large share of the world's rough stones.

The riding is hardly the point here: Antwerp's centre is a tangle of cobbled lanes, trams and one-way systems, and the ring road, the R1, is among the busiest in Belgium, with heavy truck traffic and constant lane changes. Treat the city as a base and head out by the quieter roads to the east and north. The Campine country towards Wortel and Hoogstraten is flat, sandy and wooded, with long, quiet lanes between fields and pine, and the beguinage in Mechelen to the south, a walled enclave of small houses and gardens, is the sort of quiet that cities forget. Cobbles, tram tracks and wet leaves are the hazards, and the weather in Flanders can turn grey without warning.

Fuel is no problem in a city this size, and neither is food. Go for a paper cone of fries from a frietkot with a dollop of mayonnaise, or a bowl of stoofvlees, beef stewed in dark beer. The old town has brown cafes that serve Belgian beer by the glass, and the sweet shops sell Antwerpse handjes, small biscuits shaped like hands, a reference to a legend about a giant and a severed hand. May and September are the best months, when the terraces are open and the light is gentle on the stone.
t.london motorcycle escapes@51.1,0.6:
Cranbrook stands in the High Weald of Kent, a hilly, wooded country of sandstone ridges and winding lanes, and in the Middle Ages it was one of the richest towns in the county, thanks to the cloth trade. Edward III encouraged Flemish weavers to settle here in the fourteenth century, and the broadcloth they made brought wealth to the town, visible today in the big timber-framed houses and the huge church known as the Cathedral of the Weald. On the edge of the town stands Union Mill, an eighteenth-century smock mill that is the tallest working windmill of its kind in Britain.

A few kilometres away, Sissinghurst is famous for its castle garden, created in the 1930s by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her husband Harold Nicolson among the ruins of an Elizabethan house. The white garden and the tower, which was Vita's writing room, are widely known, and the property belongs to the National Trust. Hawkhurst, a village of nearly four thousand people, is bigger, with a long street of shops and an old pond called the Moor. Tenterden, eight kilometres away with just over seven thousand people, has the nearest fuel and a handsome wide high street lined with weatherboarded houses.

The swim stop on the label should be taken lightly, because there is no beach here, and the pools of the Weald are mostly private. For a rider, the pleasure is in the lanes themselves, which are narrow and twisting, with high banks, overhanging trees and sudden dips where a stream crosses. Take them slowly, because blind bends and farm vehicles are common. The surface is often patched and the verges soft, and in wet weather mud can wash across the road in the low spots.

The High Weald is at its best in spring, when the woods are carpeted with bluebells and the orchards bloom, and in autumn, when the beeches and oaks turn bronze. Summer brings crowds to Sissinghurst, so aim for a weekday or an early start. A cream tea in one of the village tearooms is a very English way to finish.
t.cambridge fen edge and ely@51.3,0.3:
Culverstone Green and Meopham lie on the dip slope of the North Downs in Kent, a landscape of chalk hills, steep woods and fields of wheat, and they feel remote from London although the M25 is only a few kilometres to the west. Meopham, with about four thousand four hundred people, has one of the largest village greens in the county, with a cricket pitch, and its smock windmill is one of the best preserved in Kent. Wrotham, a little further south, is on the Pilgrims' Way and the North Downs Way, ancient routes along the chalk ridge. West Kingsdown, six kilometres off, is the nearest bigger place and has the shops and fuel stations a long ride demands.

The label says fuel gate, and the business is simple. Top up here before heading north and east, because the villages around have few stations and the long rides across Essex and Cambridgeshire have stretches where services are far apart. Meopham and Culverstone have a couple of shops and cafés for a first coffee and a pastry. The Downs here give a good start to the day, with roads that wind up wooded slopes and over ridges, with views opening out toward the Medway and the Thames estuary.

The surface is generally good, but the lanes are narrow and the banks high, and fallen leaves or mud can make bends slippery. Traffic is light except around the main roads toward the motorway. The chalk soil gives the hedgerows a rich variety of wild flowers in summer, including orchids on the road verges, and the beech hangers on the steep slopes are lovely in autumn. The area is also a favourite with cyclists and horse riders, so slow down for them.

The Downs are a good reminder that the best of the English countryside lies close to the capital, and it is worth a few minutes to enjoy it before the motorway miles. A quiet moment on Meopham Green, watching the cricket if it is a Saturday, is one of the pleasures of the county. On a clear day the Thames estuary glints far away to the north.
t.cambridge fen edge and ely@51.7,0.9:
The Dengie peninsula is one of Essex's quiet corners, a flat, windswept tongue of land between the Blackwater and the Crouch, and it feels a long way from London. Southminster, with just over four thousand people, is its main village, with a small high street, a railway station that connects to the capital and a pair of pubs. Burnham-on-Crouch, seven kilometres south, is the sailing town of the area, a Georgian waterfront on the north bank of the river, lined with yacht clubs and chandlers, where Burnham Week, a regatta that has been held since the nineteenth century, fills the water with sails every August.

Food is the point of the stop. Burnham, with about seventy-five hundred people, has fuel, bakeries, fish and chip shops and a handful of good pubs along the quay, and Mayland, a smaller place on the opposite shore, has a few more. Oysters from the nearby Blackwater estuary and salt from Maldon, a few kilometres north, are part of the local larder, and a plate of fresh seafood on a summer evening is hard to beat.

The roads on the Dengie are long, flat and exposed, with big skies and big wind, and they run between fields of wheat and beet, with the sea wall always somewhere beyond the next rise. Be ready for crosswinds, especially when the weather turns, and for farm vehicles that take the whole width of the lane. In summer the heat haze can make the horizon shimmer, and in winter the wind from the North Sea is bitter. The surface is mostly good, apart from patches by field entrances.

At the far end of the peninsula stands St Peter's Chapel at Bradwell-on-Sea, built in the seventh century of Roman bricks, one of the oldest surviving churches in England. It stands alone on the sea wall, with salt marsh on one side and the grey estuary on the other, and it is a haunting place, especially in the evening light. If you have time, it is worth the extra miles, though you will need to walk the last stretch.
t.cambridge fen edge and ely high point@51:
Takeley is known for two things that could hardly be more different: Stansted Airport, which has swallowed much of the surrounding farmland, and Hatfield Forest, one of the best surviving examples of a medieval royal hunting forest in England. The forest, owned by the National Trust, has ancient pollarded oaks and hornbeams, grassy glades, a lake and a small shell house, and the wood has been managed in much the same way for nearly a thousand years. It lies just south of the village and offers a sudden stillness amid the roar of jets and the M11.

The high point on this ride is a low rise on the boulder clay plateau of north-west Essex, where the land swells enough to give long views over big fields and scattered woods, and the church towers of Thaxted and Great Dunmow can be picked out on a clear day. Great Dunmow, five kilometres away with nearly seven thousand eight hundred people, has the fuel and shops, and Takeley, with over three thousand three hundred, has a village shop and a pub. The area's flat, open character means the wind is a constant companion.

The riding here is straightforward. The roads run in long gentle curves between hedgerows, with a few villages to slow you down, and the surface is mostly good. Aircraft pass low overhead as they approach Stansted, and the noise is a strange contrast to the pastoral view. Traffic near the airport can be heavy, especially at holiday times, with taxis and coaches filling the lanes, so choose the minor roads to the north and west where it is much quieter.

If you stop at Hatfield Forest, you can walk under the old trees and sit by the lake, where families feed the ducks and children play in the shallows. The forest was a hunting ground for the Norman kings, and the ancient trees seem to remember. It is a good example of how the English countryside can survive beside modern infrastructure, and a few minutes in the shade give the day a different rhythm.
t.westerham lanes@51.3,0.1:
Westerham is a small Kent town of about three thousand people, tucked into the Darent valley under the escarpment of the North Downs, and it has a bigger history than its size suggests. General James Wolfe, who captured Quebec in 1759, was born here, and his statue stands on the green opposite a statue of Winston Churchill, who lived at Chartwell, a few kilometres to the south. Squerryes Court, a seventeenth-century manor house with gardens, stands on the edge of town and has been home to the same family for centuries.

Chartwell, a short ride away, is where Churchill lived from 1924 until his death, and the house, garden and studio, with its easel and brushes, are kept much as he left them. It is a National Trust property with a good café, and the view over the Weald from the terrace explains why he chose it. Biggin Hill, up on the Downs to the north, was one of the key fighter airfields in the Battle of Britain, and its history is commemorated with a chapel and a museum.

The lanes around Westerham are among the best in the Home Counties. The road climbs the escarpment in a series of bends through beech woods, with views south across the Weald, and the lanes beyond wind through farmland and small villages. The A25 runs through the town and carries much of the traffic, so the minor roads are quieter, and they are best on a weekday morning when the cyclists and weekend drivers have not yet arrived. The surface can be rough in places, with potholes and mud.

Fuel is available in Oxted, five kilometres away, with over thirteen thousand people, and at a few stations on the main road. Sundridge, a village nearby, has a church and a pub, and Westerham itself has several cafés and a good bakery. It is a fine place to finish a ride, with the light sinking behind the Downs, the old pubs glowing and the smell of woodsmoke on the evening air.
t.surrey hills and box hill bends@51.7,0.1:
Epping Forest begins almost at the edge of London and runs north-east for some twenty kilometres, a remnant of the great royal forest that once covered most of Essex. Its ancient hornbeams, cut for centuries by commoners who were allowed to take firewood from the upper branches, have grown into gnarled, twisted shapes that give the woods a strange and beautiful character. In 1878 an Act of Parliament saved the forest from enclosure and handed it to the City of London Corporation as a public space, and it remains one of the great gifts of Victorian conservation.

The villages at its edge, Theydon Bois, Abridge and Epping, are all within a few kilometres. Epping, a market town of just over ten thousand people, is the northernmost stop on the Central Line of the Underground, and it has fuel stations, supermarkets and a good selection of cafés and pubs. Theydon Bois, with its village green and its pubs, feels a world away from the city, while Abridge is a small village on the River Roding with a handful of old buildings.

The fuel gate is a practical start, and the ride heads north from here into Essex and Hertfordshire. Roads through the forest are generally good, but the speed limits are low and enforced, and for good reason: deer wander across the roads, cyclists and horse riders are common, and the traffic on the A104 and A121 can be heavy at peak hours. Early on a weekday morning is the best time, when the mist lies among the trees and the forest feels silent.

If you have time before setting off, a walk among the beeches and hornbeams, especially in autumn, is rewarding. The forest has two ancient hill forts, Ambresbury Banks and Loughton Camp, and the legend that Boudicca made her last stand at Ambresbury Banks, though not proven, adds a certain drama to the place. Fill the tank, buy a coffee and enjoy the last bit of woodland before the open country.
t.surrey hills and box hill bends high poi:
Wrotham sits at the foot of the North Downs, at a point where the Pilgrims' Way and the old road from London to the Channel ports pass, and its flint church and small square have the look of a village that has seen centuries of travellers. Borough Green, a larger village of over four thousand people beside it, has the shops and fuel. Kemsing, a short distance west, has about seven thousand people and a church dedicated to St Edith, a tenth-century princess who is said to have been born there and whose holy well still attracts visitors.

The high point is the top of Wrotham Hill, where the road crosses the chalk escarpment and the land drops away to the Weald. From the lay-by and the viewpoint you can see a vast stretch of Kent, with orchards, oasts, woods and distant church spires, and on a clear day the view reaches to the Sussex Downs. The M26 and A20 run through here, so the hum of traffic is constant, but a few minutes' walk along the North Downs Way brings you to quieter places among the trees.

Riding up the hill, the road makes a series of broad bends through beech and yew, and the surface is generally good. At the top, the wind can be strong and the weather quite different from that of the valley below, so a layer of clothing is useful. The lanes that branch off along the ridge are narrow and quiet, with high hedges and glimpses of the plain.

Chalk grassland on the slopes is home to rare orchids and butterflies in summer, and the yew woods are among the oldest in Kent. In autumn the beeches turn brilliant copper. For coffee, Borough Green has cafés, and a few of the villages have good pubs. Choose a clear day, bring a camera and pause at the viewpoint, where the Weald lies spread out like a map.
t.surrey hills and box hill bends scenic r:
Grays is a Thames-side town of nearly ninety thousand people on the Essex shore of the river, and the stretch of land around it is among the most industrial and the least visited in the whole region. Tilbury, a few kilometres east, has one of the country's major container ports, and its docks are where the Empire Windrush landed in 1948 carrying hundreds of Caribbean migrants. The old Tilbury Fort, a star-shaped artillery fortress built in the seventeenth century, still guards the river, and nearby is the spot where Elizabeth I is said to have given her famous speech to the troops in 1588 as the Armada approached.

Across the river, Swanscombe, on the Kent side, is the site where the skull of Swanscombe Man was found in the 1930s, a human ancestor about four hundred thousand years old. These two shores, Essex and Kent, face each other across the water, linked by the great QEII bridge and the Dartford Crossing, and a trip along the estuary gives a sense of the power and the grit of the Thames. It is not a pretty landscape, but it has a raw grandeur.

The ride ends here, and the practical needs are easy. Grays has everything, with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Tilbury has a few cafés near the docks. Roads are busy with lorries and port traffic, and the roundabouts and slip roads call for care. The best views are from the sea wall paths, where you can watch container ships pass.

The light over the estuary is often wonderful in the evening, with long shadows, orange sky and the silhouettes of cranes against the water. The air smells of salt, diesel and mud, and gulls wheel overhead. Take a short walk on the riverbank before the traffic swallows you again, and think about the great ships that have passed here. It is a rough-edged ending to a day, but a memorable one.
t.chilterns ridge and thames valley high p:
Royal Tunbridge Wells owes its existence to a spring. In 1606 a young nobleman, Dudley, Lord North, found a chalybeate spring here that he believed cured his ailments, and soon the court was visiting to take the waters. Queen Henrietta Maria stayed after the birth of a son, and the town became a fashionable resort. Its colonnaded walkway, the Pantiles, where visitors promenaded and drank the iron-rich water, still survives, lined with shops, cafés and restaurants, and the spring can still be seen under its canopy. The town has nearly sixty-nine thousand people and every service imaginable.

The sandstone outcrops of the High Weald are a feature of the town's surroundings. At Rusthall Common, the Toad Rock, a weathered boulder shaped much like its name, has been a Victorian curiosity for generations, and High Rocks, a few kilometres west, is an outcrop of dramatic cliffs and gorges. Speldhurst, a village of about fourteen hundred people, has a church with Pre-Raphaelite stained glass by Edward Burne-Jones, and a pub that claims to be one of the oldest in Kent.

The high point is the ridge that carries the town, where the road climbs from the valley and offers glimpses of the Weald through gaps in the woods. The riding around is excellent, with narrow lanes, steep banks, and sandstone cuttings, and the bends are tight enough to hold your attention. The surface is variable, and mud and leaves collect in the sunken sections, so take care in wet weather.

The phrase Disgusted of Tunbridge Wells has long been used for the stereotypical letter-writer of a conservative persuasion, and the town takes it with good humour. A pot of tea on the Pantiles is a delight, and the town has some excellent independent shops. Weekends can be crowded, especially in summer, so plan for a weekday if you can. In autumn, the woods around the town are golden.
t.chilterns ridge and thames valley scenic:
The land east of Sevenoaks is a hinge between two Kents, with the chalk ridge of the North Downs to the north and the clay and sandstone of the Weald to the south, and the lanes that run between them are among the best in the county. Sevenoaks, five kilometres away with nearly thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Tonbridge is a similar distance in the other direction. Hadlow, a village known for its gothic tower, lies a little further on.

Knole, a vast house at Sevenoaks, is one of the great houses of England, a medieval palace of the archbishops of Canterbury that later passed to the Sackville family and is said to have a room for every day of the year. Its deer park, with a herd of fallow and sika deer, is open to walkers, and the house inspired Virginia Woolf's novel Orlando, written for her friend Vita Sackville-West, who grew up there. Ightham Mote, a few kilometres east, is a moated manor house of the fourteenth century, one of the best preserved in the country, with a half-timbered courtyard.

The ride here finishes on a pass of sorts, a ridge crossing on the Greensand escarpment, where the road climbs through woods and gives a view south over the Weald. The roads are narrow and winding, with beech and oak overhanging, and the bends are of the kind that reward a smooth rhythm. The surface is patchy, with potholes and mud, and cyclists are numerous, particularly at weekends. Take it slowly and enjoy the scenery.

At the end of a day, a pub in one of the villages makes a pleasant finish, and many of them have gardens for fine evenings. The light on the Weald in the low sun, with long shadows across the fields and the oast houses glowing, is among the most characteristic sights in Kent. Fill the tank before you go home, because the back lanes have few stations.
t.peak district overnight escape photo pul:
Leysdown-on-Sea is on the Isle of Sheppey, a flat island off the north coast of Kent, separated from the mainland by the narrow channel of the Swale, and its beach, caravan parks and amusement arcades give it a faded seaside character. It also has a place in aviation history. In 1909, the pioneers of British flying, including the Short brothers and members of the Aero Club, set up an airfield at Leysdown, and John Moore-Brabazon made the first official powered flight by a British pilot in Britain there. A few kilometres inland, Eastchurch took over as the centre of the flying, and the Royal Navy trained some of its first pilots there.

At the eastern tip, Shellness has a long shingle spit covered with shells and backed by marshland of the Swale National Nature Reserve, with huge numbers of wading birds in winter. Whitstable, on the mainland across the water, with over thirty thousand people, is the nearest large place with fuel and food, and it is famous for its oysters, eaten fresh at the harbour or at a seafood restaurant. The journey across the Sheppey Crossing, a high bridge, offers a wide view of the estuary.

The riding on Sheppey is flat and exposed, with wind the main factor, and the roads run between marshes and fields with little shelter. The surface is generally good, but the road onto the island can be congested, especially in summer when the caravan parks are full. For a photo, the beach and the long sea wall are good subjects, and the sky is huge, with spectacular sunsets over the estuary.

Services on the island are limited, so fill the tank on the mainland. Leysdown has cafés and fish and chip shops, and a quiet pause here, with the sea air and the cry of gulls, is a welcome change from the roads. The peak district is a long way off, and the road there starts with the long grind through Kent and the motorway.
t.essex saltmarsh photo pull off@51.7,0.8:
The Dengie peninsula is the bit of Essex that most people drive past on the way to somewhere else, which is exactly why it is worth the detour. Mayland sits at the head of a tidal creek on the northern shore of the Blackwater estuary, and the pull-off here looks out over saltmarsh that changes colour with the season: grey-green in summer, rust and purple in the autumn, silver when the tide is full and the sky is low. The land is so flat that clouds seem to do most of the scenery work.

The riding that gets you here is quiet Essex lane stuff, narrow, hedged, with sharp ninety-degree bends where a field boundary once demanded them. It is not a road for pushing on. Farm tractors, mud on the tarmac after harvest and the occasional cyclist mean you take it at a walking-pace-plus, and the reward is the smell when you stop the engine: mud, salt, a trace of seaweed and diesel from the boats. Wind can come off the estuary with nothing to slow it, so a crosswind on an exposed causeway is worth respecting.

Maldon, seven kilometres away, is the sensible place for fuel and a proper meal, and it has a long story for a small town. The Battle of Maldon was fought on the estuary in 991, when a Viking army faced Essex levies on the causeway to Northey Island, and an Old English poem about it survives. Today the town is better known for its flaky sea salt, boiled from the estuary water in the same family workshop tradition for generations, and for the tan-sailed Thames barges that still moor along the Hythe. Heybridge Basin, just beyond, is where the canal meets the tide and is a pleasant place for a tea and a look at the boats.

Birdwatchers will tell you this coast matters far more than it looks. The saltmarsh and mudflats of the Blackwater are an internationally protected wintering ground for brent geese, and on a cold morning the sky fills with them. Go early, in spring or autumn, when the light is low and gold on the water and the lanes are empty. Bring a layer even in July, because the wind never really stops here.
t.hampshire test valley roads scenic road@:
Northwest Essex is a quiet landscape, a land of big skies, wide arable fields and gentle valleys, and it hides in the shadow of the airport. The pin is near Newport and Elsenham, with Stansted Mountfitchet a few minutes away, and the roads here are among the best lanes in the county. They are narrow, undulating and often empty, with lines of hedge and the odd village pond, and they are a good place to learn how Essex can be rolling and generous when you leave the main roads.

The ground is chalky boulder clay, heavy and fertile, and the fields are famous for wheat, barley and oilseed rape. In May the rape flowers turn whole hillsides a shocking yellow, in July the wheat goes gold, and in autumn the ploughed earth turns a deep brown. The valleys are modest but real, and the villages sit in them, with timber-framed houses, thatch and plastered walls painted in soft pinks and creams. It is a landscape where the buildings are as interesting as the roads.

Stansted Mountfitchet has a surprising claim. A motte-and-bailey castle was built here after the Norman Conquest, and a reconstruction of it now stands on the original site, with wooden palisades and timber houses that give a real sense of how a Norman stronghold looked. The village also has a windmill, one of the best preserved in the county. The airport, which opened as an American air base in the war, sits just beyond, and you can often see jets climbing over the fields as you ride.

The practical side is easy. Stansted Mountfitchet has fuel, shops and cafes, and Newport has pubs and a few places for lunch, so you will not go hungry. Roads can be greasy after rain and muddy at harvest, and farm vehicles are a hazard around the villages, so keep your speed down on blind bends. The lanes between Newport and Saffron Walden, just to the north, are among the best in the county, and an early start on a dry spring morning, with mist in the hollows, is the best way to enjoy them.
t.hastings cliffs and high weald high poin:
The Blackwater estuary is the biggest in Essex, and this corner of it, the north shore of the Dengie and the lanes behind Mersea Island, feels as far from London as you can get without leaving the county. The coordinates sit among low fields and sea walls, close to the water, and the horizon is dominated by sky. Southminster, Tollesbury and West Mersea all lie within a short ride, and each has its own character: a market village, a sailing harbour and an island town.

West Mersea, nine kilometres away, is the place to go for food and fuel. The island is reached by a causeway called the Strood, which floods at the highest tides, so check the tide table before you cross. Oysters have been farmed here since Roman times, and Mersea natives are still prized, so a plate of them at the waterfront is a fine reward after the ride. Tollesbury, on the other side of the creek, is a sailing village with rows of old boats and a long history of yacht crews, and its saltmarsh is a joy for walkers.

Further along the Dengie coast, near Bradwell-on-Sea, stands one of the oldest churches in England: the chapel of St Peter-on-the-Wall, built in the seventh century by St Cedd, using stones from a Roman fort. It stands alone on the sea wall, a plain stone barn of a building, and it is a place that makes you think about how long people have lived on this edge of the world. A short walk takes you out to it from the car park, along a track with the sea on one side and the fields on the other. The nuclear power station that stands nearby is being decommissioned, and its silhouette dominates the skyline in an odd, silent way.

The roads out here are narrow and quiet, with sharp bends where they follow old field boundaries, and a strong wind can push you about on the open stretches. Late summer, when the samphire is ready and the saltmarsh turns purple with sea lavender, is the best time. Winter brings flocks of brent geese and bitter cold, so wrap up and keep your visor clear. Allow time to take the long way round, because this is a coast that rewards being slow.
t.cambridge@52.2,0.1:
Cambridge is flat, and for a motorcyclist that is both its weakness and its secret. The city sits where the chalk of the Gog Magog hills runs out into the fens, and the River Cam wanders through its heart past the colleges, between lawns and willows, under little bridges where punts jostle on summer afternoons. King's College Chapel, begun in the fifteenth century and finished under the early Tudors, has a fan-vaulted ceiling that looks as if it were carved from lace, and its choir sings evensong most days of term. More than 158,000 people live here, so fuel, food and a bed are never in doubt.

The city is a very hard place to ride in the middle. Cyclists rule the narrow streets, bus gates and one-way systems cut across the centre, and parking for anything with an engine is scarce and expensive. Do the sensible thing: park at the edge, perhaps near one of the big park-and-ride sites, and walk in. The old courts and lanes are best seen on foot anyway, and the Backs, the lawns behind the colleges along the river, are impossible to see from a saddle.

Leave the city and the reward arrives. East and north, the land opens into the fens, a country drained from marsh by Dutch engineers in the seventeenth century, black-soiled and so level that the sky seems to take up three-quarters of the view. The roads here run dead straight along dykes and drains, and every so often take a sharp right angle for no reason except the line of an old ditch. Wind is the main hazard, and in winter, fog and frost. To the south-east the Gog Magog hills offer the only real climbing for miles, a gentle ridge of beech and chalk grassland.

For a start or finish, Cambridge has a very good rhythm. A morning coffee in a bakery, a quiet departure while the students are still asleep, and an evening return along the river, when the college windows light up one by one and the bells begin. It is a city of long memories, and a few of them linger in the way the evening light falls on the old stone.
t.exmoor moorland@51.5,0.3:
Orsett is a quiet Essex village with a surprising amount of history. The pin lands between it and South Ockendon, in Thurrock, on the north bank of the Thames, where the land is flat, open and marshy, and the great river is only a few kilometres south. Tilbury, with its Tudor fort and its docks, lies about six kilometres to the south, and Grays and the big Lakeside shopping centre are to the west.

It is far from the Exmoor and Norfolk coast of the ride's name, and it is a cheerful, low-key final point. The roads here are fast and mostly straight, linking the A13, the M25 and the Dartford Crossing, and heavy goods traffic is constant. The Thames marshes give long views and large skies, and on a clear evening, the sunset over the water and the cranes of the docks has a harsh beauty. Orsett and its neighbours have narrow lanes between farmland that reward a slower pace, though surfaces are patchy.

The area's history is tied to the river. Tilbury Fort was built by Henry VIII and used by Elizabeth I when she gave her famous speech to the troops in 1588 to face the Spanish Armada. In 1948 the ship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, bringing one of the first large groups of Caribbean migrants to Britain. Orsett Fen, in the village, has a nature reserve with ponds and wildfowl, and the village itself retains its old church and green.

For fuel, South Ockendon and Grays have stations and supermarkets, and the Lakeside area has a full range of chain restaurants. Orsett has a few pubs, a small shop and a village hall, and a pint at a village inn is a traditional way to relax. The riverside at Tilbury has a ferry to Gravesend and a pleasant walk along the sea wall.

Take your time here, because the light over the estuary is worth an extra hour. It is an unpretentious place with a long history and a big sky.
t.cambridge fen@51.3,0.3:
Brands Hatch is only a few minutes' ride west, and for any motorcyclist the name needs no explanation. The pin lands in the North Downs of Kent, near Culverstone Green and Meopham, with West Kingsdown, the nearest town of any size, six kilometres away, and the circuit close to it. The hills here are chalk, wooded and gently folded, and the lanes run along the ridges and through the dry valleys.

For a ride that began among the fens near Cambridge, this is a kinder landscape. The roads are narrow, with sharp bends, hedges and old trees, and the surface is variable, patched and sometimes gritty. Traffic is light on the lanes, though it builds on the A20 and the A227. The best riding is on a dry morning in spring or early autumn, when the beech woods are fresh and the air is clear. On race weekends at Brands Hatch, the roads around are busy with bikes and cars.

Meopham is an old village with a large green, a cricket pitch and a windmill that has stood on the hill for two centuries. The Pilgrims' Way, the old route from Winchester to Canterbury, runs along the foot of the Downs not far south, and its chalk path is popular with walkers. Wrotham and Trosley, villages nearby, have old churches and country parks with long views over the Weald, and are worth a short detour.

Fuel is available at West Kingsdown and Gravesend, and the village shops in Meopham sell basic supplies. For a coffee or a bite, the country pubs along the lanes are friendly, and a bacon roll at a roadside cafe near the circuit is a motorcycling tradition. The Medway valley, down to the south, has more choice.

As the closing stage of a long day, it is a landscape that eases you down: open chalk, old woods and a small circuit with a big name.
t.surrey hills@51.7,0.1:
Epping Forest is the main reason to come, and the pin lands on its edge, between Abridge and Theydon Bois, a few kilometres south of Epping. The forest is what is left of a huge royal hunting ground, and it covers about two thousand hectares of ancient woodland, heath and ponds, running from the edge of London to the Essex countryside. The trees are mostly hornbeam and beech, many of them pollarded, cut high in the past to give a crop of wood, and they have an odd, twisted shape.

After a ride that started in the Cotswolds, it is an easy and calm place to finish. The roads through the forest are narrow and winding, with gentle bends, overhanging trees and a surface that is often patchy, with leaves, mud and branches after storms. Deer, including fallow and muntjac, wander across without warning, and dusk is the most dangerous time. Traffic is moderate on weekdays, but heavy on sunny Sundays, with cyclists and walkers in large numbers.

Theydon Bois is a pleasant village with a green and a Central line station, which makes a quick journey into London possible. The forest was saved from enclosure in the nineteenth century by a public campaign, and the City of London Corporation took it over in 1878, an act that kept it open to everyone. Queen Elizabeth's Hunting Lodge, a Tudor timber building at Chingford, stands at the southern end and holds a small museum.

Fuel and food are easy at Epping, a market town with stations, supermarkets and cafes, and Theydon has several pubs and a bakery. The forest has a number of tea huts, small cafes in wooden buildings along the roads, and a mug of tea and a bacon roll from one of them is a London rider's tradition.

Walk a few steps into the trees if you have time. In autumn the leaves are thick underfoot and the smell of damp earth is strong.
t.dorset jurassic coast long day@51.1,0.0:
Ashdown Forest is the place where Winnie-the-Pooh lives, and the villagers of Forest Row and Hartfield know it. A. A. Milne had a country home nearby, and his son Christopher Robin played among the heather and pines that he turned into the Hundred Acre Wood, so the open heathland, with its clumps of Scots pine, a lookout called Gills Lap and a little bridge for the game of Pooh Sticks, has become a place of pilgrimage. It is also real, rough, windswept heath on sandy soil, one of the largest areas of open access land in south-east England, and in August the heather turns purple.

The fuel gate here is on the edge of this country, near Forest Row, Horsted Keynes and Ardingly, in the High Weald of West Sussex and East Sussex, a region of small fields, ancient woods, sunken lanes and half-timbered farms. Forest Row is the largest, with about three and a half thousand people, and the stations in the area are modest, so top up the tank in a larger town such as East Grinstead or Haywards Heath if you need to. At Horsted Keynes a preserved steam railway, the Bluebell, runs old locomotives through the woods, and at Ardingly a large reservoir offers a quiet walk and a view of the water.

The ride is called the Dorset Jurassic Coast Long Day, and it heads south and west across the South Downs and along the coast. It is a long day and an early start helps. The roads in the Weald are twisty and narrow, with high hedges and blind corners, and the surfaces can be rough, so ride cautiously in the first hour. The lanes can be muddy after rain, with hay and leaves, and fog is common in the valleys in autumn mornings.

The best seasons are spring, with bluebells in the woods, and autumn. In summer, weekends bring walkers and cyclists in large numbers. A coffee at one of the village tea rooms is a pleasant way to start, and the heath is a good place to take a photograph before you set out, with the forest stretching away in the early light.
t.dorset jurassic coast long day@51.9,1.2:
Great Bentley has the largest village green in England, or so its residents will tell you, and the claim is plausible, because the green covers dozens of acres, with a cricket pitch in the middle and old houses all around. It is a lovely sight on a summer afternoon, with the click of bat on ball and children running across the grass. The neighbouring villages of Thorpe-le-Soken and Little Clacton are similarly quiet and rural, set among the flat fields and creeks of the Tendring peninsula, in the north-east corner of Essex.

The soil is rich and the farms are large, and the landscape is open, with big skies and long views, with tidal creeks and salt marshes on the coast a few kilometres away. Brightlingsea, Walton-on-the-Naze and Clacton are the nearest seaside towns, and fish and chips on the sea wall is a good way to finish a day. Thorpe-le-Soken has an unusual name, because soken was an old word for a district with its own jurisdiction, and the village still has an old church, a few shops and a railway station on the line to Clacton and Walton.

The ride that ends here is a long one, along the Jurassic Coast and across the south of England, and by this stage the pleasure is in the quiet. The roads here are narrow and flat, with a few bends where they cross creeks, and little traffic apart from tractors. In summer, the verges are full of wild flowers, and in autumn the stubble fields attract geese. The coastal wind can be sharp, and rain comes in from the east.

For a meal, the pubs and tea rooms in the villages serve traditional English food, and in summer many have gardens. The nearest fuel is in Little Clacton, the biggest of the three, which has about four and a half thousand people, and in Clacton itself, so make sure you have enough if you come in on a Sunday evening. It is a calm, unhurried place to end a long day, with the smell of cut grass, the sound of birds, and a pint to follow.
t.chilterns ridge and thames valley@51.6,0:
Cranham, Bulphan and Ingrave lie on the south-eastern edge of London, in the flat country where Essex meets the Thames, and it is surprising how much open land survives here. Upminster, next to Cranham, has a handsome white windmill, built in 1803, and a long suburban street, while Ingrave, near Brentwood, lies beside Thorndon Country Park, a large area of woods and parkland with the ruins of an old hall and ancient oaks. Bulphan, the quietest, sits on the low fen of the Thames marshes, a land of drainage ditches, flat fields and big skies that few people ever visit.

The reason to be here is practical. The M25 passes close by, and the A127 and A13 run through the area, so it is a quick way to get on the main roads out of London. Fuel is plentiful at the stations on the approach roads, and it is wise to fill up here before the ride, because the Chilterns, where the day is headed, lie far to the north-west. The route crosses the Thames at Dartford, via the big bridge, or loops around the north of the capital on the motorway, so check the traffic and the toll arrangements before you leave. The crossing has a charge, which is paid online and not at a booth.

The Chilterns, when you get there, are worth the trouble. They are a range of chalk hills with beech woods, steep lanes and attractive villages, and the Thames winds below them. The roads there are narrow and bendy, with a lot of variety, and in autumn the woods turn a rich copper.

On the way out of Essex, the early part of the ride is easy, but be aware of the traffic. Weekday mornings are slow, with commuters heading into the city, and Friday evenings are worse. Leave early on a Saturday or Sunday, when the roads are clear. The best seasons are late spring and autumn, and a coffee at a roadside café on the A127 or in Brentwood is a good way to prepare.
t.chilterns ridge@51.6,0.3:
Upminster has a windmill. The pin lands near it, between Cranham, Bulphan and Upminster, on the eastern edge of Greater London, where the suburbs give way to Essex farmland and the great belt of the M25. The windmill, a tall white smock mill built in the 1800s, stands on a hill above the town and is open to visitors on some days, and the sight of it among suburban roofs is oddly cheering.

After a ride along the Chilterns ridge and the Thames valley, the end is a very different landscape. The roads here are flat and fast, with long straight sections and roundabouts, and the countryside is open fields, small woods and the occasional lake. Thames Chase, a community forest being planted across the area, gives a green setting, and the paths and lanes through it are quiet. The surface is usually good, though heavy traffic on the A127 and M25 can disrupt things.

The area was once fairly empty, with farms and scattered villages, and the arrival of the railway in the nineteenth century turned Upminster into a commuter town. Bulphan has a quiet fen-like character, with drains, flat fields and old farmhouses, and its church is worth a look. The soil is heavy London clay over gravel, so the fields stay wet well into spring, and the ditches hold water and the odd heron. Old maps show how thinly settled the district was before the commuter railways arrived. Cranham has a pleasant green and an old village church.

Fuel is available at Upminster, which has stations and supermarkets, and the town has a small centre with cafes and pubs. A weekend market on the green offers fruit and snacks. The Tube and rail station connects the town with central London, which is useful for tired riders. If you want a short quiet loop before going home, the lanes around Bulphan and Orsett are less busy on Sundays than anywhere nearer the A13.

Come in the late afternoon, when the light is long and the fields are gold. It is a gentle end to a day, with a mill on the skyline.
t.north wessex downs flow photo pull off@5:
Little Dunmow and Great Dunmow lie in the valley of the River Chelmer in north-west Essex, in a country of gentle hills, big fields and old thatched villages, and the pair are best known for a quaint tradition. Since the thirteenth century, according to the records, a couple who could prove that they had not quarrelled or wished themselves unmarried for a year and a day could claim a flitch, a side of bacon, at Little Dunmow, and the Dunmow Flitch Trials are still held every four years, with a jury of local men and women and lots of ceremony. The remains of the priory church where the custom began still stand in Little Dunmow.

The photo pull-off in the name is a reasonable idea in this soft countryside. Essex is often dismissed as flat and dull, but the land here rolls, with long views across wheat fields and hedged lanes, and in summer the whole landscape is the colour of straw. From the higher roads you can see church towers rising out of the trees, and on a calm evening the light is gold. Spring brings the bright yellow of the rape fields.

Great Dunmow, a market town of about eight thousand people, has an old high street with timber-framed houses, a few good pubs and cafés, and the usual supermarkets and fuel stations. Stansted Airport is only ten kilometres away, so now and then a plane roars overhead, but the lanes are quiet, and the traffic is mostly local. The roads wind between villages with greens and ponds, and on a fine weekend they are used by cyclists and riders from London.

The ride is called the North Wessex Downs Flow, and it heads to the chalk downs of the west. The early part is across the plain of Essex and Hertfordshire on mostly flat roads, so it is a gentle start. Wind can be strong in the open fields, and surfaces are patchy in places. Fuel is best found in Great Dunmow or Great Leighs, and an early stop for coffee in the town is a good way to begin the day.
t.north wessex downs flow scenic road@51.8:
The label says Wessex Downs, but these coordinates sit a good two hours east of any chalk escarpment of that name. They put you in the far west of Essex, a few kilometres from Old Harlow, with Hatfield Heath and Little Hallingbury as the smaller villages in the frame. This is boulder-clay country: gently rolling arable fields, big hedgerows, small woods and a sky that always seems larger than you expected so close to London.

Nobody comes here for mountains, and the riding reflects that. The lanes are narrow, often with a hedge close on both sides, and corners tend to be tight right-angled bends around old field boundaries rather than flowing sweepers. Mud and tractor debris are the real hazards, especially after harvest and in wet autumns. Early morning on a dry weekday is the best time, before the commuter shortcuts around Harlow fill up. Stansted airport lies close enough that you will hear jets climbing out now and then, and the M11 hums away to the west.

The most interesting thing nearby is Hatfield Forest, just east of the Hatfield Broad Oak lanes. It is a surviving medieval royal hunting forest, now looked after by the National Trust, with ancient pollarded trees, a lake and wood pasture that has been managed in much the same way for centuries. It is one of the few places in England where you can still see how a Norman hunting preserve worked. The village names around here, with their Broad Oaks and Heaths, hint at the same woodland past.

Harlow itself, to the west, is one of the post-war new towns laid out outside London, with sculpture dotted around its neighbourhoods, which is an odd contrast to the thatch and weatherboard of the villages just beyond its edge. If you need fuel, Old Harlow, about seven kilometres away, is the sensible place; the villages here are too small to count on a pump. A pub lunch in one of the villages is an easy win, and you can usually find one with a garden.

Treat this as a connecting road rather than a destination: a gentle, rural way to put some quiet miles between you and the capital before the real riding starts.
t.hampshire test valley roads@51.2,0.2:
Royal Tunbridge Wells sits on the border of Kent and Sussex, and its story begins with a spring. In 1606 Lord North, a courtier, is said to have found iron-rich water running from the ground here and it became a fashionable spa. The Pantiles, a colonnaded walkway built in the following century, is still the most elegant corner of the town and a good place to stroll after you have filled up. The town later gave rise to the old joke about the disgusted letter-writer.

The fuel gate is on the outskirts, close to Speldhurst and Rusthall, both small villages on sandstone. Rusthall Common has Toad Rock, a weathered outcrop of Tunbridge Wells Sandstone that really does look like a toad, and the High Weald around here is full of such rocks, many of them popular with climbers. The area is hilly, wooded and criss-crossed with lanes, and lies within the High Weald National Landscape, one of the most densely wooded parts of England.

With nearly seventy thousand people, Tunbridge Wells has plenty of petrol stations, supermarkets and cafes, so there is no shortage of facilities. Start early, as the A21 and the roads around the town fill quickly with commuters and weekend traffic. If you want a proper breakfast before a long day, there are plenty of places around the Pantiles and the old high street.

The ride heads west toward Hampshire and the Test Valley, so this is the first of many hours in the saddle. The lanes immediately around Speldhurst are narrow, with steep banks, sunken tracks and sudden bends, and the surface varies considerably, so give the first few kilometres some patience while the tyres warm up.

In late spring the woods here are flooded with bluebells, and in autumn the oak, beech and chestnut turn spectacular colours. It is easy to enjoy the countryside, but the traffic through the town centre can slow you, so expect to take your time on the way out.
t.hampshire test valley roads@51.2,1.0:
Chartham and Wye sit on either side of the River Stour as it cuts through the North Downs on its way to Canterbury, and this stop gives you one of the nicest bits of Kent. The chalk hills rise above gentle fields, orchards and hop gardens, and the valley feels like a sheltered green corridor. Canterbury, about nine kilometres away, is the city you will probably head to if you want a proper meal.

Canterbury is worth a short detour for its cathedral alone. Thomas Becket was murdered there in 1170, and for centuries afterward pilgrims came from all over Europe, which Chaucer turned into the Canterbury Tales. The Pilgrims' Way and the North Downs Way, which run along the base of the hills, follow some of those old routes. The streets inside the city walls are a little crowded and mostly pedestrianised, so find parking outside and walk in.

Closer to this stop, Wye has a distinctive landmark on the hillside above it: a huge crown carved into the chalk, made in the early twentieth century by students of the agricultural college to mark a coronation. The Wye Downs above it are a national nature reserve, with orchids in early summer and wide views across the Weald. Chartham has a long history of paper-making along the river, and you can still see old mill buildings and oast houses scattered around.

The roads in this area are narrow and winding, with banks and hedges on either side. They run steeply up and down the valley sides, with tight corners and occasional gravel. Traffic is usually light outside the main routes, though farm vehicles and cyclists are common. Late in summer you may smell the sweet, resinous scent of the hop fields.

Food is easy here, with village pubs, farm shops and tearooms scattered across the valley, so choose what looks best. If you need fuel, Canterbury is the place, and it has plenty. A relaxed lunch here is a good way of breaking up the long ride west from the coast.
t.hampshire test valley roads high point@5:
Silver End is one of the more unusual villages in Essex, and it is a good reason to take this road. In the 1920s the manufacturer Francis Crittall, whose company made metal windows, built a model village here for his workers, with modern flat-roofed houses, a village hall and a school designed in a clean, progressive style. The brick streets and curved terraces are still recognisable, and the whole place is now a conservation area. It feels more like a piece of Bauhaus planting than the Essex countryside around it.

Do not be misled by the label of a high point. This is some of the flattest, calmest land in the county, in the gentle country between Braintree, Witham and Coggeshall, with the River Blackwater rolling slowly nearby. The highest ground here is only a few tens of metres above sea level, so the real pleasure is not altitude but quiet lanes through arable fields, small woods and old farmhouses.

The riding is relaxed. Lanes are narrow and well hedged, mostly with gentle bends, and the surface can be rough in places where farm lorries have broken the edges. In harvest season there is dust and straw on the road, and in autumn the mud can be a real nuisance. Roads such as the old Roman route, Stane Street, run in long straight lines across the landscape and give you some pace in the quieter stretches.

Kelvedon, five kilometres away, is the closest town with fuel and shops, sitting on the old A12 with a long high street of antique shops and pubs. Coggeshall, a short ride away, is full of timber-framed buildings and has a long wool-trade history that gave the area its wealth in the Middle Ages. Rayne and Great Notley are quieter villages with pubs for a pause.

Take it gently, enjoy the villages and don't expect drama. This is the quiet, rural heart of Essex, with big skies and plenty of birdsong from the hedgerows.
t.hastings cliffs and high weald scenic ro:
Maldon sits at the head of the Blackwater estuary in Essex, where the tide runs out across wide, glistening mud flats and the old sailing barges with their tan sails still moor. It is a proper working small town of about twenty thousand people, which means there is fuel, a good choice of shops and plenty of cafes and pubs, while Heybridge Basin, just up the canal, has a lock and more places for a drink beside the boats.

The town is famous for two things. One is salt: Maldon sea salt, made by boiling estuary water in pans and producing the soft, flaky crystals that cooks across the country now use. The other is the Battle of Maldon in 991, where an Essex force under Byrhtnoth fought a Viking raiding army on the causeway to Northey Island. The Old English poem about the battle is one of the finest to survive, and a statue of Byrhtnoth stands near the old causeway.

As a photo stop it works beautifully, especially in the late afternoon. The Hythe quay is lined with the red-sailed Thames barges, with the sunset reflecting in the water and the ribbon of mud flats stretching toward the sea. The Promenade Park, with its boating lake, is a good place to sit down with an ice cream. The estuary has huge skies, and the light here can be dramatic in winter, with flocks of brent geese and waders stirring over the marsh.

The riding in this part of Essex is flat and quiet, along narrow lanes through fields that open here and there onto views of the water. The bends are gentle, and the main danger is farm vehicles and wind coming off the estuary. The A414 into town is busy at peak times, so avoid the Friday evening rush.

Maldon is an easy place to spend a couple of hours, and parking a bike near the quay is not usually hard. Bring a camera and some patience for the tide, which can change the scene completely in an hour.
t.bontoc@17.1,121.0:
Bontoc looks like exactly what it is, the administrative heart of a mountain province, with a busy market, jeepneys parked nose to tail and a river, the Chico, curling through the middle of everything. About ten thousand people live here, hemmed in by the steep green flanks of the Cordillera, and the town has long been the main trading point for the Igorot villages scattered through these hills. For a long time, Bontoc was associated with headhunting in the foreign imagination, an image the locals have grown tired of, and a visit to the small museum on the hill gives a more honest picture of the culture, with its stone houses, tattoos, weaving and rice rituals.

The Halsema Highway, which brings you here from Baguio, is the highest road in the Philippines, climbing to well over two thousand metres through pine forest and vegetable terraces before dropping toward Bontoc in a long, winding descent. It is a hard road, narrow in places, with landslide scars, cloud that rolls in off the ridges and stretches where the pavement gives way to gravel or mud. Rain makes it treacherous, and landslides can close it for a day or two in the typhoon season, from roughly July to October, so the dry months from November to April are the sensible time. Buses and trucks dominate and the drivers are good, if unhurried. Leave the early hours for the high sections, since the mist usually builds by midday.

Bontoc has fuel and plenty of small restaurants where rice and local pork are the default. From here the road runs on to Sagada, about eight kilometres away, famous for its hanging coffins, limestone caves and cool, pine-scented air, and to Banaue, where the rice terraces that built the region's reputation stand in great tiers. The terraces were cut over centuries, without machines, by people moving stone and soil by hand.

Wear layers. Mornings in the high Cordillera are cold enough for a jacket and gloves, while the afternoon sun at lower elevations can be fierce. The smoke of cooking fires, the smell of wet pine and the sound of a distant gong from a village feast are small things that stay with you long after the mud has been washed off the bike.
t.dinant river@50.3,4.9:
Dinant is a small city squeezed between a river and a cliff. The Meuse runs through it, wide and slow, and the rock face rises almost vertically behind the old houses, with the citadel perched on top. The town has about thirteen thousand people, and the first view of it, with the Gothic collegiate church and its famously bulbous spire in front of the cliff, is one of the great pictures of Belgium.

Several things come from here. Adolphe Sax, inventor of the saxophone, was born in Dinant in 1814, and the town honours him with sculptures of giant saxophones along the bridge. The hard biscuit called couque de Dinant, made of flour and honey and so tough that it can break a tooth, is a local curiosity, usually stamped with elaborate designs. The strong Leffe beers take their name from an abbey on the edge of town. And the Rocher Bayard, a rock pillar beside the river, is said to have been split by the magic horse Bayard, which carried four brothers away from Charlemagne.

For a rider, Dinant is both a destination and a gateway. The roads along the Meuse north and south, with their curves, cliffs and river views, are among the best in southern Belgium, and the route into the Ardennes plateau and the Semois valley climbs through woods and meadows. Fuel is easy, with stations on the main roads, and cafes and restaurants line the river. Moules-frites, local cheese and waffles are the standard meals, and many of the riverside places have terraces.

Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, when tourists and boats fill the quays, and the road along the river is busy with campers. Weekdays and early mornings are better, and the light on the cliff is best in the morning. The Citadel can be reached by a cable car or a steep flight of steps, and the view from the top is worth the climb.

On a damp day, mist hangs on the river and the cliffs disappear into cloud. It is moody and atmospheric, and the hot chocolate in a riverside cafe tastes better for it.
t.canterbury food@51.3,1.1:
Canterbury asks for a pause even from people in a hurry. The cathedral towers over the roofs, the little River Stour slips under footbridges and old timber houses lean over the lanes, and the whole centre is wrapped in a medieval wall that still survives in long stretches. It was already a Roman town, and in 597 Augustine arrived from Rome to begin the English church here, so this is, in a sense, where English Christianity starts.

The story most visitors know is the murder of Thomas Becket, the archbishop killed in the cathedral in 1170 by knights of Henry II. His shrine made Canterbury the great pilgrimage destination of medieval England, and the road from London became so busy that Geoffrey Chaucer used a party of pilgrims on it as the frame for his Canterbury Tales. As a rider coming down from London, you are following a very old route, and it is a nice thought for the last few miles.

As a food stop, the city is easy and varied. The centre is compact and mostly pedestrianised, with cafés, pubs and bakeries in the lanes around the cathedral, and cheaper places toward the station and the university. Parking for motorcycles is available at the edge of the centre, and a short walk gets you to everything. Weekends are crowded and coach parties are common, so a weekday or an early start is much easier. Kent produces good cheese, cider and apples, and you will find the local product on most menus.

Canterbury has about fifty-five thousand people, so fuel is straightforward, with stations on the ring road and the main approaches. The riding in and out is mostly town and A-road traffic, with roundabouts and the occasional queue, so the pleasure is saved for the lanes to the east and south, where the North Downs roll toward the coast. If you are heading to Dover or Folkestone, the road is quick, and you will see the land open toward the Channel.
t.dover white cliffs@51.1,1.4:
Dover's cliffs are not just white, they are enormous: chalk faces about a hundred metres high, bright against the sea on a sunny day, the first and last piece of England for about a thousand years of travellers. This stop sits on the clifftop on the eastern side of town, where the road gives way to open grass, a National Trust area and a long view across the Strait of Dover. On a clear day you can see the French coast, about twenty miles away, as a thin pale line.

It is also one of the most busy approaches in Britain. Dover is the busiest ferry port in the country, and the road down into the docks can be thick with lorries, particularly when there are delays across the Channel, so check traffic before you set out. On the cliff itself the mood changes. Gulls call from the ledges, skylarks sing over the downland, and the wind is almost always present, strong enough to need a firm grip on the bike at the car park edge. Stay well back from the cliff edge, where the chalk is unstable.

The history is thick here. Dover Castle, high on the hill behind the port, has stood for nearly a thousand years and holds tunnels used in the Second World War. Along the cliffs, the South Foreland lighthouse and the wartime sound mirrors recall the days when this coast was the front line, and the song about the white cliffs of Dover became a symbol of wartime hope. Down below, the cross-channel ferries still come and go every few minutes.

For fuel and food, Dover has about forty-two thousand people and all the usual services, and Deal, further up the coast, has more. The cliff area has a small café and a visitor centre, though hours vary with the season. Pack a waterproof, because the weather comes in from the Channel quickly. It is a fine place at sunset, when the cliffs turn warm gold and the ships appear as dark shapes on the sea.
t.folkestone coast@51.1,1.2:
Folkestone has quietly rearranged itself. A seaside resort that went through lean years has become a town of galleries, painted streets and a revived harbour, and it still has the long clifftop promenade, the Leas, laid out by the Victorians when the railway made this a place for the well-to-do. Today it is easy to spend an hour strolling there, watching the ships in the Channel, and it makes a sound pause before or after the road to Dover.

The label here says swim, and in summer that is possible, with a shingle beach and, at low tide, a stretch of sand to the east that the locals know well. The water is cold and the shingle is hard on bare feet, so a pair of beach shoes is a good idea. Do not leave your riding gear unattended, and check for any warning flags. The harbour arm, a long stone pier with a lighthouse at the end, is a good place for a walk, and in the evening it fills with people eating and drinking.

History is close at hand. In the First World War, Folkestone was a major departure point, and about ten million soldiers passed through the town on their way to France, marching down a steep road to the harbour that is now called the Road of Remembrance. The coast is also lined with Martello towers, small round forts built against a feared Napoleonic invasion, and the Channel Tunnel terminal sits just inland. The mixture of old and new makes the town more interesting than it first looks.

Folkestone has more than sixty thousand people, so fuel, food and parking are straightforward. Cafés, bakeries and fish-and-chip shops are plentiful along the harbour and in the old town, and it is the easiest stop on this stretch. Riding in and out, the main roads are busy, but the lanes on the downs behind, toward Hawkinge and Elham, are quiet and pleasant, and the cliffs west of town give a good ride with views of the sea.
t.royal tunbridge wells@51.1,0.3:
Tunbridge Wells owes its existence to a rusty spring. In 1606 a young nobleman, Lord North, was resting in the woods here and noticed a pool with an orange scum; he tried the water, felt better and told the world. Within a few decades the court was coming down from London to drink it, and the Pantiles, a raised, colonnaded walk with trees along it, became the place to be seen taking the waters. The town was granted its Royal prefix in 1909 by Edward VII, and has been the butt of letters to the editor ever since, usually signed by someone disgusted.

None of that matters much on a motorbike, but the setting does. Tunbridge Wells sits on the High Weald, an old ridge-and-valley country of sandstone, ancient woodland and hedges so thick the lanes run in tunnels. Right on the edge of town at Rusthall is Toad Rock, a lump of weathered sandstone that does look like a toad if you are generous, and there are many more outcrops in the woods round about. The riding south and east is some of the best in the southeast: narrow, hump-backed B-roads and unclassified lanes with blind crests and wet leaves for six months of the year. North is Penshurst and the Medway valley, west is Ashdown Forest and the road to Sussex.

As a stop on the way back to London this is a place for sensible things. It is a proper town of nearly seventy thousand, with every fuel brand, plenty of cafés in the old Pantiles and along the high street, and public toilets by the common. If you have been out in the lanes since morning, it is a gentler re-entry than going straight onto the A21. Traffic into the town on a Friday evening is slow, so leave before four or accept the queue.

Remember that most of the lanes around here are signed for far lower speeds than a bike wants to travel, and farm vehicles, horses and cyclists use them in numbers. Assume there is a tractor round every bend, because eventually there is.
t.hampshire test@51.2,0.2:
You are near Speldhurst, a quiet Kent village a couple of kilometres north-west of Tunbridge Wells, with Rusthall and its sandstone outcrops just to the south. The coordinates sit in the lanes of the High Weald, a landscape of small hills, sunken lanes, woods of oak and chestnut, and farmland where hops were grown for centuries. The oast houses with their white cowls, built to dry the hops, are still scattered across the fields, though most are now houses.

Speldhurst church is known for its stained glass, much of it by Edward Burne-Jones, the Pre-Raphaelite artist, and in the village there is an old pub that claims a very long history. It is a good example of what the area does well: small, local, a little overlooked. Rusthall's Toad Rock, a mushroom-shaped block of sandstone shaped by wind and rain, is close by, and the sandstone crops out all over these woods, giving the lanes a sunken, rocky character that looks like Devon.

The riding is enjoyable but slow. Around Speldhurst the lanes are narrow and shaded, the surface is patchy and in winter it can be greasy with mud and fallen leaves, so give them your attention. Farm tractors, delivery vans and horses all share these roads.
