The route north toward Penshurst and Leigh is lovely in spring when the bluebells are out, and to the south are the ridges of Eridge and the long, quiet roads toward Sussex. Most of the character comes from being slightly lost.

For practical needs, Speldhurst is too small to count on a petrol station, though the village has a pub and a church. Tunbridge Wells, about six kilometres away, has everything. That makes this a reasonable place to be on a long return: you are quiet, close to supplies and still in good riding country. Take the last miles gently and keep a good lookout for cyclists, and you will arrive home having enjoyed it.
t.south downs and beachy head day scenic r:
This one carries a swim label, and I would gently ignore it. The ground between Abridge and Collier Row, on the Essex side of Greater London, is a patchwork of woodland, farmland and the last green fringes of the city, with the little River Roding winding through the valley, but there is no lake, beach or pool to speak of. If you need a swim, the best plan is to wait until you reach the coast; what this place gives you is forest, not water.

That forest is the thing. Epping Forest, the great remnant of the royal hunting forest that once covered most of Essex, stretches nearby, a mixture of ancient hornbeams, oak and beech, and it has been protected as public land since the 1870s, when the City of London took over its care. The old pollarded trees have strange, knotted shapes, because for centuries villagers cut branches for firewood, and walking under them feels like stepping into an older England. Havering-atte-Bower, close by, was once a royal retreat, and its green and stocks are still there.

The riding here is quiet, winding and a little fiddly. The lanes between Abridge and the forest have tight bends, narrow stretches and dips where the surface can be damp and leaf-strewn. Speed limits are low and enforced, and horse riders use the same lanes, so a calm approach is best. Autumn is beautiful, with the beeches turning copper, and early mornings in summer have a fresh, green smell that is unlike anywhere else near London.

Abridge is a small village with a couple of pubs and a few shops, and fuel is not guaranteed, so use the bigger stations of Romford and Collier Row before you come. Collier Row has about ten thousand people and a good supply of cafés, while the forest itself has tea huts and pub gardens, which are good places to stop. Check the weather before going, as the forest holds damp, and the road can stay wet long after rain.
t.south downs and beachy head day high poi:
Chalk streams are rare in the world and England has most of them, and the Darent, which runs through this stretch of Kent, is one of the best. It is a shallow, clear, quick little river that comes out of the North Downs and heads north to the Thames, and the valley it has carved is one of the prettiest corners of the London fringe. Darenth and Horton Kirby, close to each other, sit in the lower part of the valley, with watercress beds, old mills and a long viaduct overhead where the M25 crosses the valley.

The label says swim, but I would not. The Darent is a lovely thing to look at, with its trout and kingfishers, but it is too shallow and too fragile for swimming, and it is better admired from the bank. The old paper mills along its length drew on the clean water for centuries, and Horton Kirby's mill was one of them, though most of the industry is now gone. What survives is a gentle, green valley with walkers, cyclists and fishers, a short distance from the crowds of the capital.

Upstream, the valley holds one of the best Roman remains in the south-east. The villa at Lullingstone, near Eynsford, was a wealthy country house with fine mosaics and a rare early Christian chapel, and it is a worthwhile detour if you have an hour. The ride up the valley is also rewarding: the road winds beside the river through villages with flint churches and old pubs, with hills rising on both sides, and it is quiet outside rush hour.

For fuel, Darenth has fewer than three thousand people and few services, so use Dartford or the town of Stone, about three kilometres away. Stone is small but has what you need, and the bigger centres of Dartford and Swanley are not far. A short pause in the village is a good chance to smell the water and wood, and to think that the same river has been running here since long before the road.
t.south downs and beachy head day photo pu:
The Surrey Hills begin to rise here, south of London, around Godstone and Blindley Heath, where the clay of the Weald meets the foot of the North Downs. Godstone has a big, handsome green with a pond, old inns around it and a long record as a coaching halt on the way to the south coast, and Blindley Heath is a smaller place on common land, where cows still graze. It is a gentle landscape of hedges, woods and small fields, with the escarpment of the Downs just to the north.

The label says swim, but what you have here is a viewpoint. Walk or ride up toward the ridge of the Downs, and the land opens out to a long view over the Weald to the south, a patchwork of green with the dark line of the Sussex hills on the horizon. The light is lovely in the late afternoon and the best photographs come after rain, when the air is clear and the colours deep. In summer, the common land is full of butterflies, and in spring the hedges are white with blossom.

The riding on the lanes around here is excellent for the area. The roads are narrow and winding, with short climbs and drops, tight bends and a number of blind corners, and the surface is variable, so a steady pace is wise. Cyclists are everywhere, especially on weekends, since the Surrey Hills are a favourite training ground, and horse riders also use the lanes. Early mornings are quieter, and a light fog in the valleys can add atmosphere.

Godstone has about two and a half thousand people, with a few shops, pubs and a garage or two, but Oxted, about five kilometres away, is a larger town with a station, supermarkets and several cafés, and it is the sensible place to get fuel. The village greens are fine places for a quiet stop, and the pubs around Godstone serve decent lunches. Check opening times, as some close in the afternoon, and plan to be seated by one o'clock or so.
t.seven sisters cliffs@50.8,0.2:
Seven Sisters is the name of a row of white chalk cliffs that rise and fall like a wave along the Sussex coast, between the mouth of the Cuckmere river and Birling Gap. They stand about a hundred metres high, bright against the sea, and the view of them from the clifftop path to the east is one of the most photographed in southern England. The coast here is constantly being worn away, and every winter storm brings down another piece of cliff, so the profile you see is never quite the same.

The best view for riders is from the roads around Seaford and Exceat, where the lane drops to the Cuckmere valley and you see the river wriggling through its meanders toward the shingle beach. The pull-off by the visitor centre is a good place to stop, take a few photographs and walk down to the water, where the sea breeze brings the smell of salt and seaweed. In the evening, the light on the chalk is warm and soft, and the colour of the water changes from grey to green and blue.

The area is also a nature reserve. The chalk grassland is rich in flowers and insects, skylarks sing over the downs and the rare chalkhill blue butterfly is found in summer. Offshore, the water is clear over the chalk, and seals can sometimes be seen close to the beach. Up the coast, the old lighthouse at Belle Tout sits on the cliff edge, and the far taller red-and-white one stands below Beachy Head. Keep well away from the cliff edges, because the chalk is unstable and there is no fence in many places.

The roads from Seaford and Eastbourne can be busy on summer weekends, with holiday traffic and slow-moving camper vans, and parking at Birling Gap and the country park fills early. Seaford, with about twenty-two thousand people, has fuel, cafés and shops, and it is the sensible place to fill up. Take warm clothing, since the wind on the cliffs can be bracing even on a sunny day, and be sure to leave time for a walk along the shingle.
t.beachy head@50.7,0.2:
Beachy Head is the highest chalk sea cliff in Britain, around 160 metres, and the place where the South Downs end in a white wall at the English Channel. Down on the shore a red-and-white striped lighthouse from 1902 looks tiny, and the old Belle Tout lighthouse sits on the next headland west, a squat white tower that was moved back from the cliff edge in 1999. Past it the cliffs run on in the long, undulating line of the Seven Sisters, now protected as part of the South Downs National Park.

It has been a landmark for sailors for as long as ships have used the Channel. In 1690 a French fleet beat a combined English and Dutch fleet in the Battle of Beachy Head, one of the great naval defeats in English history, and wrecks lie on the seabed. On the cliff top the turf is short and springy, full of orchids, thyme and skylarks, and the view runs over the sea and, on a clear day, as far as the Sussex coast to the east. It is also a place with a grave reputation, and you will see Samaritans signs and volunteers on patrol. Be considerate, keep your voice low, and stay well away from the edge.

For a rider, the approach is via the steep road up from Eastbourne, with a couple of tight bends and sudden views, ending in a large car park with a pub and a visitor centre. The road is narrow and the surface can be patchy, with cars pulling in and out. The wind is the main thing. On the open headland it can be fierce, and sudden gusts from the sea will push a loaded bike across the road, so keep your speed down and your hands relaxed.

Eastbourne, about four kilometres away, has filling stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafés along the seafront. The pub on the top does simple meals and tea and is a decent place to warm up, and from there it is a short, steep walk down to the viewpoint. Go early on a weekday and you will have the place almost to yourself.
t.lewes@50.9,0.0:
Lewes is one of those small county towns where you can feel the layers of time on the street. A Norman castle, built soon after 1066, sits on a mound in the middle, and the main street, the High Street, climbs steeply toward it in a long curve of old brick, tile and timber. In 1264 Simon de Montfort defeated Henry III in a battle on the slopes outside the town, a moment often seen as the start of English parliamentary government, and the place has stayed a little rebellious ever since.

The town is famous for two things. Every fifth of November it holds the biggest Bonfire Night celebrations in England, when the streets fill with processions, torches and fireworks, and the roads around the town are closed, so avoid it unless you are very keen. It also has the Harvey's brewery beside the river Ouse, a handsome Victorian building that has produced Sussex ale for more than two centuries, and the smell of malt sometimes drifts across the bridge. Thomas Paine, author of The Rights of Man, lived in the town for several years, and a statue of him stands near the station.

As a food stop, Lewes is very easy. The town is full of independent cafés, bakeries and pubs, and the side streets, known as twittens, are good for a wander. The Downs press close on every side, with the road from Brighton arriving along a green valley. Parking can be tight, but there are car parks near the station and the river, and motorcycles can usually find a spot at the edge of the centre.

The roads around Lewes are a delight. The lanes through the Ouse valley to Glynde and Firle are quiet and winding, with chalk hills rising on either side, and the A27 gives a fast link to the coast. Lewes has about seventeen thousand people, with petrol stations and supermarkets on the edges, so fuel is straightforward. Keep an eye out for the steep, narrow streets near the centre, where the cobbles can be slippery after rain.
t.new forest and solent easy ride@51.4,0.4:
Gravesend has been the gateway to London for a very long time. For centuries ships coming up the Thames stopped here to take on a pilot or pay their dues, and the town has a long river frontage with a historic pier, old pubs and a few streets that have kept their Georgian character. The Pocahontas who famously visited England in 1616 died at Gravesend the next year, as she was about to return home, and she is buried in the churchyard of St George's, with a statue to mark the spot.

Across the water lies Tilbury, and the ferry still runs between the two, carrying foot passengers and cyclists on a short crossing. Tilbury Fort, a seventeenth-century star-shaped fortress on the river bank, guarded the Thames approaches, and it is close to the spot where Elizabeth I gave her famous speech to the troops in 1588, as the Spanish Armada threatened. In 1948 the ship Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, bringing one of the first big groups of Caribbean migrants to Britain, an event now seen as a landmark in the country's history.

As a food stop, Gravesend is a good choice. The old town has cafés, pubs and takeaways, and the riverside has several places to sit and watch the ships, and a few have a good view over the water to Essex. Parking is available near the pier and in the town centre, and motorcycles can usually find a space. The town also has a sizeable market and a handful of street food places, giving a good choice for a quick lunch.

Gravesend has more than fifty thousand people and Tilbury almost twelve thousand, so fuel is easy, with stations on the main roads. The riding in the area is largely flat and busy, with lorries heading to the docks, but the Kent lanes to the south, through Cobham and Shorne, are quiet and pretty. Aim to cross the Dartford Crossing outside rush hours, and take some time to look at the river before you go.
t.dorset@51.1,0.0:
The lanes around Horsted Keynes and Forest Row run along the edge of Ashdown Forest, the great sandy heath in East Sussex that A. A. Milne turned into the Hundred Acre Wood. He lived at nearby Hartfield, and his son Christopher Robin played here with the toys that became Winnie the Pooh. The forest itself is not a forest in the modern sense; the word meant a royal hunting ground, and the land is largely open heathland with gorse, heather, bracken and clumps of Scots pine, a rare habitat that is looked after by grazing. Nightjars and Dartford warblers live there, and in July the heather turns purple.

Horsted Keynes has a real attraction for anyone who likes steam. Its station is on the Bluebell Railway, a preserved line that runs old locomotives and carriages between Sheffield Park and East Grinstead, and the Victorian station has been kept in period style, with gas lamps and milk churns. On a running day you will hear whistles across the fields. Sheffield Park gardens, nearby, is a big landscaped park with lakes and good autumn colour.

The riding is pure Sussex: narrow, winding lanes with banks and hedges on both sides, short climbs and drops, and views that open and shut. The B2110, B2028 and the roads over the forest are the best, with sections where the surface is rough and the camber is odd, so watch your lines. On the open heath the road is exposed to wind, and in sunshine you will share it with walkers, cyclists, ponies and a lot of car-borne visitors. On a weekday morning it is magic, with light low across the heather.

Horsted Keynes and Forest Row are small villages, so fuel is not guaranteed. East Grinstead, about seven kilometres away, is the town to rely on, with several stations and supermarkets. Both villages have pubs and a village shop, and the forest has a couple of car parks that make good rest stops, with wide views over the Weald on a clear day.
t.baguio@16.4,120.6:
Baguio is the city that the Philippines built to escape itself. At about 1,500 metres in the Cordillera, with pine trees, mist and an average temperature that would feel mild in Europe, it became the summer capital soon after the Americans arrived in 1900s, and the layout of the original city was drawn up by the planner Daniel Burnham. Today around 270,000 people live here, the traffic is a constant argument, and the cool air is still the main attraction for people from the lowlands.

The city has been shaken. In July 1990 a powerful earthquake brought down hotels and left hundreds dead, and the memory is still part of local life. But the city is resilient and charming in its way, with the hillside neighbourhoods of colourful houses, the market selling strawberries and fresh vegetables from the surrounding farms, and Session Road, the main street, lined with cafes and bookshops. Burnham Park, with its small lake, is where families go on weekends, and former American military land at Camp John Hay is now a leafy park.

The local food leans towards strawberries, peanut brittle and the ube jam sold in jars in the market. The indigenous peoples of the Cordillera, including the Ibaloi and Kankanaey, have shaped the culture of the region, and you will see weaving, wood carving and silverwork for sale.

For motorcyclists Baguio is the start of the Halsema Highway, one of the great mountain roads of the Philippines. It runs north through Benguet and over the Cordillera, reaching about 2,250 metres at its highest point, the highest highway in the country, passing vegetable terraces, pine forests and villages on the slopes. The road is a mixture of good concrete and rough patches, with landslides and washouts in the rainy season, and mist and fog can drop visibility to a few metres. Heavy trucks carry vegetables down to Manila, so be careful on blind bends.

Fuel is easy in Baguio, and the city has a large number of garages and parts shops. Fill up and eat well before leaving, since services on the highway are sparse.

The dry months of November to April are best, with the clearest views. Typhoon season, from about July to October, can close the road for days.
t.atok@16.6,120.7:
A sign beside the road at Atok declares that this is the highest point on the Philippine highway system, and the air agrees. At about 2,250 metres the Halsema Highway is cold and often shrouded in cloud, a surprise to anyone who flew in from the sweating lowlands, and the vegetable terraces that cover the slopes here look more like Switzerland than South-East Asia. Cabbages, carrots, potatoes, flowers and strawberries grow on slopes that appear almost vertical, and farmers carry loads up and down on their backs. Atok is a small municipality, with Baguio far to the south and Abatan and Sagada to the north.

The highway itself was laid across the Cordillera in the 1930s, linking Baguio with Bontoc, and it carries the name of an American engineer who worked on the project. It is a long, narrow, winding mountain road, now mostly paved but with sections where the surface breaks away after typhoon rains. Landslides are not rare, and in some places half the carriageway has slipped into the valley, so keep your speed down and watch for debris. The scenery is superb: pine ridges, rice terraces further north, gorges full of mist and, on a clear morning, a sea of cloud below you.

Rain and fog are the main hazards, and the road can change from dry to treacherous within a kilometre. Go in the dry season, from November to April, when the air is crisp and views carry for miles. Trucks loaded with vegetables thunder down toward the city, often overloaded and sometimes overtaking on blind bends, so give them space and hold your line. The people of the Cordillera, the Kankanaey and Ibaloi among them, are friendly, and if you stop at a roadside stall for strawberries or a hot coffee you are likely to be offered a chat.

There is little fuel in the high villages, so fill the tank in Baguio or at Abatan before you ride. The nights are cold and the temperature can drop below ten degrees even in the tropics, so bring a warm layer. For a meal, the small eateries beside the road serve rice, vegetables, grilled meat and strong coffee from local beans. This is a long day on a hard road, but few rides in Asia are as memorable.
t.sagada@17.1,120.9:
Sagada is a village in the mountains where the dead are literally placed above the living. In the limestone cliffs around the valley, the Igorot Kankanaey people have for centuries laid their dead in wooden coffins, which they hang from the rock face or wedge into crevices, in the belief that it brings them closer to the ancestors. Some of the coffins are very old, and the tradition is still practised by a few families. The best-known are at Echo Valley, reached by a short walk through the cemetery.

The village itself is a mix of old and new, with a few thousand people, wooden and stone houses, a stone church that began as an American Episcopal mission in the early twentieth century and a number of simple guesthouses and cafes. The air is cool, since it is at about 1,500 metres, and the surrounding hills are covered in pine. There are caves to explore, among them Sumaguing, a huge cavern with limestone formations, which you visit with a local guide, and rice terraces that climb the nearby slopes. At dawn, people drive to a viewpoint called Kiltepan to watch the sun rise above a sea of cloud.

Local specialities include a strong rice wine called tapuy, hot coffee grown in the hills and a lemon pie that has become the town's unofficial snack. The pace of life is slow, and the main entertainment in the evening is conversation around a fire.

The road in from Bontoc, about eight kilometres away on the map, is part of the Halsema Highway system and is a winding mountain road with generally good concrete, though landslides and washouts are common during the rains. Mist rolls over the pass and visibility can drop quickly, so slow down on the bends. The road is narrow with sheer drops, and trucks and jeepneys take the middle. Early morning is clearest.

Fuel is the critical point. Sagada is small, and services may be limited, so fill up in Bontoc, which is the larger town nearby, or in Baguio before you set out. Carry cash, since cards are rarely accepted, and dress warmly for the evenings.

The best months are from November to May, with cool, clear weather. Respect local customs at the burial sites, and ask before photographing people.
t.nelson@49.5,-117.3:
Nelson is a heritage town in the Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia, built on a steep hillside above the West Arm of Kootenay Lake. Silver strikes brought miners and money here in the 1880s and 1890s, and the town's downtown, with more than three hundred restored heritage buildings, is one of the best-preserved Victorian cores in western Canada. A vintage streetcar, number 23, runs along the waterfront, restored by volunteers, and the main street, Baker, is lined with brick storefronts, cafes and bookshops.

In the 1960s and 1970s, the town became a refuge for American draft resisters and back-to-the-land hippies, and an alternative, artistic spirit has lingered. Nelson has a lively music scene, organic bakeries and an outdoor culture of skiing, hiking and mountain biking. Hollywood noticed too: the Steve Martin film Roxanne, from 1987, was shot here. The local college, Selkirk, adds a student presence, and the steep streets are full of cyclists.

The ride east along Kootenay Lake is among the loveliest in the Canadian interior. Highway 3A follows the shoreline through Balfour, where a free ferry, claimed to be the longest in the world at about thirty-five minutes, crosses the lake to Kootenay Bay. The road then runs on to Crawford Bay and Creston, with views across blue water to the Purcell Mountains. The west side, Highway 31 and Highway 31A, climbs through the mountains toward Kaslo and the Slocan valley, with tight bends, steep grades and quiet traffic.

Nelson has fuel, a supermarket and a wide range of restaurants, and it is the main service town for the region. Castlegar and Salmo, farther away, are smaller. The best months are June and September, with clear air and the larches turning gold in October. Summer is warm, with lake swimming, and winter brings snow, so the passes can close. Wildfire smoke can fill the valleys in late summer, and weather in the mountains can change fast. Watch for deer and bears near the road.
t.kelowna@49.9,-119.5:
Kelowna spreads along the eastern shore of Okanagan Lake, a long, narrow lake in a dry valley of southern British Columbia, and the sun is its great asset. The Okanagan is Canada's fruit and wine country, with orchards of apples, cherries, peaches and apricots, and vineyards stretching along the hillsides above the water. The name comes from a Syilx word for grizzly bear, and the Syilx people have lived here for thousands of years.

The city is a big, bright, fast-growing place of about a hundred and twenty thousand people, with a lakeside park, a long beach and a boardwalk. The floating bridge across the lake, one of the longest in Canada, is a landmark, and the lake is said by some to hold a monster, Ogopogo, the Okanagan's own version of Nessie. The town also marks the site of an early mission: in 1859 Father Charles Pandosy and the Oblates founded one of the first European settlements in the valley, and the mission buildings are preserved. Wineries, many with tasting rooms, cluster on the hills.

For riders, the valley roads are the draw. Highway 97 runs south along the lake through Peachland and Summerland toward Penticton, with views of blue water and dry brown hills, and the roads above the lake, through vineyards and orchards, are quieter. The surface is generally good, and the curves are gentle, but summer traffic can be heavy, especially with tourists and tractors. The desert climate, among the warmest in Canada, brings hot summers, and mornings are the best time.

Kelowna has everything: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants, hotels and bike shops. West Kelowna, across the bridge, has more wineries. The best months are May, when the blossoms open, and September, when the grapes are harvested and the heat has eased. July and August are hot and busy, and wildfire smoke has been a problem in recent summers, so check conditions. In winter, snow comes to the hills, but the valley bottom is mild, and the lake rarely freezes.
t.louth@53.4,0.0:
Louth wears the tallest parish church spire in England, and the whole town seems arranged around it. St James' Church, with a spire of about ninety meters, rises above the rooftops of this market town in the Lincolnshire Wolds, a landmark that can be seen for miles across the surrounding countryside. The spire was completed in the early sixteenth century, and the church stands in a quiet, tight-knit town of narrow lanes, Georgian houses and independent shops, with the River Lud running through.

The town carries a memory of disaster. On 29 May 1920, after a violent storm on the hills, the Lud overflowed and a wall of water swept through the center, killing twenty-three people and destroying many houses, and a memorial marks the spot. The poet Alfred, Lord Tennyson went to school in Louth as a boy, and he was born a few miles away at Somersby, and the countryside around fed his early verse. The weekly market and the old butchers' and cheese shops give the town a strong sense of its own identity.

For riders, the Wolds are a surprise. Rising from the flat Lincolnshire plain, they form a long band of rolling chalk hills, steep-sided valleys and hedgerowed lanes, with wide views over the fens and, on a clear day, the North Sea. The A157 and the B1203 run through the hills, and narrow lanes climb to hilltop villages, with gentle curves, sudden dips and few cars. A famous ridge route, the Bluestone Heath Road, runs along the top with big views. The surface is mostly good, though farm tractors and mud on the lanes are common.

Louth has fuel, supermarkets, pubs and cafes, and it is the best base for the Wolds. Manby and Burwell, nearby, are smaller. The best months are May to September, with long light evenings, and autumn brings colored hedgerows. The wind on the open ridges can be strong, and winter fog and ice make the lanes tricky. Look out for farm vehicles and, in harvest, straw on the road.
t.namur@50.5,4.9:
Namur stands at the meeting of two rivers, the Sambre flowing in from the west and the Meuse running north to south, and above the confluence a huge citadel stretches along a rocky spur. The Walloon capital has been a fortress town since Roman times, and the citadel as you see it is a layered thing: medieval walls, a Dutch-era rebuild, and extra works added by the engineers who followed Vauban's methods. It is among the largest fortifications in Europe, and you can ride a long way up the hillside road to the top, where a panoramic view sweeps over the red roofs and the two river valleys.

Down in town the pace is easy. A university, a big cathedral and a cluster of cafes around the old squares make Namur feel lived in rather than staged. The painter and printmaker Félicien Rops, born here, has a museum in the centre. Locals are proud of their position as the gateway to the Ardennes and the Meuse valley, and quietly resent being overlooked for Brussels and Bruges.

The ride south is the reason most bikers stop. The road along the Meuse to Dinant winds under limestone cliffs, with the river on one side and rock walls on the other, passing Profondeville and the castle gardens at Freÿr. It is a gentle, flowing road in good condition, perfect for a Sunday, though it fills with traffic, cyclists and coaches at weekends. In spring the wooded slopes are fresh green and in autumn they turn copper; summer brings haze and tour boats on the water.

For fuel and food, Namur is an ideal break: more than a hundred thousand people, stations on all the ring roads, and a well-stocked riverside area where you can park the bike and grab a croque or a plate of frites. Walloon cooking leans toward hearty dishes, including rich stews and local beers.

Give yourself time for the climb to the citadel, and if you can, ride the loop early on a weekday morning, before the day trippers arrive.
t.oudenaarde@50.9,3.6:
Oudenaarde is a quiet Flemish town on the river Scheldt, and for a few weeks each spring it becomes the centre of the cycling world. The Tour of Flanders has finished here since 2012, and the town has built a museum around the event, so riders on two wheels of the pedalled kind and the engine kind share an obsession with the surrounding hills. The Flemish Ardennes, as they are called, are no mountains, only a rolling ridge of short, steep slopes laid with cobbles, but the names are legends in the sport: the Kwaremont, the Koppenberg, the Paterberg.

The town's old heart is the market square, and on it stands one of the finest town halls in Belgium, a lace-like Brabantine Gothic building from the early sixteenth century with a slender belfry. Oudenaarde was once famous for tapestry, and its weavers supplied the courts of Europe. In 1708 the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene beat a French army here in one of the great battles of the War of the Spanish Succession.

For a rider on a heavy motorbike, cobbled climbs are a different challenge. They are slick when wet, uneven and lined with fans on race days, so enjoy the scenery from the paved parallel roads unless you ride something light. The surrounding lanes through Zottegem, Kluisbergen and Ronse wind between hedges and farms and are lovely on a calm morning, though you will meet dozens of club cyclists, especially at weekends, so keep your speed polite.

Fuel is straightforward in a town of nearly twenty-eight thousand, and cafes around the Markt serve the Flemish classics: carbonnade stewed in beer, fresh waffles, and the local brown beers. The Flemish Ardennes also have a sour red ale tradition, and Oudenaarde was the home of Liefmans brewery.

April is the cycling month and also the busiest; choose September for warm, quiet days and the smell of cut hay.
t.banaue@16.9,121.1:
Banaue sits at about twelve hundred metres in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, in a valley that has been carved, over many generations, into one of the most extraordinary landscapes on earth. The Ifugao people shaped the steep slopes into rice terraces, stone-walled steps that climb to the ridgelines in curves like the contours of a map, and the system is recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage landscape. Local tradition holds that the terraces were built two thousand years ago, though scholars argue about the date. What is certain is that they are still farmed by hand, through the cycle of planting and harvest that is celebrated with chants and rituals.

The town is a small, tidy place of about two and a half thousand people, with a few inns and cafes looking over the terraces, and tricycles, or motorised rickshaws, that carry visitors to the viewpoints. The best known terraces lie nearby at Batad, an amphitheatre of green steps reached by a steep path, and at Bangaan. Ifugao woodcarvers sell figures of the rice god, bulul, in the market, and old women in traditional dress sit at viewpoints.

For a rider, the road from Banaue toward Bontoc and Sagada is pure mountain riding. It climbs and descends through forest and farmland, with steep gradients, hairpins and spectacular views, passing through villages perched on the slopes. The surface is a mixture of concrete and asphalt, with patches that are rough or washed out after heavy rain. Landslides are common in the rainy season, so be prepared for delays. Beyond Bontoc, Sagada is known for its limestone caves and the hanging coffins that cling to the cliffs.

Fuel is the main practical concern. Banaue is small, and while there are usually pumps in the area, the larger town of Lagawe, fourteen kilometres away, is the place to fill up fully. Carry some cash, since machines are scarce. The best months are March to May, when the skies are clear, though the terraces are greenest during the wet season. Typhoons between July and October can close roads for days.
t.namur food@50.5,4.9:
Namur sits at the meeting of two rivers, the Sambre and the Meuse, and a great fortress stands on the rock above them. The Citadel, one of the largest in Europe, has been rebuilt many times, by Spanish, Dutch, French and Belgian hands, and it still dominates the city's skyline. From its terraces, you look down on the red roofs, the river bends and the forested hills beyond. The city is the capital of Wallonia, the French-speaking half of Belgium, and has a university, a market, and a lively riverside.

There is plenty to eat. Namur has a good reputation for food, with restaurants ranging from traditional Walloon places to modern bistros. A local speciality is the tarte al djote, a cheese and chard tart, and the region is known for its beer, its jambon d'Ardenne and its chocolate. The old town, with its narrow streets and squares, is full of cafes and bakeries, and a stroll along the quay with a waffle in your hand is a fine way to spend an hour. The cathedral of Saint-Aubain, with its domed top, is an unusual, Baroque landmark.

For a rider, Namur is the sensible place to eat and refuel before heading into the Ardennes. It is large enough to have fuel stations on all the approaches, and there are plenty of parking spots by the river. The roads along the Meuse, south toward Dinant and Givet, are among the prettiest in Belgium, following the river between limestone cliffs, with castles, rock climbers and little villages along the way. The surface is good, and the corners are flowing, but the traffic can be heavy at weekends. To the east, the Condroz plateau offers quiet farm roads, and to the south, the Ardennes proper begins.

Namur sits on the border between the plains and the hills, and the change in landscape is clear within a few kilometres. The Meuse valley is dotted with rock formations and ruined castles, and the cliffs at Freyr are a favourite with climbers.

Weather is mild, but the Ardennes can be cold and wet, so pack a waterproof. Summer weekends are the busiest time, with riders from all over the Benelux region, so go early if you want the roads to yourself. Namur is a good city to wander, and a coffee on the Place d'Armes or by the river is a pleasure.
t.leiden@52.2,4.5:
Leiden is a university town built on canals, and it is one of the most agreeable small cities in the Netherlands. The Old Rhine, split into several branches, runs through the centre, and the old merchant houses, narrow bridges and windmills give it a charm that is lived in rather than preserved. The university, founded in 1575 as a reward for the city's resistance to the Spanish siege the year before, is the oldest in the country, and its students keep the streets busy on bicycles. Rembrandt was born here in 1606, and the Pilgrim Fathers lived here for years before sailing to America. About 120,000 people live in the city, so fuel, food and everything else are easy to find.

The Siege of Leiden in 1574 is the city's founding story. Inhabitants starved while Spanish troops surrounded the walls, and the Dutch broke the dikes to flood the countryside and bring relief ships. The day of liberation, 3 October, is still celebrated with herring and white bread, and with hutspot, a stew of potatoes, carrots and onions that the Spanish are said to have left behind in their camp. The Hortus Botanicus, one of the oldest botanical gardens in Europe, holds some of the first tulips grown in the Netherlands, which links the city to the flower region.

As a start for the Flower Route, Leiden is well placed, because the bulb fields lie just to the north, around Lisse and Keukenhof. The riding is flat, calm and a matter of small roads between dikes, canals and fields, where rows of tulips, daffodils and hyacinths stretch to the horizon in stripes of colour. Peak season is April, and especially mid-April, when the roads are busy with tourists, cyclists and slow tractors, so be patient. Wind is frequent, and the surface is usually good, though bikes and mopeds have priority in many places.

Do not ride across the fields, and do not pick the flowers, which are commercial crops. Instead stop at the roadside, and enjoy the smell, which is sweet when the hyacinths are out. Traffic in the city is heavy on weekdays, so an early start helps. Order a plate of herring, or a slice of apple pie, and sit by the canal for a while before setting off.
t.noordwijk@52.2,4.4:
On the Dutch coast the sea and the sand come with a smell of salt and frying fish, and Noordwijk has plenty of both. It is a seaside resort between Katwijk and Zandvoort, with a long wide beach, a boulevard, and a line of dunes standing between the town and the bulb fields inland. The town is also home to ESTEC, the main technical centre of the European Space Agency, which makes it a rare place where the beach crowd shares the bakery queue with rocket engineers. The Dutch coast here is flat, windy and bright, and the light has the clean, washed quality that painters came for centuries ago.

For a rider, Noordwijk is a stop on the way between the flower fields and the sea, and its charm is in the contrast. The roads that approach it run along straight dykes, past drainage ditches and rows of poplars, often with a strong wind at your side. Cyclists are everywhere, in numbers that would shock a visitor from most other countries, and they have right of way in all sorts of situations that are not obvious. Speed limits are low, speed cameras are common, and the Dutch drive politely but expect you to know the rules. The reward is a smooth, easy day, with a coffee and a sea view at the end.

The coast road through the dunes is a lovely thing in good weather, but the surface can be covered in sand after a windy day, and a loaded motorbike should be treated gently on it. Spring brings tulip and hyacinth fields in the hinterland, and the whole coastal strip fills with people at weekends, so book ahead if you plan to stay, and expect queues of cars in April.

Noordwijk-Binnen, the inland half of the place, has twenty-four thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are all easy. On the beach side you will find fish sellers and cafés that serve a decent kroket and, in season, herring with onions. Try a stroopwafel from a market stall, still warm. If the weather is clear, ride the dune road at sunset and watch the sky turn orange behind the ships out at sea.
t.lisse@52.3,4.6:
Lisse is the heart of the Bollenstreek, the bulb region, a belt of sandy land between Leiden and Haarlem where tulips, daffodils and hyacinths are grown by the million. In April the fields stretch away in stripes of red, yellow, pink and white, so strongly coloured that they seem painted. The sandy soil, a little way inland from the dunes, drains well and suits the bulbs, which is why this strip of land has been planted for four centuries. The story is a famous one: the botanist Carolus Clusius planted some of the first tulips in the Netherlands at Leiden in the 1590s, and within a few decades the flower had set off the speculative frenzy now called tulip mania.

The town itself is neat, a little sleepy, with canals, small bridges, a church and a museum devoted to the flower bulb and its history, called De Zwarte Tulp, after the novel by Dumas. The region's flower parade in spring is a great spectacle, floats covered in blooms creeping along the roads, and it can stop traffic on all the main routes for hours. Check the date before you plan a day around it.

The riding is slow by necessity. Narrow dyke roads cut between the fields, cyclists ride three abreast, and tour buses wait where they should not. A sensible rider takes the time, enjoys the colour and keeps off the verges. Do not step into the fields to take photographs: the flowers are a crop, farmers are understandably annoyed by trespassers, and you can be fined. The roads are in good condition, but windblown sand and wet leaves can make them slippery, and the wind coming off the North Sea, only a few kilometres away, is steady.

Everything you need is in Lisse: several fuel stations on the edge of town, supermarkets, cafés, and a bakery or two that are worth a stop for the appeltaart alone. If you come in April and early May, expect crowds, and if you can come on a weekday morning, do. Outside the flowering season the fields are brown or green, and the countryside is empty, with a different, plainer beauty.
t.keukenhof@52.3,4.5:
Keukenhof is a garden of about thirty-two hectares, and for around eight weeks in spring it holds several million flower bulbs in bloom, which makes it the biggest show of its kind in the world. The name means kitchen garden, and it is old: the land was once part of the hunting grounds and herb gardens of Countess Jacoba of Bavaria in the fifteenth century, supplying her castle with produce. In the nineteenth century a landscape architect designed the park around the manor house in an English style, and in 1949 the bulb growers of the region came together to turn it into a permanent showcase for their trade. They have kept it going ever since.

The gardens are laid out among old trees, ponds and winding paths, with huge beds of tulips in blocks of colour, hyacinths with a heavy sweet scent that reaches you across the lawns, and pavilions with flower arrangements inside. The season runs from about mid-March to mid-May, and the timing of the peak depends on the weather. A warm spring brings it early. The park is open only for that short period, and tickets are sold in advance, so check the dates before you ride out.

Getting there is a matter of timing and patience. The roads near Lisse get crowded with buses and cars, queues form on the approach, and the car parks fill by mid-morning on a good day. Motorcycles usually have a separate parking area, which is a small mercy. Aim for the opening hour on a weekday, or the late afternoon when the crowds thin. The surrounding fields are just as beautiful as the garden, and free, so do not skip the ride around them.

There is fuel in Lisse, about a kilometre away, and a café and snack stalls inside the park itself. Dress for a changeable climate: April can be sunny and bright, or windy and cold with a shower. A thin waterproof is better than nothing. Allow at least half a day, wear shoes you can walk in, and bring a little patience for the people who stop dead on the path to photograph a single tulip.
t.haarlem@52.4,4.6:
Haarlem is the pretty one among the big Dutch towns, a city of about a hundred and fifty thousand people that keeps its old centre in good order, with a huge market square dominated by the Grote Kerk, the great church of St Bavo. The organ inside, built in the 1730s, was played by Handel and by the ten-year-old Mozart. The Frans Hals Museum holds the paintings of the great portraitist who lived and worked here in the seventeenth century, and the Teylers Museum, founded in 1778, is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, a cabinet of fossils, instruments and drawings in an elegant building. Haarlem sits on the Spaarne river, a short distance from the dunes and the North Sea.

The city has strong links to flowers. In the seventeenth century, during the tulip mania, bulbs were traded here for staggering sums, and the surrounding area, the Bollenstreek, remains the centre of bulb growing. Haarlem's name has even given its name to a district in New York, because Dutch settlers called their new town Nieuw Haarlem. The Bavo market and the old Waag, the weigh house, add to the character, and the city is a good place to walk, with almost every street offering a view of a gabled house or a courtyard.

For a rider finishing the Dutch Flower Route, Haarlem is a pleasant and easy end. The roads between the dunes at Zandvoort and the bulb fields are gentle and flat, with little drama but plenty of colour. The coastal dunes are a nature reserve, and the road through the Kennemerland area passes forests and sand hills. Traffic in the city, as always, is controlled, with cycle lanes everywhere, so ride carefully. Parking for motorbikes is generally available, though restrictions apply in the centre.

Eat in one of the many cafes on the Grote Markt, where you can try bitterballen, deep-fried meat croquettes served with mustard, or a plate of local cheese. The best season is spring, when the bulbs are in bloom, but the city is lively all year. Finish the ride at a canalside terrace with a glass of beer, as the evening light softens on the brick.
t.maeslantkering@52.0,4.2:
The Maeslantkering is one of the largest moving structures on earth, and it sits quietly on the Nieuwe Waterweg, the channel that brings the sea to Rotterdam, in the town of Hoek van Holland. It consists of two enormous white steel arms, each about two hundred metres long, which rest in dry docks on either bank. When a severe storm surge threatens, the arms swing out, float across the channel, and sink to seal it, all by computer, without a human hand. Opened in 1997, it is the last big piece of the Delta Works, the vast series of dams, barriers and sluices that the Dutch built after the North Sea flood of 1953 drowned much of the south-west and killed more than eighteen hundred people.

You can see the whole thing from the outside, and there is a small visitor centre, the Keringhuis, where displays explain how it works and why. The arms look from the road a bit like the wings of a giant, unlikely bird. The barrier is tested once a year, usually before the storm season, though it has rarely been closed for real. It is a reminder that a country where a good third of the land lies below sea level lives with water as a daily fact.

For a rider, the roads around here are flat and wide, with industrial views and long open bends along the dyke. Wind is the main character, and gusts of side wind on the exposed stretches by the water deserve respect. Heavy lorries serve the port, the roads are busy on weekdays, and many junctions have bike lanes you need to watch. Weekends are quieter and more pleasant.

Hoek van Holland is a seaside town, a ferry port with service to Harwich in England, a beach and a few simple places to eat fish. It has fuel, and Maassluis and Rotterdam are close for more. The town is a good place for a coffee on the front, watching ships go in and out of one of the busiest ports in Europe. In clear weather the horizon is full of tankers and container ships in a line, which is a remarkable sight for those who like moving machinery.
t.oosterscheldekering@51.6,3.7:
The Oosterscheldekering is nine kilometres of concrete piers and steel gates running across the mouth of the Eastern Scheldt, and it is the longest of the Delta Works. Sixty-two piers stand in the water, and between them hang sixty-five enormous steel gates, which stay open most of the time to let the tide in and out, and close only when a storm surge threatens. It was finished in 1986, and Queen Beatrix opened it that October. Riding across it on the road that runs along the top, with the sea on both sides and the horizon flat in every direction, is one of the strangest and most impressive crossings in northern Europe.

The history is dramatic. In the night of 31 January to 1 February 1953, a storm surge broke through the dykes of Zeeland and South Holland, flooding huge areas and killing 1,836 people. The government decided to close off the estuaries with dams, but when the plan for the Eastern Scheldt came up, fishermen, shellfish farmers and environmentalists protested that a closed dam would kill the tidal habitat and the oyster and mussel beds. The result was a compromise, a barrier that is open in normal weather and closes only in danger. It cost far more than a simple dam, and many consider it a triumph of Dutch pragmatism.

The ride is flat and exposed, and the wind is the main thing to prepare for. On a blustery day, the crosswind on the barrier can be fierce, and a loaded motorbike will be pushed around, so keep both hands on the bars and a steady speed. Traffic is moderate, and the road is smooth. Seals lie on the sandbanks nearby, and the water at low tide shows a huge shining mudflat, full of wading birds.

There are parking places along the way and a visitor centre on the island of Neeltje Jans, in the middle of the barrier. For fuel, the nearest sizeable town is Zierikzee, about fifteen kilometres away, which also has restaurants and supermarkets, and Haamstede and Kamperland have smaller shops. Eat mussels in season, from September to March roughly, or a simple plate of fried fish. Bring a windproof layer, even in summer, because the sea breeze is cold.
t.neeltje jans@51.6,3.7:
Neeltje Jans is an island that was made by hand. It did not exist before the barrier works, when engineers built it as a working platform in the middle of the Eastern Scheldt, a place to build the concrete piers and gates of the storm surge barrier. When the barrier was finished, the island became a museum, and it still hosts Delta Expo, an exhibition about the Delta Works that includes the original equipment used to build them. The huge machines and the giant concrete pillars stored there give you a sense of scale that the road crossing never quite can.

Visiting the island is a natural pause on the Zeeland ride. There is a car and motorbike park, a restaurant and a café, and a water park that fills with families in summer. From the exhibition you can walk out on part of the barrier itself and see the gates from below, and when the weather permits, boat trips take you out to see seals on the sandbanks. The engineering society of the United States once named the Delta Works among the seven wonders of the modern world, a claim the Dutch mention with modest pride.

The wind is constant. On a calm day, it is mild, but a stiff breeze brings a chill and sometimes a harsh, drenching rain that arrives sideways. Ride with a windproof jacket and take care on the exposed causeway, where gusts can catch you. Traffic is light in winter and heavier in summer, when day trippers and holidaymakers head for the beaches of Zeeland. The roads are well kept and flat, and the surface is generally excellent.

Landscape is the other attraction: wide skies, mudflats, wheeling birds, and the long line of the barrier disappearing into the haze. Bird watchers come in autumn and winter for geese and waders, and in clear light the whole estuary has a silvery look. Mussels and oysters are the local specialities, and the cafés here serve them in season with fries and a cold beer.
t.tynda@55.2,124.7:
Tynda is the capital of the BAM, the Baikal-Amur Mainline railway, and it feels like a town that was designed for that purpose. It was a small settlement until the 1970s, when thousands of young volunteers arrived from across the Soviet Union to build the railway through the mountains and permafrost, and the city that grew around the junction now has about thirty-seven thousand people. The apartment blocks, the station and the monuments to the builders have a uniform, ambitious look, and the whole place carries the memory of a huge communal project.

For a rider, Tynda is an important stop on the road toward Neryungri. The route follows the line of the railway through the forests of the Stanovoy Highlands, with long straights, gentle hills and wide bends. The surface varies, with good asphalt in some sections, rough patches in others, and gravel where repairs are under way. Heavy trucks carry the main load of traffic, so watch for them on blind corners. Summer weather is warm but changeable, with sudden storms, and winter is brutally cold, with snow on the ground for more than half the year. June to September is the best period.

Tynda has fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and several hotels, and it is the last large town for a long way, so it is the place to fill up, buy food and check the bike. The railway museum and the monument to the builders are worth a short visit, and give a good picture of what the construction meant for the people who took part. Food in the cafes is basic and filling, with soup, meat and potatoes, and the portions are large.

The landscape around is taiga, with larch and pine on the hills and swampy valleys between, and the air smells of resin and wet earth. Mosquitoes are fierce in summer, so carry repellent, and in autumn the larch turns gold, which makes a good time to ride. Look for trains on the line, long freight convoys that carry coal and timber, because the railway is part of the identity of the region. It is an honest, hard-working place that rewards a little curiosity.
t.voormalig stadhuis met belfort@51.0,2.7:
Lo is one of the smallest towns in Belgium, a cluster of brick houses around a market square in the flat polders of the Westhoek, a few kilometres from the French border. Its former town hall, built in the sixteenth century in Renaissance style, has a small belfry tower, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Belfries of Belgium and France, alongside much grander towers in Bruges, Ghent and Lille. It is a reminder that even tiny towns had civic pride and privileges worth announcing to the world.

The town's other claims to fame are a medieval gate, the Westpoort, and an old yew tree beside it, to which, according to local legend, Julius Caesar tied his horse. The legend is improbable, but the tree is genuinely ancient, its trunk hollowed and propped, and the townspeople guard it fondly. Lo is now part of the municipality of Lo-Reninge, and the surrounding countryside is a patchwork of fields, pastures, drainage ditches and willow rows.

This was the front line in the First World War. A few kilometres east, the Yser river and its flooded plain stopped the German advance in October 1914, when the Belgians opened sluices at Nieuwpoort to inundate the land. Diksmuide, ten kilometres away, has the Yser Tower, a memorial and museum, and the Trench of Death, a preserved section of Belgian trenches. Military cemeteries dot the landscape, and the poppies that grow along field edges in early summer feel anything but decorative here.

For riders, the Westhoek is flat and windy, with narrow, straight roads between fields, cobbled village squares, and lots of cyclists. It is not dramatic, but it is peaceful, especially early in the morning, when mist lies over the fields. Fuel is easy in Diksmuide or Alveringem. Try the local beers from small breweries, many of them run by monks or families, and the regional cheeses. Across the border, Dunkirk and the Flemish part of France are within easy reach.
t.beguinage de dendermonde@51.0,4.1:
Push open the gate of the Dendermonde béguinage and the traffic noise of the ring road simply drops away. Inside is a quiet triangle of grass, whitewashed houses with green shutters and a modest church, where for centuries communities of beguines lived. These were laywomen who chose a shared religious life without taking permanent vows, earning their keep with lacework, nursing and teaching. The béguinage is one of thirteen in Flanders listed together by UNESCO, and it is among the most intimate of them.

Dendermonde stands where the Dender flows into the Scheldt, a strategic spot that made it a fortress town for most of its history. That cost it dearly in September 1914, when invading German troops set much of the town on fire. The béguinage survived better than many streets, and a few of its houses now hold small museums about beguine life and local folk traditions. Dendermonde is also home to the Ros Beiaard, a giant wooden horse carried through the streets with four young brothers on its back, a procession held only once a decade that draws enormous crowds and fierce local pride.

Riding here is gentle Flemish lowland work. The country roads along the Scheldt dykes are flat and narrow, shared with tractors, cyclists in matching kit and the occasional heron lifting off a ditch. Wind is the real enemy; on a westerly day you will feel every exposed stretch. Expect cobbles in the old centre, low speed limits around schools and plenty of cameras, so ride as the locals do and keep it relaxed. Small foot and bike ferries cross the Scheldt along this stretch, and following the river's loops on the dyke roads is half the fun of a ride here.

Dendermonde is a town of over forty thousand, so fuel, bike parking and food are all close. Settle on the Grote Markt under the belfry, itself a World Heritage site, with a Flemish beer and a plate of local fare, and enjoy the bells ringing over a square that has seen a great deal and still manages to look content.
t.stadhuis en belforttoren@51.1,4.6:
Lier's Grote Markt is one of those squares that makes you slow down without being asked. In the middle stands an elegant eighteenth-century town hall in pale stone, and grafted onto its side is something much older: a slim Gothic belfry from the fourteenth century, its four corner turrets giving it the look of a castle chess piece. Together they belong to the group of Belgian and French belfries listed by UNESCO, symbols of the moment when medieval towns won their freedoms and built towers to prove it.

Lier is a small town between Antwerp and Mechelen, laced with branches of the river Nete and still ringed by a green belt where its walls once stood. Locals carry the nickname schapenkoppen, sheep's heads, from a story that the town was once offered a university and chose a cattle market instead; the university went to Leuven, and Lier has never quite lived it down. A few steps from the square, the Zimmer Tower holds an astonishing astronomical clock built by a local clockmaker in the 1930s, with dials for tides, moon phases and planetary cycles. The writer Felix Timmermans, who celebrated Flemish joie de vivre in his novel Pallieter, was born here, and the béguinage, another UNESCO site, is one of the loveliest in the country.

The roads around Lier are the Flemish standard: flat, well signposted, busy around rush hour and full of cyclists who know they have priority. The centre is compact, with cobbles, one-way loops and limited access for motor vehicles, so park at the edge of the old town and walk in. Short rides out along the Nete valley towards the Kempen bring quieter lanes, pine woods and heathland, and a good afternoon can link Lier with Mechelen and Antwerp without ever touching a motorway.

Fuel stations line the ring roads. On the square, order a coffee with a Lierse vlaaike, a small, dark, spiced tart that the town has been making for generations, and watch the light move slowly across the belfry stones.
t.terril 140@50.4,3.1:
Rising out of the flat fields north of Douai, the black, cone-shaped hill of Terril 140 is not a natural feature at all: it is a heap of mining waste, the spoil left over from decades of coal extraction. The mining basin of Nord-Pas-de-Calais, listed by UNESCO in 2012 as a cultural landscape, is studded with hundreds of these terrils, some flat-topped, some pointed, and together with the pitheads, workers' housing and railways they tell the story of an industry that shaped the region for nearly three centuries.

Coal was found here in the eighteenth century, and by the late nineteenth century the basin was one of the great industrial centres of Europe, drawing workers from across France, Belgium, Poland, Italy and North Africa. Émile Zola set his novel Germinal in this world of mines and miners, describing the hardship and danger of life underground. The last mine in the region closed in 1990, and since then many terrils have been reclaimed by nature, with birch trees, wild orchids and rare insects colonising the black slopes, while some have become viewpoints, ski slopes or nature reserves.

Riding around the mining basin is mostly flat, with straight roads, roundabouts and towns that run into one another, punctuated by canals, terrils and old pitheads. Traffic can be heavy around Douai, Lens and Valenciennes, but smaller roads through villages and fields are quieter. For a more interesting ride, head west to the hills of Artois or south to the battlefields of the First World War around Arras. Wind and rain are common, and cobbled stretches remain in some villages, as fans of the Paris–Roubaix cycle race know well.

Auby, a small town nearby, and Douai, the main city of the area, will cover fuel and a meal. Northern cooking is built for cold days: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, and maroilles cheese, served in a tart or on its own. Wash it down with a local beer, and if you are brave, try climbing to the top of a terril for a view across the flat land.
t.cites de la solitude@50.4,3.1:
On the edge of Waziers, near Douai, the cités de la Solitude are rows of brick houses built by a mining company for its workers, laid out in neat streets with small gardens. Such company towns, the cités minières, were the backbone of life in the coal basin of northern France, providing housing, schools, churches and shops for miners and their families, and they are among the most important elements of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012. The name Solitude seems almost ironic for a place built to house so many people close together.

The houses vary in style according to their era and company: early barracks-like terraces, later semi-detached houses with gardens and, in the twentieth century, garden-city layouts with trees and green spaces. Each family typically had a vegetable garden, a shed and sometimes a pigeon loft, as racing pigeons were a passion among miners. Life revolved around the pit, the church and the café, and the mining companies controlled much of daily life. Many cités have since been renovated and are still lived in, often by descendants of miners.

Douai, close by, is a historic town with a magnificent Gothic belfry, one of the UNESCO-listed belfries of Belgium and France, and every summer it celebrates the Gayant festival, when giant figures representing a family of giants parade through the streets. The Scarpe river runs through town, and the old centre has elegant eighteenth-century buildings. The surrounding countryside is flat and agricultural, punctuated by terrils and pitheads.

Riding in this area means flat roads, roundabouts and traffic around the towns, but quieter routes through villages and along canals. The region is known for its cobbled roads, some of which feature in the Paris–Roubaix cycle race, and they can be challenging on a motorcycle, especially when wet. Waziers and Douai have fuel stations and restaurants. Try local specialities like waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish, and a glass of local beer, and visit the old pitheads and terrils nearby to complete the picture.
t.ensemble minier des argales@50.4,3.2:
At Rieulay, in the middle of the Scarpe valley, the terril des Argales is one of the largest spoil heaps in France, a vast, flat-topped plateau of mining waste stretching for well over a kilometre. Once a stark, black wasteland, it has been transformed into a nature and leisure area, with a lake at its foot, trails, viewpoints and a nature reserve where rare plants and birds have found a home. The site, together with nearby mining remains, is part of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012.

The landscape around is part of the Scarpe-Escaut Regional Natural Park, a region of wetlands, forests, canals and farmland, with ponds formed by mining subsidence that now attract waterbirds. The nearby Mare à Goriaux, at Wallers, is one such lake, and the Arenberg pithead, made famous by cinema and by the cobbled forest track used in the Paris–Roubaix cycle race, is close by. Marchiennes, a short distance away, has the remains of a large abbey, and the town and villages around are full of brick houses, small churches and cafés.

Riding here means flat roads through villages, forests and farmland, with long straight stretches and frequent roundabouts. Traffic is light outside the towns, but watch for tractors, cyclists and cobbles in some villages. The roads along the canals and through the forest of Saint-Amand offer pleasant, relaxed riding, and the nearby Belgian border opens up more options, including the hills and valleys of Hainaut. Rain arrives often and the wind rarely rests, so pack accordingly.

Pecquencourt, the nearest town of any size, has fuel and shops, and Douai and Valenciennes are within easy reach. Rieulay itself has a few cafés and restaurants. The local cuisine is rich and hearty, with dishes like flamiche, a tart filled with leeks or cheese, and welsh, a dish of melted cheese, beer and ham on toast, borrowed from across the Channel and now a northern French classic. From the top of the terril the plain spreads out in every direction, and pitheads, church spires and wind turbines punctuate the horizon.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville d arras@50.3:
Arras has two great squares, the Grand-Place and the Place des Héros, surrounded by tall Flemish-baroque houses with curved gables and arcades, and towering above them is the belfry of the town hall, over seventy metres high. It looks medieval, but most of it is a careful reconstruction: Arras was devastated by German artillery during the First World War, when the front line ran just east of the town for years, and the belfry was destroyed in 1914. After the war, the people of Arras rebuilt it, along with the squares, and today it is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO.

Beneath the town lies a maze of chalk quarries and cellars, the boves, used for centuries for storage and as shelters. During the war, New Zealand tunnellers extended them to hide thousands of soldiers before the Battle of Arras in April 1917, and the Wellington Quarry, now a museum, tells this story. The town was also the birthplace of Maximilien Robespierre, one of the leading figures of the French Revolution. Around Arras, the battlefields of Artois are scattered with cemeteries and memorials, including the Canadian memorial at Vimy Ridge and the French national cemetery at Notre-Dame-de-Lorette.

Riding around Arras is easy and often moving. The countryside is rolling farmland, with long views and straight roads, interrupted by small villages and countless war cemeteries. The roads are generally good, with little traffic outside the towns, though the main routes towards Lens and Lille can be busy. Wind is a constant companion on the open plains, and weather can change quickly, with rain and fog common.

Arras has around forty-seven thousand people and plenty of fuel, food and accommodation. Park near the squares and walk around the centre, where cafés and restaurants line the arcades. Local specialities include andouillette, a sausage made from tripe, and coeurs d'Arras, gingerbread biscuits shaped like hearts. Climb the belfry for a view across the town and the surrounding countryside, and visit the boves for a glimpse of the underground world beneath your feet.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de bailleul@:
Bailleul sits in French Flanders, so close to the Belgian border that you can hear Flemish place names on every signpost, and its town hall belfry, rising over the main square with a pointed spire and a carillon, looks every bit as Flemish as the towers of Ypres or Bruges. Like much of the town, it is a rebuilding: Bailleul was almost entirely destroyed in the spring of 1918, during the German offensive in Flanders, and was reconstructed in the 1920s in a neo-Flemish style of brick, stepped gables and decorative stonework. The belfry is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO.

Bailleul has a strong Flemish identity and traditions to match. The carnival, held around Mardi Gras, features a giant called Gargantua, who parades through the streets and is fed huge quantities of porridge. The town was famous for its lace-making, and there is still a school dedicated to the craft. Just to the north rise the Monts de Flandre, a line of low hills, including the Mont Noir and Mont des Cats, which seem like mountains in this flat country and offer views across the plain to the North Sea on a clear day. The Trappist abbey of Mont des Cats produces a well-known cheese.

The riding here is gentle and rolling, with small roads winding through farmland, hop fields and villages with brick churches, and short climbs over the Monts de Flandre that are more fun than their modest height suggests. Crossing into Belgium is easy, and the roads around Kemmel and Ypres are full of history from the First World War, with cemeteries, memorials and museums. Be careful of cobbles in some villages, wet surfaces after rain and tractors in the farming season.

Bailleul, a town of around fifteen thousand, has fuel stations, shops and restaurants. Flemish cuisine dominates: potjevleesch, carbonnade, waffles and local beers, often served in estaminets, traditional taverns with old wooden furniture and board games. Climb the belfry for a view across the town and the plain, and on a clear day you might see the towers of Ypres on the horizon.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de charleroi:
Charleroi has a reputation, unfairly earned or not, as one of the grittiest cities in Belgium, and its belfry is a fine reason to look again. Rising from the town hall on the Place Charles II, the belfry was built in the 1930s in an elegant Art Deco style, replacing an older tower, and it is one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO. Its slender shape, topped with a dome and carillon, is a symbol of the city's pride and resilience, and inside, the town hall has a sumptuous Art Deco interior.

Charleroi was the heart of the Pays Noir, the Black Country of Wallonia, where coal mines, steelworks and glassworks powered Belgium's industrial revolution. The landscape around is still marked by terrils, slag heaps now covered in trees, and the remains of mines and factories. The Bois du Cazier at Marcinelle, on the edge of the city, was the site of a mining disaster in 1956 that killed hundreds of miners, many of them Italian immigrants, and it is now a museum and memorial, part of the UNESCO listing of major mining sites of Wallonia. The city has been reinventing itself with street art, culture and urban renewal.

Riding in and around Charleroi is mostly urban and suburban, with busy roads, ring roads and industrial areas. Traffic can be heavy, and cobbles appear in some streets. Escape south and the landscape changes quickly: the Entre-Sambre-et-Meuse region, with its forests, rivers and villages, offers pleasant, winding roads, and further south, the Ardennes has some of the best riding in Belgium, with hills, valleys and forests. The weather is changeable, with frequent rain and wind.

There is no shortage of pumps or brasseries in Charleroi. Walloon cooking is generous: try boulettes, meatballs in a rich sauce, often served with fries, and a glass of local beer, perhaps a Trappist from Chimay, not far to the south. Climb the belfry for a view across the city and the terrils, and take time to explore the street art and the renewed city centre.
t.ensemble minier de la fosse cornuault@50:
The flat country between Douai and Lens does not look like much from a motorway, but it holds one of the great industrial landscapes of Europe. For more than two centuries coal was dug from under these fields, and the mining basin of the Nord-Pas de Calais was listed by UNESCO in 2012 as an evolving cultural landscape of pits, slag heaps, railway lines and workers' housing. The Fosse Cornuault at Évin-Malmaison is one piece of that vast mosaic, a former colliery site with its associated buildings, set among the brick villages of the eastern part of the basin.

The history is deep and often harsh. Coal was found in the area in the eighteenth century, and by the late nineteenth century the mines employed tens of thousands of workers, including waves of immigrants, particularly from Poland and Italy, who came to work underground. Not far from here, in 1906, the Courrières mining disaster killed well over a thousand miners, the worst mining catastrophe in European history. The last pit in the region closed in 1990, just a few kilometres away at the Fosse 9-9bis in Oignies, now a cultural venue with its headframes preserved.

The riding is flat and generally straightforward, with a dense network of roads linking towns and villages. Traffic can be heavy, especially around the larger towns and the motorway junctions, and you will need patience with roundabouts and traffic lights. The landscape has its own beauty, though, especially in the evening light, when the slag heaps, the terrils, stand out against the sky like dark pyramids, some of them now covered in trees and wildflowers. The cobbled sectors of the Paris-Roubaix cycle race lie further to the east, and riding one of them on a motorbike is an experience your fillings will remember.

Évin-Malmaison, Ostricourt and Leforest are all small towns with basic services, and you will find fuel easily throughout the area. The local food is hearty: chips cooked in beef fat, carbonnade flamande, and the strong-smelling Maroilles cheese, best enjoyed with a local beer. The weather is often grey and damp, but that only adds to the atmosphere of the place, which rewards those who take the time to look beyond the surface.
t.cite foch@50.4,3.0:
Row upon row of identical brick houses, each with its small garden, outbuilding and front door painted in the colour of the mining company: that is a cité minière, and Cité Foch, between Hénin-Beaumont and Montigny-en-Gohelle, is one of the many hundreds that the coal companies built across northern France. They were designed to house miners and their families close to the pits, and they came in different forms over the decades, from the long terraces of the nineteenth century, the corons, to the garden cities of the early twentieth century, with semi-detached houses, wide streets and green spaces. Many of these neighbourhoods are included in the UNESCO listing of the mining basin.

The cités were more than housing. The companies built schools, churches, shops, dispensaries and sports grounds, creating whole communities that revolved around the pit. After the First World War, when the northern mines had been devastated by the fighting, large numbers of Polish workers were recruited, and their influence is still visible today in surnames, churches, and the pastries in local bakeries. Walking or riding slowly through a cité gives you a sense of that shared life, with its strong traditions of solidarity, brass bands and pigeon racing.

Around Hénin-Beaumont, the landscape is dominated by the slag heaps, the largest of which, the twin cones of Loos-en-Gohelle near Lens, rise to well over a hundred and fifty metres and can be climbed on foot for a view over the whole basin. Lens itself is home to a branch of the Louvre museum, built on a former pit site, and to a football club with a famously loyal following.

As for riding, this is urban and suburban terrain, flat and busy, with plenty of traffic lights, roundabouts and speed bumps. Navigation is easy enough, but it pays to ride calmly and enjoy the details rather than hurrying through. Hénin-Beaumont, with about twenty five thousand residents, has fuel, food and all the services you need. The local cafes are friendly and unpretentious, and a plate of chips or a welsh, the regional take on cheese on toast, drenched in beer and melted cheese, will set you up for the rest of the afternoon.
t.beffroi de porte de lucheux@50.2,2.4:
Lucheux is a small village in a wooded valley in the north of the Somme, close to the border with the Pas-de-Calais, and its belfry is something of an oddity. Rather than rising above a town hall or a market square, as in the larger towns of Flanders and Picardy, it is built into a fortified gateway, a stout stone tower straddling the road through the village. It is part of the group of belfries of Belgium and France listed by UNESCO, a symbol of the civic freedoms that towns and villages won from their feudal lords in the Middle Ages. Above the village stand the ruins of a castle that belonged to the Counts of Saint-Pol, with a great hall and towers in a romantic state of decay.

The forest of Lucheux, which surrounds the village, is one of the largest in the area, a dense beech and oak wood crossed by quiet roads and walking paths. The riding here is gentle and pleasant, with gently rolling hills, fields of wheat and sugar beet, and small villages built of brick and chalk. The roads are generally well surfaced but narrow, with some steep, short climbs and descents in the valleys. Traffic is light, and the area is a pleasant contrast to the busier industrial towns to the north.

Doullens, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with a population of over six thousand, and it has fuel, shops and restaurants. It holds an important place in the history of the First World War. On 26 March 1918, during the German spring offensive, Allied leaders met in the town hall at Doullens and agreed to give General Foch the coordinating command of the Allied armies on the Western Front, a decision that helped turn the tide of the war. The room where the meeting took place is preserved and can be visited. Doullens also has a large citadel, built over several centuries and later used as a prison.
