The valley of the Authie, just to the south, is another lovely area to explore, with water meadows, poplars and old mills along the river. The weather in this part of France is mild but often damp, with grey skies and drizzle common, so waterproofs are a sensible addition to any pack.
t.landhuis met belfort@51.1,2.7:
Veurne's market square is one of the most complete in Flanders, and the old Landhuis, with its belfry rising behind it, is the reason. The Landhuis was the seat of the castellany, the regional administration that governed the surrounding countryside, and its belfry is part of the group of Belgian and French belfries protected by UNESCO. Around the square stand the town hall, the old meat hall and a row of gabled houses, many dating back to the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when Veurne was under Spanish rule, which explains the stepped gables and ornate facades.

The town is famous for its Penitents' Procession, held on the last Sunday of July, when hooded figures carry crosses through the streets in a tradition that goes back centuries. It is a strange and moving spectacle, and the town fills with visitors for the day. Veurne also played an important role in the First World War, when it was close to the front line along the Yser river and served as a base for the Belgian army and for King Albert I, whose forces held the last unoccupied corner of the country.

The riding around Veurne is flat and open, through the polders of the Westhoek, the low-lying land reclaimed from the sea and crossed by canals and drainage ditches. The roads are straight and well surfaced, with little traffic outside the towns, but the wind can be a real challenge, blowing hard off the North Sea and across the fields with nothing to stop it. Cyclists are everywhere, and cycling is taken seriously in Flanders, so give them space and respect.

The coast is just a few kilometres away, with the resorts of Koksijde, Oostduinkerke and De Panne offering beaches, dunes and seafood restaurants. Oostduinkerke is known for its shrimp fishermen, who ride heavy horses into the surf to drag nets, a tradition recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage. Veurne itself, with about twelve thousand residents, has fuel, shops and plenty of cafes around the square, perfect for a coffee or a local beer. The Westhoek is also home to several abbey breweries, and the beers from the area are among the most celebrated in the world.
t.stadhuis met belfort@51.0,2.9:
Diksmuide was almost wiped from the map in the First World War. The town stood right on the front line along the Yser, and from 1914 to 1918 it was pounded into rubble, along with its town hall, belfry and church. In October 1914, the Belgian army halted the German advance by opening the sluices at Nieuwpoort and flooding the low-lying plain, creating a watery barrier that held for four years. After the war, the town was rebuilt in the old style, with the town hall and belfry carefully reconstructed on the market square, and the belfry is now part of the UNESCO listing of the belfries of Belgium and France.

The great landmark of Diksmuide is the IJzertoren, the Yser Tower, a tall concrete tower on the bank of the river, built as a memorial to the Flemish soldiers who died in the war, and bearing the letters AVV-VVK, which mean All for Flanders, Flanders for Christ. It houses a museum about the war and the Flemish movement, and the view from the top over the Yser plain and the coast is outstanding. Just north of the town, the Trench of Death, the Dodengang, is a preserved section of Belgian trenches, only a few hundred metres from the German lines, where soldiers lived and died under constant fire.

The riding around Diksmuide is through the flat polders of the Westhoek, a land of fields, canals, poplars and small villages, with church towers rising in the distance. The roads are generally good, with little traffic outside the towns, but they can be narrow, and the wind blows hard across the open land. Cyclists are everywhere, and they deserve plenty of space. War cemeteries and memorials are scattered across the landscape, especially around Ypres, about twenty kilometres to the south.

Diksmuide, with about fifteen thousand people, has fuel, shops and cafes around the market square, and its butter and dairy products were once famous across the region. The coast, with the resorts of Nieuwpoort and Koksijde, is only a short ride away, and the abbey breweries of the Westhoek, including the famous Westvleteren, are within easy reach. The weather is mild but often wet and windy, so waterproofs are a sensible choice.
t.beguinage de lier@51.1,4.6:
Through a gateway off a busy street in Lier, you step into another world. The béguinage is a small walled neighbourhood of narrow cobbled lanes, whitewashed brick houses and a baroque church, where for centuries communities of beguines lived. These were religious women who chose a life of prayer, work and service without taking the permanent vows of nuns, living independently in their own houses but sharing a communal life. The béguinages of Flanders, about a dozen of them, were listed by UNESCO in 1998, and the one in Lier, with its quiet lanes and doorways topped with statues of saints, is one of the most charming.

Lier itself is a pleasant town on the Nete rivers, south east of Antwerp, with a historic centre of canals, gabled houses, a fine Gothic church dedicated to Saint Gummarus, and a market square with a town hall and belfry. Its most famous attraction is the Zimmer Tower, a medieval tower converted into a clock tower in the 1930s by the local clockmaker Louis Zimmer, who installed an astronomical clock with many dials, showing the time around the world, the phases of the moon, the tides and much more. The people of Lier are nicknamed schapenkoppen, sheep heads, after a legend in which their ancestors chose a cattle market over a university, and the local pastry, the Lierse vlaaike, is a small tart filled with a spiced syrup.

The riding around Lier is flat, through a densely populated landscape of towns, villages, fields and woods, with plenty of traffic and plenty of cyclists. It is not a destination for spectacular roads, but the town makes a good stop on a ride through Flanders, and the countryside to the east, in the Kempen region, offers quieter roads through heathland, pine forests and small villages. Antwerp, with its great port, cathedral and museums, is only a short ride away to the north west, and Mechelen, with its own béguinages and cathedral tower, is just to the south west.

Lier, a town of over thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of cafes and restaurants, especially around the market square. Belgian beer and food are excellent, and a plate of mussels and fries, followed by a local tart and coffee, makes a fine lunch. The weather is mild and often damp, with rain possible at any time of year.
t.belfort en stadhuis@50.8,3.1:
British soldiers marching to the front in the First World War left Ypres by the road that led east towards Menen, and the gate they passed through became the Menin Gate, now a memorial bearing the names of more than fifty thousand soldiers with no known grave. Menen itself, about twenty kilometres from Ypres, sits right on the French border, on the river Leie, which the French call the Lys, and its town hall and belfry, standing on the market square, are part of the UNESCO listing of the belfries of Belgium and France. The belfry, like much of the town, was damaged in the war and rebuilt, and it remains the proud symbol of the town's civic history.

Menen and its French neighbour Halluin form a single built-up area, divided by the river and the border, and crossing between them is as simple as crossing a street. The area has a long history as a centre of textile production, especially linen, made from flax grown in the surrounding fields and retted in the waters of the Leie, which were said to give the linen its quality. The Leie valley was once lined with flax mills and warehouses, and the National Flax Museum in Kortrijk, a few kilometres downstream, tells the story.

The riding around Menen is flat and urban, with busy roads, industrial areas and plenty of traffic. It is not a destination for spectacular roads, but it makes a good starting point for exploring the battlefields of the Ypres Salient, with cemeteries, memorials and museums scattered across the landscape. The Menin Road, now a busy main road, leads to Ypres, where the Last Post is played every evening at the Menin Gate, a moving ceremony that has taken place almost without interruption since 1928. To the south, across the border, Lille is a large and lively city with a fine old town and excellent food.

Menen, a town of over thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The local food is a mix of Flemish and French, with mussels and fries, stews cooked in beer, and the cheeses and pastries of northern France. The weather is mild but often grey and damp, with rain possible at any time of year, and the wind can be strong across the flat land.
t.droogmakerij de beemster@52.5,4.9:
In 1612 a lake north of Amsterdam disappeared. Wealthy merchants, flush with money from the Dutch trading boom, financed the draining of the Beemster, and the engineer Jan Adriaenszoon Leeghwater used dozens of windmills to pump the water out into a ring canal. What remained was a polder several metres below sea level, laid out in a perfectly regular grid of roads, canals and fields based on Renaissance ideas of order and proportion. The Beemster was inscribed by UNESCO in 1999 as a masterpiece of creative planning, and from above it looks like a ruled sheet of paper.

On the ground the landscape is flat, green and calm, divided by straight roads lined with trees and long ditches full of reeds. Grand farmhouses with pyramid roofs, many dating back to the seventeenth century, sit in their own little islands of trees. The Stelling van Amsterdam, a ring of forts built around the capital in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, also runs through the polder, and its forts can be seen at intervals. Beemster cheese, made from the milk of cows grazing on the rich clay soil, is famous throughout the Netherlands.

Riding here is about geometry rather than corners. The roads are straight, flat and narrow, often on dykes above the fields, and you share them with cyclists, tractors and the occasional herd of cows being moved. Wind is the main challenge, and it can be very strong across the open landscape. Speed limits are low, and cyclists have priority in many places. Early morning, when mist lies over the fields, or late evening, with the sun setting over the flat land, is the best time to ride.

Purmerend, six kilometres south, has petrol and every other practical thing, and Middenbeemster, the village at the centre of the polder, has cafés, a museum and a church. Try the local cheese, of course, and perhaps a glass of beer from a local brewery. Amsterdam is close enough for an evening, and De Rijp, a pretty village nearby, is a lovely place for a coffee.
t.neolithic flint mines at spiennes@50.4,4:
Beneath the fields south-east of Mons lies a honeycomb of shafts and galleries dug by Neolithic farmers more than six thousand years ago. They were after flint, the essential raw material for axes and tools, and they dug shafts up to fifteen metres deep through the chalk to reach the best seams, using antler picks and stone hammers. The mines at Spiennes, covering more than a hundred hectares, are the largest and earliest in north-western Europe, and they were inscribed by UNESCO in 2000. An interpretation centre allows visitors to descend into one of the shafts, and on the surface the ground is still scattered with flint flakes.

Mons itself, the capital of Hainaut, is an old town with a Gothic collegiate church, a Baroque belfry, also a World Heritage Site, and a lively main square. Its festival, the Doudou, held every year on Trinity Sunday, re-enacts the fight between Saint George and the dragon in a wild, crowded spectacle that is also listed by UNESCO. Mons saw the first battle between British and German forces in August 1914, and the last day of the war in November 1918, when Canadian troops liberated the town. The surrounding Borinage was a coal-mining region, where the young Vincent van Gogh lived and worked as a preacher before turning to art.

The riding around Mons is mixed: the area is flat and densely populated, with busy roads, industrial areas and towns, but the countryside to the south, towards the French border, offers quieter roads through farmland and forests. Watch out for cobblestones in the towns and villages, which can be slippery when wet. The roads are generally good, and traffic is moderate outside rush hour.

Mons is a city of ninety thousand people, so petrol, food and beds are easy, and the Grand-Place is ringed with terraces where Belgian beers come in their proper glasses alongside frites and carbonnade, beef stewed in dark beer. Touch the little bronze monkey on the town hall facade with your left hand, the locals say, and good luck will follow. The interpretation centre at Spiennes opens on a limited schedule, so check before planning the descent into the shaft, and wear proper shoes rather than riding boots for the ladders.
t.beffroi de rue@50.3,1.7:
Rue is a small town of three thousand people that used to be a seaport, and the belfry in the middle of it is one of the reasons it still feels more important than its size suggests. Over centuries the Baie de Somme silted up and the sea pulled back, leaving Rue stranded a few kilometres inland among salt meadows and polders, but the stone tower that once watched the harbour still stands over the square. It is part of the group of belfries of Belgium and northern France on the UNESCO list, symbols of civic freedom built by towns that wanted the world to know they governed themselves.

Look also for the Chapelle du Saint-Esprit, a small but astonishingly ornate piece of late Gothic carving. Rue was a pilgrimage stop because of a crucifix that, the legend says, washed up on the shore in a boat without sail or crew in the twelfth century, and the money of pilgrims paid for the chapel's lace-like stonework.

The landscape around is flat as a table and full of sky. To the west lie the dunes of the Marquenterre, with its bird reserve, and the Baie de Somme itself, a huge tidal estuary where the sea retreats for kilometres at low tide and seals haul out on the sandbanks. Le Crotoy, on the north shore of the bay, is the place for a seafood lunch looking south across the water to Saint-Valery. Salt-marsh lamb, the agneau de pré-salé, is the local speciality, grazing on the meadows the tide covers.

Riding here is about wind rather than corners. The D940 coast road and the little lanes across the polders are straight and exposed, and a westerly off the Channel will lean you over more than any bend. Summer weekends bring holidaymakers and cyclists in numbers; early autumn, with the bird migration in full swing and the light going silver over the bay, is better. Rue has a fuel station and shops; for a bigger choice, Berck to the north is the nearest real town. Cobbles in the old centre are short but slippery when wet.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de loos@50.6:
Loos is a town on the southwestern edge of Lille, and its town hall belfry is part of the same UNESCO family as the medieval towers of Bruges and Ghent, though it is a much more modern member. In this corner of Europe a belfry was the symbol of a town's independence from lord and church, and when the industrial towns of the Nord built new town halls in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, they gave them belfries too, as a statement that they had grown up. Loos's tower, in brick and stone, does exactly that.

Let's be frank about the setting. This is the dense urban fabric of the Lille metropolis, with Haubourdin, Emmerin and Lille itself running into each other, and the riding is traffic, roundabouts and red lights. The Deûle canal runs nearby, with barges and towpaths, and the old textile and brewing past of the area is visible in red-brick mills turned into flats or offices. Loos was for a long time best known in France for its large prison, which has since been replaced, and for being on the outskirts of everything.

Still, it makes a sensible start or finish. The A25 and A1 motorways are minutes away, so you can be heading for the Flanders hills around Cassel, the battlefields of Artois near Vimy, or the Belgian border in no time. Once you leave the metropolis the land opens into the flat, wind-scoured farmland of French Flanders, with straight roads, big skies and the occasional slag heap rising out of the mining basin to the south.

For food, you are in the north, so think carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, potjevleesch, and waffles from Lille's famous tea rooms if you head into the city centre. Beer here is a serious subject, and there are good regional brews in any bar. Fuel and shops are everywhere in Loos and the neighbouring towns. Watch out for cobbled sections that still survive in older streets of the region, slippery in the frequent drizzle, and for the very real speed camera density around Lille.
t.coastal fort near ijmuiden@52.5,4.6:
At the mouth of the North Sea Canal, where giant locks let ocean-going ships into the waterway that leads to Amsterdam, a round island fort sits in the middle of the harbour. This is Fort IJmuiden, also called Forteiland, built in the 1880s as the westernmost stronghold of the Defence Line of Amsterdam, a ring of forts, dikes and flood fields designed to protect the capital by inundating the land around it. The Defence Line, now part of the UNESCO-listed Dutch Water Defence Lines, is one of the more ingenious military systems ever devised: rather than walls, it relied on water a few decimetres deep, too shallow for boats and too deep for marching.

During the Second World War the Germans occupied the fort and added it to their Atlantic Wall, building bunkers on and around it; the coastline of IJmuiden and Wijk aan Zee still has many of them, some of them open as museums. Forteiland can be visited on guided tours by boat in season.

IJmuiden itself is a working port town, dominated by the steelworks of Tata Steel on the northern side of the canal, whose blast furnaces and chimneys loom over the dunes. The North Sea lock, opened in 2022, is the largest sea lock in the world, and watching container ships and cruise liners squeeze through is quite a sight. The beach at IJmuiden aan Zee is wide and popular with kite surfers.

The riding is coastal and flat, as you would expect in the Netherlands. The dune roads along the coast, between Zandvoort, IJmuiden and Wijk aan Zee, run through landscapes of marram grass, pine woods and low sand hills, with the North Sea glinting beyond. Wind is the big factor, often strong and gusty. To cross the canal you take a free ferry, or the tunnels further east. Speed cameras are common in the Netherlands, and limits are strictly enforced. IJmuiden has plenty of fuel, supermarkets and fish restaurants; the harbour area is famous for fresh fish, especially kibbeling, battered chunks of cod, and herring served raw with onions. Wijk aan Zee hosts a famous chess tournament every January.
t.chateau de l hermitage@50.5,3.6:
On the Franco-Belgian border, in a forest that has never much cared which country it is in, a pale classical château stands in a clearing. The Château de l'Hermitage was built in the eighteenth century for the dukes of Croÿ, one of the great aristocratic families of the region, as a refined country retreat, and it sits just inside France, near Condé-sur-l'Escaut, at the edge of the forest of Bon-Secours. The family's title went back centuries, and their estates spread across both sides of what is now the border.

A few hundred metres away, on the Belgian side, the twin-towered basilica of Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours rises above the trees in Péruwelz. It is a pilgrimage church built in the late nineteenth century around a much older devotion to a statue of the Virgin, and the border runs almost at its doorstep; a café on one side of the street can be in France while the shop opposite is in Belgium. Customs houses and border stones hint at the smuggling that once thrived here, especially of tobacco, coffee and butter.

The surrounding landscape belongs to the Scheldt plain, the Escaut in French, a flat, watery country of meadows, marshes, canals and woods, protected on both sides of the border by cross-border natural parks. To the south lies the old mining basin of the Nord, where slag heaps and pithead frames rise above towns like Wallers-Arenberg, and the mining landscape is now on the World Heritage list. Ponds created by mining subsidence have become nature reserves full of birds.

The riding here is gentle, on small roads through forest, farmland and villages, with few hills and a great deal of brick. Cobbles still turn up in places, and they are dangerously slick in the wet; the famous cobbled sections of the Paris-Roubaix cycle race are not far to the west. Traffic is moderate, heavier near the towns. Péruwelz, a small Belgian town of about sixteen thousand people, two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and frites stands, and Condé-sur-l'Escaut and Vieux-Condé on the French side have the same. Fuel tends to be a little cheaper in Belgium, so it is worth checking the prices. A Belgian beer in a border café, with a plate of cheese, is an excellent way to end a ride here.
t.beguinage de hoogstraten@51.4,4.8:
A béguinage is one of the most peaceful places in the Low Countries: a walled enclosure of small houses around a green courtyard and a church, built in the Middle Ages for béguines, women who lived a religious life of prayer and work without taking permanent vows. They could own property, leave if they wished and support themselves by weaving, teaching or nursing, which made the béguinages a unique form of female independence in medieval Europe. The béguinage at Hoogstraten, in the north of Antwerp province near the Dutch border, is one of thirteen Flemish béguinages on the World Heritage list, and it is a quiet, charming place, with whitewashed houses, a baroque church and a garden where time seems to slow.

Hoogstraten itself is a pleasant small town with a long, wide main street lined with lime trees and dominated by the tower of St Catherine's church, one of the tallest church towers in Belgium at over a hundred metres. The original tower was blown up by German troops in 1944 and rebuilt after the war in its original style. The town is famous in Belgium for its strawberries, grown in greenhouses and sold at a large auction; Hoogstraten strawberries are considered among the best in the country.

The landscape is the Kempen, a flat region of heaths, pine woods, sandy soils and small farms, with nature reserves like the Strijbeekse Heide on the Dutch border. Just across the border, the town of Baarle is a geographic curiosity, with Belgian enclaves within the Netherlands and Dutch enclaves within the Belgian enclaves; borders run through houses and shops.

The riding is flat and easy, along quiet country roads through woods and farmland, with cycle paths separated from the road in most places. There are no real hills, but the scenery is pleasant, especially in late spring and summer when the heath flowers. Speed limits are strictly enforced, with average speed cameras on some roads in Flanders. Hoogstraten, a town of about eighteen thousand people, has fuel, shops, cafes and restaurants; the main street is a good place to stop. In early summer, try the strawberries with cream, and finish with a local beer; the Trappist abbey of Westmalle, famous for its beers, is a short ride to the southwest.
t.beffroi de bergues@51.0,2.4:
Bergues found a new kind of fame in 2008, when the comedy Bienvenue chez les Ch'tis, filmed here, became one of the most successful French films of all time, and suddenly the whole country wanted to see the town where a postman from the south is exiled to the cold north and ends up falling in love with it. The film's best-known scenes include the belfry, from which the hero rings the carillon, and the town still welcomes visitors who come in search of the locations. But Bergues was a proud place long before cinema arrived. It is a small fortified town in French Flanders, surrounded by ramparts and canals, with fortifications improved by Vauban in the seventeenth century.

The belfry is part of the World Heritage site of the Belfries of Belgium and France, towers that symbolised the power and freedom of the medieval towns. The original tower was blown up by retreating German troops in 1944, and the present belfry was rebuilt after the war in a style inspired by Flemish tradition, with a carillon that plays regularly. Climbing to the top gives you a view across the flat Flemish plain to Dunkirk and the sea, with church towers and wind turbines on the horizon.

The landscape around Bergues is the Flemish maritime plain, land won from the sea and marshes over centuries, crossed by canals and drainage channels. It is flat, green and windy, with big skies and fast-moving clouds. Riding here is about gentle roads along canals, through villages with red-brick houses and Flemish names. To the south, the Monts de Flandre, such as Mont Cassel, rise from the plain and offer short climbs, cobbled streets and views across to Belgium. Watch for cobblestones in the towns, slippery when wet, and for strong crosswinds on the open plain.

Téteghem and Dunkirk have fuel and supermarkets, and Bergues has cafés, bakeries and restaurants around the main square. The local cuisine is rich and hearty: carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer; potjevleesch, a cold terrine of meats in jelly; and the strong cheeses of the north, including the Bergues cheese washed in beer. Wash it all down with a local beer from one of the breweries of French Flanders.
t.beffroi de l hotel de ville de binche@50:
Once a year, on the Tuesday before Lent, the little town of Binche in Belgian Hainaut goes completely mad. The Gilles, men dressed in costumes decorated with heraldic lions, crowns and stars, wearing wooden clogs, padded humps and, in the afternoon, enormous hats of ostrich feathers, dance through the streets to the beat of drums from dawn until late at night, throwing oranges into the crowd. The carnival of Binche is one of the oldest and most famous in Europe and is listed by UNESCO as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity. If you are hit by an orange, it is considered a sign of luck, and throwing it back is not done.

The rest of the year, Binche is a quiet town with a well-preserved ring of medieval walls, one of the most complete in Belgium, and a fine town hall on the main square, topped by a belfry. This tower is part of the World Heritage site of the Belfries of Belgium and France, which honours the towers that symbolised the freedom and wealth of the medieval towns. Binche also has an international museum of carnival and masks, where you can see the costumes of the Gilles up close, along with masks from all over the world. In the sixteenth century, Mary of Hungary, governor of the Netherlands, built a lavish palace here, and its ruins can still be seen in the park.

The surrounding area is the old industrial heartland of Wallonia, with former coal mines, slag heaps and workers' housing, some of which are now World Heritage sites, such as Bois-du-Luc and Grand-Hornu. The royal domain of Mariemont, nearby, has a large park and a museum of art and archaeology. Riding here is a mix of small country roads through fields and villages and busier roads between towns, with plenty of cobbles in town centres that become slippery in the rain, and Belgian drivers who can be impatient.

Binche has fuel, shops and restaurants. Belgian food is a delight: fries with mayonnaise, steamed mussels, waffles and, of course, beer, with hundreds of local varieties. The best time to visit is during the carnival, but be warned that the town is very crowded and that parking a motorcycle can be a real challenge.
t.terrils 87 et 92@50.4,3.0:
From a distance they look like hills, which in this flat country is reason enough to stare. The terrils numbered 87 and 92, on the edge of Noyelles-Godault and Dourges next to Hénin-Beaumont, are spoil heaps from the coal mines of the Nord-Pas de Calais basin, made of the shale and rock that came up with the coal over a century and more of mining. They are part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2012 as a whole cultural landscape: pits, headframes, miners' housing, schools, churches and these artificial black mountains, more than a hundred of which are protected.

Nature has been quietly reclaiming them. Some heaps are still bare and dark, others are covered in birch, buddleia and grasses, and because the black shale warms quickly in the sun, they host plants and insects more at home further south. Ecologists find rare orchids, lizards and nesting birds on these slopes, and several heaps have marked paths to the top, where on a clear day you can look across a landscape of towns, canals, motorways and other terrils stretching to the horizon.

The riding here is not about scenery in the conventional sense. Roads are flat, often straight, and busy with traffic around the A1 and A21 motorways and the commercial zones of Noyelles-Godault, one of the biggest shopping areas in the region. Cobbles turn up in older streets, and roundabouts come thick and fast. But the mining landscape has a strange beauty, and riding between the heaps and the cités, the long rows of brick miners' houses, gives a real sense of what this place was.

The last coal pit in the region closed in 1990, and the area has struggled since with unemployment and change. Hénin-Beaumont is the main town nearby, and Douai and Lens are not far. Fuel and food are easy to find in the commercial zones and the towns. For a local taste, try a carbonnade flamande, beef braised in beer, or a welsh, a regional dish of cheddar melted with beer over bread and ham, and a beer from one of the many breweries of the north.
t.cite d auchy@50.5,2.8:
Rows of identical brick houses with small gardens, laid out in straight lines or gentle curves, each with its own vegetable plot and outhouse: the cité at Auchy-les-Mines is a textbook example of the miners' housing built by mining companies in northern France. The companies provided homes, schools, churches and shops, both to attract workers and to control them, and the cités, with their distinctive layouts and architecture, are a central part of the World Heritage listing of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin.

Auchy-les-Mines and neighbouring Haisnes lie near La Bassée, on the canal linking the Deûle to Béthune. This area was in the front lines of the First World War: the Battle of Loos in 1915, in which British troops used poison gas for the first time, was fought just to the south, and memorials and cemeteries dot the landscape. Loos-en-Gohelle, a few kilometres away, is home to the twin heaps of the 11/19 pit, among the tallest in Europe, which you can climb for a view over the whole basin.

The riding in this area is flat and urban, with towns merging into one another, busy roads and cobbles in places. It is not a place for curves, but for history and atmosphere. The brick of the houses and the black of the heaps give the landscape a unique character, and in the evening light the colours are warm and rich.

Look closely at the houses and you can read the social order of the old company towns. Engineers and foremen had larger detached houses, often set apart, while miners lived in terraces or in semi-detached pairs with identical doors and chimneys. Many cités had a company school and church at their centre, and gardens were not decoration but part of the household economy, with leeks, potatoes and rabbits feeding big families. Pigeon racing, brass bands and the local football club filled Sundays.

La Bassée, two kilometres away, has fuel and services, and Béthune, Lens and Lille are all within easy reach. The local food is hearty, with dishes such as potjevleesch, a cold terrine of mixed meats in jelly, and maroilles, a pungent cheese, and the beer is excellent. The cités are lived in, so respect the privacy of residents when visiting.
t.monument commemoratif de la catastrophe:
On the morning of 10 March 1906, an explosion tore through the galleries of the Courrières mining company, killing well over a thousand miners. It remains the worst mining disaster in European history. Most of the victims came from the towns of Méricourt, Sallaumines and Billy-Montigny, and many were buried in a mass grave nearby. Twenty days after the explosion, thirteen survivors emerged from the darkness, having found their way through the ruined galleries, and their story became famous across Europe. The memorials in and around Sallaumines honour the dead and the rescuers, including German miners from Westphalia who came to help.

The disaster had huge consequences. Anger at the company's handling of the crisis led to strikes across the coalfield, and it pushed France to improve mine safety and labour laws, including the weekly day of rest, made law later that year. The memorials are now part of the World Heritage listing of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin.

Sallaumines and the towns around it are part of the dense urban landscape of the former coalfield, with cités, heaps and old pits. The riding here is urban and flat, with busy roads, roundabouts and cobbles. It is not a place for a ride for its own sake, but a place to stop, reflect and understand the history of the region and its people.

The cause was never settled beyond doubt, though a fire in the workings and a coal dust explosion that swept through more than a hundred kilometres of galleries were at the heart of it. Families waited at the pit heads for days in the cold, and the funerals drew huge crowds. Today the names on the memorials, row after row, many of them boys in their teens, make the scale of it painfully concrete, and local schools still bring children here to learn what their great-grandparents lived through.

Fuel and services are easy to find in Sallaumines, Lens and the surrounding towns. Lens, a few kilometres away, has the Louvre-Lens museum, a branch of the Paris Louvre built on the site of a former pit, and the football stadium of RC Lens, whose fans are known for their passion. The memorials are free to visit and often decorated with flowers.
t.terrils 143 et 143 a@50.4,3.2:
East of Douai, the Scarpe river winds through a green valley of marshes, woods and meadows, and rising out of it, near Pecquencourt and Lallaing, are the heaps numbered 143 and 143a, spoil from the mines that once operated here. Today they are part of the Scarpe-Escaut regional nature park and the World Heritage listing of the mining basin, and they are covered with trees and paths, home to birds and plants.

The area has a long history before the mines. At Pecquencourt, the ruins of the Benedictine Abbey of Anchin, founded in the eleventh century and once one of the richest in Flanders, stand near the Scarpe; little remains today but a tower and fragments. Douai, the nearby city, has a magnificent Gothic belfry, one of the belfries of Belgium and France listed as a World Heritage Site, and a carillon that plays regularly. Douai is also home to the Gayant giants, huge wicker figures paraded through the streets during the town's festival in summer.

The riding here is flat and gentle, with roads along the Scarpe and through the marshes and woods of the regional park. Traffic is moderate, and the roads are mostly good, with some cobbles in older streets. The landscape is greener than the western part of the mining basin, with canals, lakes and forests.

The marshes of the Scarpe are a fine place for birds: herons, grebes and marsh harriers over the reeds, kingfishers on the ditches, and in spring a loud chorus of frogs and warblers. Former subsidence ponds, created where the ground sank above old mine workings, have filled with water and become wetlands in their own right, so the mining past shaped even the nature you see.

Pecquencourt and Lallaing are small towns with basic services, and Douai, a few kilometres away, has everything. The local food includes dishes such as carbonade, potjevleesch and waffles, and the beer is excellent. The heaps can be climbed on paths for views over the valley and the surrounding landscape, and the nature park offers walking and cycling routes.
t.voorburg arentsburg@52.1,4.4:
Under the suburbs between The Hague and Delft lie the remains of Forum Hadriani, the northernmost Roman town on the continent, founded in the early second century AD and named after the emperor Hadrian. At Arentsburg, a country estate in Voorburg, excavations revealed streets, houses, a harbour and a canal, the Fossa Corbulonis, dug by Roman soldiers to link the Rhine and the Meuse. The site is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes World Heritage Site, listed in 2021, which follows the Rhine frontier through the Netherlands and Germany.

Little is visible above ground, but the park at Arentsburg and markers in the streets show the outline of the town, and a museum in Voorburg displays finds. It takes imagination to picture a Roman town among the modern houses, but the idea of soldiers and traders at the edge of the empire, here on the flat, wet coast of the North Sea, is fascinating.

The landscape around The Hague is flat, green and watery, with polders, canals and dunes along the coast. Delft, a few kilometres south, is a beautiful old town with canals, the famous blue and white pottery, and the churches where William of Orange and the Dutch royal family are buried. The Hague has the Mauritshuis, with Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, and the beach resort of Scheveningen.

Riding here is flat and urban, with bike paths everywhere, which motorcyclists may not use, and many cyclists to watch for. Traffic is heavy around The Hague and Rotterdam, and roads are well maintained. Wind can be strong, especially near the coast. The Dutch Water Defence Lines, a system of forts and flooding zones, are another World Heritage Site worth exploring by bike.

Voorburg has stations and supermarkets, and The Hague has everything. Try haring, raw herring, from a fish stall, and a bitterbal with a beer in a café.
t.plantin moretus house workshops museum c:
In 1555 a French bookbinder called Christophe Plantin set up a printing press in Antwerp, then one of the richest cities in Europe, and his business became the largest printing house of its time, printing Bibles, atlases, scientific works and books in many languages. His son in law, Jan Moretus, and the Moretus family carried on the business for three centuries, and their home and workshops on the Vrijdagmarkt, preserved almost intact, are now a museum. It holds the two oldest surviving printing presses in the world, a huge collection of type, woodblocks and copper plates, a library and portraits painted by Rubens, a friend of the family. In 2005 it became the first museum listed as a World Heritage Site.

The house is a beautiful example of a merchant's home, with a courtyard, panelled rooms, leather wallpaper and a printing room full of presses. The archives of the business, also preserved, are listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

Antwerp itself is a lively city on the Scheldt, with a great Gothic cathedral, Rubens's house, a diamond district, fashion designers and an excellent food and beer scene. The old town around the Grote Markt is full of guild houses and cafés.

Riding in Antwerp is city riding, with heavy traffic, tunnels under the Scheldt, tram lines and cobbles. The city has a low emission zone, and the ring road is often congested. Parking a bike in the centre is easier than parking a car, but be aware of restrictions. Flanders beyond the city is flat, and the roads are busy, but there are pleasant routes along the Scheldt and toward the Kempen.

Antwerp can see to fuel and lunch. Try the local beer, De Koninck, served in a bolleke glass, Antwerpse handjes, biscuits shaped like hands from the city legend, and stoofvlees with frites.
t.compagnie des mines d anzin ensemble com:
In 1757, a group of aristocrats and entrepreneurs founded the Compagnie des Mines d'Anzin to work the coal seams found under the plains near Valenciennes. It grew into one of the largest industrial companies in France, owning dozens of pits, thousands of workers' houses and its own schools, churches and shops. The ensemble here at Fresnes-sur-Escaut, close to the Belgian border, includes buildings connected with the company's long history, and it is part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

Anzin has a special place in French history. A major strike by its miners in 1884 inspired Émile Zola, who visited the area to research his novel Germinal, a raw portrait of mining life and labour struggle that is still read in schools today. The company's history is also linked with the early days of the steam engine and industrial capitalism in France. Fresnes-sur-Escaut claims to be the place where coal was first found in the region, in the early eighteenth century.

The landscape is flat and green, with the Escaut river, called the Scheldt in Belgium, running through it on its way to Antwerp. Spoil heaps, terrils, rise like small mountains above the plain, many now covered with trees and turned into nature reserves. The old mining towns have rows of brick houses, red and orange, built by the company for its workers. Not far away, the forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers is a large woodland that includes the Arenberg pit, where the coal mine closed in 1989 and the cobbled road through the forest, the Trouée d'Arenberg, is one of the most famous sections of the Paris-Roubaix cycle race.

The riding here is flat and urban, with lots of roundabouts, small towns and traffic. Cobbled roads remain in places, which can be tricky on a motorcycle, especially when wet. The forest roads are pleasant, and the area is easy to explore, but this is not a place for curves. The real reward is the history and the atmosphere.

Fresnes-sur-Escaut, just over a kilometre away, has fuel and basic services. Valenciennes, about fifteen minutes away, is a larger city with a lively centre. Try a carbonnade flamande, beef stewed in beer, or a slice of tarte au maroilles, a strong cheese tart, washed down with a local beer.
t.monument aux morts et grilles de la cite:
In the mining towns of northern France, the companies built not only pits and houses but whole communities, with churches, schools, dispensaries and, after the First World War, monuments to the dead. This war memorial and the iron gates of a mining cité in Mazingarbe are small parts of that story, included in the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site. They stand among rows of brick houses, gardens and allotments in a town shaped by coal.

The landscape around Mazingarbe is dominated by two huge black cones: the twin terrils of Loos-en-Gohelle, spoil heaps from the 11/19 pit that rise to over 180 metres above the plain, among the highest in Europe. You can climb one of them for a view over the whole mining basin, with its towns, pit heads and fields stretching to the horizon. The 11/19 site itself is now a centre for culture and sustainable development, with a theatre and offices in the old buildings.

This area was also on the front line during the First World War. The Battle of Loos in September 1915 was one of the major British offensives of 1915, and the first time the British army used poison gas. Thousands of soldiers died in the fields around here, and cemeteries and memorials dot the landscape, including the Dud Corner Cemetery and the Loos Memorial, which lists over twenty thousand names of men with no known grave.

The riding is flat and industrial, with busy roads, roundabouts and towns that blend into each other. The A21 motorway runs nearby, but the local roads are more interesting, through mining towns and past terrils and memorials. Cobbles appear in places, so be careful in the wet. The area is not about scenery in the conventional sense, but about history and atmosphere.

Mazingarbe, about a kilometre and a half away, has fuel and basic services. Bully-les-Mines, Lens and Béthune are nearby, with more options. Lens is home to the Louvre-Lens museum, built on the site of a former pit, a striking modern building with an outstanding collection. Try the local frites from a friterie, served with a variety of sauces, or a hearty potjevleesch, a terrine of meats in jelly.
t.cites sainte marie@50.4,3.2:
Pecquencourt sits on the edge of the Scarpe valley east of Douai, where the coal basin meets a land of marshes, ponds and forests, and the Cités Sainte-Marie are rows of miners' houses built for the workers of the nearby Sainte-Marie pit. Like many mining settlements, they follow a regular pattern, with brick houses in pairs or rows, gardens at the back and wide streets, designed by the company to house its workforce and keep them close to the pit. They are part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

What makes this area different is the nature that has reclaimed the industrial landscape. Just north, near Rieulay, the Terril des Argales is one of the largest spoil heaps in the region, now a nature reserve with a lake, walking trails and a surprising variety of plants and birds. The Scarpe-Escaut Regional Nature Park covers much of the area, with marshes, forests and wetlands that are home to herons, kingfishers and dragonflies. The forest of Marchiennes, a large woodland, is a pleasant place for a walk.

The history of Pecquencourt goes back long before coal. The Abbey of Anchin, founded in the eleventh century on an island in the Scarpe, was one of the richest Benedictine monasteries in the region, though little remains today. The town grew around the abbey and later the pits, and the mix of old and new is still visible.

The riding is flat and quiet, with small roads winding through villages, fields and forests. Cobbled sections and rough surfaces appear in places, and the roads can be muddy after rain. The area is not about curves, but about exploring a landscape that has been transformed by industry and nature. Spring and autumn are pleasant, with mild temperatures and beautiful light over the marshes.

Pecquencourt, about a kilometre away, has fuel and basic services. Douai, a few kilometres west, is a larger town with a famous Gothic belfry, one of the belfries of Belgium and France on the World Heritage list. The local cuisine is hearty, with dishes like waterzooi, a creamy stew, and tarts made with sugar or cheese. A glass of local beer is the perfect end to a ride.
t.fosse delloye@50.3,3.4:
The name on the label belongs to the most famous pit in the whole northern coalfield. Fosse Delloye, at Lewarde a short ride west of here, closed in 1971 and became the Centre Historique Minier, France's largest mining museum, where former miners once guided visitors through reconstructed galleries and the old lamp rooms, showers and machine halls still stand as they were left. The point itself, though, sits beside Denain on the Escaut, and Denain deserves a story of its own.

In July 1712, during the War of the Spanish Succession, Marshal Villars surprised and routed an allied army here in a battle that saved France from invasion and helped bring the long war to an end. A monument outside town still recalls it. A century and a half later, the town's fortunes were made by coal and then steel. The Usinor steelworks dominated Denain for decades, and when they closed around 1980 the town lost thousands of jobs at a stroke. Like much of the mining basin, it has been slowly finding a new shape since, and the brick cités, chapels and pit buildings scattered around are now part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

For a rider, this is honest, workaday country. The roads between Denain, Lewarde, Douai and Valenciennes are flat, frequently interrupted by roundabouts and small towns, and in places still paved with the old cobbles, the pavés that make the region famous among cycling fans. Wet cobbles under a motorcycle tyre are slippery and unforgiving, so take them upright and slow. The joy here lies in the details: a lone headframe against the sky, a terril turned green with birch trees, a corner café full of retired miners.

If you go to Lewarde, give it at least two hours. The museum does a fine job of explaining what life underground meant, from pit ponies to the firedamp explosions that killed so many men, and it ends with the gradual closure of the pits through the late twentieth century.

Denain, half a kilometre away, has fuel, supermarkets and places to eat. Douai and Valenciennes are larger and offer more choice. A plate of chicons au gratin, endives rolled in ham under a cheese sauce, is the sort of northern comfort food that makes sense after a grey day on the cobbles.
t.hotel de ville@50.5,2.5:
Bruay-la-Buissière is a mining town that grew from almost nothing into a busy industrial centre in less than a century, and its town hall, an imposing building in the heart of town, is a statement of that civic pride. The label points to the Hôtel de ville, one of the many urban and public buildings of the mining era that are part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site. It sits on the western end of the coalfield, where the plain begins to rise towards the chalk hills of Artois.

The town's most famous building, though, is underwater, or at least built around water: the Art Deco swimming pool, opened in the 1930s and recently restored, with its mosaic tiles, curved lines and a light-filled hall. Pools like this were built by mining towns and companies so that miners could wash and their families could swim, and Bruay's is one of the finest. Nearby, the Cité des Électriciens, one of the oldest surviving miners' settlements in the region, has been transformed into a heritage centre with exhibitions about mining life, gardens and houses that you can visit.

Riding here is a curious experience. The landscape is flatter in the east and rolls more to the west, with chalk valleys and small villages. A short way north, at Nœux-les-Mines, a ski slope has been built on the side of a spoil heap, a typically northern piece of reinvention. To the south and west, the hills of Artois offer quiet country roads through farmland, with gentle curves and views over the plains. Expect cobbles and rough surfaces in the towns, and traffic around the main roads.

The region suffered greatly in both world wars. The front line of the First World War ran close by, and the hills of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette and Vimy saw some of the fiercest fighting of the war. Memorials and cemeteries are scattered across the countryside, and the views from these heights over the mining basin are sobering.

Bruay-la-Buissière, a few hundred metres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Béthune, a few kilometres north, is a larger town with a belfry and a lively main square. The region is known for its beer, its cheeses, such as Maroilles, and its friteries, where chips are fried in beef fat and served with a choice of sauces.
t.terril 80 et cite des garennes@50.4,2.8:
Liévin is a town that knows grief. On 27 December 1974, a firedamp explosion at the Saint-Amé pit killed forty-two miners, one of the last great mining disasters in France, and it is still remembered every year. The town sits on the southern edge of the coal basin, next to Lens, and its landscape is still marked by the industry: Terril 80, a spoil heap from one of the pits, and the Cité des Garennes, a settlement of miners' houses, are part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

Terrils like this one were once bare black heaps, smoking and sliding. Today many are covered with trees and grass, and some have become nature reserves with rare plants and insects that thrive in the warm, dry soils. Climbing one gives you a view over the whole area: the brick towns, the pit heads, the fields and, on the ridge to the west, the memorials of the First World War.

That ridge is Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, the site of one of the largest French military cemeteries, with a basilica and a lantern tower, and since 2014 the Ring of Remembrance, a striking elliptical memorial that lists the names of almost six hundred thousand soldiers of all nationalities who died in the region, alphabetically and without distinction of rank or country. A short ride south, the Canadian National Vimy Memorial stands on the crest of Vimy Ridge, its twin white pylons visible for miles.

The riding here is a mix of town and country. The roads through Liévin, Lens and the surrounding towns are busy and full of roundabouts, but heading west into the hills of Artois, the roads become quieter and more scenic, with gentle curves and views over the plains. The roads up to Lorette and Vimy are short climbs with good surfaces. Weather is changeable, with rain and wind common throughout the year.

Liévin, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Lens, next door, is home to the Louvre-Lens museum and the Stade Bollaert-Delelis, the stadium of the beloved local football club, RC Lens, whose supporters are among the most passionate in France. The atmosphere on match days is electric, even if you never set foot inside the ground.
t.cites de montigny et du moucheron@50.4,3:
Montigny-en-Ostrevent is a small town in the Ostrevent, the strip of land between the Scarpe and the Escaut rivers east of Douai, and its miners' settlements, the Cités de Montigny and du Moucheron, are typical of the housing built by the mining companies in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Rows of brick houses with small gardens, built along straight streets, often with a church, a school and a shop nearby, formed the backbone of community life in the coalfield. These cités are part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

The town also has a château, a reminder of the aristocratic landowners who held the area before the coal companies arrived. Nearby, the town of Douai is one of the most historic in the region, a former capital of French Flanders with a parliament and a university. Its Gothic belfry, a tall tower with a carillon of bells, is one of the finest in France, and the town is famous for its giants, Gayant and his family, huge wicker figures paraded through the streets every July in a festival that dates back to the sixteenth century.

The riding here is gentle and flat, with small roads winding through villages, fields and woods. The Scarpe valley offers pleasant routes along the river and its canals, with towpaths and old locks. The forests of Marchiennes and Raismes are not far, with shady roads and paths. Cobbles appear in some villages, and the roads can be slippery in wet weather. This is not a place for adrenaline, but for a relaxed ride through a landscape that tells a story.

The area has a quiet beauty, especially in spring and autumn, when the light over the fields and marshes is soft and golden. The terrils, now green, add an unusual element to the landscape, and some have walking paths and viewpoints. Birdlife is rich in the wetlands, with herons, ducks and occasionally storks.

Montigny-en-Ostrevent, under a kilometre away, has basic services. Pecquencourt, Lallaing and Douai have fuel and more options. In Douai, look for a brasserie on the main square, where you can enjoy a plate of moules-frites or a welsh, a northern dish of bread, ham and melted cheddar soaked in beer, perfect after a day on the bike.
t.cite crombez@50.4,3.0:
Cité Crombez is a miners' settlement at Noyelles-Godault, on the eastern edge of Hénin-Beaumont, in the heart of the old coal basin between Lens and Douai. Built by the mining company to house its workers, it has the classic layout of brick houses, gardens and straight streets, and it is part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site. Today it is a quiet residential area, surrounded by shopping centres, motorways and the remains of heavy industry.

The area has a difficult environmental legacy. For most of the twentieth century, the Metaleurop lead and zinc smelter at Noyelles-Godault was one of the largest in Europe, and it left the soil around it heavily contaminated. The plant closed abruptly in 2003, leaving hundreds of workers without jobs and a polluted site that has since been partly cleaned up. The story of Metaleurop is a symbol of the industrial decline and environmental problems of the region.

Despite this, the area has its charms. The terrils around Hénin-Beaumont and Courcelles-lès-Lens are now green and some are nature reserves. The Deûle canal, running north towards Lille, offers pleasant towpaths for walks or bike rides. And the towns themselves, with their brick houses, churches and markets, have a strong sense of community.

The riding here is mostly urban and suburban, with busy roads, roundabouts and traffic lights. The A1 and A21 motorways meet nearby, making it easy to get in and out, but the local roads are not particularly scenic. Head south towards Arras or west towards the hills of Artois for more interesting rides, with country roads through farmland and villages. Weather is changeable, so be prepared for rain.

Noyelles-Godault, a few hundred metres away, has fuel and large shopping centres. Hénin-Beaumont and Courcelles-lès-Lens have more options for food and services. The region is known for its hearty cuisine, with dishes like carbonnade, potjevleesch and maroilles tart, and for its beers, brewed in many small breweries across the north. Stop at a local friterie for a cone of chips and a fricadelle, a long sausage of minced meat, a quintessential northern snack.
t.cite du pont@50.5,2.9:
Wingles sits on the northern edge of the coal basin, between Lens and La Bassée, where the mining towns give way to the canals and fields of the Weppes and the outskirts of Lille. The Cité du Pont is one of its miners' settlements, rows of brick houses built for the workers of the local pits, and it is part of the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site. The name, the bridge settlement, hints at the importance of the waterways that crisscross this flat land.

The Canal de la Deûle runs just east of Wingles, connecting the coal basin with Lille and the canal network of northern France and Belgium. Barges once carried coal from the pits to factories and ports, and some still pass today, carrying gravel, grain and containers. The canal banks are now pleasant places for walks and cycling, with locks, bridges and wildlife.

Wingles was badly damaged during the First World War, when the front line ran nearby, and much of the town was rebuilt in the 1920s. The church and many houses date from this period of reconstruction, with the solid brickwork of that reconstruction era. The mining companies rebuilt the cités and pits quickly, and coal production resumed, continuing until the late twentieth century.

The riding here is flat and practical, with small roads connecting towns and villages, and busier roads leading to Lens, Lille and the motorways. The landscape is a mix of farmland, industrial sites and residential areas, with terrils and canals adding interest. Cobbles appear in places, and the roads can be slippery in wet weather. For a more scenic ride, follow the canal north towards Lille, or head west towards the hills of Artois.

Wingles, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Meurchin and Billy-Berclau are nearby villages with basic services. Lille, about half an hour away, is a vibrant city with a beautiful old town, excellent museums and a lively food scene. In Lille, look for a traditional estaminet, a cosy tavern serving northern dishes like carbonnade and welsh, with a wide choice of local beers.
t.cites chabaud latour ancienne et nouvell:
Old and new: the label names two generations of company housing at Chabaud-Latour, and walking between them is a short lesson in how mining employers thought about their workers. The older cité is a grid of long brick rows, the corons of Zola's novels, packed close to the pit so that men could be at the shaft in minutes. The newer one, built later, spreads out in pairs and small groups of houses set in gardens, with wider streets and green space, part of a shift towards the garden-city ideal in the early twentieth century. Both belong to the Nord-Pas de Calais Mining Basin World Heritage site.

These houses mattered beyond their walls. The company owned everything: the house, the school, the church, often the shop and the doctor. A miner who lost his job lost his home too, and strikes could mean eviction. At the same time, the gardens behind every house fed families, and the cités built tight communities with brass bands, pigeon racing clubs and cafés that survive to this day. Pigeon fanciers' lofts are still a common sight in back gardens around here.

The Escaut flows past nearby, canalised for barge traffic towards Valenciennes and Belgium. Denain and the towns around it were once among the most industrial in France, with steelworks and pits side by side. Today the skyline is quieter, but the scale of the old industry is still readable in the width of the rail lines, the size of the terrils and the number of brick houses stretching across the plain.

Riding around here is short-hop stuff: flat roads, lots of roundabouts, town after town merging into each other. Watch for cobbles, tram lines in Valenciennes and poorly marked speed bumps. If you want curves, the Avesnois to the south-east, with its hedges, bocage and rolling hills towards the Belgian Ardennes, is about an hour away and well worth it.

Denain, under a kilometre away, has fuel, food and shops. Valenciennes, a little further, is a lively city with a rebuilt centre, a good fine-arts museum and plenty of restaurants. Sit down in a brasserie and order a plate of andouillette or a maroilles tart, and you will be eating what the miners ate on a Sunday.
Oignies holds a special place in the history of northern France: it is where coal mining in the Pas-de-Calais began and where it ended. In 1842, coal was found here during a search for water on the estate of a local landowner, Henriette de Clercq, starting a rush that transformed the region. And on 21 December 1990, the last tonne of coal in the Nord-Pas de Calais basin was brought up from the 9-9bis pit in Oignies, ending more than two and a half centuries of mining in the region. The old Fosse n°2 and its mine-image, a training gallery where young miners learned their trade above ground, are part of the World Heritage site.

The 9-9bis site has been transformed into a cultural centre, with concert halls, exhibition spaces and a music venue in the old machine halls, while keeping the headframes and buildings that tell the story of mining. The mine-image, recreated galleries where trainees practised with real equipment, gives visitors a sense of what it was like to work underground, in cramped, dark and dangerous conditions.

Oignies sits on the edge of the coal basin, near the border between the Nord and Pas-de-Calais departments, where the mining towns give way to farmland and the forests of the Pévèle. The landscape is flat, with terrils, canals and fields, and the roads are straight and quiet outside the towns.

The riding here is relaxed, with small roads winding through villages and fields. The Pévèle, to the north-east, offers pleasant country roads through farmland and woods, with old farms and churches. The forest of Phalempin, just north, is a large woodland with shady roads. Cobbles appear in some villages, and the roads can be muddy after rain. This is a gentle landscape for a slow ride, with history at every turn.

Oignies, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Libercourt and Carvin are nearby towns with more options. The region is known for its beers, with several small breweries producing traditional ales, and for its cheeses, such as Maroilles and Vieux-Lille. A visit to a local estaminet for a beer and a plate of cheese is the perfect way to end a ride.
t.w arly pendjari complex@11.9,2.2:
West Africa's last great savanna wilderness lies where three countries meet, and it is a place with a fierce beauty and a difficult present. The W–Arly–Pendjari complex spans Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger, and its name comes from the shape of the Niger river as it bends in a W through the W National Park. It is the biggest block of protected savanna in West Africa and holds the region's largest population of elephants, as well as lions, cheetahs, hippos, buffalo and many antelope. UNESCO listed it in 2017 as a transboundary site.

The land is a mosaic of open woodland, grassland, rocky outcrops and seasonal rivers. In the dry season, from December to March, animals gather at waterholes and pools in the Pendjari and the Niger, and that is when they are easiest to see. The rains transform the park into green bush, and many tracks become impassable. Local people, including the Gourmantché and Fulani, have lived around the edges for generations, and their villages with round mud-brick houses and granaries are part of the scenery.

I have to be careful with advice about travel. Security in this region has deteriorated in recent years, with armed groups active in the border areas, and in 2019 two French tourists were kidnapped in the Pendjari park in Benin, an event that changed travel patterns. Government advice for the northern parts of Benin and for Burkina Faso and Niger is restrictive, and independent riding is not something I could recommend. If you are interested in the park, check the current situation with official sources and with reputable operators who work in the area.

The tracks within the park are mostly unpaved laterite, with sand and rocks, and roads outside are patchy, with heavy goods vehicles on the main routes. There are no reliable fuel stops close to the coordinates, and supplies are limited, so any trip would need serious logistics, including spare fuel, water and recovery equipment. It is a place that deserves to be seen and protected, but at the moment it is better seen in documentaries and photographs than from the saddle.
t.cite n 2 62 pas de calais@50.4,2.8:
The mining basin of Nord-Pas-de-Calais is flat country made hilly by hand. Around Lens, the heaps of slag left by two centuries of coal digging rise like black pyramids above the fields, and the red-brick miners' houses stand in long, tidy terraces, row after row, called corons. This particular stop lies in the town of Lens, in a cité, the name for a company-built miners' estate, and the numbers in the label come from the way the mining companies numbered their pits and estates.

Coal was first found here in the middle of the nineteenth century, and for a hundred years the region produced much of France's energy. The work was dangerous and the communities were close. At Courrières, a few kilometres east, an explosion in March 1906 killed more than a thousand miners, the worst mining disaster in Europe, and it led to strikes and reforms. The last pit in the basin closed in 1990. Since then the landscape has been reinvented, and in 2012 the mining basin was inscribed on the World Heritage list as a living cultural landscape, with the pit heads, the slag heaps and the housing estates together. The best known of the heaps, the twin terrils of Loos-en-Gohelle, are the highest in Europe, with a path to the top and a view for miles over the plain.

In Lens itself, the Louvre-Lens museum, a long, low building of glass and aluminium, opened in 2012 on the site of an old colliery. The town was almost destroyed in the First World War, and then again heavily bombed in 1944, and its centre has a surprising Art Deco look as a result.

For a rider, this is a flat, straight, practical landscape with cobbled sections on some of the old roads, so wet pavé needs respect. The reward is in the details: pit-head frames, the church spires, slag heaps with silver birch trees on their slopes, and small museums. Winter days are short and grey, and rain is frequent, so spring and early autumn are the best seasons. Vimy Ridge, with its Canadian memorial, is ten minutes away.

Lens has thirty-eight thousand people and has all the fuel, cafes and supermarkets you need. Local food is hearty: frites with a carbonnade of beef stewed in beer, maroilles cheese and strong ale, and the town's brasseries do them well, especially on a cold day.
t.cite n 2@50.5,2.7:
Mazingarbe is a small town on the northern edge of the mining basin, with the terraced rows of a miners' cité running down streets of red brick, and nearly twelve thousand people live in neighbouring Bully-les-Mines. The Cité Foch and the Cité Bellevue are two of the estates that mark this stretch of the basin on the map. The cité, built by the coal company for its workers, usually came with a school, a church, a company shop and a community hall, so that the pit shaped a whole life.

The company that worked here also built a large chemical plant at Mazingarbe, which turned coal into gas, fertiliser and other products, and the town was industrial as well as mining. In the First World War the whole district was in the front line. In September 1915 the British attacked at Loos, a few kilometres north, in the first big battle where the British army used poison gas, and the fighting was fierce around the slag heaps and the pit-head frames of the mines. The cemeteries around Loos are among the largest British cemeteries of the war, with long white rows of headstones, and the memorial lists the names of many men with no known grave. Anyone who rides through the area will pass them in the fields without warning.

The terrain is flat and open, and the roads between Mazingarbe, Bully and Sains-en-Gohelle are straight and fast, crossing old railway lines and canals, and passing beneath slag heaps that are now grown over with trees. Old cobbled lanes survive between the villages and can be treacherous when wet, and the traffic is steady around Lens and Béthune at rush hour. The best rides are at the weekend, in spring or autumn, when the light is clear and the fields green or golden.

Mazingarbe has seven and a half thousand people and enough shops and fuel for a short break. Bully-les-Mines and the larger towns around have more choice. Local specialities are plain and hearty: a plate of frites, a pot of mussels near the coast, and the strong, spicy maroilles cheese. Try the welsh, a regional dish of bread and cheese baked in beer, if you are cold. A warm drink is easy to find, and the people in the cafes are friendly to travellers who stop and ask about the area.
t.monument a madame declercq@50.5,3.0:
Oignies is a small town in the Pas-de-Calais, at the edge of the old coal basin near the border with the Nord, with a monument at its heart to the people who lived and died by the pits. I do not know who Madame Declercq was, and the name belongs to a local monument that I cannot describe, so I will tell you about the place, which has one of the most poignant stories of the whole coalfield.

Oignies was where coal mining in the region ended. The last working pit of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais basin, Fosse 9-9 bis, closed in December 1990, ending almost two centuries of mining here. The buildings, red-brick sheds and a headframe, were kept, and the site has been reinvented as a centre for music and culture, with concerts in the old pit sheds. Two great slag heaps rise behind it, twin cones planted with trees and open to walkers. Nearby Courrières, three kilometres away, was the scene of the great explosion of March 1906, which killed nearly eleven hundred men and boys, and the memorial there is a moving place to stop. Émile Basly, the miners' leader named in the label of this ride, was born in 1854, worked as a miner, became a union organiser and later the mayor of Lens, and is remembered across the district.

On a motorcycle, the country is flat and the roads are straight, with many roundabouts, level crossings and stretches of old setts that can be slippery in wet weather. Industrial buildings, canals and new warehouses alternate with fields of sugar beet and wheat, and the horizon is broken by terrils with silver birch and pine. It is not a landscape for corner-hunters, but it has a character you cannot find elsewhere in France. In winter, the days are short and the sky heavy, and the best time to visit is late spring or September.

Oignies has ten thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and a supermarket, and Libercourt and Courrières are close by if you need more. For food, try a plate of frites with a fricadelle, the local sausage, and a glass of local beer. The cafes are friendly, and the old miners' cités nearby offer a gentle walk on a quiet afternoon.
t.canterbury cathedral@51.3,1.1:
Canterbury Cathedral has been the mother church of English Christianity for fourteen hundred years, and it stands in the middle of a compact walled city in east Kent, rising out of a tangle of medieval lanes. The central tower, called Bell Harry, was finished in the late fifteenth century and can be seen for miles across the surrounding farmland, a pale spire above the orchards and hop gardens.

The story begins in 597, when a Roman monk called Augustine arrived on the coast of Kent sent by Pope Gregory the Great, to convert the English. King Æthelberht of Kent, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian, allowed him to settle in Canterbury, and Augustine became the first archbishop. The cathedral itself grew over the following centuries, and its fame increased dramatically after the murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket in the north-west transept on the 29th of December 1170, killed by four knights who believed that the king, Henry II, wanted him silenced. Becket was made a saint within three years, and pilgrims flooded in. Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, written in the late fourteenth century, follows a group of them. In 1538, Henry VIII destroyed the shrine and scattered the relics, and today a single candle marks the place. The cathedral, together with the ruins of Saint Augustine's Abbey and the church of Saint Martin, was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1988.

The riding here is mostly about getting in and out. The city centre is largely pedestrianised, with a ring road that is busy at rush hour, and parking near the cathedral is limited, so use the park-and-ride sites on the edge and walk through the narrow streets. Beyond the walls, the best roads are the small lanes across the North Downs, through villages with oast houses and flint churches, and the coast road to Whitstable, famous for its oysters, is about ten kilometres to the north. Rain is frequent, and the lanes can be slippery with mud and leaves in autumn.

Canterbury has everything: fuel on the ring road, supermarkets, and countless cafes and pubs inside the walls, many in wonky timbered houses. Sturry and Blean, on the northern side, are quieter. Visit on a weekday morning in spring, before the school groups arrive, and take time for the choir stalls and the stained glass.
t.beguinage de turnhout@51.3,4.9:
Turnhout lies in the Kempen, the sandy, wooded heath of northern Belgium, only a few kilometres from the Dutch border, and the beguinage here is a small village within the town, with brick houses, a church and quiet courtyards behind a wall. The city has nearly forty thousand people, and the beguinage is about half a kilometre from the centre. It is one of thirteen Flemish beguinages inscribed by UNESCO in 1998.

The beguines were communities of lay women who lived a religious life without taking permanent vows, and who earned their living by weaving, nursing and teaching. The movement began in the Low Countries in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and in Flanders it grew into walled enclosures with their own streets, churches, infirmaries and gardens. Turnhout's beguinage was founded in the thirteenth century, and the houses seen today mostly date from the seventeenth century, with stepped gables and low doorways. The last beguines died out over the twentieth century, but the buildings survive, and many are now used as homes and small museums. You can wander in freely, and the enclosed feeling, with bells in the church tower, is special.

Turnhout has its own claim to fame as the capital of playing cards. The industry began in the nineteenth century, and a long-standing printing company turned the town into a world supplier of cards, and a museum dedicated to them is in the centre. The Kempen to the north is a land of pine woods, heaths, fens and small lakes, with good cycling routes, and just across the border Baarle-Hertog and Baarle-Nassau form a bizarre tangle of Belgian and Dutch enclaves, with the border running through shops and houses.

For a rider, the Kempen is flat and rather uniform, but the country roads between woods and fields are quiet, well surfaced and run in long straight lines with sudden bends at the old farms. Speed limits are strict, and cameras and radar traps are common. Winter days are grey and rainy, and the best months are May to September. Turnhout has everything, with filling stations on the ring road, bakeries, and cafes serving Belgian beer, frites and waffles. The town has several breweries nearby, and a Trappist ale is brewed at Westmalle, thirty minutes to the west.
t.rice terrace clusters of mayoyao mayoyao:
High in the mountains of northern Luzon, the hillsides are carved into thousands of rice terraces, rising in curved steps from the river to the ridge, and the Mayoyao cluster is one of five inscribed by UNESCO in 1995 as the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras. The cluster is in Ifugao province, about seven kilometres from the town of Lagawe, and the terraces here feel more intimate than those of the better-known Banaue, with the houses of the villages set among the paddies and the forest above.

The Ifugao people built and maintained the terraces for centuries, by hand, with stone walls and bamboo pipes, and the system of irrigation channels carries water from the forest on the ridge to the fields below. A popular claim that they are two thousand years old is disputed, and many scholars believe that most of the terraces are a few centuries old. What is certain is that the system depends on community work, ritual and knowledge handed down by the elders, and that the Ifugao grow native heirloom rice that is harvested once a year. Their culture has a rich oral tradition, including the hudhud, a long chant sung at harvest and funerals, and carved wooden guardians called bulul stand in granaries to protect the rice. Traditional houses at Mayoyao stand on four posts, with pyramid roofs of thatch.

The roads here are not for the hurried. The highway from Lagawe to Mayoyao winds up through the mountains, steep and narrow, with a mixture of concrete and rough patches, and landslides and washouts are frequent from July to November, when typhoons cross the island. Rain and fog can reduce visibility. Tricycles and jeepneys are common and drivers make sudden stops, so keep your speed down.
