The best months are from December to April, when skies are clearer, though planting season, from about January to March, shows the terraces at their brightest green or silvery with water.

Lagawe has nearly seven thousand people, a market and fuel stations, and Mayoyao has small shops and simple lodges. Fill up in Lagawe, because fuel in the mountains can run out. Try local red rice, grilled pork and bamboo shoots, and the strong local rice wine, which is part of every celebration.
t.stadhuis@51.2,4.4:
Antwerp's Stadhuis faces the Grote Markt with all the confidence of a city that once ran the world's busiest port. It was built between 1561 and 1565 to a design by Cornelis Floris de Vriendt, a Renaissance palace with a long, symmetrical front, tiers of columns and a central tower topped by statues. Four hundred and more years later it still serves as the city hall, and its gilded flags, carved reliefs and rows of tall windows catch the evening light beautifully.

In the square in front stands the Brabo fountain, a muscular bronze figure hurling a giant's severed hand into the river. The legend says that the giant Druon Antigoon demanded tolls from sailors on the Scheldt and chopped off the hands of those who refused to pay, until the hero Silvius Brabo defeated him and threw the hand away. The name Antwerp is said to come from that hand-throwing, hand werpen, though linguists have their doubts. The guild houses that line the square, with their stepped gables and golden ornament, add to the theatrical feel.

Riding into the old centre is a mixed pleasure. Cobbles and tram rails are slippery in the wet, narrow streets limit access, and parking is tight, so many riders leave the bike at a car park on the edge and walk in. Belgium also has low-emission zones in Antwerp, so check the current rules for your vehicle before you arrive. Fuel is plentiful in the surrounding city and along the ring road, and the Grote Markt is ringed with cafés and restaurants serving mussels, stoofvlees, a Flemish beef stew, and strong local beer.

The cathedral of Our Lady, with its towering spire, and Rubens's house are within a short walk, and the city's diamond district sits near the central station. Early morning is the best time to see the square before it fills up, and Sunday is quieter, though the shops are shut. Spring and early autumn are comfortable, while the winter months bring grey drizzle and an early dusk. The Scheldt waterfront, a short stroll away, is worth a sunset walk.
t.beguinage de bruges@51.2,3.2:
The Princely Beguinage of Bruges, Ten Wijngaerde, is the sort of place that makes people lower their voices without being asked. White-washed houses surround a grassy courtyard planted with old trees, and in spring thousands of daffodils bloom under them. A beguinage was a community where lay women lived a religious life without taking full vows, and Flanders had many of them from the thirteenth century. This one was founded around 1245 under Margaret of Constantinople, Countess of Flanders, and the UNESCO listing of Flemish Beguinages covers it, along with Diest and others.

Today the beguinage is occupied by Benedictine nuns, and there is a small museum in one of the houses. Visitors may walk through the courtyard and the church, but silence is expected, so keep the engine off and the voices low. Right beside it, the Minnewater, often called the Lake of Love, reflects a small bridge and swans, and a stroll along it makes a calm interlude after the bustle of the Markt.

Riding into Bruges needs a bit of thought. The historic centre is a maze of one-way streets and cobbles, much of it restricted to residents and deliveries, and the best approach is to park outside the ring and walk or take a short bus ride. Brugge is a town of well over a hundred thousand, and fuel and parking are easy to find around the ring road. In summer, tourist crowds are heavy by midday, so aim for early morning or evening when the light on the canals is golden.

The Flemish countryside around is flat and open, with straight roads, poplars, canals and fields stretching to the North Sea, and the wind can be strong from the west. Take the road to Damme, along the canal lined with trees, for a gentle ride on a sunny afternoon. Belgian chocolate, waffles and fries with mayonnaise are available on every corner, and a Trappist beer in a brown café is a good way to end the day. March and April are best for flowers.
t.chevalement du n 3 bis de lens@50.4,2.8:
A headframe is the most honest piece of architecture in a mining country, because it exists only to hold up a wheel. The chevalement of Pit 3 bis at Lens is one of those tall, simple frames of concrete or steel, once used to raise coal and men from hundreds of metres underground, and it is now one of the markers of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012 as a living cultural landscape. At the height of the industry, hundreds of such frames stood on this flat country, and the sky was filled with smoke and steam.

The mining basin is an odd, powerful place. Around Lens and Liévin the land is flat, and the only hills are man-made: the terrils, slag heaps of waste rock, some of them as high as a small mountain, now covered in birch, broom and rare orchids. The twin terrils at Loos-en-Gohelle, about a hundred and eighty metres high, are the tallest in Europe and can be climbed, with a wide view over the plain. Between them stand the brick cités, the rows of workers' houses built by the companies.

Lens itself has reinvented itself with culture. The Louvre-Lens, a long, low museum of glass and aluminium, opened in 2012 on the site of an old pit, and its gallery runs through centuries of art in a single space. Lens is also a football town: Racing Club de Lens, with its red and gold shirts and a fiercely loyal crowd, has played at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis for generations. Fuel and food are easy, with Liévin less than a kilometre away.

Local food is generous and unpretentious: carbonade flamande, a beef stew with beer, frites, strong maroilles cheese and local beer. The language of the region, Picard or ch'ti, still lingers in older speech. For riding, the roads are flat and straight, with cobbles in places, and weather is changeable, often grey. Spring and early autumn are most pleasant, and the low light on the red brick of the cités is memorable.
t.temple protestant@50.4,2.8:
Liévin is a town of thirty-four thousand people that grew up around coal, and the Protestant temple on its streets is a small reminder of how mixed the mining population was. The pits drew workers from Belgium, Poland, Italy and North Africa as well as from the French countryside, and the mining companies built churches, schools, shops and entire districts for them. In a region that was overwhelmingly Catholic, a temple stood a little apart, and its quiet presence says something about the way the basin took in newcomers.

The mine was never gentle on this place. In December 1974 an explosion in the Saint-Amé pit at Liévin killed forty-two miners, one of the last great disasters of the French coalfield, and the memory is still strong. The last pits in the basin closed in 1990, and the towns have had to find a new identity since. Today the landscape of cités, the rows of brick workers' housing, with their small gardens, and the slag heaps rising from the plain, forms the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin that UNESCO listed in 2012.

Liévin itself has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and a few decent restaurants, and the town centre is an easy place to stop. Lens, with the Louvre-Lens museum, is a few minutes away. You can pick up a coffee in the square, and in the evening, the bars fill with football talk, since Racing Club de Lens is a passion for the whole area. The accent you hear, ch'ti, has a warm, singing quality that visitors enjoy.

Riding here is flat and often grey, with straight roads, roundabouts and brick houses. The cités are quiet and clean, with a dignity that comes from their uniform rows, and slowing down to look is rewarding. Light is best in early morning or late afternoon, when the brick turns warm red. Spring brings flowers to the gardens, and autumn mist drifts across the terrils. In winter, rain and wind can be bitter, but the cafés are warm.
Number 1 bis at Liévin was one of the shafts of the old Compagnie des mines de Liévin, and its headframe still stands, a lean tower against a sky that is often low and grey. It is protected as part of the Mining Basin World Heritage Site, listed in 2012, together with the terrils, the cités and a hundred or so other elements across the old coalfield. What strikes you is how ordinary it looks, a plain frame in an urban setting, and yet it stands for generations of men who went down in cages and came back up with faces black with coal.

Daily life in the pits was hard and highly structured. The shift began at the lamp room, where each miner took a numbered lamp, then the cage dropped to the working levels, hundreds of metres down, where the seams ran in narrow layers. Dust, heat and firedamp were constant dangers, and silicosis haunted retired miners. The nicknames, the gueules noires, black faces, were worn with pride, and the solidarity among workers shaped the politics and culture of the whole region.

Outside the shaft, the company took care of everything, building housing, clinics, schools and sports clubs, and the cités around Liévin, such as the Cités de la Justice and du Moulin, show the type: long, uniform rows of brick houses with gardens, laid out in neat grids. Many are still lived in, so be considerate and keep noise to a minimum. A short walk takes you to one of the terrils, where a path climbs through birch scrub to a view over the plain.

Liévin has all the practical services you need, with fuel stations and supermarkets close to the old pit, and the neighbouring villages of Angres and Éleu-dit-Leauwette are quiet. The roads around are flat, with brick houses and the occasional cobbled stretch, so slow down on wet stones. A plate of frites with a carbonade, or a slab of Maroilles tart, is the proper post-ride meal. Grey days suit the place, giving the brick and steel their character.
t.fosse n 13 bis@50.5,3.0:
Oignies holds a special place in the story of French coal, because it was the last place in the Nord-Pas-de-Calais where a pit closed. The final coal came up at Oignies in December 1990, ending nearly three centuries of mining in the basin, and the old pit buildings there have since been turned into a concert hall and cultural centre. Fosse 13 bis, a few kilometres off, belonged to the Compagnie des mines de Courrières, one of the great names of the coalfield, and the whole district falls inside the Mining Basin World Heritage Site that UNESCO recognised in 2012.

The Courrières name carries a heavy memory. On the tenth of March 1906, a firedamp and coal dust explosion tore through the company's galleries, killing around eleven hundred men, still the worst mining disaster in Europe. Rescue teams came from Germany and elsewhere to help, and the aftermath triggered strikes, reforms and a national mourning. The cités nearby, such as Montigny and Le Moucheron, were built for the families of such men, and the monuments scattered around the district keep the memory of the community alive.

Oignies is a town of about ten thousand people, with Libercourt and Carvin close by, and fuel and food are easy to find. You are in the Pévèle plain, north of Lens, a landscape of farms, canals, brick villages and slag heaps. Further north, the cobbled sectors of the Paris–Roubaix cycle race, including the famous trench through the forest at Arenberg, are not far off, and in April the roads here are full of cycling fans.

For a rider, this is flat, open country, with long straight roads, small roundabouts and a lot of brick. In the early morning, mist hangs over the fields and the terrils appear like blue hills. The light in September, low and golden, is lovely. Cobbles can be treacherous when wet, so take care, and the weather can change quickly, with rain blowing across the plain. A plate of Flemish beef stew with a strong local beer is the ritual reward.
t.chevalement du vieux deux@50.5,2.5:
Marles-les-Mines is a small town of about six thousand people west of Béthune, in the hilly western fringe of the coalfield, and the headframe known as the Vieux-Deux, the old Number Two, stands among its houses as a stubborn monument. The Compagnie des mines de Marles sank its shafts here in the nineteenth century, and the pit worked until the twentieth. The tall frame has been preserved, and together with the nearby terril and the cités around it, forms part of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, the World Heritage Site listed in 2012.

This corner of the basin is more undulating than the plain near Lens, with low hills, hedgerows and little valleys, and you feel the Artois uplands nearby. The terrils here have been colonised by nature: birch, buddleia and rare plants have taken root, and in summer butterflies and warblers fill the slopes. Some are open for walking, and the view from the top, across the old pit villages and out to the Béthune plain, is a good lesson in the shape of the coalfield.

The cités of Marles, among them Cité n°10, show the paternal design of the companies, with brick houses in rows, gardens at the back and little squares at the end. Auchel, a larger neighbour of about eleven thousand people, has shops, fuel and cafés, and Lozinghem is a village close by. Béthune itself, a short ride away, has a splendid Grand'Place and a belfry, also on the UNESCO list, and its market is lively.

On a bike, the roads here are a pleasant surprise: gentle climbs, curves through hedgerows, and long views across fields toward the next terril. The surface can be rough in places, and cobbles appear without warning, so keep an eye ahead. Mist and drizzle are common, and the brick takes a deeper colour in the damp. A pause at a bakery for a sweet tart and a coffee is an excellent way to end the day. Spring blossom is lovely, and autumn light is warm and golden.
t.grands bureaux de la societe houillere d:
The Grands Bureaux of the mining company at Liévin are the opposite of a pit: a big, solid brick office building where the engineers, accountants and managers ran the underground world from desks. Built in the style of company headquarters across the basin, with generous windows, a formal entrance and a clock, the building announces that coal was a serious business, with a payroll, a hierarchy and a public face. It sits in the town centre, a few hundred metres from the heart of Liévin, and it forms part of the Mining Basin that UNESCO listed in 2012.

The company ran more than offices. It built houses, schools, churches, clinics, sports halls and shops, and it expected loyalty in return. The system, often called paternalism, shaped life in places like Liévin so thoroughly that a miner's family might live in a company house, send the children to a company school, and see the company's name on the clinic and the sports club as well. The system also bred a fierce sense of class identity, and strikes in the coalfield were among the biggest in French history.

The cités around the office, such as the Cité des Sœurs, and the neighbouring terril 31, a slag heap now covered in vegetation, are within walking distance, and you can combine them in a leisurely stroll. Other sites on the wider mining route, as far off as Wallers-Arenberg, belong to the same story, spread across the plain.

Liévin has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and a market. The town is lively on football match days, when the red and gold of Lens colours spill over from the neighbouring city. The ride is mostly flat and urban, with brick buildings and roundabouts, though a few quiet lanes lead out into the fields. In misty weather the brick looks almost black, and in sun it glows. A strong coffee and a slab of tarte au sucre in a local bakery are the best way to start the morning.
t.chevalement de la fosse n 9@50.4,3.1:
The tall steel frame that stands over a coal pit shaft is called a chevalement in French, and a headframe in English, and in the old mining basin of northern France they are the cathedrals of a vanished industry. This one stands at the Fosse n°9, a few kilometres north of Douai, in the plain of the Pévèle, where coal was dug for more than two centuries. The basin of Nord-Pas-de-Calais stretches for over a hundred kilometres across flat farmland, and its pits, slag heaps, workers' villages and railway lines are now protected by UNESCO, listed in 2012 as an evolving cultural landscape. The last pit closed in 1990, and the people here still talk about the mine in the present tense.

The slag heaps, called terrils, are the other great feature. Some have been planted with birch and pine and are now nature reserves, and a few stand more than a hundred metres high, a strange conical hill in the flattest of plains. The two at Loos-en-Gohelle are the highest in Europe. The miners' houses, the corons, stand in long red brick terraces, each with a garden for vegetables and a shed for pigeons, and the people who live in them are famous for their warmth and their dry humour. The local dialect, called ch'ti, was made known to the world by a comedy film.

The food is hearty. Frites in paper cones, carbonnade flamande, a beef and beer stew, and maroilles, a strong, orange-rinded cheese, are the staples, and the local beers are good. A Sunday lunch here is long.

The riding is flat and easy, in a landscape of beet fields and long straight roads, with farm tracks and villages with brick churches. Cobbled stretches, famous from the Paris-Roubaix cycle race, lie to the east, near Wallers and Arenberg, and are rough and slippery for a motorcycle, so take care. Wind is strong on open ground. Roost-Warendin has fuel and bakeries, Raimbeaucourt and Râches are smaller villages, and Douai has everything. The best time is spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the fields are green or gold.
t.monument aux morts 1914 1918@50.4,2.8:
Lens is a mining town that was flattened in the First World War and rebuilt in brick, and the monument to the dead of 1914 to 1918 stands as a reminder of what happened here. Lines of trenches ran across this plain for years, and the surrounding ridges, Vimy and Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, were the scene of huge battles. At Vimy, the great white Canadian memorial stands on the ridge, commemorating the attack of April 1917 in which Canadian troops took the hill, and the preserved trenches and tunnels can be visited. At Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, a vast French military cemetery and a lantern tower hold the remains of tens of thousands of soldiers. They are quiet places, and the silence is part of the experience.

The mining story is just as present. Fosse n°13 bis, on this ride, is one of the pits in the basin protected by UNESCO as a cultural landscape, and the coal fields employed tens of thousands of people for generations. In the middle of Lens, on the site of an old pit, stands the Louvre-Lens, a long, low gallery of glass and aluminium opened in 2012, which brought a branch of the Parisian museum to a place that had been written off. Its location in a former mining town is no accident, and the building and the park around it are worth an hour.

Lens also has football. The Racing Club de Lens, known as the Sang et Or, the blood and gold, plays in the Stade Bollaert-Delelis, and on a match day the town fills with fans in red and yellow and the noise is extraordinary. The supporters are among the most loyal in France.

For a rider, this is flat, gritty country, with a mix of motorways, town streets and quiet roads between slag heaps. The surface is uneven, there are speed cameras and the traffic can be dense. Fuel is easy to find, since Lens, Loison-sous-Lens and the neighbouring towns have stations and supermarkets. Come in spring or autumn, and take care on wet cobbles.
t.cite des sports wingles@50.5,2.9:
Wingles is a town of nine thousand people in the old mining basin, sitting on the edge of the plain where the Lens-Béthune coal fields meet the canal of La Bassée. The coal here was dug from the mid-nineteenth century, and the town still bears the marks: rows of workers' houses, a handful of pit headframes, and slag heaps that rise from the farmland. The sports complex that gives this stop its name is a modern echo of the old social life of the mine, when companies built stadiums, bandstands and gymnasia for their workers, and brass bands and football clubs were as central to the community as the pit itself.

The area belongs to the Nord-Pas-de-Calais mining basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012. The listing covers more than a hundred separate elements, from pit heads to miners' villages and even railway lines, and it is unusual for including the living towns and not just the monuments. The result is a landscape in which history is lived rather than displayed. A short ride away at Douvrin stands one of the big engine factories of the French motor industry, a reminder that the region has moved from coal to cars.

North of here, the town of Béthune has a belfry, a tall brick and stone tower on the Grand'Place that is part of the UNESCO list of Belfries of Belgium and France. These towers, which stood for the freedom of the medieval towns, are a distinctive sight in this part of Europe, and Béthune's, with its carillon, is one of the finest. The town square is lined with Flemish-style gabled houses, rebuilt after the war, and is an excellent place for a coffee.

The roads are flat and the country is open. Straight lanes run between beet fields and rows of poplars, and a canal path is popular with cyclists. A rider may find the landscape plain, but on a clear day the skyline of pit heads and slag heaps has a sort of beauty. Wingles has fuel and shops, and Vendin-le-Vieil and Douvrin do as well. Spring is the best time to visit, and wind is a constant companion.
t.dispensaire societe de secours mutuel@50:
A dispensary may seem an odd thing to visit, but this is a monument to something remarkable. In the nineteenth century the coal companies of northern France built housing, schools, churches and clinics for their workers, partly out of paternalism and partly to keep a stable workforce, and the miners themselves set up mutual aid societies, the sociétés de secours mutuel, to pay for doctors, medicines and funerals. The dispensary at Bully-les-Mines belongs to that world of care and control, and it is one of the buildings that explain why UNESCO listed the whole mining basin in 2012. The brick architecture has a plain, solid dignity, and the sense of a community looking after its own is easy to feel.

The population here is varied. In the 1920s the mines recruited thousands of workers from Poland, and the families who came stayed, so that Polish surnames are common in the basin and Polish churches and cultural associations still exist. Italians, Belgians and North Africans came as well, and the local identity is a mixture of all of them, held together by shared work and shared dangers. Grenay and Bully-les-Mines were both pit towns, with whole districts of corons laid out in straight rows around a central church or school.

After the mines closed, the region had to reinvent itself, and the slag heaps have been turned into parks, ski slopes and nature reserves. The twin heaps at Loos-en-Gohelle, a short ride to the north, are the highest in Europe, with a hiking trail to the top and a view across the flat country to Arras and Lille. On a clear day the climb is rewarding.

Riding here is easy and flat, with long straight roads, cobbled sections in the town centres, and plenty of traffic around Lens. Bully-les-Mines, Grenay and Mazingarbe all have fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, so fuel is no problem. A traditional lunch of frites and a stew, with a Belgian-style beer, is a good way to end the stop. Spring and autumn are best.
t.paysage et ensemble miniers de fouquiere:
On 10 March 1906 a fire in a pit at Courrières, a few kilometres from here, set off a coal-dust explosion that ran through the galleries of three linked mines and killed 1,099 men and boys. It is the worst mining disaster in European history. Rescue teams came from Germany's Westphalian coalfield and worked alongside French crews, a rare moment of cooperation between two countries that would be at war within a decade. Twenty days after the explosion, thirteen survivors were found alive, which astonished the country. The disaster led to strikes and a national debate on safety and the role of the state, with the interior minister, Georges Clemenceau, sending troops to the area, and it changed mining law in France.

The landscape of Fouquières-lès-Lens, Billy-Montigny and Noyelles-sous-Lens is part of the UNESCO-listed mining basin, with corons, slag heaps and pit headframes scattered among the modern suburbs. Many of the cemeteries and memorials in the area honour the victims of that day, with rows of simple graves and a monument. They are worth a quiet visit.

The people are warm and direct, and the old mining communities have a strong identity. Football, brass bands and pigeon racing are all part of the culture, and the Sunday market is a good place to see it. The beer is local and the frites are very good. The pit villages hold a festival for Sainte-Barbe, the patron saint of miners, in early December, with processions and banners.

For a rider, the roads are flat, mostly straight, and often busy. The surface is generally fair, though cobbles appear in town centres and slippery rails cross the roads. Fuel is easy to find in the neighbouring towns of Billy-Montigny, Noyelles and Fouquières, all of which have supermarkets and petrol. A visit to the Louvre-Lens, a short drive away, fits well with the day. Spring and autumn give the best light, and winter brings fog and drizzle.
t.corbulo s canal romeinsepad@52.1,4.4:
Some two thousand years ago, in the year 47, the Roman general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo had a canal dug between the Old Rhine and the Maas to give his ships a safe route behind the dunes and avoid the dangerous coastal sea. Tacitus mentions it, and later sources say that Corbulo, recalled by the emperor Claudius from further conquests in Germania, kept his soldiers busy with the digging rather than let them grow idle. The channel is known as the Fossa Corbulonis, and in today's landscape it is usually identified with the Vliet, the old waterway that runs between Leiden and Delft through Voorburg.

Voorburg, which is part of the Hague region, was Forum Hadriani, a Roman town named after the emperor Hadrian and the only Roman town of that status in this part of the Netherlands. The marks it left are modest: a few remains, a museum and a signposted Roman Path that runs along the waterside. But as part of the Lower Germanic Limes, the Rhine frontier of the empire, the area holds the memory of one of the largest frontiers the Romans ever built.

On a bike, this is flat, built-up country, and the interest is more in the quiet backroads than in drama. The Vliet is lined with old villas, small bridges, rowing clubs and weeping willows, and the roads along the water are narrow, brick-paved in places, and shared with many cyclists, who have priority in their own way. Traffic around The Hague is dense, trams complicate junctions, and parking is expensive, so a short walk is better than a long ride here. Spring blossom and autumn mist add atmosphere; winter brings grey skies and wet cobbles that deserve respect.

Voorburg has thirty-eight thousand people and a full supply of fuel, shops, bakeries and cafes; the Hague is on the doorstep. Herring and raw onion at a fish stall is the classic local snack. Amsterdam and the canal ring, which is the destination of the ride, lie about fifty kilometres to the north, where the seventeenth-century merchants made their own engineering marvel, a ring of canals that is arguably the more famous descendant of the Romans' modest ditch.
t.rice terrace clusters of kiangan nagacad:
Nagacadan is a village in Kiangan, in the province of Ifugao in northern Luzon, and its rice terraces are shaped like a vast green amphitheatre, with stone-walled steps climbing the slope in tight curves above the Ibulao river. The Ifugao rice terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras are UNESCO listed, and older guidebooks describe them as two thousand years old, though more recent research suggests that many of the surviving terraces are younger, perhaps a few centuries. What nobody doubts is the effort: dry-stone walls, bamboo irrigation pipes and generations of hand labour, all passed on without machines.

The terraces are not just farming but a whole culture. Rice is a sacred crop for the Ifugao, and harvest rituals involve chants, sacrifices and the drinking of tapuy, the local rice wine. Carved wooden figures called bulul guard the granaries and the fields. The same hills saw a very different moment in history in September 1945, when the Japanese general Yamashita surrendered at Kiangan, a small town you pass on the way, and the end of the Pacific War reached this remote valley.

The look of the terraces changes with the season. In planting time, around February and March, the water-filled steps mirror the sky; in April and May they are a brilliant green, and by June the rice has ripened to gold. The rainy season and typhoons from July to October can bring landslides on the mountain roads, so check the weather before you go. Early morning is best, with mist pooling in the valleys and the light low.

The riding is memorable but demanding. The roads into the Cordillera are narrow, winding and steep, often cut into the hillside with a sheer drop on one side, and surfaces can be broken by landslides and rain. Traffic is slow, with jeepneys, tricycles and trucks sharing the lane, and the cultural rule is to take your time. The villages of Hapao and Monamon are close, and Banaue, another famous terrace town, is a little farther along. Fuel is scarce in the hills, so load up in the bigger towns on the approach, such as Lagawe, and carry some cash, since rural places seldom take cards. Local guides from the villages are a good way to understand the terraces and to support the community.
t.sonian forest forest reserve joseph zwa@:
Brussels has a forest on its doorstep, and a very good one. The Sonian Forest, Forêt de Soignes or Zoniënwoud depending on who is speaking, spreads over the south-eastern edge of the city in a dark green arc of about four and a half thousand hectares, and its core is beech, tall, grey and straight as columns. The forest is shared among three regions of Belgium, and the Joseph Zwaenepoel reserve is a protected section in the Flemish part, where the managers let nature take its course and fallen trees are left to rot. It is part of the UNESCO listing for ancient and primeval beech forests, extended in 2017 to include the Sonian Forest.

Honesty matters here: this is not a primeval forest in the strict sense. People have used it for centuries as a hunting ground and wood supply, and the great beech stands you see were largely replanted from the late eighteenth century onward, when the forest was managed for timber under Austrian rule and its successors. What makes it special is that so large a mature beech wood has survived beside a European capital, and that the dead wood and old trees in the reserve host fungi, beetles, woodpeckers and bats that need exactly that.

Walking in it, especially in early summer, is like being inside a cathedral, with light falling through the new leaves in green shafts and the ground covered in bluebells in April. In autumn the colours turn to gold and copper. The forest is popular with walkers, cyclists, horse riders and joggers, so a rider on the narrow roads has to be patient and gentle. Speed limits are low, and the authorities enforce them, with cameras in the villages around.

Hoeilaart, nearby, is known for its greenhouse grapes, a local tradition for over a century, and the town of Tervuren to the north has a museum on Central Africa, a grand building that raises complex questions about Belgium's colonial past. Waterloo, only five kilometres away, is the village that gave its name to the great battle of 18 June 1815, when Napoleon was finally defeated, and the Lion's Mound, a huge artificial hill with a bronze lion on top, marks the battlefield.

Fuel is no problem here: Waterloo, Sint-Genesius-Rode and Hoeilaart are all sizeable towns with stations and restaurants. The ride goes east to Tienen, with its church of Saint Germanus, across the gentle fields of Brabant. Try a Belgian waffle or a plate of mussels and fries, and expect rain at any time of year, so keep a waterproof close.
France's coalfield is a long, narrow band that runs from Béthune in the west to the Belgian border in the east, and at its eastern end, around Valenciennes, the ground still carries traces of the first mines. The Anzin company, which controlled much of this area in the nineteenth century, dug shafts, built pumping stations and laid out workers' housing, and in 1884 Émile Zola came to the district to research Germinal, his great novel of a miners' strike. The ensemble at La Sentinelle includes the old pumping engine house of the Sarteau pit, a survivor from that early industrial age, and the nearby Cités de Beaurepaire, rows of company housing for miners and their families. The whole mining basin was listed by UNESCO in 2012.

The country is flat and gently rolling, a mix of fields, small towns and the dark cones of old slag heaps, called terrils, which now sprout birch and wildflowers. Roads here are mostly straight and well surfaced, with roundabouts every few hundred metres and plenty of traffic. This is not scenic riding in the Alpine sense, but it has a strong character, and the sight of a terril against a pale northern sky is unforgettable. Cobbled sections, called pavé, appear on some minor roads, and they are slippery in rain, so take care.

La Sentinelle has about three thousand people and Petite-Forêt about five thousand, so fuel and food are within reach, and Valenciennes, the nearest city, is a short ride away with all services. The region's cuisine is hearty, with beer, potatoes, cheese and the strong-smelling Maroilles. A plate of carbonade flamande and a glass of local beer after a day in the cold is the right kind of reward.

Spend a little time on the human story. The mines were hard and dangerous, and generations of families lived and worked within sight of the pithead. The pump house, quiet now, carries something of that history in its brick walls and tall windows. Look for the brickwork, which is rich in detail, and imagine the engine breathing.
t.monument emile basly@50.4,2.8:
Émile Basly was a miner who became a union leader, a deputy and for a long time the mayor of Lens, and his monument stands in the town as a salute to the people who worked underground. He led the great strike of 1884 at Anzin, which inspired Zola's Germinal, and later rose to national politics as a socialist. In Lens, a town of over thirty-eight thousand people at the heart of the Pas-de-Calais coalfield, he remains a local hero. The town was razed in the First World War and rebuilt in the 1920s, so much of the centre has the brick-and-concrete look of that rebuilding.

You come to Lens for the landscape of the mining basin, which UNESCO listed in 2012. The twin slag heaps at Loos-en-Gohelle, a few kilometres away, are among the tallest in Europe, rising nearly two hundred metres above the plain, and they can be climbed on foot. From the top you see a wide, flat country of fields and small towns, with other terrils scattered across the horizon like a chain of low volcanoes. The Louvre-Lens, a satellite of the Paris museum, opened in 2012 on the site of an old pit, with a long, low building of glass and aluminium that reflects the sky.

Riding is easy but not thrilling. Straight roads cross the plain, lined with brick houses and the occasional chimney, and cobbles break the surface now and then. Weather is changeable, with wind and rain from the North Sea, so pack a waterproof. The football stadium, home of RC Lens, is a place of passion, and on match days the town is full of red and yellow shirts.

Fuel and food are no problem in Lens, and the old brewery bars and frites stands are good for a cheap, filling meal. A visit to the memorial to the Courrières disaster of 1906, in which over a thousand miners died in the worst mining accident in European history, is a sober but worthwhile stop. The monument to Basly says, in its own way, that the people who dug here counted.
t.cite de la solitude@50.5,3.6:
The Cité de la Solitude sounds like the name of a novel, but it is a real miners' housing estate in the far east of the French coalfield, near Vieux-Condé and Condé-sur-l'Escaut, within a few kilometres of the Belgian border. Here the mining basin merges into the Hainaut country on the other side, and the two halves share a single history of coal, iron and hard work. The French basin was listed by UNESCO in 2012, and on the Belgian side the major mining sites of Wallonia, including the Grand-Hornu and the Bois-du-Cazier, were listed in the same year. The Beffroi de Thuin, in the Belgian town of Thuin, is one of several belfries in the region recognised by UNESCO as symbols of civic pride.

A cité is a planned estate of brick houses built by mining companies, often arranged in tidy rows with gardens, a school and a church, and the best preserved ones feel like small, self-contained towns. They are low, uniform and warmly red, with slate roofs and chimneys, and they say a great deal about how the companies thought about their workers. Riding through them is a slow, quiet affair, on streets that are narrow, sometimes cobbled and often lined with parked cars.

The surrounding country is flat, with the River Scheldt, called the Escaut here, meandering through canals and meadows. Roads are straight and the traffic is moderate, though the border area is busy with commuters. Weather is changeable and often grey, so take rain gear. In autumn the mist hangs low over the fields, and the terrils, now wooded, stand out like dark islands.

Vieux-Condé and Condé-sur-l'Escaut, each with over ten thousand people, have fuel, bakeries and cafes, and Valenciennes is not far. Cross into Belgium and you reach Mons, a short ride away, where the beer and the frites are excellent and the border check is nothing more than a change of road signs. If you like industrial heritage, the contrast between the two sides of the border makes a rewarding day.
t.terril 31@50.6,2.3:
A terril is a coal slag heap, and in the old Artois coalfield they punctuate the horizon like unfinished pyramids. This one, numbered 31 in the local inventory of the mining basin, lies on the southern fringe of the field, near Norrent-Fontes and Mametz, where the plain of the Lys starts to tilt against the low hills of Artois. Heaps like this were built up over decades from the waste rock hauled out of the pits, and many are conical, a few are flat-topped and some stretch in long ridges. Left alone, they have turned into oddities of nature, with warm black soil that suits unusual plants, birch scrub, and in summer a surprising number of butterflies.

The ride here is rural and quiet. The country between Lillers, Auchel and Aire-sur-la-Lys is a patchwork of fields, hedgerows and small brick villages, with roads that run in long lines and sudden right-angle turns, a pattern inherited from old field boundaries. The surface is fair, though cobbled stretches and farm mud appear without warning, especially in autumn. Wind can be strong across the open plain, and rain comes in from the Channel, so a waterproof is wise. In spring the fields glow yellow with rapeseed.

Aire-sur-la-Lys, eight kilometres away, has over ten thousand people and is the practical choice for fuel and a meal. Its main square is framed by Flemish-style brick houses, and the belfry, listed by UNESCO along with others in northern France and Belgium, rises over the market place. The cités of the label, the miners' housing estates of the Justice and the Moulin, belong to the former mining villages nearby, with their long rows of identical houses, each with a chimney and a patch of garden.

To climb a terril, check first that it is open, because some are protected nature reserves and others are private. If you can, go up at sunset. The slope is loose, the view is wide, and the whole district spreads out below, with church spires and chimneys catching the last light. It is a landscape made by human hands, but time has given it a certain strange beauty.
t.coron des 120@50.4,3.5:
The Coron des 120 is among the most famous rows of miners' houses in France, partly because a film crew chose it. A coron is a long terrace of identical brick cottages built by a mining company, and this one, with its endless line of doors, chimneys and small gardens, was used in the 1993 film of Germinal, Zola's novel of the miners' strike. It lies near Anzin and Petite-Forêt, in the Valenciennes area, at the heart of the mining basin that UNESCO listed in 2012. I believe the film's location is in the adjoining commune of Raismes, so treat the exact placement with a little caution.

What you notice most is the scale of the company's thinking. Rows of this kind were designed to house a workforce close to the pit, and each family had a few rooms, a garden and an outbuilding. The bricks are dark red, the roofs grey slate, and the effect, even now, is of order and uniformity, with a little human variety in the paint of doors and the flowers in the front gardens. The old pits have gone, but the houses endure, lived in and loved.

Riding here is pleasantly flat. Roads from Anzin through the forest of Raismes, St-Amand and Wallers are lined with trees and brick houses, and the traffic is moderate. The Arenberg site, with its great steel pithead frame, is another film location and a major heritage attraction, and it stands only a few kilometres away. Cobblestones appear unexpectedly on minor roads, so slow down on wet days. The best months are May and September, when the forest is green and the light is soft.

Anzin has over fourteen thousand people and Petite-Forêt five thousand, so you are never short of either. The Anzin company traces its beginnings to the finding of coal at nearby Fresnes in 1720, an event that launched French deep mining. The company grew into one of the largest in the country, and its legacy is written in the streets and chimneys around you. A visit here is a small lesson in how a landscape of work gets made.
t.w arly pendjari complex@11.9,2.7:
This is the great wildlife country of West Africa, where three nations meet at a bend of the Niger river. The W park takes its name from the shape of the river's loops, and together with the Arly reserve in Burkina Faso and the Pendjari in Benin it forms the largest protected savannah area in the region. Elephants, buffalo, hippos and several kinds of antelope live here, and so do lions and a small, precious population of cheetahs. In the dry months from January to April animals gather at the remaining waterholes, which is when watching is best.

The landscape is open woodland, grassland and gallery forest along seasonal rivers, with baobabs standing like upturned trees and flat-topped acacias. Rock outcrops catch the evening sun, and the harmattan wind from the Sahara fills the air with a pale dust that turns sunsets red. Birds are plentiful, with hornbills, bee-eaters, kingfishers and, along the river, Egyptian plovers and herons.

I have to be plain about the riding. Roads into and between these parks are laterite tracks of variable quality, and the rainy season from June to October makes many of them impassable. More serious still is security, since the border zone around the W has been affected by armed groups over recent years, and several governments advise against travel there. The Pendjari side in Benin has also seen incidents. Anyone thinking of riding here should consult current official advice and local park authorities before making any plan, and be ready to accept that the answer may be no.

If conditions are open, the nearest services are in the towns outside the park boundaries, since there is no town listed at these coordinates, and fuel must be carried in from larger centres such as Kandi or Natitingou in Benin or Niamey in Niger. Park entry usually requires a fee and often an escort or guide, and camping or lodges are the only accommodation. Carry more water than you imagine and a spare tyre. In the heat of the day the animals rest, and so should you, with morning and evening for movement.
t.tour de saint rombaut@51.0,4.5:
Saint Rumbold's Tower dominates the skyline of Mechelen like a very tall stone cliff. It is the bell tower of the cathedral, and it rises to about ninety-seven metres. It was begun in the fourteenth century and was meant to go higher, with a spire that would have made it among the tallest in Europe, but the money ran out and the tower was left with a flat top in the sixteenth century. That unfinished stump is somehow more memorable than a completed spire would have been. It is part of the UNESCO list of belfries of Belgium and France, and a ring of bells hangs inside, including two carillons, one of which is played by hand from a keyboard of wooden batons.

Mechelen was once the capital of the Burgundian Netherlands, under Margaret of Austria, who governed from here in the early sixteenth century, and the town still has the elegant palaces, guildhouses and quays of a place that used to matter. Climbing the tower is a stiff trial, with more than five hundred steps, but the view across the Flemish plain, with Brussels and Antwerp on the horizon, repays the effort. In the evening the carillon concerts drift down over the square.

Riding in the area is flat and easy. The roads between Brussels, Antwerp and Mechelen are dense with traffic, with ring roads, roundabouts and the usual Belgian cobbles on older streets, which are slippery in rain. For a gentler ride, head out along the Dyle or Nete rivers, or toward Leuven, on quiet lanes through market gardens, poplars and brick villages. The weather is changeable, with rain at any time of year, so a waterproof layer is not optional. Spring and early autumn are the pleasant seasons.

Mechelen is a city of nearly eighty thousand, and you will find fuel stations, cafés, brasseries and bike shops without trouble. It is known for the Mechelse koekoek, a famous chicken, and for the local beer of the Gouden Carolus brewery, whose name comes from a coin. Parking is easy in the underground garages near the centre. A Belgian speed camera is rarely far away, and city centres often have low-emission zone rules, so check before you enter a large city with a foreign-registered vehicle.
t.cites anatole france et des electriciens:
Bruay-la-Buissière is a town built on coal, and the rows of brick houses that spread around it were designed to keep miners close to their pits. The Cités Anatole France and des Électriciens belong to the great mining landscape of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais, a basin of coalfields, slag heaps and company towns that UNESCO inscribed in 2012. Coal was mined here from the early eighteenth century until the last pit closed in 1990, and the memory of that work is still everywhere.

A cité is a planned company village: terraces of identical brick houses, each with a small garden, laid out in streets or in half-moons, with a school, a church and a shop built by the mining company. The idea was to keep families housed, healthy and obedient, and to ensure that miners lived close enough to answer the siren. The cités of Bruay have a particular orderliness, with brick in warm orange and red, steep tiled roofs and long, neat streets. If you stop and look carefully you can see that the houses vary from period to period, with later ones larger and better equipped.

The people who lived here included Frenchmen, Belgians, Italians and, after the First World War, thousands of Poles, who came to work in the pits. They called themselves gueules noires, black faces, with pride, and their culture of brass bands, pigeon racing and local football is still alive in the small towns. The region's cuisine is hearty: carbonnade, stewed in beer, frites, and strong cheeses such as Maroilles. Look for an estaminet, the old-style local pub, for a proper lunch.

Riding here is not about mountains but about atmosphere. The land is flat, apart from the great conical slag heaps, the terrils, that rise from the plain like green pyramids. Roads run straight between brick villages, with the occasional stretch of cobbles, so take care in wet weather. Light traffic is usual on Sundays, and in autumn, with mist and wet leaves, the whole landscape turns to sepia.

Bruay-la-Buissière has twenty-four thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and many cafés. Everything you need is close.
t.monument du soldat marche@50.4,2.7:
Bully-les-Mines lies just below the long ridge of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, where the great French military cemetery overlooks the coalfield, and the juxtaposition says something about this part of France. The land around is a battlefield and a mining basin at the same time. In 1914 and 1915 the front line ran through here, and the villages were shattered. After the war they were rebuilt, and the new mining estates, the cités de la Victoire and des Arbres, took names that spoke of recovery.

The Monument du soldat Marche belongs to that story, a small memorial in a landscape full of them. Every village in the Pas-de-Calais has a war memorial, and many have more than one, and they are quiet reminders of how much was lost. Not far north, Vimy Ridge is the Canadian national memorial, with its twin white pylons visible for miles, and the vast cemetery at Notre-Dame-de-Lorette holds the remains of tens of thousands of French soldiers.

The mining cités here belong to the UNESCO listing of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, inscribed in 2012. They are rows of red-brick houses, each with a garden and often a pigeon loft, built in a rebuilding wave after the First World War, when the companies replaced destroyed housing with something more regular and more modern. Today their gardens are bright with dahlias and vegetables, and many have been renovated with care.

Riding in the Pas-de-Calais is very flat, and the road surface can be harsh, with patches of cobbles and frost damage. It is best enjoyed in the early morning or on a quiet weekend, when the light is soft and traffic is thin. In spring and summer the air smells of cut grass and turned earth, while autumn brings mist across the fields and the terrils glow with birch and broom.

Bully-les-Mines has twelve thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and small cafés, and the larger town of Lens is a short ride away. A visit to the memorial park at Vimy or the cemetery at Lorette is a thoughtful addition to a day.
t.cite de la gare@50.5,2.9:
Wingles is a small town of nearly nine thousand people on the southern edge of the Lens coalfield, and its Cité de la Gare takes its name from the railway station that once carried coal away. This is the logistics of the mining basin laid bare: pit, rail, canal and village. The coal came up the shafts, was hauled to the sorting plants and loaded on trains that ran to the factories of the north and the ports of the Channel, while the people who dug it lived in neat brick rows within sight of the headframes.

The Cité de la Gare is one of the sites that make up the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, listed by UNESCO in 2012. Its houses are typical of the cités: terraced, built in brick, with small gardens, and arranged to be convenient for the railway and the pit. The company provided everything from schools to sports clubs, and loyalty was expected in return. The streets are quiet today, with bright shutters and flower boxes, and the neatness of the plan is still obvious.

Near Wingles stands one of the highest slag heaps in the basin, and the double cone of the terrils at Loos-en-Gohelle, which are the tallest in Europe, are a short ride away. You can climb them on foot, and the view from the top across the plain, with the old mining towns, wind turbines and church spires, is a good way to understand the scale of the old industry.

The ride is flat and the roads are straightforward, with long runs between brick villages. The surface can be rough after winter, and cobbled stretches appear on minor roads, particularly in the countryside around Lens and Béthune. In rain these can be slippery. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summer is mild by southern standards, though showers are common.

Wingles has pumps, a few shops and cafés, with larger supermarkets on the road to Lens. Try the local beer and a plate of carbonnade in a village estaminet, and bring a waterproof, because the sky in the north can change quickly.
t.grand hornu@50.4,3.8:
A coal mine designed like a neoclassical palace sounds like a joke, but Grand-Hornu is real, and the man behind it meant every column. Henri De Gorge, a mining entrepreneur, took over a failing colliery at Hornu in the early nineteenth century and built, between about 1810 and 1830, a complex of workshops, offices and workers' housing around a great oval courtyard. The buildings are in pale stone and brick, with arcades, pediments and a perfect sense of proportion. De Gorge was an idealist, and he wanted his workers to live in decent houses with gardens, which was unusual in an age of slums.

The site closed with the mine in 1954 and was threatened with demolition before being rescued and restored. Today it houses the MAC's, a contemporary art museum, in the old workshops, and visitors walk around the courtyard under the arches where horses and carts once passed. It is one of the Major Mining Sites of Wallonia that UNESCO listed in 2012, and it is a good place to understand how the first generation of mine owners saw themselves as civilisers as well as employers.

This is the Borinage, a coal region in the west of Belgium that is also linked to the young Vincent van Gogh, who worked here as a lay preacher among the miners in the late 1870s, and whose first serious drawings were of the people he met. The landscape is flat and industrial in places, with the green cones of old slag heaps and rows of brick houses, and Mons, the nearby city that was European Capital of Culture in 2015, makes a good base.

The ride is not about thrills but about texture. Roads here are mostly flat, with small towns, canals and factories, and surfaces that can be bumpy, with cobbles in the older streets. The weather is changeable and often damp, and the best days are those with high cloud and cold sunshine. Spring and early autumn are agreeable.

Saint-Ghislain, a couple of kilometres away, has twenty-two thousand people, and offers fuel, supermarkets and cafés, as does Mons. Belgian frites and a glass of beer in a local café make a satisfying end to a visit.
t.gare de lens@50.4,2.8:
Lens station looks like a locomotive, which is exactly what its architects intended. The Art Deco building, completed in the 1920s to replace a station destroyed in the First World War, has a long low front with a tall central block that suggests a train at speed, and its brick and stone are laid out with real flair. Inside and out it was designed to tell people that this was a town that had survived and meant to thrive, and few stations of its date achieve the effect so well.

Lens was almost wiped off the map in the First World War. The town stood on the front line, and by 1918 most of its buildings had been flattened. Rebuilding gave it an Art Deco character, and you can see it in the streets around the station. A short walk takes you to the Louvre-Lens, a branch of the Paris museum that opened in 2012 on the site of an old pit, designed as a long, low glass and aluminium building that reflects the sky. The gallery is full of well-lit space, and entry to the main collection has often been free or cheap.

The Cité Crombez is one of the mining estates of the Nord-Pas-de-Calais Mining Basin, which UNESCO inscribed in 2012. Rows of brick houses, neat gardens and the patterns of company planning give it a distinct and rather moving atmosphere. Lens is also the home of RC Lens, whose red-and-yellow supporters fill the Bollaert-Delelis stadium, and the town's football culture is as much a part of its identity as the mines.

For riders, Lens is a hub rather than a destination, and a very easy one to reach, since it sits at the meeting point of motorways and main roads from Paris, Lille and the coast. The landscape is flat, the roads are mostly straight and surfaces vary, with occasional cobbled stretches. Fine days are best, because rain on cobbles is greasy.

Lens has thirty-eight thousand people, so fuel, parking and food are easy to find. Try a plate of local cheese, such as Maroilles, or a waffle with a coffee in a café near the station.
t.st augustine s abbey@51.3,1.1:
Canterbury has been the centre of English Christianity for fourteen centuries, and the ruined abbey of Saint Augustine is where it began. In AD 597, Augustine, a Roman monk sent by Pope Gregory the Great, landed in Kent with a small group of companions to convert the English. King Aethelberht of Kent, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian, received them, and the king himself was baptised soon afterwards. Augustine founded a monastery outside the city walls, where he and his successors were buried, and it grew into one of the richest abbeys in England.

The abbey was dissolved by Henry VIII in 1538, and much of it was demolished or turned into a royal palace. What remains is a field of low ruins, outlines of walls and chapels, and a museum that tells the story. It is a quiet, moving place, and seen together with Canterbury Cathedral and the little church of Saint Martin, it forms the World Heritage site that UNESCO listed in 1988. Saint Martin's is among the oldest churches in England still in use, and probably dates from Roman times in part.

The cathedral, a short walk away, is the mother church of the Anglican Communion, and the site of the murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket in 1170, which turned Canterbury into a pilgrimage destination. Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, written in the late fourteenth century, follows a group of pilgrims on the road from London to Becket's shrine, and the city still plays on that connection with everything from walking tours to a visitor attraction.

For a rider, the Kent countryside around Canterbury is soft and green, with orchards, hop gardens and flinty lanes. The roads are narrow and hedged, with tight bends and the odd muddy patch, and they are best explored on weekday mornings. The A2 and A28 bring most traffic into the city, and the medieval centre is largely pedestrianised, so use a car park or park-and-ride on the edge.

Canterbury has fifty-five thousand people, with fuel on the ring road and plenty of cafés and pubs in the old streets. Allow a couple of hours for the abbey and cathedral.
t.leiden roomburg park matilo@52.1,4.5:
Leiden gave the world a university, a painter and a puzzle about a Roman fort. The fort was called Matilo, and it stood on the south bank of the Oude Rijn, the old arm of the Rhine, in what is now the Roomburg district west of the old town, between about AD 40 and 270. It guarded the frontier that ran along the river from Germany to the sea, with a garrison of auxiliary troops and a civilian settlement beside it, and its name survives on the Roman road maps. Today the site is a green park, Park Matilo, where the outlines of the fort are marked out, and information panels tell the story. The Lower German Limes was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

The city that grew up later is a delight. Leiden got Holland's first university in 1575, as a reward for withstanding a Spanish siege, and its canals, gabled houses and windmills are among the most attractive in the country. Rembrandt was born here in 1606, and the Pilgrim Fathers lived here for a decade before sailing to America. The Hortus Botanicus, one of the oldest botanical gardens in the world, is where the first tulips in the Netherlands were planted.

Riding in this part of Holland is calm and flat. The roads across the polders are narrow and straight, with ditches on both sides, and every junction has bicycles, since the Dutch cycle everywhere and have priority in every sense. Speed limits are low and enforced by cameras, and a motorcycle is expected to move at the pace of the general flow. The weather is changeable, with a sea wind that can push you sideways, and rain showers pass through, so wear waterproofs. April and May, when the bulb fields along the coast are in bloom, are glorious, and the fields around Lisse are a short ride to the north.

Leiden is a city of over a hundred thousand, so fuel is no trouble, and Leiderdorp, next door, has stations on the main road. Parking in the old centre is restricted, and the best option is to leave the bike in a car park by the station and walk. The ride list heads east to the Dutch Water Defence Lines, a chain of forts and flooded fields built to protect Amsterdam, which is a very different sort of frontier.
t.corbulo s canal knippolder@52.1,4.4:
In AD 47, a Roman general on a quiet frontier had a problem, which was how to keep his legions from getting restless. Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, newly appointed to command in Lower Germany, solved it, according to the historian Tacitus, by making his troops dig. The result was a canal, the Fossa Corbulonis, linking the mouth of the Rhine with the Maas, so that ships could pass between the two rivers on a sheltered inland route rather than risk the open North Sea. It is one of the earliest known large engineering works of its kind in the Netherlands.

The canal's line is thought to run through the area of the Knippolder, between Leidschendam, Voorburg and Voorschoten, in what is now a quiet landscape of polders, ditches and suburbs. The Vliet, an old waterway that still connects Leiden and Delft, follows the same course in part, and the idea is that Corbulo's soldiers dug a channel along the line of an existing creek. Close by, in Voorburg, stood Forum Hadriani, a Roman town named after the emperor Hadrian. The canal is part of the Lower German Limes, which was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

There is not much to see on the ground, and I would be doing you a disservice if I promised remains. What you get is a very Dutch ride along a line of water. The roads are narrow, often one-way for cars, with dedicated cycle lanes and speed bumps in the villages, and an occasional lift bridge that holds you up while a barge passes. Everything is well kept, with tidy gardens, little harbours and windmills. In spring the bulb fields to the north colour the horizon, and in winter, mist hangs over the polders in the early morning.

Voorschoten, a town of more than twenty thousand, has fuel and cafes, and larger towns like Leiden and The Hague are close. The Hague has its own interest, with the seat of government, a fine art museum with Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, and a beach at Scheveningen, so a ride here can take in a lot in a single day.

Sit by the water for ten minutes and think of the legionaries with their shovels.
t.corbulo s canal vlietvoorde@52.1,4.4:
A straight line on a Dutch map is nearly always a canal, and this one is two thousand years old. The Fossa Corbulonis, or Corbulo's canal, was dug in AD 47 by Roman soldiers under the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, to link the Rhine with the Meuse and give supply ships a safe route that avoided the open sea. It ran through the dunes and marsh of what is now South Holland, and today the line of the Vliet, the canal between Leiden and Delft, follows part of it. Corbulo, so the story goes, dug it to keep his idle legions busy, and the emperor Claudius called his troops back from beyond the Rhine soon afterwards. Vlietvoorde, near Voorschoten, is one of the places where the route can be traced, and the site is part of the Lower German Limes, which won World Heritage status in 2021.

The landscape here is the classic Dutch polder: flat fields below sea level, drained by ditches, with cows, windmills, rows of poplars and red-tiled farmhouses reflected in the water. The sky does most of the work, with huge clouds sailing across, and the light is clear and soft. Leiden, the university town, is a few kilometres to the north, and the Hague to the south, while the dunes and North Sea beaches lie a short ride west. In April and early May, the bulb fields around Lisse bloom in long stripes of colour.

The ride goes on to the Dutch Water Defence Lines, the system of flooded fields and forts that protected Holland for centuries by letting the water in, and it is a gentle journey over dikes and along canals. The roads are narrow, often with a cycle lane, and the speed limit is low, usually eighty on the open road and fifty or thirty in villages, with cameras and police who enforce it. Cyclists are everywhere, so patience is a virtue, and the wind, often from the west, can be a nuisance on the open stretches.

Voorschoten, a small town of about twenty thousand, has fuel stations, a few cafes by the canal and a pleasant old centre. Dutch food is simple: herring with onions at a market stall, cheese from Gouda, and thick pancakes. The best months are May, June and September, when the days are long and the light is golden. If rain comes, as it does, a good waterproof will save the day.
t.rice terrace clusters of banaue battad@1:
Nobody knows exactly how old the rice terraces of Ifugao are. The popular figure of two thousand years has been questioned by archaeologists, who suggest that the great walls went up more slowly and perhaps more recently, but the effort involved remains staggering. The Ifugao people shaped these steep slopes in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon by hand, building stone and mud retaining walls, digging channels to bring water from the forest above, and planting rice on narrow steps that climb the mountainside in tiers. Laid end to end, the walls would run for many thousands of kilometres. The terraces were listed as a World Heritage landscape in 1995, and Battad, with its rice fields arranged in a bowl like a natural amphitheatre, is one of the clusters people come to see.

The terraces change with the season. In the planting months, around February and March, the paddies are flooded and shine like pieces of the sky, and by April and May the young rice colours the steps a brilliant green. Harvest comes in June and the slopes turn gold, followed by a bare, brown period when the fields are fallow. Rain can fall at any time, and between July and October typhoons come off the Pacific and can cut the mountain roads with landslides. The dry season, from about November to April, is the best for riding.

The roads are the thing to understand. The highway from the lowlands climbs to Banaue through a long run of bends, with steep drops, patched surfaces and the occasional fallen rock, and the road continues on to Bontoc over a high pass with fog and cold air. Jeepneys and trucks crowd the narrow sections, and the light can fail early in the mountain gloom. Go carefully, sound the horn on blind corners, and avoid night riding. The side road to Battad ends at a saddle, from which a footpath drops down to the village, and the walk takes an hour or so on stone steps, so a pair of sturdy shoes is wise.

Banaue is a small town of a couple of thousand, with a few guesthouses, shops and small restaurants, and fuel is sold there, though supplies can run short, so fill up in a larger town on the way. Barlig, thirteen kilometres by the map, is the nearest bigger settlement. The Ifugao are known for their carved wooden rice guardians, called bulul, and for the hudhud chants that women sing at harvest and funerals, which are recognised as a part of intangible cultural heritage. In the evening, a bowl of red rice and a cup of strong mountain coffee make a good ending.
t.exmoor moorland weekend@51.5,0.3:
Orsett sits on a low ridge above the Thames Estuary in Thurrock, and it has the look of an Essex village that has been surrounded by modern development but has refused to give in. Its green and church are still there, along with an annual agricultural show, while in the lowlands around it are the vast shopping centres, warehouses and housing estates of Thurrock. South Ockendon and Chafford Hundred, each with well over thirteen thousand people, are packed with fuel stations and supermarkets, so there is no shortage of places to start the day.

Chafford Hundred has an unusual origin. It is built in the floor of an old chalk quarry, where for generations the pale rock was dug out for cement and lime, and the quarry lake and the cliffs that remain are now a nature area beside the Lakeside shopping centre. The whole of this part of Thurrock is chalk, which is why the area was so heavily quarried and why the Thames here is lined with cement works and wharves. The Dartford crossing and the M25 are only a few kilometres away, which makes the area a kind of gateway to the north and the east.

The start of a weekend ride like this is usually all about getting out of London's orbit quickly. The roads here are busy with lorries and commuters, and the junctions are many, so a calm and early departure is the best plan. Once you move north and west, the countryside opens out into the farmland of south Essex, with fields, woods and low hills, and the pace changes as the traffic thins. Be careful on the roundabouts, where lorries and cars jostle for position and the surface can be greasy.

Practical advice is simple. Fill the tank, check your tyre pressures and maybe grab a coffee at one of the roadside cafés that open early for the lorry drivers, who are usually a good guide to a decent breakfast. The big day ahead is on the far side of the motorway, and it will feel far away from this tangle of roads and warehouses.
t.exmoor moorland weekend@51.9,0.4:
Great Bardfield is the sort of Essex village that artists love, and in the middle of the last century a group of them settled there, among them Edward Bawden and John Aldridge, and made it known across the country for its open studios and exhibitions. The village still has the look of it, with a long street of timber-framed and plastered houses, a pretty church and a windmill nearby. Thaxted, five kilometres away with about two and a half thousand people, is a small town of even greater charm, with a fifteenth-century guildhall raised on pillars above the market place and a spire of a church that is one of the largest in the county.

The composer Gustav Holst lived in Thaxted for some years in the early twentieth century and wrote parts of The Planets while there, and the church still holds a festival in his honour. A tower windmill on a hill above the town completes the picture. Great Dunmow, eight kilometres off with nearly seven thousand eight hundred people, is the larger centre, with fuel stations, shops and a long-standing local custom, the Dunmow Flitch, in which a married couple who can prove they have not quarrelled for a year and a day win a side of bacon.

A food stop here is easy. The villages have pubs that serve lunch, and a baker or two sells pasties and cakes, and in Thaxted you can sit on the steps of the guildhall with a coffee and watch the town go by. The roads between these places are pleasant, running over gently undulating farmland with big hedges, big skies and many a tidy village green. Corners are mostly gentle, but the narrow lanes have blind brows and the occasional tractor.

The surface is generally good on the main roads and more variable on minor ones, where the verge can be crumbly and mud can gather at field entrances. This is the quiet, unspectacular heart of rural Essex, the kind of country that rewards a slow pace. In summer the fields are golden with wheat and barley, and in late spring the lanes are lined with cow parsley. If you can, time your stop for the middle of the day and have a proper meal.
t.exmoor moorland weekend high point@51.9,:
Puckeridge announces itself as a coaching village on the old Roman road known as Ermine Street, which ran from London to Lincoln and York, and the line of the A10 here still follows it more or less. In the days of horse transport the inns here fed and watered travellers on the long road north, and the wide main street and old coaching inns still show it. Today it has about three and a half thousand people and a good selection of pubs, a couple of shops and a bypass that has restored some quiet. Buntingford, with nearly five thousand people, is a small market town on the River Rib, and Bishop's Stortford, eight kilometres to the east, is the major centre, with nearly thirty-eight thousand people and plenty of fuel.

The high point on this ride is not a mountain but a broad chalk rise in east Hertfordshire, where the land swells enough for the view to open across fields and woods to the horizon. It has the quality of English countryside that grows on you slowly, a patchwork of hedges, copses and church towers set against big skies. The chalk beneath gives the roads good drainage, so they dry quickly after rain, and the soil shows pale in ploughed fields.

Much Hadham, a village of about two thousand people to the south-west, is home to the Henry Moore Foundation at Perry Green, where the sculptor lived and worked for more than forty years and where large bronze figures stand in the fields among grazing sheep. The studios and gardens are open to visitors in summer, and the sight of massive abstract forms in a quiet Hertfordshire landscape is oddly right. Moore's reclining figures echo the hills around.

The riding here is easy, with sweeping views, gentle gradients and mostly good surfaces. Wind can be a nuisance on the exposed ridge, and the narrow lanes between villages have bends that tighten unexpectedly. Late afternoon light on the stubble is lovely, and in spring the verges are full of cow parsley. A pause at the crest, with the engine off and the sound of larks overhead, is a good way to spend ten minutes.
t.highest point@16.8,120.8:
Halsema Highway does not shout about its summit. There is a sign, a small pull-off and a few stalls selling strawberries, fresh vegetables and woolly hats, and that is the highest point on the whole Philippine highway network, around 2,255 metres above the sea. It sits close to Atok, in Benguet, and the road goes on north toward Bontoc and Sagada as if nothing special had happened. For a country associated with beaches, a pine-scented ridge where you need a jacket is a pleasant shock.

Getting here is the reward. From Baguio the road climbs and descends through the Cordillera, clinging to hillsides carved into rice terraces and vegetable terraces so steep they look like green staircases. The highway is named after an American engineer called Halsema, who worked on the route in the early twentieth century, and many people still call it the Mountain Province road. It is mostly paved but narrow, with cliffs on one side, blind bends, trucks hauling cabbages and potatoes, and landslides that can shut sections in the typhoon months. Check conditions before setting out, because rain and fog turn the scenery into a grey wall.

Up at the top the air is thin and cool, the pines smell of resin, and the vegetable farms of Atok, Buguias and Kabayan spread across the slopes around you. This is where much of Manila's salad comes from. If you can, stop at one of the roadside stands for fresh strawberries, which are sweet and cheap, and sip a hot coffee from the local shacks. The fog usually rolls up by midday, so mornings give the best views of the terraces falling into the valleys.

Fuel needs planning. Baculongan and Atok have shops and some pumps, but remote stretches farther north do not, so fill up in Baguio or at a larger town before the climb and carry a little extra if you can. Daylight is precious on this road: driving it after dark in fog is a stressful business, and the locals will tell you honestly that you should be at your night stop before the light goes.

The ridge is also close to the country of the Igorot people, whose highland culture, weaving and rice terraces shape this region. Greet people warmly, drive slowly through villages, and you will be met with the same.
t.steptoe butte@47.0,-117.3:
Steptoe Butte is a pointed hill in a landscape that is otherwise all curves, and that is exactly why you can see so much from it. The Palouse is a region of south-eastern Washington where the earth rolls in endless, smooth, wheat-covered dunes, the product of wind-blown dust, called loess, piled up over many thousands of years. Steptoe rises abruptly out of this sea of soft hills, a steep cone of ancient quartzite that was once a mountaintop and was buried by the lava flows that covered the surrounding land, leaving only its summit exposed.

That odd history has given geologists a word, kipuka, borrowed from Hawaiian, for a hill left standing amid a younger lava flow. From the top, at a little over three thousand feet, you can look out over a patchwork of fields in greens, golds and browns, stretching away to the Blue Mountains, the Rockies of Idaho and the horizon beyond. The colours change by season: the fields are emerald in spring, gold in summer and bare earth by autumn. Photographers come at dawn and dusk to catch the low light on the rolling hills, which look like velvet, and the summit can be crowded then.

The butte is named after Colonel Edward Steptoe, whose troops were defeated by a force of Native warriors nearby in 1858, a battle that led to a larger war on the plateau. The summit is a state park now, with a narrow, winding road to the top, a small car park and a picnic area. The road is paved, but steep and tight, with little room to pass, and it is not suitable for large vehicles. It is a short, rewarding ride, with hairpin bends and gradually widening views. Gravel and wet leaves can make the corners slippery, and strong winds can blow at the top, especially in spring and autumn.

Weather is the main factor. Clear mornings give the best views, but the Palouse is dry and dusty in summer, and haze or smoke from wildfires can obscure the view, while winter brings ice and snow. There are no services on the butte. Colfax, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest small town, and Pullman, thirty-five kilometres south, has fuel, food and everything else, so fill the tank before you go.

Stay for the light, if you can. Sunset on the Palouse is unforgettable.
t.pullman@46.7,-117.2:
Pullman is a college town surrounded by wheat, and it carries the confidence of both. Washington State University, founded in 1890, sits on the hill above the town, with its red-brick buildings, clock tower and sports stadium, and the whole place hums with students for most of the year and falls quiet in the summer. The town sits among the rolling Palouse hills, with fields of wheat, peas and lentils curving away on all sides, and the smell of cut grass, dust and diesel drifts in on the wind.

The college is the town's big institution, and one of its better-known products is cheese.
