The university creamery makes a sharp, aged cheddar in tins called Cougar Gold, which is sold by mail order and has a loyal following across the country. The college mascot is the cougar, and the town takes its football seriously. The nearby town of Moscow, Idaho, lies a few miles away across the state line, home to a rival university, and the two towns share a cheerful rivalry and a regional airport. The Palouse region also produces most of the nation's dry peas and lentils, and farmers can be seen working enormous combines on the hillsides in late summer.

The riding around Pullman is a gentle, rolling affair. The roads run over the hills in long, easy bends, with wheat fields on both sides and views of the swelling land, and traffic is light outside university events. In spring, the hills are bright green, and in July and August the fields turn gold and the dust rises behind tractors. Wind can be strong on the ridgelines, and winters are cold and snowy, with ice on the back roads, so check the weather. Watch for farm vehicles, particularly during harvest, and for deer at dusk.

As a stop, Pullman is excellent. It has more than thirty thousand residents, with petrol stations, supermarkets, cafés, bakeries, brewpubs and cheap, hearty restaurants aimed at students, so it is easy to find fuel, a good meal and a warm bed. The main street has a pleasant, old-fashioned feel, and the creamery shop on campus is worth a visit if you like cheese.

After a long day in the saddle, a coffee in a student café and a look at the hills from the campus is hard to beat.
t.joseph oregon@45.4,-117.2:
Joseph is a small town at the foot of a very large mountain range. The Wallowa Mountains, sometimes called the Alps of Oregon, rise sharply behind it, with snow on the high summits for much of the year and a long glacial lake, Wallowa Lake, tucked into the valley mouth just south of town. It is a place that feels a long way from anywhere, in the far northeastern corner of the state, at the end of a long road that runs up through Enterprise and has no real continuation.

The town takes its name from Chief Joseph, the Nez Perce leader whose people, the Wallowa band, lived in this valley long before settlers arrived. In 1877 the government's demand that they leave for a reservation in Idaho led to a conflict and a long, desperate retreat of more than a thousand miles, which ended in Montana just short of the Canadian border. Chief Joseph's speech of surrender is remembered, and the Nez Perce still have a presence in the valley. His father, Old Chief Joseph, is buried by the lake. It is a story worth knowing before you arrive.

For a rider, the Hells Canyon Scenic Byway loop begins here, and the approach is the best bit: the road crosses a broad, flat valley of ranches and hayfields with the mountains filling the horizon. It is a gentle ride, with long straights and easy bends, and the real excitement lies ahead on the climbs and descents toward the canyon. Weather can turn cold even in summer, and winter closes some of the more remote routes. The summer months are the best, with warm days and cool nights, and autumn brings golden larches higher up.

Joseph itself is a pleasant little place, with a main street lined with bronze statues, a nod to the foundries that work here, along with galleries, cafes, a brewery and a few shops. It has fuel, and so does Enterprise, about nine kilometres away, which is slightly larger and has a supermarket and more services. Motels and cabins are available but fill up in summer. If you can, ride out to Wallowa Lake in the evening, when the light is low and the mountains turn pink.
t.hells canyon overlook@45.1,-116.8:
Hells Canyon is the deepest river gorge in North America, cut by the Snake River between Oregon and Idaho, and it is deeper than the Grand Canyon, though far less visited and far less famous. Across the gulf, the Seven Devils range in Idaho tilts up to more than 2,400 metres, nearly eight thousand feet above the river. What strikes you is the lack of a crowd. A couple of other vehicles in the car park and a lot of silence is normal.

The Snake here has been tamed by three dams, Brownlee, Oxbow and Hells Canyon, built by a power company in the mid-twentieth century. The reservoirs lie in the canyon floor like long green ribbons, and the hydropower they produce is an important part of the regional economy. Below the lowest dam the river returns to wild water, with rapids and a protected corridor. The canyon walls are layered with basalt, in grassy slopes with a scattering of ponderosa pine and juniper, and in spring they are green and in late summer they are the colour of lions.

The riding up to a canyon overlook is worth more than the destination. The roads here are quiet, mostly paved and sometimes gravel, with a mix of long climbs, tight bends and sudden views. It is a ride that rewards a relaxed rider, and the lack of traffic means you can take it slowly. Be aware of cattle, deer, and loose gravel on corners. Summer heat is intense in the canyon bottoms, and snow can block the high roads from late autumn into spring. The Nez Perce knew this country as home and hunting ground, and the whole region is part of the story of their homeland.

There are no services at the overlook. Fuel is available at Halfway and in Joseph and Enterprise on the Oregon side, and at small towns in Idaho on the other, but opening hours are limited and the distances are long, so fill up whenever you can. Take water, food and a good map, because mobile coverage is poor and help is far away. Evening light on the canyon is magnificent.
t.rotterdam@51.9,4.5:
Rotterdam is a young city by Dutch standards, and that is because the old one was destroyed. German bombers flattened the centre in May 1940, and rather than rebuild a historic town the Dutch built a modern one, bold and experimental, with towers, bridges and cubic houses that tilt on their corners. Nothing here is quiet or pretty in the postcard sense, and that is its appeal. The Erasmus Bridge, a white swan-necked span over the Maas, is the city's symbol, and the Markthal, a vast arched market hall with a ceiling painted in giant fruit and flowers, is the best place to eat. Cheap, quick, varied food is sold from stalls there, and Dutch herring, eaten raw with onion, is available at every street corner.

The port is the heart of the matter. For decades Rotterdam was the largest port in the world, and it remains the biggest in Europe, with container cranes and refineries lining the river for kilometres. A harbour tour by boat gives a sense of the scale. Out beyond the city, at the mouth of the Nieuwe Waterweg near Hoek van Holland, stands the Maeslantkering, a huge storm barrier whose two arms swing across the channel when a surge approaches.

That barrier is the first of the Delta Works, the great programme of dams, dykes and sea gates built in the south-west after the flood of 1953, which killed more than eighteen hundred people in Zeeland and South Holland. The ride south follows the islands of Zeeland over a chain of bridges and causeways, and the Oosterschelde barrier, finished in 1986, is the showpiece, a long line of concrete piers with steel gates that stay open except in storms. The roads are flat and smooth, the wind is stiff and the skies are huge. Wind can push a bike hard on the exposed sections, so ride with a firm grip.

In the city itself, traffic is calm and cycle lanes are everywhere, so give way to bikes. Speed cameras and police checks are common in the Netherlands, and the fines are steep. Fuel is easy to find in Rotterdam and along the motorway. For the Delta Works, fill up before heading onto the islands, where stations are less common. Spring brings the tulips and clear light, and autumn is moody and golden.
t.amsterdam@52.4,4.9:
Amsterdam is built on water and wood. The city was founded in the thirteenth century as a fishing village on a dam across the Amstel, and in the seventeenth century it grew into the richest trading city in the world, and the canals that circle the centre in concentric arcs were dug in that Golden Age. Merchants built tall, narrow houses along them, with gabled fronts and hoisting beams so that goods could be lifted to the upper floors. The canal ring is on the UNESCO list. The houses lean forward slightly, partly by design, and sink on their wooden piles, so that some visibly tilt.

Riding in the centre is a poor idea, and Amsterdammers will tell you so with some feeling. The streets are narrow and shared with trams, bicycles, scooters and pedestrians, and parking for motorbikes is limited and sometimes charged. A good approach is to park on the edge of town and walk or take a tram. Bicycles rule here, and a cyclist who has the right of way will use it without hesitation. The ring motorway, the A10, can be heavy with traffic during rush hours, but the roads in and out are well signed.

The ride that begins here heads toward the Roman frontier. The Rhine in the Netherlands was the northern limit of the Roman Empire, and the line of forts, watchtowers and roads that ran along it, the Limes, is now a UNESCO site. The old river road near Utrecht runs along a levee, with farms, orchards and low houses, and there are traces of Roman forts at places like Vechten, near Utrecht. It is a gentle, flat ride, with wide skies and a pleasant, rural feel. Wind off the polders can be strong, and rain comes and goes.

Fuel is plentiful on the outskirts, and food ranges from cheap fried snacks to world-class cooking. Try stroopwafels, thin waffles filled with caramel syrup, sold fresh in the markets, and pickled herring, eaten by tipping your head back. Spring is the best time, when the tulip fields near Lisse bloom and the days lengthen. In winter, the city is damp and dark but the canals look lovely under a dusting of snow.
t.the hague@52.1,4.3:
The Hague is where the Dutch government sits, but not where the capital is, which is a characteristic Dutch compromise. Amsterdam is the capital, but the parliament, the ministries, the royal working palace and the embassies are all here, and the city has an air of quiet formality. The Binnenhof, a cluster of medieval buildings around a courtyard, is the centre of Dutch politics, and the Mauritshuis next door holds Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and some of the finest Dutch paintings in the world. Close by, the Peace Palace, a vast, fairy-tale neo-Gothic building finished in 1913, houses the International Court of Justice. The city has long been the seat of international law.

Scheveningen, the seaside district, is the other face of The Hague. A broad beach, a pier with a Ferris wheel, a boulevard of cafes and a harbour of fishing boats form a popular resort, and on sunny weekends the whole city seems to go there. The sand is wide and pale, and the dunes behind it make a nature reserve for walkers and cyclists. In the dunes, the road runs past old bunkers from the Atlantic Wall, built by the Germans during the occupation, and the coast to the north is dotted with such remains.

For a rider, the day ahead leads to the Van Nelle Factory in Rotterdam, a brilliant piece of 1920s modernism built for a coffee, tea and tobacco firm. Its glass walls and rounded corners were meant to bring light and fresh air to the workers, and it is on the UNESCO list. The road between the cities runs through a belt of greenhouses, which glitter in the sun, and past the old centres of Delft and Schiedam. Delft is worth the detour, a small canal town of blue-and-white pottery, and a good place for coffee.

The Hague has plenty of fuel and food, and good Indonesian restaurants, a legacy of the colonial past. Traffic is moderate, with tram lines to watch and cyclists in every direction. Speed enforcement is strict, so keep to the limits. The best time is spring or early autumn.
t.church of san agustin@18.1,120.5:
The church at Paoay looks like it is built to withstand a siege, and in a way it is. San Agustin stands on a flat stretch of Ilocos Norte, in the northwest corner of Luzon, and its sides are propped by enormous stepped buttresses, as massive as bastions, that march along the flanks like the legs of a great animal. The Augustinian friars who built it between about 1694 and 1710 were working in earthquake country, and the buttresses were their answer. The walls are coral stone and brick, laid in thick layers and held with a mortar that, according to local lore, included sugar cane juice and egg white. The result is a heavy, dark, strangely beautiful church that belongs to the family of Baroque Churches of the Philippines, listed by UNESCO in 1993.

The bell tower stands apart, a few metres from the church, and its separation was also a safety measure, so that a falling tower would not crush the nave. It rises in tiers of coral stone, and during the Philippine Revolution and later the Second World War it served as a lookout. The facade is more earthbound than elegant, with a mixture of Baroque, Gothic and Asian motifs, and the odd carved flourish near the base.

The road here is a quiet coastal plain, and a good riding area. Highways in Ilocos are straight and flat, running between rice fields, tobacco plots, salt pans and sandy stretches, with the Cordillera on one side and the South China Sea on the other. Near Paoay, a small lake spreads behind the town, and beyond it, to the west, are the sand dunes of La Paz, where the film industry sometimes shoots desert scenes. Hot, dry winds blow most of the year, and from July to October typhoons can arrive.

The nearby city of Batac is the home of Ilocano empanada, a crisp orange pastry filled with grated papaya, egg and sausage, fried on the spot. Eat one as soon as it comes out. Laoag, the provincial capital, is about twenty kilometres north and has all the fuel and supplies a rider needs, and Paoay itself has a few stations. The best months are November to February, when the air is cooler and drier. Mass is held on weekends, and visitors should dress modestly.
t.church of la nuestra senora de la asunci:
Santa Maria is the church that makes you earn the view. It stands on a hill above the town of the same name in Ilocos Sur, and reaching it means climbing an imposing stone staircase of about eighty steps, flanked by walls, which opens onto a broad, open terrace. The church was built in the eighteenth century by Augustinian friars, and it looks more like a fortress than a house of prayer, with a long, plain, buttressed brick facade and a separate bell tower standing on the hill's edge. Walls surround the whole complex, because during the colonial period a church could also be a refuge and a stronghold. It is one of the four Philippine churches in the UNESCO group of Baroque Churches.

The hilltop location gives it a feeling of watchfulness. From the terrace you can see the river valley and the line of the Cordillera in the east, and the town spread beneath. In the cool of the early morning, with doves on the walls and light across the bricks, the place is quiet. The interior is simple and dim, with a carved wooden altar and old, worn floors. A small convent next door holds a museum.

The ride here makes a fine day. Highway roads in Ilocos Sur, particularly the coastal national road between Vigan and Candon, are straight and flat for long stretches, with rice fields, tobacco and fishing villages to the sides. Farm vehicles, tricycles and buses share the road, so expect abrupt turns. Hot weather is the norm, and from July to October the rains and typhoons can be heavy. From December to February, the air is gentler.

Vigan, the old Spanish town to the north, is the main stop. It preserves a grid of cobbled streets and old houses with heavy shutters and tiled roofs, built by Chinese and Filipino merchants, and horse-drawn carriages called kalesa take visitors along Calle Crisologo. The town is famous for its longganisa, a garlicky local sausage, and its empanada. Fuel is easy to find in Vigan and along the highway, and Santa Maria has a few shops and eating places.

Cover your shoulders and knees inside the church, and come outside Sunday service hours.
t.lille@50.6,3.1:
Lille is a Flemish city that happens to be in France, and its brick and gables show it. The Grand'Place, with its tall merchants' houses and a theatre that looks like a wedding cake, is the centre of a lively old town of cobbled streets, and the nearby Vieille Bourse, the old stock exchange, is a courtyard of carved stone where secondhand-book sellers set out their stalls. The citadel, built by Vauban for Louis XIV, still stands to the west, a star-shaped fortress inside a park.

The city is also a place for eating. Moules-frites, mussels with chips, are the regional classic, as are carbonnade, a beer-braised beef stew, and waffles filled with sweet vanilla sugar. Each year in early September the whole city turns out for the Braderie de Lille, an enormous flea market that spreads over dozens of streets, and the mound of mussel shells outside the restaurants becomes a competition. If you plan to ride around that weekend, expect closures and crowds.

Lille has some 228,000 people, and fuel and parking are straightforward at the edge, with the ring roads giving access to Belgium, which lies only a few kilometres away. The centre is dense, with tram lines, one-way streets and cobbles that become slick when wet. Park outside and walk, or leave the bike at a secure garage. The countryside around is flat, with long straight roads across fields of sugar beet and wheat, and small canals and brick villages, and it is not a landscape for dramatic corners. But there are pleasures in the wind, the wide sky, and the old battlefields that lie to the south.

Winters are grey, wet and cold, and summers mild, so pack for rain whenever you come. Then, as the lights come on in the Grand'Place, with a beer in hand, the city makes a good case for itself.
t.middelburg@51.5,3.6:
Middelburg is the sort of Dutch town that makes you slow down on purpose. It is the capital of Zeeland, set on the old island of Walcheren, and the canals, brick houses and a huge Gothic town hall give it a settled, prosperous look. Around forty-six thousand people live here, enough to guarantee fuel, coffee and a proper lunch, but small enough that you can see the centre on foot in an afternoon.

The history is heavier than the pretty brickwork suggests. In May 1940, during the German invasion, bombing and fire destroyed a large part of the historic centre, and the town was rebuilt in the years that followed, with the abbey complex and the town hall restored. The abbey, with its tall Lange Jan tower, is the heart of the place and was a major religious centre in the Middle Ages. Zeeland was also deeply tied to the Dutch East India Company, which had one of its chambers here, so a lot of old wealth and trade runs under the streets.

Then there is the water, which is the reason a rider comes to Zeeland at all. In 1953 a storm surge broke through the dikes, flooded much of the province and killed well over a thousand people across the Netherlands. The answer was the Delta Works, a vast system of dams, dikes and storm surge barriers, and a few kilometres from town you can ride across the Oosterschelde barrier, a long gate-lined structure which is among the great pieces of engineering in Europe. Seals haul out on the sandbanks nearby, and the sky is enormous.

The riding is flat and gentle, with long causeways, dike-top roads and quiet lanes among polder fields, and the main enemy is the wind, which comes in from the North Sea and can push a bike sideways on exposed bridges. Traffic is calm outside the summer weekends, when cyclists and holiday makers fill the roads. Keep to speed limits, which are strictly enforced with cameras.

Finish here with something Dutch and straightforward. Mussels from Yerseke are famous in the region, and a plate of fish by the harbour makes a fair end to a day on the dikes.
t.neryungri@56.7,124.7:
Neryungri exists because of coal. In the 1970s, geologists and builders arrived in the empty taiga of southern Yakutia to open one of the largest open-cast coal mines in the Soviet Union, and a new city grew beside it, with straight avenues, apartment blocks and a power station. Today it is a town of about sixty-six thousand, and the biggest settlement for a very long way in any direction. Serebryany Bor, a smaller satellite town on the river, lies a short distance away.

For a rider coming up the Lena Highway from the south, or along the Amur-Yakutsk road, this is a landmark in every sense. There is fuel, there are cafes, there is a mechanic who has seen a hundred tired trucks, and there are beds. The road north toward Yakutsk is long, remote and very much a test of preparation: stretches of excellent tarmac alternate with gravel, mud and construction, the distances between fuel stops can be several hours, and the weather is extreme. Summer brings heat, dust and mosquitoes, and winter brings temperatures that freeze everything. The best time is July to early September.

The landscape here is the southern edge of the great Siberian taiga, with larch, pine and birch covering low hills, wide marshy valleys and rivers that run brown with peat. Permafrost lies under much of the ground, and the buildings in town stand on piles driven deep into it to avoid melting the frozen soil. The air in summer smells of warm resin and wet moss, and in autumn the larch turns gold before shedding its needles, one of the few conifers to do so.

The area's story is tied closely to the Baikal-Amur Mainline railway, which passes through Tynda to the south and brought the heavy machinery. The Yakut, or Sakha, people have lived in the region for centuries, herding horses and cattle and hunting, and their culture is visible in place names, food and festivals. The city's cafes may serve Yakut specialities such as frozen fish and horse meat dishes, and a bowl of hot soup is welcome.

Before leaving, fill up completely and carry spare fuel if you are heading north. Bring repair gear and a warm layer, and let someone know your plans, since mobile coverage can be patchy.
t.spokane@47.7,-117.4:
Spokane is the biggest city between Seattle and Minneapolis, about two hundred thousand people in the dry country on the eastern side of Washington state, and it exists because of a waterfall. The Spokane River drops through a basalt gorge in the middle of downtown, a thundering set of falls that is the heart of Riverfront Park, a space created for the 1974 World's Fair. The Spokane tribe lived and fished here for thousands of years, and the name means children of the sun.

The city grew in the late nineteenth century as a hub for silver mining in Idaho, timber and wheat farming, and railroads, and a fire in 1889 destroyed much of the downtown, which was then rebuilt in brick and stone. You can still see the grand old buildings of that period, and the neighbourhoods on the South Hill, with their large houses and green parks, feel somewhat like an old eastern city. It is a good place to eat, with a lively food and brewing scene, and a very easy place to fill the tank and top up supplies before you leave.

The ride south follows the Palouse Scenic Byway, which crosses one of the most unusual landscapes in America. The Palouse is a region of rolling loess hills, deep, wind-blown soil laid down over thousands of years, and the hills are covered in wheat, peas and lentils, in broad swells of gold and green that look almost like sand dunes under a blanket. Steptoe Butte, a quartzite peak that pokes out above the farmland, offers a vast view from its summit, and the roads wind between small farm towns such as Colfax and Pullman.

Roads in the Palouse are quiet, well paved, and mostly gentle, with long climbs over the hills and sudden dips into stream valleys. The best seasons are late spring, when the fields are bright green, and midsummer, when the wheat turns gold. There is little shade and the wind can be strong, so allow for that, and remember that distances between towns are significant. Tractors and combines are common, especially at harvest time, and they take up a lot of road.
t.clarkston@46.4,-117.0:
Clarkston sits on the Washington bank of the Snake River, directly opposite Lewiston in Idaho, and the two towns, one on each side of a bridge, effectively form a single community in a river canyon of dry hills. The river here is wide and green, and the elevation is low, only about eight hundred feet, which makes it one of the warmest places in the Pacific Northwest. In summer the heat can be fierce, with temperatures well above thirty-five degrees Celsius, but the winters are mild.

The town is named for William Clark of the Lewis and Clark expedition, which came through here in the autumn of 1805 and again on the return journey the following spring, with help from the Nez Perce people, whose homeland this is. The river has changed since then. A series of dams on the Snake and the Columbia now turns the river into a chain of reservoirs, and ocean-going barges can reach Lewiston, making it the farthest inland seaport on the West Coast. Grain from the Palouse wheat fields is shipped from here to Asia.

For a rider, Clarkston is the end of a rolling descent from the Palouse, and the last stretch is a big drop down into the canyon on a road that wiggles down the hillside with views over the valley. It is a relief to hit the river, with its greenery and shade, after the open wheat country. The roads here are paved and good, and traffic can be heavy around the bridges. This is also the gateway to Hells Canyon, the deepest river gorge in North America, which lies upstream and can be seen by jet boat from the town.

Everything is close at hand, with fuel stations, supermarkets and motels, and the riverside parks make a pleasant place to rest. The Lewis and Clark interpretive centre and the Nez Perce historical park, on the Idaho side, are well worth a visit if you want to know more about the region. Summer evenings are warm and long, and you can eat outside by the water. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and the light on the hills turns golden, a good time to be here.
t.la grande oregon@45.3,-118.1:
La Grande lies flat as a table in the middle of the Grande Ronde Valley, a wide bowl of farmland in north-eastern Oregon ringed by the Blue Mountains to the west and the Wallowas to the east. It is a railroad town of about thirteen thousand people, with a college, a brick downtown and a long, wide main street, and it feels more like Idaho or Montana than the rainy Oregon of the coast. Wheat, hay and cattle fill the valley, and the air is dry and clear.

The Oregon Trail came through here in the 1840s and 1850s. After weeks crossing the plains, emigrants descended the Blue Mountains into the valley, and many camped in the open grass before facing the Columbia and the Willamette beyond. The ruts of the wagons are still visible at an interpretive site on Blue Mountain, a few miles west of town, where you can walk among them. The name Grande Ronde, French for great round, is said to have come from trappers who saw the circular valley.

Your ride leaves the valley to the east, into the country of the Nez Perce, where Chief Joseph and his people lived before they were forced out in 1877. The road crosses the foothills into the Wallowa valley and continues toward Hells Canyon, the deepest river gorge in North America, a gash cut by the Snake River that drops almost eight thousand feet from the rim peaks to the water. The scenery shifts from farm fields to forest, then to dry canyon country, with a lot of curves and climbs and impressive views. Traffic is light, and the surface is mostly good, although winter frost can damage it.

La Grande has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, so it is a sensible place to start. Beyond, supplies get thin, and the best strategy is to fill up in town and again at the larger villages. Summer days are hot and dry, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, while autumn brings cold nights and colourful larches in the high country. In winter, snow and ice can close the mountain passes, so check road conditions before you leave. Look out for deer and elk, particularly at dusk.

t.lisse@52.3,4.5:
Lisse is the heart of the Bollenstreek, the bulb region, a belt of sandy land between Leiden and Haarlem where tulips, daffodils and hyacinths are grown by the million. In April the fields stretch away in stripes of red, yellow, pink and white, so strongly coloured that they seem painted. The sandy soil, a little way inland from the dunes, drains well and suits the bulbs, which is why this strip of land has been planted for four centuries. The story is a famous one: the botanist Carolus Clusius planted some of the first tulips in the Netherlands at Leiden in the 1590s, and within a few decades the flower had set off the speculative frenzy now called tulip mania.

The town itself is neat, a little sleepy, with canals, small bridges, a church and a museum devoted to the flower bulb and its history, called De Zwarte Tulp, after the novel by Dumas. The region's flower parade in spring is a great spectacle, floats covered in blooms creeping along the roads, and it can stop traffic on all the main routes for hours. Check the date before you plan a day around it.

The riding is slow by necessity. Narrow dyke roads cut between the fields, cyclists ride three abreast, and tour buses wait where they should not. A sensible rider takes the time, enjoys the colour and keeps off the verges. Do not step into the fields to take photographs: the flowers are a crop, farmers are understandably annoyed by trespassers, and you can be fined. The roads are in good condition, but windblown sand and wet leaves can make them slippery, and the wind coming off the North Sea, only a few kilometres away, is steady.

Everything you need is in Lisse: several fuel stations on the edge of town, supermarkets, cafés, and a bakery or two that are worth a stop for the appeltaart alone. If you come in April and early May, expect crowds, and if you can come on a weekday morning, do. Outside the flowering season the fields are brown or green, and the countryside is empty, with a different, plainer beauty.
t.near cranbrook on the way back@51.1,0.6:
Cranbrook stands in the High Weald of Kent, a hilly, wooded country of sandstone ridges and winding lanes, and in the Middle Ages it was one of the richest towns in the county, thanks to the cloth trade. Edward III encouraged Flemish weavers to settle here in the fourteenth century, and the broadcloth they made brought wealth to the town, visible today in the big timber-framed houses and the huge church known as the Cathedral of the Weald. On the edge of the town stands Union Mill, an eighteenth-century smock mill that is the tallest working windmill of its kind in Britain.

A few kilometres away, Sissinghurst is famous for its castle garden, created in the 1930s by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her husband Harold Nicolson among the ruins of an Elizabethan house. The white garden and the tower, which was Vita's writing room, are widely known, and the property belongs to the National Trust. Hawkhurst, a village of nearly four thousand people, is bigger, with a long street of shops and an old pond called the Moor. Tenterden, eight kilometres away with just over seven thousand people, has the nearest fuel and a handsome wide high street lined with weatherboarded houses.

The swim stop on the label should be taken lightly, because there is no beach here, and the pools of the Weald are mostly private. For a rider, the pleasure is in the lanes themselves, which are narrow and twisting, with high banks, overhanging trees and sudden dips where a stream crosses. Take them slowly, because blind bends and farm vehicles are common. The surface is often patched and the verges soft, and in wet weather mud can wash across the road in the low spots.

The High Weald is at its best in spring, when the woods are carpeted with bluebells and the orchards bloom, and in autumn, when the beeches and oaks turn bronze. Summer brings crowds to Sissinghurst, so aim for a weekday or an early start. A cream tea in one of the village tearooms is a very English way to finish.
